text: These are brief answers and hints, not full solutions: they give the result and the key step, so that you can check your own work. Try each exercise properly before looking. 1.1 A Prime Factory Suppose p_1, ldots, p_k are all the primes; then p_1cdots p_k + 1 has a prime factor not in the list, a contradiction. The Fermat-number proof is constructive: it exhibits infinitely many pairwise coprime numbers F_0, F_1, ldots , each of which supplies a new prime. For n ≥ 2 , 2^n is a multiple of 4 , so 2^2^n = 16^2^n-2 , and every power of 16 ends in 6 . Hence F_n ends in 7 . (a) Induction: a_n+1 - 1 = a_n(a_n - 1) = a_n · a_1cdots a_n-1 . (b) A common factor of a_m and a_n ( m < n ) divides a_1cdots a_n-1 = a_n - 1 and a_n , so it is 1 ; each term has a prime factor shared with no other. (c) (1)/(a_n) = (1)/(a_n - 1) - frac1a_n+1 - 1 ; the sum telescopes to 1 - frac1a_n+1 - 1 . (a) p mid F_n gives 2^2^n equiv -1 ; squaring gives 2^2^n+1 equiv 1 . (b) d divides every e with 2^e equiv 1 , so d mid 2^n+1 ; d nmid 2^n since 2^2^n equiv -1 notequiv 1 (as p is odd). So d = 2^n+1 . (c) 2^p-1 equiv 1 , so 2^n+1 mid p - 1 . (d) 641 = 64 × 10 + 1 . The primes of the form 64k + 1 below 641 are 193 , 257 , 449 and 577 : only four candidates to try, which is how Euler found 641 . The n th prime is at most the largest prime factor of any of F_0, ldots, F_n-1 , so p_n ≤ F_n-1 = 2^2^n-1 + 1 . For n = 5 the bound is 65\,537 , while p_5 = 11 : correct but extremely weak. 1.2 How Thinly Spread Are the Primes? P_1,10 = 210 , P_1,20 = 9\,699\,690 , P_1,30 = 6\,469\,693\,230 . Compare 4^30 approx 1.15 × 10^18 and e^30 approx 1.07 × 10^13 : the product is far below 4^n and grows roughly like e^n (in fact P_1,n sim n , a form of the Prime Number Theorem). binom2mk+1big/binom2mk = (2m - k)/(k + 1) , which exceeds 1 exactly when k < m , so the coefficients rise to the middle and then fall. The largest of 2m + 1 terms adding to 4^m is at least their average. The primes in (sqrt n, n] each exceed sqrt n and their product is less than 4^n , so (sqrt n)^π(n) - π(sqrt n) < 4^n ; take logarithms. Since 24 approx 2.77 and π(sqrt n) ≤ sqrt n , the bound follows. It has the right shape n/ n , with the constant 2.8 instead of the true 1 . Use the primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 13, 23, 43, 83 , each less than twice the one before. For any n ≤ 50 , the first prime in this list greater than n is less than twice the previous one, which is at most n , so it lies between n and 2n . 1.3 The Smallest Counterexample If ksqrt3 is an integer for a smallest positive integer k , then k' = (sqrt3 - 1)k is a smaller positive integer with k'sqrt3 = 3k - ksqrt3 an integer. The number sqrt3 - 1 plays the role of sqrt2 - 1 . With 0 < sqrt N - m < 1 , k' = (sqrt N - m)k is a positive integer smaller than k , and k'sqrt N = kN - mksqrt N is an integer: a contradiction. With N = 4 , m = 2 = sqrt4 , so sqrt N - m = 0 and k' = 0 is not a positive integer. The step “ 0 < sqrt N - m ” fails. In the picture, the two overlapping squares of side b inside the square of side a cover a central square of side 2b - a twice and leave two uncovered squares of side a - b . Algebraically, (2b - a)^2 - 2(a - b)^2 = 2b^2 - a^2 = 0 . 1.4 e Is Irrational, and So Is e^2 If frac1e = frac pq , multiply frac1e = sum_k ≥ 0((-1)^k)/(k!) by q! . The terms with k ≤ q are integers, and the tail sum_k > q(-1)^kq!/k! is an alternating series of decreasing terms, so it lies strictly between 0 and (1)/(q+1) in absolute value. So q!/e is not an integer: contradiction. If sin 1 = frac pq , multiply by (2n + 1)! with 2n + 1 ≥ q . The left side is an integer, and so are the terms of the series up to (1)/((2n+1)!) ; the tail is alternating with first term of size (1)/((2n+2)(2n+3)) < 1 , so it is not an integer. The method needs a series with rational terms whose tails shrink faster than the denominators grow, like (1)/(k!) ; no such series is known for π . Niven’s proof uses int_0^π(x^n(π - x)^n)/(n!)sin x\,dx , which would be a positive integer smaller than 1 for large n if π were rational. The roots of x^2 - (e + π)x + eπ are e and π . If e + π and eπ were both algebraic, π would be a root of a polynomial with algebraic coefficients, hence algebraic, contradicting Lindemann’s theorem. 1.5 Infinite Descent 3 mid a ; writing a = 3a_1 gives 9a_1^3 + b^3 = 3c^3 , so 3 mid b , then 3a_1^3 + 9b_1^3 = c^3 , so 3 mid c , and (a_1, b_1, c_1) is a smaller solution: descent. For p^4 + 2q^4 = 5r^4 : fourth powers are 0 or 1 modulo 5 (they end in 0 , 1 , 5 or 6 ), so p^4 + 2q^4 equiv 0 forces 5 mid p and 5 mid q ; then 5^4 mid 5r^4 , so 5 mid r , and descent again. Squares are 0 or 1 modulo 4 , so x^2 + y^2 is 0 , 1 or 2 , never 3 . A rational point (frac ac, frac bc) would give a^2 + b^2 = 3c^2 with c ≠ 0 , which part (iii) rules out. For fixed x , y , the equation is the quadratic z^2 - 3xyz + (x^2 + y^2) = 0 , whose two roots add to 3xy . From (1,1,1) : (1,1,2) ; replacing the 1 opposite (1, 2) gives 3 · 1 · 2 - 1 = 5 , so (1,2,5) ; then (1,5,13) and (2,5,29) . 1.6 Sums of Two Squares Squares are 0 or 1 modulo 4 , so a sum of two squares is never 3 modulo 4 . 65 = 1^2 + 8^2 = 4^2 + 7^2 and 85 = 2^2 + 9^2 = 6^2 + 7^2 . With 65 = (2 + i)(2 - i)(3 + 2i)(3 - 2i) : (2 + i)(3 + 2i) = 4 + 7i and (2 + i)(3 - 2i) = 8 - i . Similarly (2 + i)(4 i) gives 7 + 6i and 9 - 2i for 85 . 1105 = 4^2 + 33^2 = 9^2 + 32^2 = 12^2 + 31^2 = 23^2 + 24^2 . Each of 5 , 13 , 17 splits as a Gaussian integer times its conjugate; choosing one factor from each pair gives 8 products, which pair up into conjugates (the same sum of squares), leaving 4 . Taking moduli squared, 9 = (a^2 + b^2)(c^2 + d^2) . Since 3 is not a sum of two squares, one factor is 1 . 1.7 When Factorisation Fails 693 = 9 × 77 = 21 × 33 , all four factors being S -prime. Recipe: take four primes p, q, r, s of the form 4k + 3 ; then (pq)(rs) = (pr)(qs) gives two factorisations into S -primes. The E -primes are the numbers 2 pmod 4 (they cannot be products of two even numbers). 60 = 2 × 30 = 6 × 10 . N(zw) = N(z)N(w) by expanding (ac - 5bd)^2 + 5(ad + bc)^2 . a^2 + 5b^2 is never 2 or 3 . Since N(2) = 4 , N(3) = 9 and N(1 sqrt-5) = 6 , a factorisation into non-units would need a factor of norm 2 or 3 . Let n be the smallest number with two different factorisations p_1cdots p_r = q_1cdots q_s . By Euclid’s lemma p_1 divides some q_j , so p_1 = q_j ; cancelling gives a smaller number with two different factorisations, a contradiction. 1.8 Counting the Rationals frac35 : parents (3, 5) leftarrow (3, 2) leftarrow (1, 2) leftarrow (1, 1) , giving positions 1 → 2 → 5 → 10 , so f(10) = frac35 . frac53 : (5, 3) leftarrow (2, 3) leftarrow (2, 1) leftarrow (1, 1) , positions 1 → 3 → 6 → 13 , so f(13) = frac53 . Newman’s rule x_n+1 = (1)/(2lfloor x_nrfloor - x_n + 1) gives 1 , frac12 , 2 , frac13 , frac32 , frac23 , 3 , frac14 , frac43 , frac35 , matching f(1), ldots, f(10) . Choose the n th digit to be 5 unless the n th number’s n th digit is 5 , in which case choose 4 . The new decimal differs from every number in the list, and avoiding 0 and 9 means it has only one decimal expansion, so it really is a different number. Every positive integer is uniquely a power of 2 times an odd number, 2^m-1(2n - 1) , so (m, n) mapsto 2^m-1(2n - 1) is a bijection. 1.9 Tangents to a Cubic Substituting y = t(x + 1) into x^2 + y^2 = 1 gives (1 + t^2)x^2 + 2t^2x + t^2 - 1 = 0 , with roots -1 and (1 - t^2)/(1 + t^2) . With t = frac qp the point is bigl((p^2 - q^2)/(p^2 + q^2), (2pq)/(p^2 + q^2)bigr) , giving the triples (p^2 - q^2, 2pq, p^2 + q^2) . The line is x + y = 3 , and x^3 + (3 - x)^3 = 9 reduces to 9x^2 - 27x + 18 = 0 : the cubic terms cancel, leaving only x = 1, 2 . The line is parallel to the asymptote y = -x , and the third intersection is at infinity. The tangent has gradient (x^2)/(y^2) = (289)/(400) , and meets the curve again at bigl(-(188479)/(90391), -(36520)/(90391)bigr) . Clearing denominators, 188479^3 = 36520^3 + 90391^3 + 180782^3 . The line meets x^3 + y^3 = 1729 again at bigl(-(37)/(3), (46)/(3)bigr) , so 46^3 = 37^3 + 27 × 1729 = 37^3 + 3^3 + 36^3 (using 27 = 3^3 and 27 × 1728 = 36^3 ).

title: Counting the Rationals
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Different sizes of infinity Stern’s sequence The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2020, Question 8 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP III paper in OCR’s download of the 2020 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/696589-2020-past-papers.zip The hook Can you list all the positive fractions, one after another, so that every fraction appears exactly once? It seems impossible: between any two fractions there are infinitely many more, so there is no “next” fraction to write down. Georg Cantor showed in the 1870s that it can nevertheless be done, which means that, in a precise sense, there are no more fractions than there are whole numbers. Cantor’s list was clumsy: it included (2)/(4) as well as frac12 , and the repeats had to be crossed out. This question builds a list with no repeats at all, from a sequence with an absurdly simple rule. It was published by Neil Calkin and Herbert Wilf in 2000, though the sequence itself was studied by Moritz Stern in 1858. Before you start Before proving anything, compute the first fifteen or so terms. What do you notice about the ratios u_n / u_n+1 ? The sequence begins 1,\ 1,\ 2,\ 1,\ 3,\ 2,\ 3,\ 1,\ 4,\ 3,\ 5,\ 2,\ 5,\ 3,\ 4,\ 1,\ 5,\ ldots and the ratios u_n / u_n+1 are tfrac11,\ tfrac12,\ tfrac21,\ tfrac13,\ tfrac32,\ tfrac23,\ tfrac31,\ tfrac14,\ tfrac43,\ tfrac35,\ tfrac52,\ tfrac25,\ tfrac53,\ tfrac34,\ tfrac41,\ ldots Every fraction appears in lowest terms, and none is repeated. The question asks you to prove that this goes on for ever, and that every positive fraction eventually turns up. Working it through Stage 1 Odd beats even Consecutive terms are either (u_2k, u_2k+1) or (u_2k+1, u_2k+2) . Write each of these pairs in terms of u_k and u_k+1 . Which term is bigger? (u_2k, u_2k+1) = (u_k,\ u_k + u_k+1) and (u_2k+1, u_2k+2) = (u_k + u_k+1,\ u_k+1) . Since every term is a positive integer (an easy induction), u_k + u_k+1 is bigger than both u_k and u_k+1 . The only exception is the first pair, (u_1, u_2) = (1, 1) , which doesn’t fit either pattern because u_1 is defined directly. ■ Stage 2 Consecutive terms are coprime Suppose d > 1 divides both u_2k and u_2k+1 , that is, both u_k and u_k + u_k+1 . What else does d divide? d divides (u_k + u_k+1) - u_k = u_k+1 , so d divides the consecutive pair u_k, u_k+1 , which is earlier in the sequence. The other case is identical: if d divides u_k + u_k+1 and u_k+1 , it divides u_k . So a common factor of a consecutive pair is passed back to an earlier pair, then an earlier one, and so on. Positions can’t decrease for ever (well-ordering yet again), so eventually d would have to divide the first pair, u_1 = u_2 = 1 . That is impossible for d > 1 . So every consecutive pair is coprime. ■ Stage 3 No pair appears twice Stage 1 tells you something useful: if you see a consecutive pair (a, b) , you can tell whether a sits at an odd or an even position. How? And can you then recover the pair that came before it, in the sense of Stage 2? If a < b , then (by Stage 1) b is at the odd position, so the pair is (u_2k, u_2k+1) = (u_k, u_k + u_k+1) for some k , and the “parent” pair (u_k, u_k+1) is (a,\ b - a) . If a > b , the pair is (u_2k+1, u_2k+2) and its parent is (a - b,\ b) . If a = b , Stage 1 shows the pair must be the very first pair, (1,1) . So each consecutive pair other than the first determines its parent pair, and the position of the parent (you can see this structure as a tree in Figure 1.8.1): the parent is at position k when the child is at 2k or 2k+1 . Now suppose (a, b) appeared at two different positions. Their parents would be the same pair at two positions, and so would their parents, and so on. Following this back, we would eventually find (1,1) at a position other than 1 , which Stage 1 rules out. ■ Stage 4 Every coprime pair appears Suppose some coprime pair (a, b) never appears consecutively. Which such pair should you look at? Take the “missing” coprime pair with the smallest possible value of a + b : a minimal counterexample. It can’t be (1,1) , which does appear, so a ≠ b (coprime and equal forces a = b = 1 ). If a > b : the pair (a - b, b) is coprime (any common factor of a-b and b divides a ), and its sum a is smaller than a + b . By minimality it does appear, say at positions k, k+1 . But then u_2k+1 = u_k + u_k+1 = a and u_2k+2 = u_k+1 = b , so (a, b) appears after all. If a < b : similarly (a, b - a) appears at some k, k+1 , and then (u_2k, u_2k+1) = (a, b) . Either way, contradiction. So every coprime pair of positive integers appears consecutively. ■ (The question phrases part (iv) as a descent: a missing pair produces a smaller missing pair. That is the same argument, read the other way.) Stage 5 A list of all fractions Every positive rational number can be written uniquely in lowest terms as a/b with a, b coprime. By Stage 4, (a, b) appears as some consecutive pair (u_n, u_n+1) , so f(n) = a/b : the range of f is all positive rationals. By Stage 3 it appears only once, and by Stage 2 every value f(n) is already in lowest terms, so two different n can’t give the same fraction. Hence f is a bijection from the positive integers to the positive rationals, and has an inverse. ■ Looking back Descent and its reverse. Common factors and repeated pairs were chased back to the start of the sequence. Missing pairs were handled by a minimal counterexample, building forward . A bijection needs two halves. “Every fraction appears” (onto) and “no fraction appears twice” (one-to-one) are separate claims, proved separately. Compute first. Writing out fifteen terms made the claims believable and suggested the parent–child structure that drove the proofs. What’s really going on The Calkin–Wilf tree Arrange the positive fractions in a tree: put frac11 at the top, and give each fraction (a)/(b) two children, (a)/(a+b) on the left and (a+b)/(b) on the right. Reading the tree row by row, left to right, gives exactly the list f(1), f(2), f(3), ldots from this question (Figure 1.8.1). Stage 3 says every fraction has a unique parent, and Stage 4 says every fraction is in the tree. In 2003 Moshe Newman found that you don’t even need the tree: each fraction in the list can be computed from the one before by x_n+1 = (1)/(2lfloor x_n rfloor - x_n + 1). Different sizes of infinity A set that can be listed like this is called countable . The fractions are countable, which is surprising, since they seem so much more numerous than the whole numbers. In your first term at university you will also meet Cantor’s diagonal argument , which shows that the real numbers are not countable: any list of real numbers must miss some. So there really are different sizes of infinity, and the real numbers form a strictly bigger infinity than the rationals. This is one of the most startling results you will meet in a first-year course. Stern’s sequence The sequence u_n is Stern’s diatomic sequence , and it has many other lives. For example, u_n+1 counts the number of ways to write n as a sum of powers of 2 with each power used at most twice. It is closely related to the Stern–Brocot tree and to continued fractions, which give the best rational approximations to irrational numbers. The thinking skill Building a bijection To show two sets are the same size, match them up exactly: prove that every element of the target is hit (onto), and that nothing is hit twice (one-to-one). Bijections are the foundation of counting, finite and infinite, and you will use them constantly at university. Here both halves were proved by chasing a structure back to its starting point. Try this next Find the fraction. For which n is f(n) = (3)/(5) ? And f(n) = (5)/(3) ? Use the parent rule to work backwards to frac11 . Newman’s formula. Check that Newman’s formula produces the first ten fractions of the list, starting from x_1 = 1 . Cantor’s diagonal argument. Suppose you had a list of all real numbers between 0 and 1 , written as decimals. Construct a decimal that differs from the n th number in the list in its n th digit. Why does this show the list is incomplete? (What care is needed with decimals like 0.0999ldots = 0.1 ?) Countable unions. harder Show that the set of all pairs (m, n) of positive integers is countable by giving an explicit bijection with the positive integers. (Try 2^m-1(2n-1) .) Further reading Neil Calkin & Herbert Wilf, “ Recounting the rationals ” ( American Mathematical Monthly , 2000). Four pages, entirely readable. Aigner & Ziegler, Proofs from THE BOOK , Chapter 17, “Sets, functions, and the continuum hypothesis”, which includes the Calkin–Wilf tree. Ian Stewart & David Tall, The Foundations of Mathematics (Oxford University Press). Countability, Cantor and the real numbers, as in a first-year course.

title: e Is Irrational, and So Is e^2
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on What we still don’t know Approximation The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: This section uses two questions. The first, from 1997, proves that e is irrational. The second, from 2024, uses a cleverer version of the same idea to prove that e^2 is irrational, which turns out to be genuinely harder. Warm-up STEP III 1997, Question 7 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/97-s3-q7 Main question STEP III 2024, Question 7 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP III paper in OCR’s download of the 2024 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/725753-2024-past-papers.zip The hook In Section 1.3 we proved that sqrt2 is irrational using the fact that sqrt2 satisfies a simple equation, x^2 = 2 . But e doesn’t satisfy any such equation that we know of. All we have is its series, e = 1 + (1)/(1!) + (1)/(2!) + (1)/(3!) + cdots. How can a series tell you that a number is not a fraction? The answer is one of the most useful ideas in number theory: a whole number cannot lie strictly between 0 and 1 . If you can show that some quantity is a whole number, and also that it is strictly between 0 and 1 , you have a contradiction. Everything in this section is a variation on that theme. Before you start Suppose e = p/q . Multiplying e by q gives an integer. What does multiplying by q! do to each term of the series for e ? Multiplying (1)/(k!) by q! gives an integer whenever k ≤ q . So q!\,e splits into a whole-number part (the first q+1 terms) and a “tail” (everything after). If e = p/q then q!\,e is itself an integer, so the tail must be an integer too. The plan is to show the tail is strictly between 0 and 1 . Working it through Stage 1 The warm-up: e is irrational The series b_n is geometric with first term and ratio both (1)/(n+1) , so b_n = (1/(n+1))/(1 - 1/(n+1)) = (1)/(n). Compare a_n and b_n term by term. Which is bigger? The first terms are equal. After that, (n+1)(n+2) > (n+1)^2 , and in general (n+1)(n+2)cdots(n+k) > (n+1)^k for k ≥ 2 , so each later term of a_n is smaller than the corresponding term of b_n . Hence 0 < a_n < b_n = 1/n . Now look at what a_n really is. Multiply the series for e by n! : n!\,e = underbrace(n!)/(0!) + (n!)/(1!) + cdots + (n!)/(n!)_an integer + underbrace(n!)/((n+1)!) + (n!)/((n+2)!) + cdots_=\,a_n. Since 0 < a_n < 1 , the integer part of n!\,e is the first bracket and a_n is the fractional part: a_n = n!\,e - [n!\,e] . Now finish the proof. Suppose e = p/q . Which value of n should you choose? Take n = q . Then q!\,e = (q-1)!\,p is an integer, so its fractional part a_q is 0 . But a_q > 0 . Contradiction: e is irrational. ■ This proof is due to Joseph Fourier, in about 1815. Stage 2 Why e^2 is harder Try the same idea on e^2 . Its series is sum 2^k/k! . What goes wrong when you multiply by n! and look at the tail? The tail is now dfrac2^n+1n+1 + dfrac2^n+2(n+1)(n+2) + cdots , and the powers of 2 ruin everything: the tail is no longer small. Multiplying by n! doesn’t help with the 2^k in the numerators. The 2024 question’s trick is to avoid e^2 altogether. If e^2 = p/q , then qe = (p)/(e). Now we have two numbers, e and 1/e , each with a factorial series and no troublesome powers of 2 : e = sum_k=0^∞ (1)/(k!), qquad frac1e = sum_k=0^∞ ((-1)^k)/(k!). Stage 3 The two tails Part (i) is exactly the warm-up: 0 < f(n) < 1/n . For part (ii), g(n) is an alternating series whose terms decrease in size. For an alternating series t_1 - t_2 + t_3 - cdots with t_1 > t_2 > t_3 > cdots > 0 , why is the sum between 0 and t_1 ? Group the terms in pairs: (t_1 - t_2) + (t_3 - t_4) + cdots is a sum of positive brackets, so it is positive. Group them the other way: t_1 - (t_2 - t_3) - (t_4 - t_5) - cdots is t_1 minus positive brackets, so it is less than t_1 . Here t_1 = (1)/(n+1) , and the terms decrease because each is the previous one divided by something bigger than 1 . So 0 < g(n) < (1)/(n+1) . Stage 4 Integers again Multiply e by (2n)! and split off the tail, exactly as in the warm-up: (2n)!\,e = (integer) + f(2n). So (2n)!\,e - f(2n) is an integer. Now do the same for 1/e : ((2n)!)/(e) = sum_k=0^2n (-1)^k ((2n)!)/(k!) + sum_k=2n+1^∞ (-1)^k ((2n)!)/(k!). What is the sign of the first term of the tail, k = 2n+1 ? How does the tail compare with g(2n) ? The first term of the tail has k = 2n+1 , which is odd, so it is negative. The tail is -(1)/(2n+1) + (1)/((2n+1)(2n+2)) - cdots = -g(2n). So ((2n)!)/(e) + g(2n) is an integer. ■ This is why the question uses 2n rather than n : with an even multiplier, the tail of 1/e is exactly -g , with a predictable sign. Stage 5 The contradiction Suppose qe = p/e . Multiply both sides by (2n)! and use Stage 4: qbigl(integer + f(2n)bigr) = pbigl(integer - g(2n)bigr). Rearranging, q f(2n) + p g(2n) equals a combination of integers, so it is an integer. That is part (iv). Now use the bounds from Stage 3. What happens to q f(2n) + p g(2n) when n is very large? Both f(2n) and g(2n) are positive, so q f(2n) + p g(2n) > 0 . And q f(2n) + p g(2n) < (q)/(2n) + (p)/(2n+1) < (p+q)/(2n). Choose n > (p+q)/2 . Then q f(2n) + p g(2n) is an integer strictly between 0 and 1 . That is impossible, so e^2 is irrational. ■ Looking back The engine is “no integer lies strictly between 0 and 1”. Both proofs build a quantity that must be an integer and then trap it. Factorials make tails small. Multiplying by n! turned the start of the series into integers and left a tail that shrinks like 1/n . When a direct attack fails, rearrange. Rather than attacking e^2 = p/q head-on, we rewrote it as qe = p/e , which spread the difficulty across two easier numbers. The details matter. The choice of 2n rather than n fixed the sign of a tail. Many proofs hinge on a small detail like this. What’s really going on How irrational is e ? Joseph Liouville proved in 1840 that e^2 is irrational, and in fact that it doesn’t satisfy any quadratic equation with integer coefficients. In 1873 Charles Hermite went much further: he proved that e is transcendental , meaning it is not a root of any polynomial with integer coefficients. His proof is a sophisticated version of exactly the argument above: build an integer, show it is strictly between 0 and 1 . Nine years later Ferdinand von Lindemann adapted Hermite’s method to show that π is transcendental, finally proving that the ancient problem of “squaring the circle” with ruler and compass is impossible. What we still don’t know For all the power of these methods, embarrassingly simple questions remain open. Is e + π irrational? Is eπ ? Nobody knows, although at least one of them must be transcendental (exercise 4). Is zeta(3) = 1 + (1)/(8) + (1)/(27) + cdots irrational? Yes: Roger Apéry astonished the mathematical world by proving it in 1978. Is zeta(5) ? Nobody knows. Approximation Behind these proofs lies a deeper idea: a number is irrational if it can be approximated by fractions too well . The partial sums of the series for e are fractions that get very close to e very quickly; a fraction can’t be approximated by other fractions that well. This is the starting point of Diophantine approximation , a branch of number theory you can explore further in Section 2.9 , where a different family of integrals produces even better fractions closing in on e . The thinking skill Trapping an integer To prove a number is irrational, assume it is a fraction, build from it a quantity that must be a whole number, and show that the quantity is strictly between 0 and 1 . The art lies in choosing the quantity. Here, multiplying by a factorial made most of a series into integers and left a tail that was small but positive. Try this next Using 1/e alone. Prove that e is irrational by supposing 1/e = p/q and using only the alternating series for 1/e . sin 1 is irrational. Use sin 1 = 1 - (1)/(3!) + (1)/(5!) - cdots to prove that sin 1 is irrational. (Multiply by a suitable odd factorial.) Why not π ? Explain why this method doesn’t work directly for π . Then look up Ivan Niven’s one-page proof (1947) that π is irrational, which uses an integral instead of a series. It is within reach of a strong A-level student. One of them is transcendental. harder Show that e and π are the roots of x^2 - (e+π)x + eπ = 0 . You may assume that a root of a polynomial whose coefficients are algebraic numbers is itself algebraic, and that π is not algebraic (Lindemann). Deduce that at least one of e + π and eπ is transcendental. Further reading Aigner & Ziegler, Proofs from THE BOOK , Chapter 8, “Some irrational numbers”. Proves that e , e^2 , e^4 and π^2 are irrational, using exactly these ideas. Ivan Niven, Irrational Numbers (Mathematical Association of America). A short classic covering everything from sqrt2 to transcendence. Julian Havil, The Irrationals (Princeton University Press). A readable history of irrational numbers.

title: When Factorisation Fails
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on What makes the integers special A smaller example to remember The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP I 2016, Question 7 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/16-s1-q7 The hook Every whole number greater than 1 can be written as a product of primes in exactly one way: 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 , and there is no other way to do it. You have probably used this fact so often that it feels too obvious to need proof. This question builds a small world of numbers that looks perfectly sensible but in which that “obvious” fact is false. It is a STEP I question, so the mathematics is gentle, but the lesson is a deep one. It is exactly the lesson that defeated a famous attempted proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 1847 and led to the invention of a whole new branch of algebra. Before you start List the first few members of S and T . Which members of S are S -prime , according to the definition in part (iv)? S = \1, 5, 9, 13, 17, 21, 25, 29, 33, ldots\ and T = \3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, ldots\ . A number in S is S -prime if it can’t be written as a product of smaller members of S (other than 1 ). Notice that 9 is S -prime, even though 9 = 3 × 3 in the ordinary integers, because 3 is not in S . “Prime” depends on which numbers you are allowed to use. Working it through Stage 1 Union, intersection and products S cup T is the set of all positive odd numbers, since every odd number leaves remainder 1 or 3 on division by 4 . S cap T is empty, because no number leaves two different remainders. How do you write a general member of S ? What is the product of two of them? Members of S are 4a + 1 for a ≥ 0 , and (4a+1)(4b+1) = 16ab + 4a + 4b + 1 = 4(4ab + a + b) + 1 S. So S is closed under multiplication. For T : (4a+3)(4b+3) = 16ab + 12a + 12b + 9 = 4(4ab + 3a + 3b + 2) + 1, which is in S , not T . For example, 3 × 7 = 21 S . So T is not closed under multiplication. Stage 2 A prime factor in T Take a number in T that isn’t prime. Its prime factors are all odd. What would happen if they were all in S ? The number is odd, so all its prime factors are odd and lie in S or T . If they were all in S , then since S is closed under multiplication, their product would be in S . But the product is our number, which is in T . So at least one prime factor is in T . ■ Stage 3 An odd number of factors If you multiply together an even number of members of T , where does the product land? What about an odd number? Each pair of T -numbers multiplies to an S -number, and S -numbers multiply to S -numbers, so an even number of T -factors gives a product in S . An odd number gives (something in S ) × (one element of T ), which is in T by the same kind of calculation. Now take t T . If t is T -prime, we are done. Otherwise, write t as a product of members of T , each bigger than 1 and so smaller than t . Any of those that are not T -prime can be broken down further, and so on. The factors get smaller each time, so the process stops (well-ordering again), leaving t as a product of T -primes. Since the product is in T , the number of factors must be odd. ■ Stage 4 Two factorisations Find a number in S with two genuinely different factorisations into S -primes. Hint: use numbers like 9 , which are S -prime only because their ordinary prime factors are missing from S . The S -primes begin 5, 9, 13, 17, 21, 29, 33, 37, 41, 49, ldots . Now 21 = 3 × 7 and 9 = 3 × 3 and 49 = 7 × 7 are all S -prime, because 3 and 7 are not in S . And 441 = 21 × 21 = 9 × 49. Two different factorisations of 441 into S -primes (Figure 1.7.1). Unique factorisation fails in S . ■ Looking back Being “prime” depends on the system. 9 and 21 are composite in the integers but prime in S , because the numbers you would need to factorise them are missing. Closure matters. S is closed under multiplication; T is not. That single difference drove parts (iii) and (iv). An obvious fact can be a theorem. Unique factorisation in the integers needs a proof. This question shows why: in a system that looks very similar, it is false. What’s really going on What makes the integers special Why does factorisation work in the ordinary integers? The key fact is Euclid’s lemma : if a prime p divides a product ab , then p divides a or p divides b . It is proved using the Euclidean algorithm, and it is exactly what fails in S . There, the S -prime 9 divides 21 × 21 = 441 (because 441 = 9 × 49 ), but 9 doesn’t divide 21 in S . In your first year at university you will prove Euclid’s lemma carefully and see that unique factorisation follows from it. The failed proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem On 1 March 1847 Gabriel Lamé announced to the Paris Academy that he had proved Fermat’s Last Theorem. His idea was to factorise x^n + y^n using complex roots of unity, x^n + y^n = (x + y)(x + zeta y)(x + zeta^2 y) cdots (x + zeta^n-1 y), qquad zeta = e^2π i/n (for odd n ), and then argue about the prime factors of each bracket. Joseph Liouville immediately objected: why should numbers built from zeta factorise uniquely? Weeks later it emerged that Ernst Kummer had already shown that they often don’t. The first failure is at n = 23 . Kummer rescued what he could by inventing “ideal numbers”, extra objects that restore unique factorisation, and proved Fermat’s Last Theorem for a large class of exponents. Richard Dedekind turned Kummer’s ideal numbers into ideals , one of the central concepts of modern algebra. A smaller example to remember In the number system mathbbZ[sqrt-5] = \a + bsqrt-5 : a, b mathbbZ\ , 6 = 2 × 3 = (1 + sqrt-5)(1 - sqrt-5), and all four factors are “prime” in that system (exercise 3). Compare this with the Gaussian integers of Section 1.6 , where factorisation is unique. Which systems of this kind have unique factorisation is a deep question. Gauss conjectured that, among systems of the form mathbbZ[sqrt-d] and their close relatives, only nine have it. This was finally proved by Heegner, Baker and Stark between 1952 and 1967. The thinking skill Questioning what you take for granted When a fact feels too obvious to prove, ask what it depends on, and look for a setting where it fails. Building a counterexample, a world where the “obvious” fact is false, is one of the best ways to find out what a proof really needs. Much of undergraduate algebra consists of asking which familiar properties of the integers survive in more general systems. Try this next Another example. Show that 693 has two different factorisations into S -primes. Can you find a general recipe for producing such examples? Even numbers. Let E = \2, 4, 6, 8, ldots\ . Which numbers are E -prime? Show that 60 has more than one factorisation into E -primes. mathbbZ[sqrt-5] . Define the norm N(a + bsqrt-5) = a^2 + 5b^2 . Show that N(zw) = N(z)N(w) . By showing that no element has norm 2 or 3 , deduce that 2 , 3 and 1 sqrt-5 cannot be factorised further in mathbbZ[sqrt-5] . Euclid’s lemma in action. harder Assuming Euclid’s lemma (if a prime divides ab , it divides a or b ), prove that every integer greater than 1 has only one factorisation into primes, apart from the order of the factors. Further reading Ian Stewart & David Tall, Algebraic Number Theory and Fermat’s Last Theorem (CRC Press). The opening chapters tell the story of Lamé, Kummer and ideals at a level a keen first-year student can follow. John Stillwell, Elements of Number Theory . Unique factorisation in the integers and in the Gaussian integers, compared side by side. Harold Edwards, Fermat’s Last Theorem: A Genetic Introduction (Springer). For the ambitious: Kummer’s work explained through its history.

title: A Prime Factory
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Fermat primes and constructing polygons One theorem, many proofs The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 2002, Question 3 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/02-s2-q3 The hook You almost certainly already know that there are infinitely many primes. Euclid proved it around 300 BC, and it is one of the first proofs anyone meets. So why would a STEP question ask you to prove it again ? Because this proof works in a completely different way. Euclid’s argument says: give me any finite list of primes and I will show you it is incomplete. This one says: here is a single, explicit sequence of numbers, written down in advance, and every one of them contains a prime that none of the others contain. It is a machine for manufacturing new primes, and the reason it works is a beautifully simple identity that the question walks you towards. Along the way you will meet numbers that fooled Fermat himself. Before you start Read the question through once and notice its shape. It has four stages: compute some examples; spot (well, be told) a pattern, and check it on those examples; prove the pattern in general; use the pattern twice: first to deduce something about common factors, then something about primes. This “examples → conjecture → proof → consequences” structure is how a great deal of mathematics is actually done, and STEP questions often follow it. When you see it, the early parts are usually not just warm-up: they are where you build the intuition you will need later. The last line asks about infinitely many primes . The middle asks about common factors . What could possibly connect “no two Fermat numbers share a factor” with “there are infinitely many primes”? Hold on to that question. We will come back to it. Working it through Stage 1 Getting a feel for the numbers Be careful with the notation: 2^2^n means 2^(2^n) , not (2^2)^n . The exponent is itself a power of 2, so these numbers grow very fast. beginaligned F_0 &= 2^1 + 1 = 3, &qquad F_2 &= 2^4 + 1 = 17,\\ F_1 &= 2^2 + 1 = 5, &qquad F_3 &= 2^8 + 1 = 257. endaligned What do you notice about these four numbers? They are all prime. (Check 257 : it is not divisible by 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 or 13 , and 17^2 = 289 > 257 , so we can stop.) The next one, F_4 = 2^16 + 1 = 65537 , is also prime. Pierre de Fermat noticed exactly this in 1640 and conjectured that every number of this form is prime. Keep that in mind; we will see later whether he was right. Stage 2 Checking the identity Now check (*) for small k : k = 1 : the left-hand side is just F_0 = 3 , and F_1 - 2 = 3 . k = 2 : F_0 F_1 = 3 × 5 = 15 , and F_2 - 2 = 15 . k = 3 : F_0 F_1 F_2 = 15 × 17 = 255 , and F_3 - 2 = 255 . Look at the step from k = 2 to k = 3 . We took 15 , multiplied by 17 , and got 255 . In terms of Fermat numbers, we computed (F_2 - 2) × F_2 and got F_3 - 2 . Is that a coincidence? That observation is the whole proof in miniature. Let’s see why it should be true. Stage 3 Proving the identity Before reading on, try to show directly that (F_k - 2)\, F_k = F_k+1 - 2. Hint: write everything in terms of powers of 2. What does F_k - 2 look like? We have F_k - 2 = 2^2^k - 1 and F_k = 2^2^k + 1 , so (F_k - 2)\, F_k = bigl(2^2^k - 1bigr)bigl(2^2^k + 1bigr). This is a product of the form (a - 1)(a + 1) . What is that? It is a difference of two squares, a^2 - 1 . With a = 2^2^k , a^2 = bigl(2^2^kbigr)^2 = 2^2 · 2^k = 2^2^k+1, so (F_k - 2)\, F_k = 2^2^k+1 - 1 = F_k+1 - 2. tag$dagger$ That is the engine. Notice what squaring does: it doubles the exponent, and doubling 2^k gives 2^k+1 . The definition of the Fermat numbers is perfectly tuned to the difference-of-squares factorisation. Now the induction is almost automatic. What exactly do we need to show in the inductive step? We assume (*) holds for some k ≥ 1 , F_0 F_1 cdots F_k-1 = F_k - 2, and we want to show it holds for k + 1 : F_0 F_1 cdots F_k-1 F_k = F_k+1 - 2. Multiply both sides of the assumption by F_k and use (dagger) : F_0 F_1 cdots F_k-1 F_k = (F_k - 2)\, F_k = F_k+1 - 2. We have already checked k = 1 , so by induction (*) holds for every k ≥ 1 . ■ Could we have avoided induction altogether? Yes, and it is worth seeing how. Apply (dagger) repeatedly, starting from F_0 - 2 = 1 : F_k - 2 = (F_k-1 - 2) F_k-1 = (F_k-2 - 2) F_k-2 F_k-1 = cdots = (F_0 - 2)\, F_0 F_1 cdots F_k-1. Since F_0 - 2 = 1 , we are done. This “unrolling” is really the same induction written out in full, but some people find it easier to see. Stage 4 No common factors We want to show that if m ≠ n then F_m and F_n have no common factor greater than 1 . Suppose some number d divides both F_m and F_n , with m < n . Where does F_m appear in (*) ? Take k = n in (*) : F_0 F_1 cdots F_m cdots F_n-1 = F_n - 2. Since m < n , the number F_m is one of the factors on the left. So if d divides F_m , then d divides the whole left-hand side; that is, d divides F_n - 2 . Now d divides F_n and F_n - 2 . What else must it divide? Their difference: d divides F_n - (F_n - 2) = 2 . So d = 1 or d = 2 . Can d be 2 ? No: every Fermat number is a power of 2 plus 1, so it is odd. Hence d = 1 , and no two distinct Fermat numbers share a factor greater than 1 . ■ Mathematicians say the Fermat numbers are pairwise coprime . Stage 5 Infinitely many primes Now we return to the question we asked at the start. Every whole number greater than 1 has at least one prime factor. Pick one prime factor of each Fermat number. What can you say about the primes you have picked? Let p_n be any prime that divides F_n . If two of these were equal, say p_m = p_n with m ≠ n , then that prime would be a common factor of F_m and F_n greater than 1 , which we have just shown is impossible. So the primes p_0,\; p_1,\; p_2,\; p_3,\; ldots are all different . There are infinitely many Fermat numbers, so there are infinitely many different primes. ■ Notice that we never needed to know which prime divides each Fermat number, or even whether the Fermat numbers are themselves prime. All we needed was that they never share a factor. Each one is forced to “use up” at least one prime that no other can use. Looking back It is worth pausing to see what made this work, because the same ideas will come back many times in this book. The examples weren’t decoration. Spotting that 15 × 17 = 255 was “ (F_2 - 2) × F_2 = F_3 - 2 ” was the key idea. When a question gives you small cases, ask what each step is doing, not just whether the numbers match. A single identity did all the work. Everything flowed from (a-1)(a+1) = a^2 - 1 . Hard-looking STEP questions are often driven by one simple piece of algebra. The final argument is about structure, not size. We proved there are infinitely many primes without finding a single new one. Instead we showed that an infinite family of numbers needs infinitely many primes to build them. What’s really going on Was Fermat right? No. In 1732 Leonhard Euler showed that F_5 = 2^32 + 1 = 4\,294\,967\,297 = 641 × 6\,700\,417. Euler didn’t find 641 by luck. He proved that any prime factor of F_n must have a very special form (for n = 5 , it must be one more than a multiple of 64 ), which drastically cut down the candidates. You can prove this yourself in Exercise 4. Since then, every Fermat number anyone has managed to test, from F_5 up to F_32 , has turned out to be composite. As far as anyone knows, F_0 to F_4 may be the only Fermat primes, but nobody has been able to prove it. It is a genuinely open problem. The delightful twist is that our proof doesn’t care. Prime or composite, the Fermat numbers still produce infinitely many primes. Fermat primes and constructing polygons Fermat primes turn up somewhere quite unexpected. The ancient Greeks knew how to construct an equilateral triangle and a regular pentagon with ruler and compass, and notice that 3 = F_0 and 5 = F_1 . For two thousand years nobody could construct any other regular polygon with a prime number of sides. Then in 1796, aged 19, Carl Friedrich Gauss showed how to construct a regular 17-gon , and 17 = F_2 . Gauss went further: a regular N -gon can be constructed with ruler and compass exactly when N is a power of 2 multiplied by distinct Fermat primes . (Pierre Wantzel completed the proof in 1837.) So which polygons can be constructed depends on how many Fermat primes there are. You will meet the key calculation behind Gauss’s 17-gon in Section 6.2 (STEP II 1991, Question 4), and the full story belongs to Galois theory , one of the highlights of an undergraduate degree. One theorem, many proofs Why would mathematicians bother proving the same theorem more than once? Because different proofs reveal different things. This proof, usually credited to Christian Goldbach in a 1730 letter to Euler, shows that any infinite sequence of pairwise coprime whole numbers greater than 1 forces infinitely many primes. Fermat numbers are just one convenient example. (Exercise 3 gives another.) It also gives more than Euclid’s proof does. The primes p_0, p_1, ldots, p_n-1 are n different primes, each at most F_n-1 . So there are at least n primes no bigger than 2^2^n-1 + 1 . That is a quantitative statement about how the primes are spread out. It is very weak (the truth is much better), but it is a first step towards one of the great results of nineteenth-century mathematics, the Prime Number Theorem , which describes exactly how the primes thin out. Section 1.2 takes the next step. The thinking skill Building an argument from a structural property To show that infinitely many objects of type A exist, find infinitely many objects of type B, each of which needs its own object of type A. Here A = primes and B = Fermat numbers, and “needs its own” means “has a prime factor not shared with any other”. The same pattern appears in counting arguments, in linear algebra (infinitely many independent vectors force infinite dimension) and in analysis. You also practised induction , and in particular the habit of asking “what does the step from k to k+1 actually do?” That question is often more useful than the formal template. Try this next Euclid’s version. Write out Euclid’s proof that there are infinitely many primes. In what sense is it “by contradiction”, and in what sense is the Fermat-number proof “constructive”? The last digit. Show that for n ≥ 2 the Fermat number F_n ends in the digit 7 . Sylvester’s sequence. Define a_1 = 2 and a_n+1 = a_n^2 - a_n + 1 , so the sequence begins 2, 3, 7, 43, 1807, ldots Show that a_n+1 - 1 = a_1 a_2 cdots a_n . Deduce that the terms are pairwise coprime, and hence give another proof that there are infinitely many primes. harder Show that (1)/(a_1) + (1)/(a_2) + cdots + (1)/(a_n) = 1 - dfrac1a_n+1 - 1 . Euler’s trick. This needs Fermat’s Little Theorem: if p is prime and p nmid a , then a^p-1 equiv 1 pmodp . Suppose a prime p divides F_n . Show that 2^2^n equiv -1 pmod p , and hence that 2^2^n+1 equiv 1 pmod p . Let d be the smallest positive integer with 2^d equiv 1 pmod p . Show that d divides 2^n+1 but not 2^n , and conclude that d = 2^n+1 . Using Fermat’s Little Theorem, show that d divides p - 1 . Deduce that p equiv 1 pmod2^n+1 . For n = 5 , this says any prime factor of F_5 has the form 64k + 1 . Check that 641 does. How many primes of this form are smaller than 641 ? A bound on the primes. Use the argument in One theorem, many proofs to show that the n th prime is at most 2^2^n-1 + 1 . How good is this bound when n = 5 ? Further reading Martin Aigner & Günter M. Ziegler, Proofs from THE BOOK (Springer), Chapter 1, “Six proofs of the infinity of primes”. It includes this proof alongside Euclid’s and four others, one of which uses topology. One of the best books you can read before university. Harold Davenport, The Higher Arithmetic (Cambridge University Press), Chapters 1–2. A beautifully written introduction to primes and factorisation, ideal for the summer before university. Michal Křížek, Florian Luca & Lawrence Somer, 17 Lectures on Fermat Numbers (Springer, 2001). Everything about Fermat numbers, from Euler’s factorisation to Gauss’s polygons. Dip into the early chapters. Ian Stewart, Why Beauty Is Truth (Basic Books), the chapter on Gauss. The story of the 17-gon told for a general reader.

title: Number Theory and Proof
headings: Pure, useless, and running the internet What you will meet at university The questions that run through this chapter A chapter about proof How to read this chapter
text: Chapter 1 · Introduction Why Whole Numbers? Mathematics is the queen of the sciences, and number theory is the queen of mathematics. — Carl Friedrich Gauss Whole numbers are the first mathematical objects anyone meets. You learned to count before you could read. And yet the simplest questions about them can be fiendishly hard. Is every even number greater than 2 the sum of two primes? Nobody knows: Christian Goldbach asked in 1742, computers have checked it beyond 4 × 10^18 , and it has still never been proved. Are there infinitely many pairs of primes that differ by 2, like 11 and 13 , or 101 and 103 ? Nobody knows that either, although in 2013 an almost unknown mathematician called Yitang Zhang stunned the world by proving that there are infinitely many pairs of primes differing by at most 70 million, a number since brought down to 246 . Pierre de Fermat scribbled in a margin in 1637 that x^n + y^n = z^n has no solutions in positive whole numbers when n ≥ 3 . It took more than 350 years, and some of the most sophisticated mathematics ever created, before Andrew Wiles proved him right in 1994. This mixture of questions a child can understand and answers that can take centuries is what makes number theory addictive. It is also why number theory has always been the training ground for proof . When you cannot check every case, because there are infinitely many whole numbers, you have to find an argument that covers them all at once. Most of the proof techniques you will use for the rest of your mathematical life were first sharpened on questions about whole numbers. Pure, useless, and running the internet In 1940 the Cambridge mathematician G. H. Hardy wrote, with some pride, that number theory was the purest of all mathematics, too remote from ordinary life to be put to any practical use, and so too remote to be put to any harmful use either. He could hardly have been more wrong. Every time you buy something online, send a secure message or unlock your phone, you are relying on number theory. The RSA system (1977) depends on the fact that multiplying two large primes is easy but recovering them from their product seems to be impossibly hard. Modern systems use the arithmetic of the very curves you will meet at the end of this chapter. The “useless” mathematics of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries became the security of the twenty-first. What you will meet at university If you study mathematics at university, number theory will be one of your first destinations and one of your last. In your first term you will almost certainly take a course with a name like Numbers and Sets or Foundations . It will teach you to write proofs properly, and much of its raw material is number theory: induction, the Euclidean algorithm, modular arithmetic, Fermat’s Little Theorem, the Chinese Remainder Theorem, and the surprising fact that some infinite sets are bigger than others. In group theory , usually in the first year, you will discover that many number-theory facts are shadows of a single theorem about symmetry, Lagrange’s Theorem. In the second year a course in Number Theory typically covers quadratic reciprocity (Gauss’s “golden theorem”), continued fractions and Pell’s equation. Later you can go further: algebraic number theory , where new number systems such as the Gaussian integers rescue unique factorisation; analytic number theory , which uses calculus and complex analysis to count primes; and the theory of elliptic curves , which lies behind the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem and one of the seven million-dollar Millennium Prize Problems. The questions that run through this chapter The nine STEP questions in this chapter circle around three big questions. Keep them in mind as you work; we will come back to them at the end. How many primes are there, and how are they spread out? Everyone knows there are infinitely many. But how thinly do they thin out, and what kind of argument can tell us? How can you prove that a number is not a fraction? Showing that a number is rational just needs an example. Showing that it is irrational means ruling out infinitely many possibilities. How is that ever done? Which equations have whole-number solutions, and what happens when we change the number system? Sometimes we can show an equation has no solutions at all. Sometimes the best way to understand whole numbers is to step outside them, into the complex numbers or onto a curve. A chapter about proof Running underneath those three questions is a fourth theme: how to prove things . Each section has been chosen partly because it shows a different method of proof in action, and between them they make a fair toolkit for a first-year undergraduate. § Topic Way of thinking 1.1 Fermat numbers An infinite family that needs infinitely many primes 1.2 Products of primes Strong induction; information hidden in binomial coefficients 1.3 sqrt2 again “Take the smallest one”: the well-ordering principle 1.4 e and e^2 Trapping a whole number strictly between 0 and 1 1.5 Impossible equations Infinite descent; working modulo n 1.6 Sums of two squares Changing the setting: complex numbers 1.7 A strange number system Questioning what you take for granted 1.8 Listing the fractions Building a bijection; descent in reverse 1.9 Cubes and curves Geometry solving arithmetic How to read this chapter Each section starts with a link to a STEP question, exactly as it was set. Try it yourself first, for at least half an hour, before you read on. You will learn far more from a question you have struggled with than from one you have only read about. When you do read on, the Ask yourself boxes are invitations to stop and think before the answer arrives, and the Pause and try boxes mark the moments where the key idea is within your reach. Then the What’s really going on part of each section looks past the exam to the mathematics you will meet at university. The sections increase roughly in sophistication, but they are largely independent. If one doesn’t grip you, move on and come back to it later.

title: Infinite Descent
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Local obstructions An equation that does have solutions The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2022, Question 2 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP III paper in OCR’s download of the 2022 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/696587-2022-past-papers.zip The hook How can you prove that an equation has no whole-number solutions? You can’t try every possibility; there are infinitely many. Pierre de Fermat, in the 1630s, found a way: show that any solution would produce another solution with smaller numbers, and then another, smaller still, and so on for ever. But positive whole numbers can’t keep getting smaller for ever. So there was never a solution in the first place. Fermat called this the method of infinite descent , and he was very proud of it. It is the reverse side of the well-ordering principle from Section 1.3 , and it is still one of the main tools for proving that equations have no solutions. Before you start All four parts have the same shape: assume a solution, shrink it, contradict. The question is how to shrink. In part (i), look at a^3 + 2b^3 + 4c^3 = 0 . Two of the three terms are obviously even. What does that tell you about the third? That is the kind of observation that starts every descent: some divisibility is forced on you. Working it through Stage 1 The first descent Since a^3 = -2b^3 - 4c^3 , the number a^3 is even, and so a is even (the cube of an odd number is odd). Write a = 2p . Then |p| = |a|/2 < |a| , and substituting, 8p^3 + 2b^3 + 4c^3 = 0 quadLongrightarrowquad 4p^3 + b^3 + 2c^3 = 0. The new equation is 4p^3 + b^3 + 2c^3 = 0 . It has the same coefficients, just rotated. Can you do the same trick again? Now b^3 = -4p^3 - 2c^3 is even, so b = 2q with |q| < |b| , and dividing by 2 gives 2p^3 + 4q^3 + c^3 = 0 . Once more, c must be even: c = 2r with |r| < |c| , and dividing by 2 , p^3 + 2q^3 + 4r^3 = 0. This is the original equation, with p , q , r in place of a , b , c . Each is half the size, and none of them is zero, because halving a non-zero number can’t give zero. Turn this into a proof that no non-zero solution exists. What, exactly, should you assume is the “smallest”? Among all solutions in non-zero integers, choose one with |a| as small as possible. (The well-ordering principle lets us do this, if any solutions exist at all.) The argument above produces another non-zero solution with |p| < |a| , contradicting minimality. So there are no non-zero solutions. ■ An equivalent way to say it: from one solution we could build an infinite sequence of solutions with |a| > |p| > cdots , an infinite strictly decreasing sequence of positive integers, which is impossible. Stage 2 A different prime In 9a^3 + 10b^3 + 6c^3 = 0 , parity doesn’t obviously help. Look at the coefficients 9 , 10 , 6 . Which prime divides two of them? The prime 3 divides 9 and 6 , so 3 divides 10b^3 , and hence 3 divides b . Write b = 3q and divide by 3 : 3a^3 + 90q^3 + 2c^3 = 0. Now 3 divides 2c^3 , so c = 3r ; dividing by 3 again gives a^3 + 30q^3 + 18r^3 = 0 . So 3 divides a : a = 3p , and dividing by 3 once more, 9p^3 + 10q^3 + 6r^3 = 0. Exactly the original equation, with smaller non-zero numbers. By the same descent argument, there are no non-zero solutions. ■ Stage 3 Squares modulo 3 Every integer is of the form 3n , 3n+1 or 3n-1 . What are their squares, modulo 3 ? (3n 1)^2 = 9n^2 6n + 1 = 3(3n^2 2n) + 1 , one more than a multiple of 3 . And (3n)^2 is a multiple of 3 . So a square leaves remainder 0 or 1 on division by 3 , never 2 . Now if a^2 + b^2 is a multiple of 3 , the possible remainders are 0+0 , 0+1 , 1+0 and 1+1 , which give 0 , 1 , 1 , 2 . Only the first is a multiple of 3 , so both a and b must be multiples of 3 . If a^2 + b^2 = 3c^2 and a = 3p , b = 3q , what can you say about c ? We get 9p^2 + 9q^2 = 3c^2 , so c^2 = 3(p^2 + q^2) is a multiple of 3 , and hence c = 3r . Then 9p^2 + 9q^2 = 27r^2 , so p^2 + q^2 = 3r^2 : the same equation, smaller numbers. Descent again. ■ Stage 4 A twist: the equation changes In a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 4abc the right-hand side is a multiple of 4 . What are the squares modulo 4 ? Even squares are multiples of 4 and odd squares are one more than a multiple of 4 ( (2n+1)^2 = 4n^2 + 4n + 1 ). So a^2 + b^2 + c^2 leaves remainder 0 , 1 , 2 or 3 on division by 4 , according to how many of a , b , c are odd. Since the right-hand side is a multiple of 4 , none of them can be odd. Write a = 2p , b = 2q , c = 2r : 4(p^2 + q^2 + r^2) = 32\,pqr quadLongrightarrowquad p^2 + q^2 + r^2 = 8\,pqr. This is not the same equation: the 4 has become an 8 . Does the descent still work? Here is the trick: prove something stronger . Consider all equations of the form x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 2^m\, xyz qquadwith m ≥ 2. For any such m , the right-hand side is a multiple of 4 , so exactly the same argument shows x , y , z are all even. Halving them gives a solution of the equation with 2^m+1 , which is again of this form. So from a non-zero solution of the m equation we get a smaller non-zero solution of the m+1 equation. Taking the solution, of any equation in the family, with |x| smallest gives a contradiction. In particular, a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 4abc has no non-zero solutions. ■ Sometimes the statement you want to prove is too weak to support its own induction, and the cure is to prove a more general statement that is self-supporting. This is a surprisingly common trick at university. Looking back Descent needs a source of divisibility. Each time, we found a prime p (here 2 or 3 ) that was forced to divide all the variables, and divided it out. Working modulo n is the way to find it. Looking at remainders mod 2 , 3 or 4 turned “could anything work?” into a short finite check. If the equation changes, generalise. Part (iv) needed a whole family of equations, closed under the descent step. What’s really going on Fermat, descent and his Last Theorem Fermat used infinite descent to prove that x^4 + y^4 = z^2 has no solutions in positive integers. This is the only case of his famous “Last Theorem” for which he left a proof, and it settles the case n = 4 of x^n + y^n = z^n . Euler later used descent, with a gap that was later filled, for n = 3 . Descent is still the starting point of the modern theory: the proof of the Mordell–Weil theorem about curves like the one in Section 1.9 is a sophisticated descent. Local obstructions Every proof in this section worked by looking at remainders modulo some number. If an equation has no solutions modulo n for some n , or no solutions in real numbers, it certainly has no solutions in integers. Such reasons are called local obstructions , and at university you will meet the p -adic numbers , a way of studying all the remainders modulo p, p^2, p^3, ldots at once. A wonderful theorem of Hasse and Minkowski says that for quadratic equations like a^2 + b^2 = 3c^2 , local obstructions are the only obstructions: if there are no “local” reasons to fail, there really is a rational solution. For cubic equations this breaks down spectacularly. Ernst Selmer showed in 1951 that 3x^3 + 4y^3 + 5z^3 = 0 has solutions modulo every whole number, and in real numbers, but no solution in non-zero integers. Explaining when and why the “local-to-global” principle fails is a major theme of modern number theory. An equation that does have solutions Part (iv) has a famous cousin: x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 3xyz , the Markov equation . It has infinitely many solutions in positive integers, starting with (1,1,1) , (1,1,2) , (1,2,5) , (1,5,13) and (2,5,29) , and they are connected to how well irrational numbers can be approximated by fractions. See exercise 4. The thinking skill Infinite descent To show an equation has no solutions, show that any solution would produce a strictly smaller one. Then the smallest solution can’t exist. Pair this with working modulo n to find the divisibility that drives the descent, and be ready to generalise the statement if it isn’t preserved by the descent step. Try this next A STEP I warm-up. (STEP I 2010 Question 8.) Show that the only integer solution of a^3 + 3b^3 = 9c^3 is a = b = c = 0 . Then, by considering final digits, show the same for p^4 + 2q^4 = 5r^4 . A modulus with no descent needed. Show that x^2 + y^2 = 4z + 3 has no integer solutions at all, just by working modulo 4 . Rational points. Use part (iii) to show that there is no point with rational coordinates on the circle x^2 + y^2 = 3 . (Contrast this with x^2 + y^2 = 2 , which contains (1,1) .) Markov triples. Show that if (x, y, z) satisfies x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 3xyz , then so does (x, y, 3xy - z) . Starting from (1,1,1) , generate the triples listed above. (This “jumping” trick is the opposite of descent.) Further reading Harold Davenport, The Higher Arithmetic , Chapters 2 and 5. Joseph Silverman, A Friendly Introduction to Number Theory (Pearson). Very readable; includes Fermat’s descent proof for x^4 + y^4 = z^2 . Simon Singh, Fermat’s Last Theorem (Fourth Estate). The story, from Fermat’s margin to Wiles’s proof, for a general reader.

title: How Thinly Spread Are the Primes?
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Bertrand’s postulate Where this goes next The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2016, Question 5 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/16-s3-q5 The hook In Section 1.1 we saw that there are infinitely many primes. But “infinitely many” is a blunt statement. The primes certainly get rarer: there are 25 primes below 100 but only 14 between 900 and 1000 . How rare do they get? This question proves something that sounds quite modest: if you multiply together all the primes up to n , the answer is less than 4^n . But that innocent inequality is the first real step towards answering “how rare?”, and it is the key lemma in one of the most celebrated short proofs in mathematics, by the young Paul Erdős in 1932. Before you start The notation P_r,s looks fussy, but the idea is simple: multiply together the primes in a range. Make sure you understand the examples. P_3,7 uses the primes greater than 3 and at most 7 , namely 5 and 7 , so it is 35 . Part (iv) asks you to prove a statement for all n ≥ 2 . Part (iii) assumes the statement for every k up to 2m . What kind of induction is that? It is strong induction: to prove the case n , you may assume all the earlier cases, not just the one immediately before. Keep that in mind; it is why the question is laid out the way it is. Working it through Stage 1 A binomial coefficient is not too big What do you get if you put x = 1 in the binomial expansion of (1+x)^2m+1 ? You get 2^2m+1 = binom2m+10 + binom2m+11 + cdots + binom2m+12m+1. All the terms are positive, so each one is less than 2^2m+1 . That is not quite good enough; we want 2^2m , which is half as much. Pascal’s triangle is symmetric. Which other term in the sum equals binom2m+1m ? By symmetry, binom2m+1m = binom2m+1m+1 , and these are two different terms of the sum (since m ≠ m+1 ). So 2binom2m+1m = binom2m+1m + binom2m+1m+1 < 2^2m+1, with strict inequality because the sum also contains other positive terms such as binom2m+10 = 1 . Dividing by 2 gives binom2m+1m < 2^2m . ■ Stage 2 Which primes divide that binomial coefficient? Write the binomial coefficient out: binom2m+1m = ((2m+1)!)/(m!\,(m+1)!) = ((m+2)(m+3)cdots(2m+1))/(m!). Let p be a prime with m + 1 < p ≤ 2m+1 . Does p divide the numerator? Can it divide the denominator? The numerator (m+2)(m+3)cdots(2m+1) contains p itself as one of its factors, so p divides it. The denominator m! is a product of numbers all smaller than p ; since p is prime, it cannot divide a product of numbers none of which it divides. So p divides the numerator but not the denominator, and therefore p divides the whole binomial coefficient (which, remember, is a whole number). We now know that each prime in the range divides binom2m+1m . Why does it follow that their product P_m+1,2m+1 divides it too? (Careful: if 4 and 6 both divide a number, 24 need not.) The difference is that our primes are distinct primes . If distinct primes p_1, p_2, ldots each divide N , then their product divides N : write N = p_1 N_1 ; then p_2 divides p_1 N_1 but not p_1 , so it divides N_1 ; and so on. (This uses the fact that if a prime divides a product then it divides one of the factors. That fact is worth a moment’s respect; Section 1.7 shows a world in which its analogue breaks down.) So P_m+1,2m+1 divides binom2m+1m , and since a divisor of a positive number is no bigger than it, P_m+1,\,2m+1 ≤ binom2m+1m < 2^2m. qed Stage 3 Splitting the product How can P_1,2m+1 , the product of all primes up to 2m+1 , be built from products we already know about? Split the primes up to 2m+1 into those up to m+1 and those above m+1 : P_1,2m+1 = P_1,m+1 × P_m+1,2m+1. The second factor is less than 2^2m = 4^m by Stage 2. For the first, we are allowed to assume P_1,k < 4^k for every k from 2 to 2m , and k = m+1 is in that range (because m ≥ 1 gives 2 ≤ m+1 ≤ 2m ). So P_1,2m+1 < 4^m+1 × 4^m = 4^2m+1. qed This is where strong induction earns its keep: to deal with 2m+1 we needed the case m+1 , which is roughly half as big, not the case just before. Stage 4 All n Part (iii) handles odd numbers. What happens for an even number n = 2m+2 ? Is it prime? Check the start: P_1,2 = 2 < 16 and P_1,3 = 6 < 64 . Now suppose P_1,k < 4^k for all k from 2 up to n-1 , where n ≥ 4 . If n is even, then n is not prime (it is bigger than 2 ), so the primes up to n are the same as the primes up to n-1 . Hence P_1,n = P_1,n-1 < 4^n-1 < 4^n . If n is odd, write n = 2m+1 with m ≥ 2 . Then part (iii) gives P_1,n < 4^n directly. By strong induction, P_1,n < 4^n for every n ≥ 2 . ■ Looking back Binomial coefficients carry arithmetic information. binom2m+1m is a single number that is small (less than 4^m ) but is forced to be divisible by many primes. Squeezing many primes into a small number tells you there can’t be too many of them. Strong induction is the natural tool when a problem halves itself. The case 2m+1 depended on the case m+1 . Small cases need checking separately. The induction only gets going once n ≥ 4 , so n = 2 and 3 had to be done by hand. What’s really going on From 4^n to the Prime Number Theorem Take logarithms of the result: P_1,n < n 4 , that is, sum_p ≤ n p < ( 4)\, n approx 1.39\,n . In the 1850s Pafnuty Chebyshev proved bounds of exactly this kind, above and below , showing that sum_p ≤ n p grows in proportion to n . Gauss, aged about 15, had already guessed from tables that the number of primes up to n is roughly n / n . This became the Prime Number Theorem , finally proved in 1896 by Jacques Hadamard and Charles de la Vallée Poussin using complex analysis. In its logarithmic form it says sum_p ≤ n p sim n, so the product of the primes up to n is roughly e^n . Our bound of 4^n is not far off at all: Figure 1.2.1 shows all three. Bertrand’s postulate In 1845 Joseph Bertrand conjectured that for every n ≥ 1 there is always a prime between n and 2n . Chebyshev proved it in 1852. Eighty years later, Paul Erdős, aged 19, found a beautiful elementary proof. Its key ingredients are this question’s lemma and a careful look at which primes divide the middle binomial coefficient binom2nn . Martin Aigner and Günter Ziegler chose it as Chapter 2 of Proofs from THE BOOK , a collection of the most elegant proofs in mathematics. Where this goes next The precise distribution of the primes is controlled by the zeros of the Riemann zeta function, zeta(s) = 1 + (1)/(2^s) + (1)/(3^s) + cdots, a function you will meet in a much humbler guise in Section 2.4 , where zeta(2) = π^2/6 . The Riemann Hypothesis , which predicts exactly where those zeros lie, would pin down the error in the Prime Number Theorem as tightly as possible. It is perhaps the most famous unsolved problem in mathematics, and one of the Millennium Prize Problems. The thinking skill Strong induction, and extracting information from a clever object If the case n depends on cases much smaller than n-1 , assume all earlier cases at once. The other idea here is subtler and very characteristic of number theory: to show something about all primes in a range, find one object (here a binomial coefficient) that every one of those primes must divide, and that you can also show is not too large. Try this next Feel the numbers. Compute P_1,n for n = 10, 20, 30 and compare it with 4^n and with e^n . (A calculator is fine here.) The middle binomial coefficient. Show that binom2mm is the largest of the 2m+1 terms in the expansion of (1+1)^2m , and deduce that binom2mm ≥ (4^m)/(2m+1) . Not too many primes. Let π(n) be the number of primes up to n . Every prime between sqrt n and n is bigger than sqrt n , and their product is at most P_1,n < 4^n . Deduce that π(n) - π(sqrt n) < (2 4)/( n)\, n , and hence that π(n) < 2.8\, n/ n + sqrt n . Compare this with the Prime Number Theorem’s π(n) approx n / n . Check Bertrand. Verify Bertrand’s postulate for n = 1, 2, ldots, 50 by finding a prime between n and 2n in each case. Can you do it efficiently using a short list of primes, each less than twice the one before? Further reading Aigner & Ziegler, Proofs from THE BOOK , Chapter 2, “Bertrand’s postulate”. Marcus du Sautoy, The Music of the Primes (Fourth Estate). A popular history of the Prime Number Theorem and the Riemann Hypothesis. G. J. O. Jameson, The Prime Number Theorem (Cambridge University Press). Rigorous but gentle, and written for undergraduates; the first chapters need only A-level calculus.

title: Tangents to a Cubic
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Elliptic curves today Sums of like powers The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP I 2009, Question 2 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/09-s1-q2 The hook This looks like a routine coordinate-geometry question: differentiate, find a tangent, solve a cubic. Then the last line asks for a cube that is the sum of three other cubes, and the geometry produces one as if by magic. The trick, drawing a line through a known point on a curve to find a new point, goes back to Diophantus of Alexandria in the third century. In modern hands it became the theory of elliptic curves , which sits at the centre of present-day number theory, underlies the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, and secures a large share of the world’s internet traffic. Before you start The point (-a, b) is on the curve. Why? And what does that have to do with sums of cubes? Substitute: (-a)^3 + a^3 + b^3 = b^3 , so yes. Points on y^3 = x^3 + a^3 + b^3 with rational coordinates are exactly what we want: if x = q/s' and y = p/s' then clearing denominators gives a relation between cubes. The plan is to start from one easy point and use the geometry to find a less obvious one. Working it through Stage 1 The tangent Differentiate y^3 = x^3 + a^3 + b^3 implicitly: 3y^2 (dy)/(dx) = 3x^2 , so (dy)/(dx) = (x^2)/(y^2) . At (-a, b) the gradient is a^2/b^2 , so the tangent is y - b = (a^2)/(b^2)(x + a) quadLongrightarrowquad b^2 y - b^3 = a^2 x + a^3 quadLongrightarrowquad b^2 y - a^2 x = a^3 + b^3. qed Stage 2 Where the tangent meets the curve again With a = 1 , b = 2 the curve is y^3 = x^3 + 9 and the tangent at (-1, 2) is 4y - x = 9 , that is, y = (x + 9)/(4) . Substitute into the curve: ((x+9)^3)/(64) = x^3 + 9 quadLongrightarrowquad x^3 + 27x^2 + 243x + 729 = 64x^3 + 576, which rearranges to 63x^3 - 27x^2 - 243x - 153 = 0 , and dividing by 9 gives 7x^3 - 3x^2 - 27x - 17 = 0 . ■ Stage 3 Solving the cubic You already know one root of this cubic without doing any algebra. Which one, and why should it appear twice ? The tangent touches the curve at x = -1 (Figure 1.9.1), and “touching” means a repeated root, just as a tangent to a parabola meets it at a double root of a quadratic. So (x + 1)^2 should be a factor. Check: 7(-1)^3 - 3(1) - 27(-1) - 17 = -7 - 3 + 27 - 17 = 0 , and the derivative 21x^2 - 6x - 27 also vanishes at x = -1 . Dividing, 7x^3 - 3x^2 - 27x - 17 = (x+1)^2 (7x - 17). So the tangent meets the curve again where x = (17)/(7) . Find y , and turn the point into a relation between cubes. y = (17/7 + 9)/(4) = (80/7)/(4) = (20)/(7) . The point bigl((17)/(7), (20)/(7)bigr) lies on y^3 = x^3 + 9 , so (20^3)/(7^3) = (17^3)/(7^3) + 9 quadLongrightarrowquad 20^3 = 17^3 + 9 × 7^3. We want 9 × 7^3 to be a sum of two cubes. Remember where the 9 came from. 9 = a^3 + b^3 = 1^3 + 2^3 , so 9 × 7^3 = 7^3 + 14^3 . Therefore 20^3 = 17^3 + 14^3 + 7^3. Check: 8000 = 4913 + 2744 + 343 . ■ Looking back Tangency means a double root. That turned a cubic with no obvious roots into one we could factorise immediately. The new root is rational for free. Once two of the three roots are rational (here both -1 ), the third must be too, because the sum of the roots, (3)/(7) , is rational. This is the heart of the method. Geometry produced arithmetic. We never searched for cubes; a tangent line found them. What’s really going on The chord–tangent method Take a cubic curve, such as y^3 = x^3 + 9 or the more standard form y^2 = x^3 + Ax + B . If you know two points on it with rational coordinates, the line through them meets the curve in exactly one more point, and that point also has rational coordinates (by the argument in Looking back ). If you know only one point, use the tangent there instead. Either way, old rational points produce new ones. Remarkably, this “chord–tangent” construction can be made into a way of adding points on the curve, and the rational points then form a group , an algebraic structure you will study in your first year. Louis Mordell proved in 1922 that this group is generated by finitely many points: all the rational points, however many there are, can be built from a finite set using chords and tangents. His proof is a version of Fermat’s descent from Section 1.5 . Elliptic curves today Curves like these are called elliptic curves (not because they are ellipses, but because of a historical link with the arc length of an ellipse). They are everywhere in modern mathematics. Fermat’s Last Theorem. In the 1980s Gerhard Frey noticed that a solution of x^n + y^n = z^n would produce a very strange elliptic curve. Andrew Wiles proved in 1994 that such strange curves can’t exist, and so proved Fermat’s Last Theorem. The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture. How many generators does the group of rational points need? A conjecture made in the 1960s, using some of the earliest computer experiments in mathematics at Cambridge, predicts the answer in terms of a function built from counting points modulo primes. It is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems. Cryptography. On an elliptic curve over a finite number system, adding a point P to itself n times is quick, even when n has hundreds of digits (double P repeatedly, much as you would calculate a high power by repeated squaring). But given P and the result nP , finding n seems to be extremely hard: this is the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem . That asymmetry protects much of today’s online communication. Sums of like powers The smallest cube that is a sum of three positive cubes is 6^3 = 3^3 + 4^3 + 5^3 ; the tangent method found 20^3 = 7^3 + 14^3 + 17^3 , which is not a multiple of it, and repeating the method keeps producing new identities (although some involve negative numbers). How many k th powers does it take to make another k th power? Euler conjectured in 1769 that you need at least k k th powers to make another k th power. For fourth and fifth powers he was wrong: in 1966 Leon Lander and Thomas Parkin found 27^5 + 84^5 + 110^5 + 133^5 = 144^5 by computer search, and in 1988 Noam Elkies used elliptic curves to find counterexamples for fourth powers. The thinking skill Geometry solving arithmetic To find whole-number or rational solutions of an equation, think of it as a curve and look for lines through known points. The algebra behind it is simple: if a polynomial with rational coefficients has all but one of its roots rational, the last root is rational too. Translating between pictures and equations in this way is one of the most powerful habits a mathematician can have. Try this next Rational points on a circle. The line through (-1, 0) with gradient t meets the circle x^2 + y^2 = 1 again. Show that the other point is left((1 - t^2)/(1 + t^2), (2t)/(1 + t^2)right) , and use this to produce infinitely many Pythagorean triples. A chord that misses. The points (1, 2) and (2, 1) lie on x^3 + y^3 = 9 . Show that the line through them meets the curve in no other point. Where has the “third point” gone? (Look up the point at infinity .) Repeat the trick. Find the tangent to y^3 = x^3 + 9 at bigl((17)/(7), (20)/(7)bigr) and the third point where it meets the curve. (A computer algebra system helps; notice how quickly the numbers grow.) Taxicab numbers. 1729 = 1^3 + 12^3 = 9^3 + 10^3 . Find the third point where the line through (1, 12) and (9, 10) meets the curve x^3 + y^3 = 1729 , and deduce a new identity of the form p^3 = q^3 + r^3 + s^3 . Further reading Joseph Silverman & John Tate, Rational Points on Elliptic Curves (Springer). Written for undergraduates; Chapter 1 needs nothing beyond A-level. Avner Ash & Robert Gross, Elliptic Tales (Princeton University Press). A popular account leading up to the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture. Simon Singh, Fermat’s Last Theorem . How elliptic curves came to solve a 350-year-old problem.

title: Sums of Two Squares
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on A new number system with its own primes Four squares and beyond The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 2023, Question 7 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP II paper in OCR’s download of the 2023 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/707102-2023-past-papers.zip The hook Which whole numbers can be written as the sum of two squares? 5 = 1^2 + 2^2 and 13 = 2^2 + 3^2 can, but 3 , 7 and 21 can’t. Here is a strange fact: 65 = 5 × 13 can be written as a sum of two squares in two different ways, 1^2 + 8^2 and 4^2 + 7^2 . Why should multiplying two such numbers give another, and why in two ways? The answer comes from an unexpected direction. The question asks you to leave the whole numbers behind and work with complex numbers. In the complex numbers, sums of two squares become simple, and some baffling-looking arithmetic becomes almost mechanical. Before you start If z = a + ib with a and b integers, what is |z|^2 ? It is a^2 + b^2 , a sum of two squares. So “ N is a sum of two squares” means exactly “ N = |z|^2 for some complex number z with integer real and imaginary parts”. Complex numbers like this are called Gaussian integers . Hold on to that translation; the whole question depends on it. Working it through Stage 1 Moduli multiply Write out zw in terms of a , b , c , d . What do you need to show about |zw|^2 ?
