The question makes this precise, and in doing so introduces one of the central ideas of numerical analysis, the subject that underlies every calculator, every weather forecast and every engineering simulation. Before you start Compute a few terms of each sequence as fractions. x_n: quad 1,\; frac32,\; frac75,\; (17)/(12),\; (41)/(29),\; (99)/(70),\; ldots qquad y_n: quad 1,\; frac32,\; (17)/(12),\; (577)/(408),\; (665857)/(470832),\; ldots Do you notice anything about the two lists? (Look at which fractions appear in both.) Every y_n appears in the x list, but further and further along: y_2 = x_3 , y_3 = x_7 , and in general y_n = x_2^n - 1 . The second recipe is skipping ahead exponentially fast through the same sequence of approximations. Keep this in mind; we will explain it at the end. Working it through Stage 1 The first recipe stays at least 1 We can write x_n+1 = 1 + (1)/(x_n + 1) . If x_n ≥ 1 then x_n + 1 > 0 , so x_n+1 > 1 . Since x_0 = 1 , induction gives x_n ≥ 1 for all n . ■ Stage 2 The error in the first recipe The question measures the error by x_n^2 - 2 rather than x_n - sqrt2 . Write x_n+1^2 - 2 as a single fraction in terms of x_n . What do you notice about the numerator? x_n+1^2 - 2 = ((x_n + 2)^2 - 2(x_n + 1)^2)/((x_n + 1)^2) = (x_n^2 + 4x_n + 4 - 2x_n^2 - 4x_n - 2)/((x_n + 1)^2) = (2 - x_n^2)/((x_n + 1)^2). The numerator is exactly -(x_n^2 - 2) . So x_n+1^2 - 2 and x_n^2 - 2 have opposite signs (the approximations alternate either side of sqrt2 ), and since x_n ≥ 1 makes (x_n + 1)^2 ≥ 4 , bigl|x_n+1^2 - 2bigr| = (|x_n^2 - 2|)/((x_n + 1)^2) ≤ frac14bigl|x_n^2 - 2bigr|. qed Stage 3 Ten steps Applying this ten times, |x_10^2 - 2| ≤ 4^-10|x_0^2 - 2| = 4^-10 = (1)/(1048576) < 10^-6 . For the sign: x_0^2 - 2 = -1 < 0 , and the sign alternates, so x_n^2 - 2 < 0 for every even n . So x_10^2 < 2 , and together these give 2 - 10^-6 ≤ x_10^2 ≤ 2 . ■ The error in x_n^2 is multiplied by at most frac14 at each step. That is called linear convergence : a fixed number of extra correct digits per step (here at least log_10 4 approx 0.6 ; in fact closer to 0.77 ). Stage 4 The error in the second recipe Write y_n+1 - sqrt2 as a single fraction. The numerator should remind you of a perfect square. y_n+1 - sqrt2 = (y_n^2 + 2 - 2sqrt2\, y_n)/(2y_n) = (bigl(y_n - sqrt2bigr)^2)/(2y_n). qed If y_n > 0 , the right-hand side is non-negative, so y_n+1 ≥ sqrt2 > 1 . Since y_0 = 1 , induction gives y_n ≥ 1 for all n . ■ (In fact y_n ≥ sqrt2 for all n ≥ 1 : after the first step, the second recipe always approaches sqrt2 from above.) Stage 5 Squaring the error Write e_n = y_n - sqrt2 , so e_n ≥ 0 for n ≥ 1 , and e_n+1 = (e_n^2)/(2y_n) ≤ (e_n^2)/(2) because y_n ≥ 1 . Prove by induction that e_n ≤ 2r^2^n for n ≥ 1 , where r = (sqrt2 - 1)/(2) . Check the base case carefully. Base case: e_1 = ((1 - sqrt2)^2)/(2 · 1) = ((sqrt2 - 1)^2)/(2) , while 2r^2 = 2 · ((sqrt2 - 1)^2)/(4) = ((sqrt2 - 1)^2)/(2) . They are equal, so the base case holds (exactly). Inductive step: if e_n ≤ 2r^2^n then e_n+1 ≤ (e_n^2)/(2) ≤ frac4r^2^n+12 = 2r^2^n+1. qed Stage 6 Six hundred digits Since sqrt2 - 1 < frac12 , we have r < frac14 , so 0 ≤ y_10 - sqrt2 ≤ 2 left(frac14right)^2^10 = 2 · 2^-2048 = 2^-2047. Now 2^10 = 1024 > 10^3 , so 2^-2047 < 2^-2040 = (2^10)^-204 < 10^-612 , which is certainly less than 10^-600 . ■ Looking back Find the error recurrence. Both parts worked by writing the new error as an exact function of the old error. Everything else followed. Linear versus quadratic. “New error ≤ constant × old error” gives a fixed number of extra digits per step. “New error ≤ constant × (old error) ^2 ” doubles the number of correct digits per step (Figure 2.7.1). Squared quantities control signs. In part (ii) the error after one step is a square divided by something positive, so it can never be negative: the iteration approaches from above. What’s really going on Newton’s method The second recipe is Newton’s method applied to f(y) = y^2 - 2 . Newton’s method finds a root of f by repeatedly replacing a guess y by the point where the tangent at y crosses the axis: y_new = y - (f(y))/(f'(y)) = y - (y^2 - 2)/(2y) = (y^2 + 2)/(2y). Near a simple root α , a Taylor expansion shows that the new error is approximately (f''(α))/(2f'(α)) × (old error)^2 , which is why Newton’s method converges quadratically. This particular case, “average y and 2/y ”, was known to the Babylonians; a clay tablet from around 1700 BC, now called YBC 7289, gives sqrt2 in base 60 with an error of less than one part in a million. Fixed points and their speed Both recipes have the form u_n+1 = g(u_n) with g(sqrt2) = sqrt2 , so sqrt2 is a fixed point , as in the cobweb diagram of Section 2.2 . Near a fixed point α , the error is multiplied by about g'(α) at each step. For the first recipe, g(x) = (x+2)/(x+1) and g'(sqrt2) = -(1)/((sqrt2+1)^2) = -(3 - 2sqrt2) approx -0.17 : the minus sign explains the alternating signs and 0.17 explains the 0.77 digits per step ( log_10(1/0.17) approx 0.77 ). For Newton’s method g'(α) = 0 , so the linear term vanishes and the error is controlled by the next term, the square. Designing iterations with g'(α) = 0 is the art of fast numerical methods. Why the same fractions appear The fractions x_n = p_n/q_n satisfy p_n+1 = p_n + 2q_n and q_n+1 = p_n + q_n , and p_n^2 - 2q_n^2 = 1 , alternating. These are the solutions of Pell’s equation p^2 - 2q^2 = 1 , and they are the convergents of the continued fraction sqrt2 = [1; 2, 2, 2, ldots] . They come from powers of 1 + sqrt2 : p_n + q_nsqrt2 = (1 + sqrt2)^n+1 . Newton’s step squares p + qsqrt2 (try it: (p + qsqrt2)^2 = p^2 + 2q^2 + 2pqsqrt2 , and (p^2 + 2q^2)/(2pq) is exactly Newton’s formula applied to p/q ). Squaring doubles the exponent, which is why y_n = x_2^n - 1 . The same pattern of “squaring” drives the iteration in Section 2.8 . The thinking skill Analyse the error, not the answer To understand how an approximation behaves, write down how the error at one step depends on the error at the step before. This is the starting point of numerical analysis. The answer itself ( sqrt2 ) is the same for both recipes; what differs, and what matters in practice, is how the error evolves. Try this next Pell’s equation. Show that if y_n = p/q in lowest terms with p^2 - 2q^2 = 1 , then y_n+1 = (p^2 + 2q^2)/(2pq) also satisfies this equation. Check that 577^2 - 2 × 408^2 = 1 . Cube roots. Write down Newton’s method for f(y) = y^3 - 2 , and show that the new error is ((y_n - α)^2 (2y_n + α))/(3y_n^2) , where α = sqrt[3]2 . Deduce that if y_n > α then the new error is at most (1)/(α) times the square of the old error. ( Hint: use α^3 = 2 .) Division without dividing. Show that Newton’s method for f(y) = frac1y - a gives y_n+1 = y_n(2 - a y_n) , which needs no division. If e_n = 1 - a y_n , show that e_n+1 = e_n^2 . (Computer processors use iterations like this to divide.) When Newton fails. Apply Newton’s method to f(y) = y^1/3 , whose only root is 0 . Show that each step doubles the distance from the root, whatever you start with. Which hypothesis of the error formula fails? Further reading Endre Süli & David Mayers, An Introduction to Numerical Analysis (Cambridge University Press). The standard undergraduate text; Chapter 1 covers fixed-point iteration and Newton’s method. Nick Higham (ed.), The Princeton Companion to Applied Mathematics (Princeton University Press). Short articles on Newton’s method and numerical analysis, written by experts for a wide audience. David Fowler & Eleanor Robson, “ Square root approximations in Old Babylonian mathematics: YBC 7289 in context ” , Historia Mathematica 25 (1998).

title: Squaring and Subtracting Two
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Finding the largest primes The Mandelbrot set The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2021, Question 8 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP III paper in OCR’s download of the 2021 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/696588-2021-past-papers.zip The hook “Square it and subtract two” is about the simplest rule you could use to generate a sequence. Yet it divides the real line into two worlds. Start outside [-2, 2] and the numbers explode to infinity, faster than exponentially. Start inside and they stay trapped for ever, wandering in a way that is, in a precise sense, completely unpredictable: one of the simplest examples of chaos . The same rule, carried out with very large whole numbers, is the engine of the Lucas–Lehmer test, an efficient test for whether a Mersenne number 2^p - 1 is prime, which has found the current record prime and most of the other very largest known primes. This question explores the escaping side of the story and finds a hidden formula that makes the sequence completely solvable. Before you start Try some starting values. With a = 3 : 3, 7, 47, 2207, ldots With a = 1 : 1, -1, -1, -1, ldots With a = 0 : 0, -2, 2, 2, 2, ldots With a = 0.3 : 0.3, -1.91, 1.648, 0.716, -1.487, 0.211, ldots Why can a number in [-2, 2] never escape? What is the largest and smallest that x^2 - 2 can be when -2 ≤ x ≤ 2 ? If -2 ≤ x ≤ 2 then 0 ≤ x^2 ≤ 4 , so -2 ≤ x^2 - 2 ≤ 2 . The interval [-2, 2] is mapped into itself. That will be half of part (ii). Working it through Stage 1 Escaping Part (i) has a 4^n-1 in it, suggesting that the distance above 2 at least quadruples at each step. Write x_n = 2 + d . What is x_n+1 in terms of d ? x_n+1 = (2 + d)^2 - 2 = 2 + 4d + d^2 . So if d ≥ 0 , the new distance above 2 is 4d + d^2 ≥ 4d . Now induct. When n = 1 , x_1 = a = 2 + 4^0(a - 2) . If x_n ≥ 2 + 4^n-1(a - 2) , then d = x_n - 2 ≥ 4^n-1(a - 2) ≥ 0 , so x_n+1 - 2 ≥ 4d ≥ 4^n (a - 2). qed Stage 2 Escape if and only if |a| > 2 “If and only if” means two separate proofs. Which direction does part (i) almost give you, and what is missing? If |a| > 2 : when a > 2 , part (i) gives x_n ≥ 2 + 4^n-1(a - 2) → ∞ . When a < -2 , the first step fixes the sign: x_2 = a^2 - 2 > 4 - 2 = 2 , and the sequence from x_2 onwards is the same sequence started at x_2 > 2 , so it tends to infinity. Only if: if |a| ≤ 2 , then a [-2, 2] , and by the observation above every term stays in [-2, 2] . A bounded sequence cannot tend to infinity. ■ Stage 3 A hidden formula Part (iii) looks forbidding. Before attempting it, it is worth finding a formula for x_n . If a > 2 , there is a number t > 1 with a = t + dfrac1t . (Why?) What are x_2 and x_3 in terms of t ? The function t + 1/t increases from 2 to ∞ as t goes from 1 to ∞ , so every a > 2 can be written this way. Then x_2 = left(t + frac1tright)^2 - 2 = t^2 + (1)/(t^2), qquad x_3 = left(t^2 + frac1t^2right)^2 - 2 = t^4 + frac1t^4, and by induction x_n = t^2^n-1 + t^-2^n-1. Squaring and subtracting 2 simply doubles the exponent. Now the question becomes manageable. Stage 4 The product telescopes What is left(t - frac1tright)left(t + frac1tright) ? What happens if you multiply the result by t^2 + frac1t^2 ? left(t - frac1tright)left(t + frac1tright) = t^2 - frac1t^2 , and then left(t^2 - frac1t^2right)left(t^2 + frac1t^2right) = t^4 - frac1t^4 , and so on: each factor x_k doubles the exponent in a difference of two powers. So left(t - frac1tright) x_1 x_2 cdots x_n = t^2^n - t^-2^n. Compute x_n+1^2 - 4 in terms of t , and compare with the product. x_n+1^2 - 4 = left(t^2^n + t^-2^nright)^2 - 4 = left(t^2^n - t^-2^nright)^2. Since t > 1 , t^2^n - t^-2^n > 0 , so sqrtx_n+1^2 - 4 = t^2^n - t^-2^n = left(t - frac1tright) x_1 x_2 cdots x_n . Therefore fracsqrtx_n+1^2 - 4x_n+1 = fracleft(t - frac1tright) x_1 cdots x_nx_n+1, which is y_n for every n exactly when A = t - frac1t . Finally, left(t - frac1tright)^2 = left(t + frac1tright)^2 - 4 = a^2 - 4 , so the condition is A = sqrta^2 - 4 , that is, a = sqrtA^2 + 4. (This is greater than 2 , as required, because A > 0 .) ■ Stage 5 Does y_n converge? With this value of a , y_n = fracsqrtx_n+1^2 - 4x_n+1 = sqrt1 - frac4x_n+1^2. Since x_n+1 → ∞ by part (ii), frac4x_n+1^2 → 0 and y_n → 1 . The sequence converges, to 1 . ■ So the infinite product x_1 x_2 x_3 cdots grows at exactly the same rate as x_n+1/A : we have found the precise growth rate of a product of rapidly growing terms. Looking back An invariant region. [-2, 2] is mapped into itself, and that one fact settles half of part (ii). A substitution that linearises. Writing a = t + 1/t turned “square and subtract 2 ” into “double the exponent”. Messy nonlinear behaviour became simple. Telescoping again. As with the products in Section 2.5 , a product of many factors collapsed because each factor fitted with the next. What’s really going on Order and chaos What happens inside [-2, 2] ? There, a = t + 1/t fails (it needs |a| ≥ 2 ), but the trigonometric version works: write a = 2cosθ . Then x_2 = 4cos^2θ - 2 = 2cos 2θ , and in general x_n = 2cosbigl(2^n-1θbigr). So inside the interval the map simply doubles an angle . That sounds harmless, but doubling an angle is chaotic. Write θ/π in binary: doubling shifts the binary point one place to the right, throwing away the leading digit. After 50 steps, x_n depends on the 51 st binary digit of θ/π , so an error in the starting value of 10^-15 (the precision of a typical computer) makes the answer after 50 steps completely unreliable. This sensitive dependence on initial conditions is the hallmark of chaos, illustrated in Figure 2.8.1. The map x mapsto x^2 - 2 is equivalent, by a change of variable, to the famous logistic map x mapsto 4x(1 - x) , which we meet again in Section 8.7 . Finding the largest primes A Mersenne number is M_p = 2^p - 1 . In 1876 Édouard Lucas found, and in 1930 Derrick Lehmer completed, a remarkable test for whether M_p is prime (for p an odd prime): start with s_0 = 4 and repeatedly square and subtract 2 , reducing modulo M_p each time. Then M_p is prime iff s_p-2 equiv 0 pmodM_p. For M_7 = 127 : s = 4, 14, 194 equiv 67, 67^2 - 2 equiv 42, 42^2 - 2 equiv 111, 111^2 - 2 equiv 0 , so 127 is prime. The connection with this question is the substitution: 4 = t + 1/t with t = 2 + sqrt3 , so s_k = (2+sqrt3)^2^k + (2-sqrt3)^2^k , and the proof of the test uses arithmetic with numbers of the form a + bsqrt3 , rather like the Gaussian integers of Section 1.6 . Because each step needs only one squaring, the test is extremely fast, which is why most of the very largest known primes, including the current record holder, are Mersenne primes (not all of them are: other special forms, such as a^2^n + 1 , have their own fast tests). As of the time of writing the record is 2^136279841 - 1 , a number with more than 41 million digits, found in 2024. The Mandelbrot set Replace -2 by any constant c and allow complex numbers: z mapsto z^2 + c . The set of c for which the orbit of 0 stays bounded is the Mandelbrot set . Our map has c = -2 , the leftmost point of the Mandelbrot set, and the set of starting values whose orbits stay bounded (its Julia set ) is exactly the interval [-2, 2] that we found in part (ii). For almost every other c , that set is a fractal. The thinking skill Change variables to make a map simple If an iteration looks complicated, look for a substitution that turns it into something simple, like doubling or adding a constant. Here x = t + 1/t and x = 2cosθ turned x mapsto x^2 - 2 into doubling. In the theory of dynamical systems this is called a conjugacy , and finding one is often the key to understanding a system completely. Try this next Inside the interval. Prove that if a = 2cosθ then x_n = 2cos(2^n-1θ) . Find all values of a for which x_3 = a but x_2 ≠ a . ( Hint: you want 4θ equiv θ , modulo 2π .) Lucas–Lehmer by hand. Use the test to show that M_5 = 31 is prime and that M_11 = 2047 is not. (For M_11 you will need nine steps; a calculator helps. Check your conclusion by factorising 2047 .) An explicit example. Take A = (3)/(2) . Find a and t , and check the formula y_1 = sqrtx_2^2 - 4/x_2 numerically. A sum that telescopes. harder With a = t + 1/t and t > 1 , show that (1)/(x_1 x_2 cdots x_n) = fract - t^-1t^2^n - t^-2^n. Using the identity (1)/(z - 1) - (1)/(z^2 - 1) = (z)/(z^2 - 1) with z = t^2^n , deduce that (1)/(x_1) + (1)/(x_1 x_2) + (1)/(x_1 x_2 x_3) + cdots = frac1t. Check this numerically when a = 3 . Further reading Ian Stewart, Does God Play Dice? (Penguin). The classic popular account of chaos, including the logistic map. Steven Strogatz, Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos (CRC Press). The standard undergraduate introduction; Chapter 10 is about one-dimensional maps like this one. Marcus du Sautoy, The Music of the Primes (Fourth Estate). Includes the story of the hunt for Mersenne primes.

title: Viète's Product
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Infinite products How quickly? The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2022, Question 4 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP III paper in OCR’s download of the 2022 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/696587-2022-past-papers.zip The hook The last line of this question is one of the most beautiful formulas in mathematics, and one of the oldest of its kind. It was published in 1593 by the French lawyer and mathematician François Viète, and it was the first time anyone had written π exactly as the result of an infinite process. Before Viète, π could only be approximated; after him, it could be defined by a formula that, carried on for ever, gives every digit. The formula looks mysterious: where could nested square roots of 2 come from? The question reveals that it comes from repeatedly using the double-angle formula, and it gets a second, less famous formula, for 2 , from the same machinery along the way. Before you start What is the double-angle formula for sinh ? (If you are not sure, write sinh 2y and sinh y cosh y in terms of exponentials and compare.) sinh 2y = 2sinh ycosh y , exactly like sin 2y = 2sin ycos y . That one identity, used over and over, drives the whole question. The question works with hyperbolic functions until the last part, where we will switch to ordinary trigonometry. Working it through Stage 1 Halving repeatedly The case n = 1 is just the double-angle formula with y = x/2 : sinh x = 2coshleft((x)/(2)right)sinhleft((x)/(2)right). Suppose the formula holds for n . The last factor is sinh(x/2^n) . How can you rewrite it to get the formula for n + 1 ? Apply the double-angle formula to it: sinh(x/2^n) = 2cosh(x/2^n+1)sinh(x/2^n+1) . Substituting, sinh x = 2^n+1coshleft((x)/(2)right)cdotscoshleft((x)/(2^n)right)coshleft(fracx2^n+1right)sinhleft(fracx2^n+1right), which is the formula for n + 1 . By induction it holds for all n . ■ For the deduction, divide both sides by x , and then multiply both sides by (x/2^n)/(sinh(x/2^n)) . On the right, 2^n sinh(x/2^n) · (x/2^n)/(x\,sinh(x/2^n)) = 1 , leaving just the product of cosh terms. ■ Stage 2 The limit From the series, for y ≠ 0 , (sinh y)/(y) = 1 + (y^2)/(3!) + (y^4)/(5!) + cdots, which tends to 1 as y → 0 , so its reciprocal y/sinh y also tends to 1 . (If you want more care: every factorial in the tail (y^2)/(3!) + (y^4)/(5!) + cdots is at least 6 , so for 0 < |y| < 1 the tail is at most (1)/(6)bigl(y^2 + y^4 + cdotsbigr) = (y^2)/(6(1-y^2)) , which tends to 0 .) Now let n → ∞ in part (i), with x fixed. Then y = x/2^n → 0 , so the left-hand side tends to (sinh x)/(x) × 1 . The right-hand side is the partial product, which therefore tends to (sinh x)/(x) . That is what the infinite product means. ■ Stage 3 A formula for 2 With x = 2 , e^x/2 = sqrt2 , so coshleft((x)/(2)right) = frac2^1/2 + 2^-1/22 = (2 + 1)/(2sqrt2) = (3)/(2sqrt2). Similarly e^x/4 = 2^1/4 , so cosh(x/4) = dfrac2^1/4 + 2^-1/42 , and multiplying top and bottom by 2^1/4 gives dfrac2^1/2 + 12 × 2^1/4 . ■ What is the general pattern for cosh(x/2^k) ? What happens when you multiply all the denominators 2 × 2^1/2^k together? The same calculation gives, for every k ≥ 1 , coshleft((x)/(2^k)right) = frac1 + 2^1/2^k-12 × 2^-1/2^k. (For k = 1 this is (1 + 2)/(2) × 2^-1/2 = (3)/(2sqrt2) , as before.) Multiplying over k = 1, 2, 3, ldots , the powers of 2 combine to 2^-(1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + cdots) = 2^-1 , and the first fraction is (1+2)/(2) = frac32 . So the infinite product is frac32 × frac12 × frac1 + 2^1/22 × frac1 + 2^1/42 × frac1 + 2^1/82 cdots. On the other side, sinh( 2) = (2 - frac12)/(2) = frac34 , so (sinh x)/(x) = (3)/(4 2) . The factor frac34 cancels from both sides, leaving (1)/( 2) = frac1 + 2^1/22 × frac1 + 2^1/42 × frac1 + 2^1/82 cdots. qed Stage 4 Viète’s formula Part (iv) has π in it, so it must come from ordinary trigonometry, not hyperbolic functions. Does everything in parts (i) and (ii) still work with sin and cos in place of sinh and cosh ? It does. The induction used only the double-angle formula, and sin 2y = 2sin ycos y . The limit used only (sin y)/(y) → 1 as y → 0 , which follows from sin y = y - (y^3)/(3!) + cdots in the same way. So for x ≠ 0 (and x not a multiple of π , so that no factor is zero along the way), (sin x)/(x) = cosleft((x)/(2)right)cosleft((x)/(4)right)cosleft((x)/(8)right)cdots. Choose x so that the left-hand side is 2/π , and work out the first few factors. The half-angle formula cos(θ)/(2) = sqrt(1 + cosθ)/(2) (for 0 ≤ θ ≤ π ) will be useful. Take x = (π)/(2) . Then (sin x)/(x) = (1)/(π/2) = (2)/(π) , and the factors are cosfracπ4, cosfracπ8, cos(π)/(16), ldots . The first is cosfracπ4 = (sqrt2)/(2) . If a factor is cosθ = (c)/(2) , the half-angle formula makes the next one cos(θ)/(2) = sqrt(1 + c/2)/(2) = fracsqrt2 + c2. So the numerators go sqrt2 , sqrt2 + sqrt2 , sqrt2 + sqrt2 + sqrt2 , …, each obtained by adding 2 to the previous one and taking the square root. That is Viète’s formula. ■ Looking back Telescoping a product. The identity in part (i) is a product that collapses, just as some sums telescope. Finite identity first, limit second. As in Section 2.4 , every step was exact for finite n , and the only limit needed was the very simple (sin y)/(y) → 1 . Hyperbolic and circular functions are twins. The same proof worked for both, because both satisfy the same double-angle formula and the same small-angle limit. This is no coincidence: cosh(ix) = cos x , as you will see in Section 5.7 . What’s really going on Archimedes’ polygons Viète’s formula has a geometric meaning that goes back to Archimedes. A regular polygon with 2^n sides inscribed in a circle of radius 1 has area A_n = 2^n-1sin(2π)/(2^n) . Doubling the number of sides multiplies the area by fracA_n+1A_n = frac2^n sin(π/2^n)2^n-1· 2sin(π/2^n)cos(π/2^n) = (1)/(cos(π/2^n)). Starting from the square ( A_2 = 2 ) and doubling for ever, the area tends to the area of the circle, π . So π = 2 div bigl(cosfracπ4 cosfracπ8 cos(π)/(16)cdotsbigr) , which is Viète’s formula. Each factor in the product is the ratio of the areas of two successive polygons in Figure 2.5.1. Infinite products Viète’s product was the first infinite product in mathematics. Others followed: John Wallis found (π)/(2) = (2)/(1)·(2)/(3)·(4)/(3)·(4)/(5)·(6)/(5)·(6)/(7)cdots in 1655, and Euler’s product for (sin x)/(x) appeared in Section 2.4 . At university you will learn when an infinite product converges. Roughly, prod(1 + a_n) with small positive a_n behaves like sum a_n , because (1 + a_n) approx a_n . Here 1 - cos(π/2^n) approx frac12(π/2^n)^2 , which shrinks by a factor of 4 each time, so the product converges quickly. How quickly? After n factors the partial product equals dfrac12^nsin(π/2^n+1) exactly, and its error is about fracπ^26 · 4^n+1 times frac2π . Each new factor makes the answer about 4 times more accurate, gaining about 0.6 of a decimal digit. Ten factors give 2/π correct to six decimal places. That is good, but nothing like as fast as the methods of Section 2.6 , which double the number of correct digits at each step. The thinking skill Iterating an identity An identity that relates f(x) to f(x/2) can be applied again and again; the result, after a limit, is often an infinite sum or product. Look for the “remainder” term after n steps (here 2^nsinh(x/2^n) ) and find its limit separately. This pattern appears all over analysis, from infinite products to the construction of fractals. Try this next The 1990 version. Try STEP I 1990, Question 8 . It reaches Viète’s product by a different route from this section, using nothing beyond the double-angle formula for sin . Which approach do you find more natural? Another angle. Use x = (π)/(3) in the product for (sin x)/(x) to write (3sqrt3)/(2π) as an infinite product, and simplify the first two factors. How many factors? Use a calculator to find how many factors of Viète’s product are needed to give π correct to 4 decimal places. Explain why each extra factor gains about 0.6 of a digit. A formula for 3 . Repeat part (iii) with x = 3 to write (1)/( 3) as an infinite product. How many factors are needed to give (1)/( 3) to two decimal places? Why does this product converge more slowly than Viète’s? Further reading Petr Beckmann, A History of π (St Martin’s Press). Archimedes, Viète, Wallis and the rest, told with gusto. Jonathan Borwein & Peter Borwein, Pi and the AGM (Wiley). The serious mathematics of computing π , including the method of Section 2.6 . Chapter 1 is accessible with this chapter behind you. Eli Maor, Trigonometric Delights (Princeton University Press). Contains a chapter on Viète and his product.

title: What We Have Learned
headings: 1. What does it mean for an infinite process to have an answer? 2. How can we prove convergence without knowing the limit? 3. How fast? 4. A toolkit for analysis Where next
text: We began with Zeno, and with three questions about infinite processes: what it means for them to have an answer, how to prove that they do, and how fast they get there. Nine STEP questions later, here is how far we have come. 1. What does it mean for an infinite process to have an answer? In Section 2.1 we learned the language. A statement about the long-run behaviour of a sequence has the shape “there exists a point m such that for all n ≥ m …”. Proving it means producing m ; disproving it means showing that every proposed m fails. The definition of a limit adds one more quantifier at the front, “for every tolerance ε > 0 ”, and with that, Zeno’s paradox dissolves: frac12 + frac14 + cdots + (1)/(2^n) is within any tolerance you like of 1 from some point on, and that is all that “the sum is 1 ” means. The language also guards against nonsense. The quick “let x equal the infinite expression” argument gave the right answer for the golden ratio in Section 2.2 , but only because we could separately prove that the limit existed. The same argument applied to 1 - 1 + 1 - cdots gives an answer that means nothing. 2. How can we prove convergence without knowing the limit? Most of the chapter’s sections used one of a handful of tools. Monotone and bounded. An increasing sequence that is bounded above must converge ( Section 2.2 , Section 2.6 ). The same applies to partial sums of positive terms ( Section 2.3 ). At university you will see that this is really a statement about the real numbers themselves: it is the property of completeness . Comparison. A series of positive terms converges if it is smaller than one that converges, and diverges if it is bigger than one that diverges. Grouping terms into blocks made the comparison easy, and showed that the harmonic series diverges while Kempner’s thinned-out version converges ( Section 2.3 ). The squeeze. Trap the quantity between two simpler ones with the same limit. This is how we proved sum 1/m^2 = π^2/6 ( Section 2.4 ) and evaluated the AGM integral rigorously ( Section 2.6 ). Exact formulas for finite stages. In Section 2.5 and Section 2.8 we found exact expressions after n steps, by telescoping, and let n → ∞ only at the very end. Once a limit is known to exist, it can often be found by “letting n → ∞ ” in a recurrence, as with L = (2L+1)/(L+1) for the golden ratio. But the order matters: existence first, value second. 3. How fast? Here the chapter held some surprises. Viète’s product ( Section 2.5 ) gains about 0.6 of a decimal digit per factor. The simple recipe for sqrt2 in Section 2.7 gains about 0.8 digits per step. Newton’s method and the AGM ( Section 2.6 ) double the number of correct digits at each step: ten steps of Newton’s method give more than 700 digits of sqrt2 . The difference is the shape of the error recurrence: “new error approx constant × old error” (linear) against “new error approx constant × (old error) ^2 ” (quadratic). And in Section 2.8 we saw the opposite extreme: starting just above 2 , the map x mapsto x^2 - 2 pushes numbers away faster than exponentially, while inside [-2,2] it amplifies tiny errors until all predictability is lost. Speed also matters for theory. The integrals in Section 2.9 produce fractions approaching e so quickly that they prove e is irrational: no fraction p/q could be approached that fast by other fractions. 4. A toolkit for analysis Method Where you used it Producing and negating quantifiers “Eventually” (2.1) Monotone bounded sequences Golden ratio (2.2); AGM (2.6) Comparison and condensation Harmonic and Kempner series (2.3) Squeezing π^2/6 (2.4); the AGM integral (2.6) Symmetric functions of roots Sum of cot^2 values (2.4) Telescoping sums and products Viète (2.5); x^2 - 2 (2.8) Invariants The AGM integral (2.6) Error recurrences Linear and quadratic convergence (2.7) Changing variables to simplify a map a = t + 1/t , a = 2cosθ (2.8) Small but non-zero integer combinations Approximating e (2.9) Notice how many of these tools came with a “theorem you may use” attached. STEP often hands you the monotone convergence theorem, or tells you to assume that limits exist. At university you will prove those theorems from the axioms of the real numbers, and you will be expected to notice for yourself when an argument quietly assumes a limit exists. When you read a solution, it is a very good habit to ask: where exactly was a limit taken, and was it justified? Where next The ideas of this chapter run through the rest of the book. Fixed points and cobweb diagrams return in Section 8.7 , where a chaotic map turns out to have an exact solution. The harmonic numbers 1 + frac12 + cdots + frac1n appear in probability in Section 9.11 and in mechanics in Section 11.12 . Another appearance of π in a limit, from probability, is in Section 12.23 . The careful attitude to limits is the theme of Chapter 3, which opens with Section 3.1 : arguments that look right but aren’t. If you want to go further before university Lara Alcock, How to Think About Analysis : what first-year analysis is like, and how to cope with it. David Bressoud, A Radical Approach to Real Analysis : analysis taught through its history, starting from the puzzles that forced mathematicians to be careful. Tom Körner, Calculus for the Ambitious (Cambridge University Press): written by a Cambridge analyst for exactly the readers of this book. Julian Havil, Gamma and William Dunham, Euler: The Master of Us All : the stories behind many of the series in this chapter. Zeno thought infinity made motion impossible. Mathematicians took two thousand years to answer him, and the answer turned out to be one of the most powerful ideas ever found: a way of making precise statements about processes that never end. You now know the first few words of that language. Analysis is where you will learn to speak it fluently.

title: Functions from Their Addition Laws
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Cauchy’s functional equation Homomorphisms The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2019, Question 2 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP III paper in OCR’s download of the 2019 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/696590-2019-past-papers.zip The hook How do you know what e^x is? At school it is introduced through compound interest, or as the function that is its own derivative, or as lim (1 + x/n)^n . This question offers another answer: e^kx is the only differentiable function that turns addition into multiplication, f(x + y) = f(x)f(y) . The rule alone, plus one number f'(0) , pins the function down completely. The second part does the same for a stranger rule, g(x + y) = (g(x) + g(y))/(1 + g(x)g(y)) . If that formula looks familiar, it should: it is Einstein’s rule for adding velocities in special relativity, with the speed of light set to 1 . The function it forces is tanh , and that explains why nothing can be accelerated past the speed of light. Before you start An equation like f(x + y) = f(x)f(y) , where the unknown is a function, is called a functional equation . The equation holds for all x and y . What is the most useful thing to try first? Special values. Setting y = 0 (or x = y , or y = -x ) often gives a lot of information cheaply. That is how both parts start. Working it through Stage 1 The value at zero Put x = y = 0 : f(0) = f(0)^2 , so f(0) = 0 or 1 . What goes wrong if f(0) = 0 ? If f(0) = 0 , then putting y = 0 gives f(x) = f(x)f(0) = 0 for every x . Then f is identically zero and f'(0) = 0 , contradicting f'(0) = k ≠ 0 . So f(0) = 1 . ■ Stage 2 The derivative everywhere from the derivative at zero In (*) , write f(x + h) = f(x)f(h) . What can you take outside the limit? beginaligned f'(x) &= lim_h → 0 (f(x)f(h) - f(x))/(h) = f(x)lim_h → 0(f(h) - 1)/(h) \\ &= f(x)lim_h → 0(f(0 + h) - f(0))/(h) = f(x)\,f'(0) = k\,f(x). qed endaligned The functional equation lets the behaviour near 0 be transported to every other point. Stage 3 Solving f' = kf Consider u(x) = f(x)e^-kx . Then u'(x) = bigl(f'(x) - kf(x)bigr)e^-kx = 0 , so u is constant, and u(0) = f(0) = 1 . Therefore f(x) = e^kx. qed (Separating the variables, int (df)/(f) = int k\,dx , gives the same answer, but needs f(x) ≠ 0 ; the trick with u avoids that worry.) Stage 4 The second rule Put y = 0 in the rule for g . What does that tell you about g(0) ? Where does |g(x)| < 1 come in? With y = 0 : g(x)bigl(1 + g(x)g(0)bigr) = g(x) + g(0) , which simplifies to g(0)bigl(g(x)^2 - 1bigr) = 0 . Since |g(x)| < 1 , the bracket is never zero, so g(0) = 0 . Now compute g(x + h) - g(x) using the rule, simplify, divide by h and let h → 0 . g(x + h) - g(x) = (g(x) + g(h) - g(x) - g(x)^2g(h))/(1 + g(x)g(h)) = (g(h)bigl(1 - g(x)^2bigr))/(1 + g(x)g(h)). Divide by h . As h → 0 , (g(h))/(h) = (g(h) - g(0))/(h) → g'(0) = k , and g(h) → g(0) = 0 (a differentiable function is continuous), so the denominator tends to 1 . Therefore g'(x) = kbigl(1 - g(x)^2bigr). qed Stage 5 Solving it Separate the variables. Which function has derivative (1)/(1 - g^2) for |g| < 1 ? Since |g| < 1 , we can divide: (g')/(1 - g^2) = k . The function artanh g = frac12(1 + g)/(1 - g) has derivative (1)/(1 - g^2) , so (d)/(dx)artanhg(x) = k and artanhg(x) = kx + C . From g(0) = 0 , C = 0 , so g(x) = tanh kx. qed Check: the addition formula tanh(A + B) = (tanh A + tanh B)/(1 + tanh Atanh B) is exactly the given rule. Looking back Special values first. Putting y = 0 found f(0) and g(0) . From one point to everywhere. The addition law moved the derivative at 0 to every x , turning a functional equation into a differential equation. Uniqueness. The argument does not just check that e^kx and tanh kx work; it shows they are the only possibilities. That is what makes a functional equation a definition. What’s really going on Velocities in relativity In everyday life, if a train moves at speed u and you walk forwards inside it at speed v , your speed relative to the ground is u + v . Einstein showed in 1905 that this is only an approximation. The correct rule, with c the speed of light, is u oplus v = (u + v)/(1 + uv/c^2). Measuring speeds as fractions of c , this is exactly the rule for g . Our result says that if we write each velocity as v = tanhφ , then velocities combine by adding the φ s. The quantity φ = artanh v is called the rapidity . Each boost from a rocket engine adds a fixed amount of rapidity, but since tanhφ < 1 for every φ , the velocity creeps closer and closer to the speed of light without ever reaching it (Figure 3.8.1). Combining 0.9c with 0.9c gives not 1.8c but (1.8)/(1.81)c approx 0.9945c . Cauchy’s functional equation The simplest functional equation is f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y) , studied by Cauchy in 1821. If f is differentiable, the method of this question shows f(x) = kx . In fact continuity is enough. But without any regularity assumption at all, there are other, utterly wild solutions, whose graphs are scattered densely over the whole plane. Georg Hamel constructed them in 1905; the construction needs the axiom of choice , and it is impossible to write any of them down explicitly. This is one reason the question insists that f is differentiable: the hypothesis is not a formality. Homomorphisms f(x + y) = f(x)f(y) says that f turns the addition of real numbers into the multiplication of positive real numbers, respecting the structure of both. In the language of first-year algebra, f is a group homomorphism from (mathbbR, +) to (mathbbR_>0, ×) , and the logarithm is its inverse. Many of the most important functions in mathematics are characterised in this way, by the structure they preserve. In Section 7.6 we meet the geometric meaning of tanh : it measures “hyperbolic angle”, and its addition law comes from composing hyperbolic rotations. The thinking skill Define a function by its properties Instead of a formula, describe a function by a rule it obeys, and prove that only one function obeys it. This is how mathematicians often think about exp , sin , cos and many other functions: not as formulas, but as the unique solutions of functional or differential equations. It explains why they matter, not just how to calculate them. Try this next A tangent rule. Suppose g is differentiable, g'(0) = k ≠ 0 , and g(x + y) = (g(x) + g(y))/(1 - g(x)g(y)) whenever both sides are defined. Show that g'(x) = kbigl(1 + g(x)^2bigr) and deduce that g(x) = tan kx near x = 0 . Cauchy’s equation. If f is differentiable and f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y) for all x , y , show that f(x) = kx . Without derivatives. harder Suppose only that f(x + y) = f(x)f(y) and f(1) = a > 0 . Show that f(n) = a^n for positive integers n , then that f(1/n) = a^1/n , and then that f(q) = a^q for every positive rational q . (Why is continuity needed to go further?) Rocket science. A rocket can increase its speed by 0.5c relative to its current frame each time it fires. Starting from rest, what is its speed (relative to the start) after 2 , 3 and 4 firings? Use rapidities. Further reading Christopher Small, Functional Equations and How to Solve Them (Springer). An accessible introduction aimed at problem-solvers. Edwin Taylor & John Wheeler, Spacetime Physics (W. H. Freeman). The classic introduction to special relativity, using rapidity throughout. Tom Körner, Calculus for the Ambitious (Cambridge University Press). Defines the exponential and trigonometric functions from their properties, exactly in the spirit of this section.

title: AM–GM, Backwards
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Many proofs of one inequality Optimisation without calculus The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 1993, Question 8 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/93-s2-q8 The hook The arithmetic mean–geometric mean inequality (AM–GM) is perhaps the single most useful inequality in mathematics. It says that for positive numbers, the ordinary average is always at least the “multiplicative average”, with equality only when all the numbers are equal. It solves optimisation problems without calculus, it proves other inequalities, and it appears in every branch of analysis. This question proves it by a strange and beautiful induction, due to Augustin-Louis Cauchy in 1821. Instead of going from n to n + 1 , it leaps from 2 to 4 to 8 to 16 , covering only the powers of 2 , and then comes back down to fill in the numbers in between. It is a reminder that “induction” is a much more flexible idea than the textbook version suggests. Before you start The version of this paper in the online archive has a misprint: it reads “ b_1 = a_2 ”. It should of course be b_1 = a_1 ; the idea is that the b s are the a s, padded out with copies of their average. Why might it be easier to go from 2^m numbers to 2^m+1 numbers than from n to n + 1 ? Because 2^m+1 numbers split naturally into two groups of 2^m , and you can apply the inductive hypothesis to each half and then use the two-number case to combine the halves. Going from n to n + 1 gives you nothing so symmetric to work with. Working it through Stage 1 Two numbers left( (a_1 + a_2)/(2) right)^2 - a_1 a_2 = (a_1^2 + 2a_1a_2 + a_2^2 - 4a_1a_2)/(4) = ((a_1 - a_2)^2)/(4) ≥ 0. ■ Stage 2 Doubling The case m = 1 is Stage 1. Suppose (*) holds for 2^m numbers, and take 2^m+1 positive numbers. Split the 2^m+1 numbers into a first half and a second half, and let P and Q be the arithmetic means of the two halves. What does the inductive hypothesis say about each half? Applying (*) to each half, a_1 cdots a_2^m ≤ P^2^m qquadandqquad a_2^m + 1 cdots a_2^m+1 ≤ Q^2^m. Multiplying (everything is positive), the product of all 2^m+1 numbers is at most (PQ)^2^m . Now the two-number case gives PQ ≤ left( (P + Q)/(2) right)^2 , and (P + Q)/(2) is exactly the mean of all 2^m+1 numbers. So a_1 cdots a_2^m+1 ≤ (PQ)^2^m ≤ left( (P + Q)/(2) right)^2^m+1 = left( fraca_1 + cdots + a_2^m+12^m+1 right)^2^m+1, which is (*) for m + 1 . By induction, AM–GM holds whenever the number of terms is a power of 2 . ■ Stage 3 Filling the gaps Now take any n , and choose m with 2^m > n . We pad the list a_1, ldots, a_n with 2^m - n copies of its own average A . What is the average of the padded list b_1, ldots, b_2^m ? The sum is (a_1 + cdots + a_n) + (2^m - n)A = nA + (2^m - n)A = 2^m A , so the average is A itself. Adding copies of the average does not change the average. So (*) applied to the b s gives a_1 cdots a_n · A^2^m - n ≤ A^2^m. Finish the proof. Divide both sides by A^2^m - n (which is positive): a_1 cdots a_n ≤ A^n . Taking n th roots, (a_1 cdots a_n)^1/n ≤ A = (a_1 + cdots + a_n)/(n). qed Looking back Induction along a different path. Stage 2 is an induction on m , covering n = 2, 4, 8, ldots Stage 3 is a way of stepping down from any power of 2 to any smaller n (Figure 3.2.1). Padding with the average. The trick of extending a list without changing its average is worth remembering; it is a way of turning a problem about any n into a problem about a convenient n . When is there equality? Tracing back through the proof, equality needs equality in every use of the two-number case, which happens only when all the numbers are equal. What’s really going on Cauchy’s induction Cauchy published this proof in his Cours d’analyse (1821), the book that began the rigorous treatment of analysis we discussed in Chapter 2. The technique is now called forward–backward induction : prove a statement for an infinite sequence of cases (here the powers of 2 ), and then show that the case n implies the case n - 1 . Together, these reach every n . Our Stage 3 jumps straight down from 2^m to n , but you can also do it one step at a time: padding n - 1 numbers with one copy of their average shows that the case n implies the case n - 1 . Many proofs of one inequality AM–GM has dozens of proofs, and comparing them is a good way to see different styles of mathematics. By convexity. The logarithm is concave, so the average of the logarithms is at most the logarithm of the average. That is AM–GM after taking exponentials, and it is the subject of Section 3.3 . George Pólya’s proof. Use e^x - 1 ≥ x (the tangent line to e^x-1 at x = 1 lies below the curve). With A the mean, apply it to each a_i/A and multiply: prod (a_i)/(A) ≤ e^sum (a_i/A - 1) = e^0 = 1 . Pólya said this proof came to him in a dream. By smoothing. If two of the numbers are unequal, replace them both by their average. The arithmetic mean is unchanged and, by the two-number case, the product increases. Repeating pushes all the numbers towards the average. Optimisation without calculus AM–GM turns many optimisation problems into one-liners. Of all boxes with a given surface area, which has the largest volume? Of all rectangles with a given perimeter, which has the largest area? (A square, by the two-number case: xy ≤ bigl((x+y)/(2)bigr)^2 , with equality when x = y .) The equality condition tells you where the optimum is, and the inequality tells you it really is the optimum, not just a stationary point. Compare the warnings of Section 3.1 . The thinking skill Flexible induction Induction does not have to go 1, 2, 3, ldots You can induct along any path that reaches every case: by doubling, by strong induction, or forwards on a subsequence and then backwards to fill the gaps. When the obvious step from n to n+1 is hard, ask which step would be easy, and whether you can reach every case using it. Try this next One step back. Show directly that if AM–GM holds for n numbers, it holds for n - 1 numbers, by padding with one copy of the average. An increasing sequence. Apply AM–GM to the n + 1 numbers 1 + frac1n, ldots, 1 + frac1n, 1 (with n copies of 1 + frac1n ) to show that left(1 + frac1nright)^n < left(1 + (1)/(n+1)right)^n+1 . The best box. A closed rectangular box has surface area S . Use AM–GM on the areas of three different faces to show that its volume is at most (S/6)^3/2 , with equality for a cube. Harmonic mean. By applying AM–GM to the numbers 1/a_i , show that the harmonic mean (n)/(1/a_1 + cdots + 1/a_n) is at most the geometric mean. Further reading J. Michael Steele, The Cauchy–Schwarz Master Class (Cambridge University Press). A wonderful, problem-driven book on inequalities, starting from exactly this level. Chapter 2 is about AM–GM. Hardy, Littlewood & Pólya, Inequalities (Cambridge University Press). The classic reference, written by three of the great analysts of the twentieth century. Arthur Engel, Problem-Solving Strategies (Springer). Chapter 7 is a large collection of inequality problems from olympiads.

Try each exercise properly before looking. 3.1 Spot the Flaw As x runs from -1 to 1 it passes through 0 , where t = 1/x is undefined: the substitution is not continuous on the interval. Correctly, int_-1^1(dx)/((1 + x^2)^2) = frac12 + fracπ4 (use x = tanθ ), while int_-1^1(-t^2)/((1 + t^2)^2)\,dt = frac12 - fracπ4 . (a) True: both sides have logarithm a b . (c) False: a non-constant polynomial is unbounded, and a constant cannot be within 10^-6 of both 1 and -1 . (d) True: x^4 + x^-4 ≥ 2 by AM–GM, with equality at x = 1 .
