title: Areas That Prove Inequalities
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on The Legendre transform The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2011, Question 4 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/11-s3-q4 The hook Here is an inequality proved by a picture so simple that it fits on a postage stamp. Draw an increasing curve through the origin. The area under it, plus the area to its left, always covers a rectangle. From that one observation comes Young’s inequality , ab ≤ (a^p)/(p) + (b^q)/(q) , which in turn is the key to Hölder’s inequality and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, two of the most important tools in analysis. The picture also contains a deeper idea. It pairs a function with its inverse in a perfectly symmetric way, and that pairing, generalised, is the Legendre transform , which connects the two great formulations of classical mechanics and the two main descriptions of thermodynamics. Before you start int_0^a f(x)\,dx is the area between the curve and the x -axis. What area does int_0^b f^-1(y)\,dy represent on the same picture? The graph of x = f^-1(y) is the same curve as y = f(x) , viewed sideways. So int_0^b f^-1(y)\,dy is the area between the curve and the y -axis, from height 0 to height b . With that, part (i) is a matter of drawing. Working it through Stage 1 The picture Draw the rectangle with corners (0, 0) and (a, b) . Shade the region under the curve from 0 to a in one colour and the region to the left of the curve from 0 to b in another. Do the two regions cover the rectangle? When is there no overlap and no excess? The two regions together cover the whole rectangle [0, a] × [0, b] , and usually some area outside it as well (Figure 3.4.1). Every point (x, y) of the rectangle is either below the curve (so in the first region, since x ≤ a ) or to the left of it (so in the second, since y ≤ b ). The total shaded area is therefore at least the area of the rectangle, ab . That is (*) . The excess is the small curved region between the curve and the corner of the rectangle. It disappears exactly when the curve passes through the corner (a, b) , that is, when b = f(a). Stage 2 Young’s inequality With f(x) = x^p-1 , what is f^-1(y) ? Compute both integrals, and use frac1p + frac1q = 1 to tidy the second. Since p > 1 , f(x) = x^p-1 is continuous and increasing with f(0) = 0 , and f^-1(y) = y^1/(p-1) . Then int_0^a x^p-1\,dx = (a^p)/(p), qquad int_0^b y^1/(p-1)\,dy = fracb^1 + 1/(p-1)1 + 1/(p-1). From frac1p + frac1q = 1 we get q = (p)/(p-1) , so 1 + (1)/(p-1) = (p)/(p-1) = q , and the second integral is (b^q)/(q) . So (*) becomes ab ≤ (a^p)/(p) + (b^q)/(q). qed Equality should hold when b = f(a) = a^p-1 . Check: then ab = a^p , and b^q = a^(p-1)q = a^p , so the right-hand side is a^pbigl(frac1p + frac1qbigr) = a^p . ■ With p = q = 2 this is ab ≤ (a^2 + b^2)/(2) , the two-number AM–GM inequality of Section 3.2 in disguise. Stage 3 An inverse sine Now take f(x) = sin x on [0, fracπ2] , which is continuous and increasing with f(0) = 0 , and f^-1 = arcsin on [0, 1] . int_0^a sin x\,dx is easy. How would you integrate arcsin y ? int_0^a sin x\,dx = 1 - cos a . For the inverse sine, integrate by parts with arcsin y × 1 : int_0^b arcsin y\,dy = Bigl[ yarcsin y Bigr]_0^b - int_0^b fracysqrt1 - y^2\,dy = barcsin b + sqrt1 - b^2 - 1. Adding, (*) gives ab ≤ barcsin b + sqrt1 - b^2 - cos a . ■ Now deduce the inequality for arcsin(t^-1) . Which value of a should you choose? (Try the simplest possible one.) Take a = 0 : then 0 ≤ barcsin b + sqrt1 - b^2 - 1 , that is, barcsin b ≥ 1 - sqrt1 - b^2 . (This is just the statement that int_0^b arcsin y\,dy ≥ 0 .) Put b = 1/t with t ≥ 1 , so 0 < b ≤ 1 , and divide by b : arcsinleft(frac1tright) ≥ tleft(1 - sqrt1 - (1)/(t^2)right) = t - sqrtt^2 - 1. qed Looking back A picture as a proof. Part (i) is a complete proof once you see the right picture. Translating a geometric fact into an inequality between integrals is a powerful technique. Specialise a general result. One general inequality, with different choices of f , gave Young’s inequality and an inequality for arcsin . The simplest choice can be the right one. The final deduction used a = 0 , where the inequality is almost trivial. Always try the easy cases. What’s really going on From Young to Hölder William Henry Young published his inequality in 1912. Its importance comes from what it leads to. Suppose sum a_i^p = 1 and sum b_i^q = 1 . Applying Young to each pair and adding, sum a_i b_i ≤ (sum a_i^p)/(p) + (sum b_i^q)/(q) = frac1p + frac1q = 1. Scaling the a s and b s to make the sums 1 gives Hölder’s inequality : for positive numbers, sum a_i b_i ≤ Bigl(sum a_i^pBigr)^1/p Bigl(sum b_i^qBigr)^1/q. With p = q = 2 this is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality , sum a_ib_i ≤ sqrtsum a_i^2sqrtsum b_i^2 , which says that the cosine of the angle between two vectors is at most 1 . Hölder’s inequality is the foundation of the theory of L^p spaces, spaces of functions in which “distance” is measured by bigl(int |f|^pbigr)^1/p , and which you will meet in courses on functional analysis and probability. The Legendre transform The picture in Figure 3.4.1 treats f and f^-1 completely symmetrically. Write F(a) = int_0^a f and G(b) = int_0^b f^-1 . The inequality says F(a) + G(b) ≥ ab , with equality on the curve, so G(b) = max_a bigl( ab - F(a) bigr). This operation, turning a convex function F into a new convex function G , is the Legendre transform , and applying it twice gets you back to F . In mechanics it converts the Lagrangian , a function of position and velocity, into the Hamiltonian , a function of position and momentum: two equivalent formulations of Newton’s laws that you will meet in a second-year course. In thermodynamics it converts between energy, enthalpy and free energy. For F(a) = a^p/p the transform is G(b) = b^q/q , which is why the two exponents in Young’s inequality are linked by frac1p + frac1q = 1 . The thinking skill Inequalities from pictures An integral is an area. Comparing areas in a well-chosen picture can prove an inequality that is hard to see algebraically. Look for pictures in which one region obviously contains another, or several regions obviously cover a third. Then translate each area into an integral. Try this next The 1987 version. Try STEP I 1987, Question 6 . It uses the same kind of picture to integrate an inverse function. Check your answer by differentiating. Cauchy–Schwarz. Use Young’s inequality with p = q = 2 to prove a_1b_1 + a_2b_2 + a_3b_3 ≤ sqrta_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2\,sqrtb_1^2 + b_2^2 + b_3^2 for positive numbers. ( Hint: first deal with the case where both square roots equal 1 .) An exponential version. Take f(x) = e^x - 1 in (*) to show that, for a, b ≥ 0 , ab ≤ e^a - 1 - a + (1 + b)(1 + b) - b. When is there equality? How good is the bound? harder Use a calculator to compare arcsin(1/t) with t - sqrtt^2 - 1 for t = 1, 2, 10 . Show that for large t , t - sqrtt^2 - 1 approx (1)/(2t) while arcsin(1/t) approx frac1t . Why is the bound off by a factor of 2 ? (Look at the picture with a = 0 : how much of the excess is wasted?) Further reading J. Michael Steele, The Cauchy–Schwarz Master Class (Cambridge University Press). Chapters 1 and 9 cover Cauchy–Schwarz and Hölder, with Young’s inequality along the way. Roger Nelsen, Proofs Without Words (Mathematical Association of America). Includes Young’s inequality and many other picture proofs. V. I. Arnold, Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics (Springer). Section 14 explains the Legendre transform with exactly this picture. Advanced, but the relevant section is short.

title: The Power of Convexity
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Convexity everywhere The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 2007, Question 7 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/07-s2-q7 The hook In Section 3.2 we proved AM–GM with a clever induction. Here it falls out in one line, as a special case of something much bigger. The bigger thing is concavity : the shape of a curve that bends downwards, like the top of a hill. A single geometric fact about such curves, that the curve lies above its chords, turns out to prove a startling range of inequalities, from a fact about triangles to AM–GM to inequalities in probability, information theory and economics. At university this idea becomes convexity , and it is one of the great unifying themes of modern mathematics. Whole subjects, such as convex optimisation, are built on it. Before you start Draw a curve that bends downwards, such as y = sin x on (0, π) . Mark two points on it and join them with a straight line. Is the chord above or below the curve? Below. For a concave curve, every chord lies below the curve between its endpoints. The average of two function values is the height of the midpoint of the chord; the function value at the average is the height of the curve above that midpoint. So “chord below curve” is exactly Jensen’s inequality for n = 2 : (f(x_1) + f(x_2))/(2) ≤ fleft( (x_1 + x_2)/(2) right). For n points, the average of the points (x_k, f(x_k)) is their centre of mass, which lies inside the region under the curve, so it is below the curve too (Figure 3.3.1). Working it through Stage 1 Checking concavity (d^2)/(dx^2)sin x = -sin x < 0 for 0 < x < π , and (d^2)/(dx^2) x = -(1)/(x^2) < 0 for x > 0 . ■ Stage 2 Triangles Which function, which points, and what is their average? Do the angles of a triangle lie in an interval where the function is concave? Take f(x) = sin x and the three points A, B, C . Each is strictly between 0 and π , where sin is concave, and their average is (A + B + C)/(3) = (π)/(3) . Jensen gives (sin A + sin B + sin C)/(3) ≤ sin(π)/(3) = (sqrt3)/(2), so sin A + sin B + sin C ≤ (3sqrt3)/(2) , with equality exactly for the equilateral triangle. ■ Stage 3 AM–GM in one line AM–GM compares a product with a sum. Which concave function turns products into sums? The logarithm. Apply Jensen to f = and the positive numbers t_1, ldots, t_n : ( t_1 + cdots + t_n)/(n) ≤ left( (t_1 + cdots + t_n)/(n) right). The left-hand side is bigl(sqrt[n]t_1 cdots t_nbigr) . Since is increasing, we can remove it from both sides, and that is AM–GM. Equality holds exactly when all the t_k are equal. ■ Stage 4 Using AM–GM For (a), the left-hand side is a sum of four terms and the right-hand side contains a product of three variables. How many terms should you apply AM–GM to, and why does the 16 help? Apply AM–GM to the four positive numbers x^4 , y^4 , z^4 , 16 : (x^4 + y^4 + z^4 + 16)/(4) ≥ sqrt[4]16\,x^4 y^4 z^4 = 2xyz. Multiplying by 4 gives x^4 + y^4 + z^4 + 16 ≥ 8xyz . ■ Now find the minimum of x^5 + y^5 + z^5 - 5xyz . ( Hint: you want a fifth root of x^5y^5z^5 , so you need five numbers. What should the other two be?) Apply AM–GM to x^5, y^5, z^5, 1, 1 : (x^5 + y^5 + z^5 + 1 + 1)/(5) ≥ sqrt[5]x^5y^5z^5 = xyz, so x^5 + y^5 + z^5 - 5xyz ≥ -2 . Equality holds when x^5 = y^5 = z^5 = 1 , that is, x = y = z = 1 , where the expression is 3 - 5 = -2 . So the minimum value is -2 . ■ Notice how the equality condition does double duty: it shows the bound is actually attained, so -2 is the minimum and not just a lower bound. Looking back One idea, many inequalities. A geometric fact about concave curves gave a result about triangles and AM–GM, with no calculation beyond checking a second derivative. Choose the function and the points. Using Jensen means deciding which function to apply it to and at which points. The logarithm, which turns products into sums, is a favourite. Pad to fit. In (b), adding two 1 s made the AM–GM fit the problem, just as padding with the average did in Section 3.2 . What’s really going on Convex functions At university the standard definition of a convex function (the upside-down version of concave) does not mention derivatives at all: f is convex if fbigl(t x_1 + (1-t)x_2bigr) ≤ t\,f(x_1) + (1-t)\,f(x_2) qquadfor all x_1, x_2 and 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, which says exactly that chords lie above the curve. This definition makes sense for functions that are not differentiable, such as |x| , and for functions of many variables. The Danish engineer and mathematician Johan Jensen made convex functions a subject in their own right in 1906, with the inequality that bears his name. Convexity everywhere Convexity appears throughout mathematics and its applications. Probability. Jensen’s inequality says that for a concave f and any random variable X , E[f(X)] ≤ f(E[X]) . In economics, with f a concave “utility” function, this explains why people prefer a certain £100 to a fifty-fifty gamble on £0 or £200, and why insurance exists. Information theory. The proof that entropy is maximised by the uniform distribution, which underlies data compression, is Jensen’s inequality for . Optimisation. A convex function has no local minima except the global one, so “walk downhill” always finds the best answer. This is why convex optimisation problems can be solved efficiently, and why so much effort goes into recasting problems in convex form. In Section 3.4 we will see a different side of convexity: a geometric duality between a function and its inverse. The thinking skill Find the general principle When several results have similar proofs, look for the single principle behind them. Then prove the principle once and apply it many times. AM–GM, the triangle inequality for sines, and many others are all instances of “a concave curve lies above its chords”. Recognising the principle turns a collection of tricks into a method. Try this next The definition. Parts (i) and (ii) of STEP II 2018, Question 2 start from the chord definition of concavity in the box above and build up to Jensen’s inequality for three points. A product of sines. Try part (iii) of STEP II 2018, Question 2 . Acute triangles. Show that tan x is convex on (0, fracπ2) , and deduce that in an acute-angled triangle, tan A + tan B + tan C ≥ 3sqrt3 . Power means. Show that x^2 is convex, and deduce that left((a_1 + cdots + a_n)/(n)right)^2 ≤ (a_1^2 + cdots + a_n^2)/(n) . Interpret this as a statement about the variance of a set of numbers. Further reading J. Michael Steele, The Cauchy–Schwarz Master Class (Cambridge University Press). Chapter 6 is about convexity and Jensen’s inequality. Claudi Alsina & Roger Nelsen, When Less Is More: Visualizing Basic Inequalities (Mathematical Association of America). Inequalities proved by pictures, many of them using convexity. Stephen Boyd & Lieven Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization (Cambridge University Press). A modern classic, free online; the first chapters show why convexity matters in practice.

title: Functions, Inequalities and Rigour
headings: Why rigour matters Inequalities: the working tools of analysis What you will meet at university The questions that run through this chapter Ideas in this chapter How to read this chapter
text: Chapter 3 · Introduction Getting It Right In mathematics you don’t understand things. You just get used to them. — John von Neumann Here is a “proof” that 1 = 2 . Let a = b . Then a^2 = ab , so a^2 - b^2 = ab - b^2 , which factorises as (a + b)(a - b) = b(a - b) . Cancelling a - b gives a + b = b , and since a = b , that says 2b = b , so 2 = 1 . You probably spotted the problem: since a = b , “cancelling a - b ” means dividing by zero. But notice how plausible every step looked, and how easily the error hid inside a routine move. Real mistakes in real mathematics are rarely so obvious, and they have fooled some of the greatest mathematicians who ever lived. This chapter is about the habits of mind that catch them: precise definitions, careful use of theorems, and a healthy suspicion of arguments that seem too easy. Why rigour matters At school, mathematics is mostly about getting answers. At university it is mostly about knowing that your answers are right , and being able to convince someone else. That shift is the biggest single change between school and university mathematics, and it can be unsettling. Why spend a page proving something that “obviously” works? The answer is that “obvious” is unreliable. The history of analysis is full of results that seemed obvious and were false: that a continuous function must be differentiable except perhaps at a few isolated points (André-Marie Ampère published a “proof” in 1806; in 1872 Weierstrass found a continuous function differentiable nowhere ), that a convergent sum of continuous functions is continuous (Cauchy believed it; Abel found a counterexample), that you can rearrange the terms of a convergent series without changing its sum (you can’t, in general). Rigour is not pedantry. It is the only reliable way to tell the true from the plausible. Inequalities: the working tools of analysis The second theme of this chapter is inequalities . In school mathematics most results are equations: this equals that. In analysis, most results are inequalities: this is at most that. To prove a sequence converges you show the error is less than any tolerance; to prove an integral exists you show some sum is bounded ; to estimate how good an approximation is, you bound the error. A professional analyst spends much more time proving inequalities than equations, and the classical inequalities you will meet here (AM–GM, Jensen, Young, Hölder, Cauchy–Schwarz) are the tools of the trade. They are also remarkable in their own right. A single inequality about functions, with a well-chosen example, proves π^2 ≤ 10 ( Section 3.7 ). A fact about the shape of the logarithm settles whether π^e or e^π is bigger ( Section 3.5 ). A chemist’s question about measurement errors leads to some of the most important polynomials in mathematics ( Section 3.6 ). What you will meet at university Rigour is the theme of first-year Analysis , and also of a course often called Numbers and Sets or Foundations , where you learn to write proofs precisely. You will meet the formal definitions of continuity and differentiability, and theorems with precise hypotheses (the intermediate value theorem, the mean value theorem, the extreme value theorem) whose hypotheses really matter. Later courses develop the inequalities in this chapter into whole subjects: functional analysis studies spaces of functions measured by integrals like those in Section 3.4 and Section 3.7 ; convex analysis and optimisation grow out of Section 3.3 ; approximation theory grows out of Section 3.6 ; and special functions like the one in Section 3.9 appear throughout applied mathematics and physics. The questions that run through this chapter Three big questions How do you know an argument is correct? What are the common ways for plausible arguments to fail, and how do you check? How do you prove an inequality? Where do the classical inequalities come from, and how do you choose which one to use? What is a function, really? Can a function be defined by a property it has, rather than by a formula? And can we invent new functions when the old ones are not enough? The chapter opens with error-spotting ( Section 3.1 ), then works through the classical inequalities, each from a different angle: an unusual induction, convexity, areas, the shape of a graph, polynomial interpolation and test functions. It closes with two sections on functions defined by their properties: e^x and tanh x from their addition laws, and a brand-new function defined as an inverse. Ideas in this chapter § Topic Idea 3.1 Plausible wrong arguments Checking calculations, logic and hidden hypotheses 3.2 AM–GM Forward–backward induction 3.3 Jensen’s inequality Concave curves lie above their chords 3.4 Young’s inequality Comparing areas in a picture 3.5 π^e or e^π ? Reducing to one function and studying its graph 3.6 Slopes of quadratics Expressing the unknown in terms of the known 3.7 π^2 ≤ 10 Test functions in a general inequality 3.8 e^x and tanh x Functions defined by functional equations 3.9 The W function Inventing a function as an inverse How to read this chapter As before, try each question before reading the solution. In this chapter, also try something else: after reading each solution, go back and find the one or two steps that a careless student would get wrong. Where would a hidden assumption slip in? Which hypothesis of which theorem needs checking? Reading in this way, critically and actively, is the single most useful habit you can build before university.

title: Inventing a New Function
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Where W appears Elementary functions The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 2021, Question 4 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP II paper in OCR’s download of the 2021 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/696588-2021-past-papers.zip The hook Can you solve e^-x = 5x ? Not with any function on your calculator. Rearranging gets nowhere: the x is stuck both inside and outside the exponential. You could find a numerical answer by trial and improvement, but there is no “formula”. Or is there? This question takes a bold step: if a family of equations has no solution in terms of known functions, invent a new function that solves them. That is exactly what mathematicians did with sqrtx (the inverse of x^2 ), with x (the inverse of e^x ) and with arcsin x . The new function here is the inverse of xe^x , now called the Lambert W function . Once you have it, a surprising range of equations, from x^x = 10 to a law of physics, can be solved exactly. Before you start What does it actually mean to “solve” an equation? Is x = sqrt2 a solution of x^2 = 2 , or just a name for the solution? Both. sqrt2 is a name for “the positive number whose square is 2 ”; we accept it as an answer because the function sqrtphantomx is well understood, easy to compute and has known properties. Whether an answer counts as a “formula” depends on which functions we have agreed to name. This question adds one more to the list. Working it through Stage 1 The curve y = xe^x (dy)/(dx) = e^x + xe^x = (1 + x)e^x , which is zero only at x = -1 , where y = -e^-1 . The derivative is negative for x < -1 and positive for x > -1 , so this is a minimum. What happens to xe^x as x → +∞ and as x → -∞ ? Where does the curve cross the axes? As x → ∞ , xe^x → ∞ . As x → -∞ , xe^x → 0 from below, because the exponential decay beats the linear growth. The curve passes through the origin. So it comes in from just below the negative x -axis, dips to its minimum (-1, -frac1e) , then rises through (0, 0) and shoots upwards (Figure 3.9.1). Stage 2 The inverse To have an inverse, f must be one-to-one, so it must be restricted to a region where it is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing. The largest such interval containing the right-hand part is [-1, ∞) , so a = -1 . On [-1, ∞) , f increases from -frac1e to ∞ , so the inverse g is defined on [-frac1e, ∞) , increases from g(-frac1e) = -1 , passes through g(0) = 0 , and grows slowly (for large x , even more slowly than x ). Its graph is the reflection of the right-hand part of y = xe^x in the line y = x , with a vertical tangent at (-frac1e, -1) . The defining property of g is g(z)\,e^g(z) = z, qquad g(z) ≥ -1. So the strategy for every part of (iii) is the same: rearrange the equation into the form (something)\,e^(the same something) = (a number) . Stage 3 Four equations (a) e^-x = 5x . Multiply by e^x and divide by 5 : xe^x = frac15 . So x = gbigl(frac15bigr) approx 0.169 . Since xe^x is negative for x < 0 , any root is positive, and xe^x is increasing for x > 0 , so this is the only root. For (b) and (c), the unknown appears as x x . What substitution turns x x into something of the form ue^u ? Put x = e^u , so x = u and x x = ue^u . (b) 2x x + 1 = 0 becomes ue^u = -frac12 . But ue^u ≥ -frac1e approx -0.368 for all real u , and -frac12 < -frac1e . So there is no real root . (c) 3x x + 1 = 0 becomes ue^u = -frac13 , and -frac1e < -frac13 < 0 . A horizontal line at height -frac13 cuts y = ue^u twice , once on each side of the minimum at u = -1 . The root on the right is u = gbigl(-frac13bigr) , giving x = e^g(-1/3) approx 0.538. The other root has u < -1 < gbigl(-frac13bigr) , and x = e^u is increasing in u , so the root we have found is the greater of the two. (The other is about 0.220 .) Now try (d), x = 3 x . ( Hint: exponentiate and aim for (something)\,e^something with the something being a multiple of x .) (d) x = 3 x means e^x/3 = x , so xe^-x/3 = 1 , and multiplying by -frac13 , left(-frac x3right)e^-x/3 = -frac13. So -frac x3 is one of the two solutions of ue^u = -frac13 found in (c). Taking the one given by g , x = -3\,gbigl(-frac13bigr) approx 1.857 . The other root comes from the other solution u < g(-frac13) , which gives a larger x = -3u . So this time the root we have found is the smaller of the two. (The other is about 4.536 .) ■ Stage 4 x^x = 10 Taking logarithms, x x = 10 . With x = e^u this is ue^u = 10 , so u = g( 10) and x = e^g( 10) approx 2.506. Since g(z)e^g(z) = z , we can also write this as x = ( 10)/(g( 10)) . ■ Looking back Name the missing function. When an equation cannot be solved with known functions, defining a new function as an inverse is a legitimate, and often illuminating, move. Rearrange to a standard form. Every part of (iii) and (iv) came down to ue^u = constant , using a substitution such as x = e^u or u = -frac x3 . Count roots with the graph. Whether ue^u = c has zero, one or two solutions depends only on where c sits relative to the minimum value -frac1e . What’s really going on A function with a long history and a recent name Johann Heinrich Lambert studied equations of this type in 1758, and Euler took them further in 1783. But the function had no standard name until the 1990s, when the developers of the computer algebra system Maple needed one. In 1996 Robert Corless, Gaston Gonnet, David Hare, David Jeffrey and Donald Knuth published a paper, “On the Lambert W function”, that collected its properties and applications. It has been cited thousands of times, and W is now built into most mathematical software. The function g in the question is the principal branch W_0 ; the dashed curve in Figure 3.9.1, which gave the second roots in (c) and (d), is the other real branch W_-1 . Where W appears Wien’s displacement law. The wavelength at which a hot body radiates most strongly is inversely proportional to its temperature. The constant comes from solving 5(1 - e^-x) = x , whose positive solution is x = 5 + Wbigl(-5e^-5bigr) approx 4.965 . That is why the Sun, at about 5800 K, looks yellow-white, and why a cooler red dwarf looks red. Power towers. The infinite tower x^x^x^·^·^· converges for e^-e ≤ x ≤ e^1/e , and its value is (W(- x))/(- x) . Population and epidemic models. The final size of an epidemic in the simplest model, and the time to reach a given population in some growth models, are both given by W. Elementary functions Is W really new, or could it be written using exp , , roots and the trigonometric functions? It is genuinely new: a theorem going back to Joseph Liouville in the 1830s shows that W is not an elementary function . The same theory shows that some innocent-looking integrals, such as int e^-x^2\,dx , cannot be done in elementary terms, which is why the normal distribution needs its own special function. The thinking skill Inverse functions as solutions An equation f(x) = c is solved by x = f^-1(c) , provided f is restricted to make it one-to-one. The restriction determines which solution you get. Many equations that look different are the same equation in disguise; finding the substitution that reveals the common form is the key step. Try this next Two, four, and one more. The equation x^2 = 2^x has the obvious solutions x = 2 and x = 4 (compare Section 3.5 ). Show that it also has a negative solution, and that this solution is x = -(2)/( 2)\,g\!left(( 2)/(2)right) approx -0.767. A derivative. By differentiating g(x)e^g(x) = x implicitly, show that, for x ≠ 0 , g'(x) = (g(x))/(xbigl(1 + g(x)bigr)). What happens at x = -frac1e ? An integral. Use the substitution x = we^w to show that displaystyleint_0^e g(x)\,dx = e - 1 . The tower. Assuming the tower T = sqrt2^sqrt2^sqrt2^cdots converges, show that T = sqrt2^\,T , and deduce that T = 2 or T = 4 . Which is it? (Compute a few terms of the sequence t_1 = sqrt2 , t_n+1 = sqrt2^\,t_n , and think about the cobweb diagrams of Section 2.2 .) Further reading Robert Corless et al., “ On the Lambert W function ” , Advances in Computational Mathematics 5 (1996). The paper that named the function. The first sections are readable with this section behind you. Brian Hayes, “ Why W? ” , American Scientist 93 (2005). A lively essay on the function’s history and uses. Free online. Brian Conrad, “ Impossibility theorems for elementary integration ” . Lecture notes, available online, explaining Liouville’s theory. Advanced.

title: A Bound on Slopes
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Interpolation Chebyshev polynomials in practice The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP I 1988, Question 7 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/88-s1-q7 The hook If you know a function stays between -1 and 1 on an interval, can you say anything about how steep it is? For a general function, no: sin(1000x) stays between -1 and 1 but has slopes as large as 1000 . But a quadratic cannot wiggle like that. This question shows that a quadratic trapped in the box |x| ≤ 1 , |y| ≤ 1 can never have slope bigger than 4 inside the box, and that 4 is the best possible. The problem has a surprising origin. In 1887 the chemist Dmitri Mendeleev, famous for the periodic table, was studying how the density of a solution depends on its concentration, and fitting quadratics to his data. He needed to know how badly errors in the data could affect the slope of his curves, and he proved exactly the result in this question. Two years later the young Andrei Markov solved the general problem for polynomials of any degree, and the answer led straight to some of the most important polynomials in mathematics. Before you start The formula for f'(x) uses only three values of f : at -1 , 0 and 1 . Why should three values be enough to determine the derivative of a quadratic? A quadratic has three coefficients, so it is determined by its values at any three points. So its derivative, which is another function of the coefficients, must be expressible in terms of those three values. The formula tells you how. And it is exactly what you need, because the hypothesis |f(x)| ≤ 1 tells you about the values of f , while the conclusion is about its derivative . Working it through Stage 1 The formula f(1) = a + b + c , f(-1) = a - b + c and f(0) = c . So the right-hand side is (a + b + c)left(x + tfrac12right) + (a - b + c)left(x - tfrac12right) - 2cx. The coefficient of x is (a + b + c) + (a - b + c) - 2c = 2a , and the constant term is frac12(a + b + c) - frac12(a - b + c) = b . So the right-hand side is 2ax + b = f'(x) . ■ Stage 2 The bound Take absolute values in the formula and use the triangle inequality, together with |f(1)|, |f(-1)|, |f(0)| ≤ 1 . What bound on |f'(x)| do you get, as a function of x ? By the triangle inequality |u + v + w| ≤ |u| + |v| + |w| , |f'(x)| ≤ |f(1)|\,bigl|x + tfrac12bigr| + |f(-1)|\,bigl|x - tfrac12bigr| + 2|f(0)|\,|x| ≤ bigl|x + tfrac12bigr| + bigl|x - tfrac12bigr| + 2|x|. Show that bigl|x + tfrac12bigr| + bigl|x - tfrac12bigr| + 2|x| ≤ 4 for |x| ≤ 1 . (Split into cases according to the signs.) If |x| ≤ frac12 , then x + frac12 ≥ 0 and x - frac12 ≤ 0 , so bigl|x + tfrac12bigr| + bigl|x - tfrac12bigr| = (x + tfrac12) - (x - tfrac12) = 1 , and the total is 1 + 2|x| ≤ 2 . If frac12 ≤ |x| ≤ 1 , both brackets have the same sign as x , so bigl|x + tfrac12bigr| + bigl|x - tfrac12bigr| = 2|x| , and the total is 4|x| ≤ 4 . Either way |f'(x)| ≤ 4 . ■ The bound is only achieved at x = 1 ; in the middle half of the interval the slope is at most 2 . Stage 3 An extreme example For the bound to be attained at x = 1 , every inequality in Stage 2 must be an equality. What values must f(1) , f(-1) and f(0) take, and with what signs? At x = 1 , the formula is f'(1) = frac32f(1) + frac12f(-1) - 2f(0) . To make this equal to 4 we need f(1) = 1 , f(-1) = 1 and f(0) = -1 . The quadratic through (-1, 1) , (0, -1) and (1, 1) is f(x) = 2x^2 - 1, so a = 2 , b = 0 , c = -1 . On |x| ≤ 1 , x^2 [0, 1] , so 2x^2 - 1 [-1, 1] , and f'(1) = 4 . ■ Looking back Express what you want in terms of what you know. The formula rewrote the derivative in terms of values of f , which is where the hypothesis gave information. The triangle inequality. Bounding a sum by the sum of the absolute values is one of the most common moves in analysis. Find the extremal case from the equality conditions. Asking when every inequality is tight produced the example 2x^2 - 1 directly. What’s really going on Markov’s inequality and Chebyshev polynomials Andrei Markov proved in 1889 that if p is a polynomial of degree n with |p(x)| ≤ 1 on [-1, 1] , then |p'(x)| ≤ n^2 qquadfor |x| ≤ 1. For n = 2 this is our bound of 4 . The extreme cases are the Chebyshev polynomials T_n , defined by T_n(cosθ) = cos nθ. For example cos 2θ = 2cos^2θ - 1 gives T_2(x) = 2x^2 - 1 , our extreme quadratic, and cos 3θ = 4cos^3θ - 3cosθ gives T_3(x) = 4x^3 - 3x . Because T_n(x) = cos nθ , these polynomials oscillate between -1 and 1 as often as a polynomial of degree n possibly can, and they are as steep as possible at the ends (Figure 3.6.1). Markov’s brother Vladimir extended the result to higher derivatives in 1892. Interpolation The formula in the question is a piece of Lagrange interpolation : given the values of a function at a few points, write down the unique polynomial of lowest degree through them, and use it to approximate the function or its derivative. Here the three points are -1, 0, 1 . Formulas like this are used everywhere in numerical analysis, for example to estimate derivatives from measured data. Markov’s inequality is the warning that comes with them: a small error in the values can be magnified by a factor of up to n^2 in the derivative, which is exactly the issue Mendeleev was worried about. Chebyshev polynomials in practice Chebyshev polynomials are the workhorses of approximation theory. Interpolating a function at the roots of T_n , rather than at equally spaced points, keeps the error under control; with equally spaced points, high-degree interpolation can go wildly wrong near the ends of the interval (Runge’s phenomenon). Software that evaluates functions to full machine precision, or solves differential equations very accurately, often works with Chebyshev expansions internally. The thinking skill Express the unknown in terms of the known If the hypothesis tells you about one kind of quantity and the conclusion is about another, look for an identity linking them, then bound term by term. And when you have a bound, ask whether it is best possible. Following the equality cases backwards usually leads you to the extreme example, and the extreme example is often interesting in its own right. Try this next The general idea. Show that if f is a quadratic then f(x) = f(-1)(x(x-1))/(2) + f(0)(1 - x^2) + f(1)(x(x+1))/(2) , and differentiate to recover the formula in the question. Uniqueness. harder Show that (2x^2 - 1) are the only quadratics with |f(x)| ≤ 1 on [-1, 1] and |f'(x)| = 4 somewhere in [-1, 1] . Chebyshev polynomials. Use cos 3θ = 4cos^3θ - 3cosθ to check that T_3(x) = 4x^3 - 3x , and verify that T_3'(1) = 9 . Show that T_n+1(x) = 2xT_n(x) - T_n-1(x) , and find T_4 . Slopes of T_n . By differentiating T_n(cosθ) = cos nθ with respect to θ , show that T_n'(cosθ) = (nsin nθ)/(sinθ) , and deduce that T_n'(1) = n^2 by letting θ → 0 . Further reading Lloyd N. Trefethen, Approximation Theory and Approximation Practice (SIAM). A beautiful modern book about Chebyshev polynomials and interpolation, readable by a strong school student, with computer experiments throughout. Peter Borwein & Tamás Erdélyi, Polynomials and Polynomial Inequalities (Springer). For the full story of Markov’s inequality and its relatives. Advanced. George M. Phillips, Interpolation and Approximation by Polynomials (Springer). An undergraduate text covering Lagrange interpolation, Chebyshev polynomials and Markov-type inequalities.

title: π^e or e^π?
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on All solutions of x^y = y^x The most economical base The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 2013, Question 1 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/13-s2-q1 The hook Which is bigger, π^e or e^π ? Your calculator will tell you in a second: e^π approx 23.14 and π^e approx 22.46 . But a calculator only tells you that ; it does not tell you why , and it cannot help with infinitely many similar questions at once. Is 3^π bigger than π^3 ? Are there any whole numbers with n^m = m^n apart from the obvious n = m ? All these questions turn out to be about a single curve, y = x , and the straight lines that cross it. This question shows how a sketch, used carefully, can settle comparisons that look hopeless by algebra, and how the number e emerges as the natural dividing point. Before you start Taking logarithms, a^b = b^a is the same as b a = a b . Rearrange this so that a appears only on one side and b only on the other. b a = a b is the same as ( a)/(a) = ( b)/(b). So every comparison of a^b with b^a is a comparison of the values of the single function h(x) = ( x)/(x) at a and b . And ( a)/(a) is the gradient of the line from the origin to the point (a, a) on the curve y = x . That is why the question is about lines. Working it through Stage 1 The tangent through the origin If y = mx touches y = x at x = x_0 , what two equations must hold? The line and curve must meet, mx_0 = x_0 , and have the same gradient, m = 1/x_0 . Substituting the second into the first, 1 = x_0 , so x_0 = e and m = 1/e . The tangent from the origin touches the curve at (e, 1) . If instead y = mx crosses the curve at x = a and x = b , then a = ma and b = mb , so ( a)/(a) = m = ( b)/(b) , which gives b a = a b and hence a^b = b^a . ■ For the sketch: a line through the origin that is slightly less steep than the tangent cuts the curve twice, once on each side of the point of tangency, so a < e < b . Lines steeper than 1/e miss the curve altogether, because x is concave and lies entirely below its tangent y = x/e . Stage 2 Lines that cut the y -axis above the origin Now the line is y = mx + c with c > 0 . What are ( p)/(p) and ( q)/(q) in terms of m and c ? From p = mp + c and q = mq + c , ( p)/(p) = m + (c)/(p), qquad ( q)/(q) = m + (c)/(q). Since c > 0 and p < q , (c)/(p) > (c)/(q) , so ( p)/(p) > ( q)/(q) . Multiplying by pq > 0 gives q p > p q , so p^q > q^p . ■ Geometrically: from the origin, the point (p, p) is seen at a steeper angle than (q, q) when the line through them crosses the y -axis above the origin. Stage 3 Chords to the right of e The chord from (p, p) to (q, q) , with e ≤ p < q , has gradient less than the gradient of the curve at p . Why? And why does that make its y -intercept positive? Because x is concave, its gradient 1/x decreases, so the chord from p to q is less steep than the tangent at p : its gradient s satisfies s < frac1p . The chord’s y -intercept is c = p - sp > p - (1)/(p) · p = p - 1 ≥ 0, using p ≥ e . So the chord crosses the y -axis above the origin. ■ Use this, and Stage 2, to decide which is greater, π^e or e^π . Take p = e and q = π . The chord between them has a positive intercept, so by Stage 2, p^q > q^p : that is, e^π > π^e. Stage 4 Chords parallel to the tangent Now suppose the chord from p to q has gradient exactly frac1e , the same as the tangent y = (x)/(e) . The chord is parallel to the tangent at (e, 1) . Since x is concave, the curve lies below that tangent. Does the chord cut the y -axis above or below the origin? The chord is the line y = (x)/(e) + c for some c . Its endpoints lie on the curve, which lies on or below the tangent y = (x)/(e) , and touches it only at x = e . The endpoints cannot both be at x = e , so at least one lies strictly below the tangent, and therefore the whole parallel chord lies below the tangent: c < 0 . Now repeat Stage 2 with c < 0 : the inequality reverses, ( p)/(p) < ( q)/(q) , and so q^p > p^q . ■ Looking back Reduce to one function. Comparing a^b with b^a became comparing h(a) with h(b) , where h(x) = ( x)/(x) . A sketch with reasons. Each “by means of a sketch” was backed up by a precise fact: concavity of (chords below the curve, tangents above it) and the sign of an intercept. The special role of e . The tangent from the origin touches at x = e , and that is the dividing point for all of these comparisons. What’s really going on The graph of ( x)/(x) Everything in this question is visible in the graph of h(x) = ( x)/(x) (Figure 3.5.1). Its derivative is h'(x) = (1 - x)/(x^2) , so h increases on (0, e) , reaches its maximum frac1e at x = e , and then decreases towards 0 . A horizontal line at height m between 0 and frac1e cuts the graph twice, at points a < e < b with h(a) = h(b) , which is exactly a^b = b^a . To the right of e , h is decreasing, so for e ≤ p < q we have h(p) > h(q) , that is, p^q > q^p . In particular e^π > π^e , and more generally e^x > x^e for every x ≠ e : no other number beats e at this game. All solutions of x^y = y^x Which pairs of distinct positive reals satisfy x^y = y^x ? A neat trick finds them all. Put y = tx with t > 1 ; then x^tx = (tx)^x gives x^t = tx , so x^t-1 = t and x = t^1/(t-1), qquad y = t^t/(t-1). Writing t = 1 + frac1n gives x = left(1 + frac1nright)^n and y = left(1 + frac1nright)^n+1 . With n = 1 this is (2, 4) ; with n = 2 it is left(frac94, (27)/(8)right) , and indeed left(frac94right)^27/8 = left((27)/(8)right)^9/4 . As n → ∞ both tend to e , the point where the two branches meet. The problem was discussed in letters between Daniel Bernoulli and Christian Goldbach in 1728, and later by Euler. The most economical base The function x^1/x = e^h(x) is also maximised at x = e . This answers a curious question: if the “cost” of a number system is the base times the number of digits needed, the most economical base is e , and among whole numbers, 3 (narrowly beating 2 ). A few experimental computers, such as the Soviet Setun of 1958, have used base 3 . The thinking skill Rearrange to separate the variables, then study one function An inequality or equation involving two quantities in a tangled way often becomes a statement about one function evaluated at two points. Once you have that function, its graph (where it increases, decreases and peaks) answers every question at once. Here a^b versus b^a became h(a) versus h(b) . Try this next Whole numbers. Try STEP I 1988, Question 1 . More comparisons. Try STEP II 2025, Question 3 (in OCR’s download of the 2025 papers, a zip file). It uses the graph from this section to settle more comparisons between a^b and b^a , including one where a numerical bound on e does the work. A one-line proof. Use e^x > 1 + x for x ≠ 0 , with x = (π)/(e) - 1 , to prove e^π > π^e directly. Further reading Eli Maor, e: The Story of a Number (Princeton University Press). The history of e , including the equation x^y = y^x . Paul Nahin, An Imaginary Tale (Princeton University Press). Not only about sqrt-1 : full of curious calculations of exactly this kind. Michael Spivak, Calculus (Cambridge University Press). Chapter 11 covers the use of derivatives to understand the shape of graphs with complete rigour.

title: Spot the Flaw
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Theorems with hypotheses A value for a divergent integral The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP I 1991, Question 6 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/91-s1-q6 The hook Most exam questions ask you to produce an argument. This one hands you two arguments and asks you to take them apart. That is a very different skill, and it is the one you will use most at university: checking your own work, reading a proof in a book and deciding whether you believe it, marking a friend’s attempt, refereeing a paper. The arguments here are bad in an instructive way. Every step looks like something you have seen a hundred times. Some steps contain arithmetic slips, but the more serious errors are errors of logic : conclusions that do not follow even when the calculations are right. Those are the errors that survive into professional mathematics, and spotting them is what this chapter is about. Before you start When you are asked to “criticise each step”, what should you check at each step? Make a list before you start. A good checklist has at least three questions. Is the calculation correct? Does this step follow from the previous ones? Are there hidden assumptions (that a function is continuous, that a limit exists, that a stationary point must be a maximum or minimum)? The question also asks whether the conclusions might be true anyway. A wrong argument can have a true conclusion, so that needs a separate check. Working it through Stage 1 Is the derivative right? Differentiate g with the quotient rule. Where is g'(x) = 0 ? Check x = 1 and x = -1 directly. By the quotient rule, g'(x) = (6x^2(x^4 + 4) - (2x^3 + 3)· 4x^3)/((x^4 + 4)^2) = (-2x^6 - 12x^3 + 24x^2)/((x^4 + 4)^2) = (-2x^2bigl(x^4 + 6x - 12bigr))/((x^4 + 4)^2). So g'(x) = 0 when x = 0 or x^4 + 6x - 12 = 0 . At x = 1 , x^4 + 6x - 12 = -5 ; at x = -1 it is -17 . Neither is a stationary point. The first claim is false . The quartic x^4 + 6x - 12 is -12 at x = 0 and tends to +∞ in both directions, so it has (at least) one positive root and one negative root; it has exactly two real roots, because its second derivative 12x^2 is non-negative, so it is convex and can cross zero at most twice. Numerically they are x approx 1.386 and x approx -2.247 . Stage 2 Are the values right? g(0) = frac34 is correct, and g(1) = (5)/(5) = 1 . But g(-1) = (-2 + 3)/(1 + 4) = frac15 , not 1 . Even on its own terms, the argument has an arithmetic error: it seems to have assumed that g is even. Stage 3 Does comparing values tell you which is a maximum? Suppose a function has exactly two stationary points, with values frac34 and 1 . Does it follow that the first is a minimum and the second a maximum? No. The nature of a stationary point is a local property: it depends on how the function behaves near that point, not on how its value compares with the value somewhere else. A function can have a local maximum lower than a local minimum (think of x + 2sin x ), or a stationary point that is neither. Here, near x = 0 , the factor x^4 + 6x - 12 is close to -12 , so g'(x) = (-2x^2(x^4 + 6x - 12))/((x^4 + 4)^2) > 0 qquadfor small x ≠ 0. The derivative is positive on both sides of 0 : x = 0 is a stationary point of inflection , not a minimum. Stage 4 Do stationary values bound a function? Even with correct stationary points, why can’t you conclude that every value of g lies between the smallest and largest stationary values? Find a value of x with g(x) < frac34 . Stationary points only describe local behaviour. The global behaviour also depends on what happens at the ends of the domain, here as x → ∞ . Since g(x) → 0 as x → ∞ , and g(x) < 0 whenever 2x^3 + 3 < 0 , that is, x < -sqrt[3]3/2 approx -1.14 , the function takes negative values. For example g(-2) = (-13)/(20) . So the conclusion frac34 ≤ g(x) ≤ 1 is false (Figure 3.1.1). The correct statement: g increases to a global maximum of about 1.083 at x approx 1.386 , then decreases towards 0 ; to the left, it decreases from 0 to a global minimum of about -0.668 at x approx -2.247 , then increases through x = 0 (where it has a horizontal inflection) up to the maximum. So -0.668 lesssim g(x) lesssim 1.083 for all x . Stage 5 The integral Differentiate -3(1-x)^-4 . Do you get (1-x)^-3 ? (d)/(dx)bigl[-3(1-x)^-4bigr] = -3 · (-4)(1-x)^-5 · (-1) = -12(1-x)^-5 . Wrong in both the power and the coefficient. The correct antiderivative is int (1-x)^-3\,dx = tfrac12(1-x)^-2 + C, as you can check by differentiating. With the correct antiderivative, bigl[frac12(1-x)^-2bigr]_-1^3 = frac12 · frac14 - frac12 · frac14 = 0 . So the answer was right after all. Or was it? It was not. The fundamental theorem of calculus, int_a^b F'(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a) , requires the integrand to be continuous on the whole interval [a, b] . Here (1-x)^-3 is undefined at x = 1 , which lies inside [-1, 3] , and near x = 1 it is enormous. The integral must be treated as an improper integral, split at the bad point: int_-1^1 (1-x)^-3\,dx = lim_ε → 0^+ Bigl[tfrac12(1-x)^-2Bigr]_-1^1-ε = lim_ε → 0^+ left( (1)/(2ε^2) - frac18 right) = +∞. The integral from -1 to 1 is infinite (and the one from 1 to 3 is -∞ ), so int_-1^3(1-x)^-3\,dx does not exist . The conclusion “ = 0 ” is false, not because the true value is something else, but because there is no value. ■ Looking back Three kinds of error. Calculation errors (the derivative, g(-1) , the antiderivative), logical errors (comparing values to classify stationary points; stationary values as global bounds), and hidden assumptions (continuity in the fundamental theorem of calculus). Right answer, wrong reason. Correcting the antiderivative in part (ii) reproduces the answer 0 , but the argument is still invalid. A correct-looking answer is no evidence that the reasoning is sound. Local versus global. Derivatives tell you about the behaviour near a point. Global conclusions need more: what happens at the ends of the domain, or at points where the function misbehaves. What’s really going on When great mathematicians got it wrong Errors of exactly this kind were made by the founders of analysis. In his Cours d’analyse of 1821, Augustin-Louis Cauchy “proved” that a convergent sum of continuous functions is always continuous. In 1826 Niels Henrik Abel pointed out a counterexample: the Fourier series sin x - tfrac12sin 2x + tfrac13sin 3x - cdots converges for every x , and every term is continuous, but the sum jumps at x = π (it equals x/2 for -π < x < π ). Working out exactly what had gone wrong in Cauchy’s argument took decades, and led to the concept of uniform convergence , which every analysis student now learns. Hidden assumptions, often about swapping the order of two limits, are the most common source of error in all of analysis. Theorems with hypotheses Two of the errors in this question come from ignoring the hypotheses of a theorem. The extreme value theorem says that a continuous function on a closed, bounded interval [a, b] attains a maximum and a minimum. To find them, check the endpoints, the stationary points, and any points where the function is not differentiable: the minimum of |x| on [-1, 1] is at 0 , which is neither. If f is differentiable everywhere inside the interval, an interior maximum or minimum must be a stationary point. On the whole real line there are no endpoints to check, and the function might not have a maximum at all; you must examine the behaviour as x → ∞ instead. The fundamental theorem of calculus needs the integrand to be continuous on [a, b] . If it is not, the integral may still exist (try int_0^1 x^-1/2\,dx ) or may not (as here), and you must check using limits. At university, every theorem you meet will come with a precise list of hypotheses. Part of the training is to check them, every time, before using the theorem. A value for a divergent integral There is a curious footnote to part (ii). The interval [-1, 3] is symmetric about the bad point x = 1 , and (1-x)^-3 is “odd” about that point. If you cut out a symmetric gap (1 - ε, 1 + ε) and let ε → 0 , the two infinite pieces cancel and you do get 0 . This is called the Cauchy principal value , and it is genuinely useful in physics and complex analysis. But it is a different definition , chosen deliberately, and an argument that arrives at it by accident has not proved anything. The thinking skill Reading arguments critically Check every step for three things: is the calculation right, does the step follow logically, and what has been assumed without being said? Then check the conclusion separately: an incorrect argument can have a true conclusion, and a “correct” answer can come from an invalid argument. Apply the same scrutiny to your own work; the arguments you are most likely to believe are your own. Try this next A substitution that lies. Try STEP I 1987, Question 8 . A substitution seems to show that a positive integral equals a negative one. Find exactly where the argument breaks, then evaluate both integrals correctly. True or false? Try STEP I 1998, Question 3 : four claims to prove or disprove. For each one, decide which you expect before you start writing. All horses are the same colour. Find the flaw in this “proof” by induction: any one horse is the same colour as itself; given n + 1 horses, the first n are the same colour by the inductive hypothesis, and so are the last n ; the two groups overlap, so all n + 1 are the same colour. An integral that does exist. Show that int_-1^1 |x|^-1/2\,dx exists, although the integrand is undefined at 0 , and find its value. Further reading E. A. Maxwell, Fallacies in Mathematics (Cambridge University Press). A classic collection of plausible wrong arguments, organised by topic, written for sixth-formers. Bernard Gelbaum & John Olmsted, Counterexamples in Analysis (Dover). Hundreds of examples showing why the hypotheses of theorems matter. Dip in once you have started an analysis course. Imre Lakatos, Proofs and Refutations (Cambridge University Press). A brilliant dialogue about how mathematicians find, and fix, errors in proofs.

title: π^2 ≤ 10
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Vibrating strings and quantum particles The calculus of variations The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 2014, Question 2 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/14-s2-q2 The hook Every school student knows that π is a little more than 3 . How would you prove an upper bound for it? Archimedes did it with polygons. This question does it in a completely unexpected way: by taking a general inequality about functions, plugging in a simple parabola, and reading off π^2 ≤ 10 . A different choice of function gives the famous approximation π ≤ (22)/(7) . The inequality (*) is Wirtinger’s inequality . It says that a function pinned to zero at both ends cannot be “big” without also being “steep”. Behind it lies one of the central ideas of mathematical physics: the vibrations of a string, the energy levels of a quantum particle, and the theory of eigenvalues. Before you start Why might a function that is zero at both ends of [0, π] have to be steep if it is large in the middle? Why does the condition f(0) = f(π) = 0 matter? To get from 0 up to some height H and back down to 0 within a distance π , a function must climb at an average rate of at least H/(π/2) . So its derivative cannot be small everywhere. Without the condition at the ends there is no such constraint: a constant function can be as large as you like with zero derivative. The inequality (*) makes this precise, measuring “size” and “steepness” by integrals of squares. Working it through Stage 1 Sine waves What is int_0^π sin^2 nx\,dx ? And int_0^π cos^2 nx\,dx ? (Use sin^2θ = frac12(1 - cos 2θ) .) Both are fracπ2 , since int_0^π cos 2nx\,dx = 0 . With f(x) = sin nx we have f'(x) = ncos nx , so int_0^π f^2 = fracπ2 ≤ (n^2π)/(2) = int_0^π (f')^2, since n ≥ 1 . ■ Notice that n = 1 gives equality, so the inequality is as tight as it could be. Stage 2 The end conditions matter Find a simple function with f(0) ≠ 0 for which (*) fails. Then find one with f(0) = 0 but f(π) ≠ 0 . The constant function f(x) = 1 has f(0) = 1 ≠ 0 , and int_0^π 1\,dx = π > 0 = int_0^π 0\,dx . For the second, f(x) = x has f(0) = 0 but f(π) = π , and int_0^π x^2\,dx = (π^3)/(3) approx 10.3 > π = int_0^π 1^2\,dx. So (*) fails in both cases. ■ Stage 3 A parabola Which quadratic vanishes at x = 0 and x = π ? (Up to a constant multiple, there is only one. Why doesn’t the multiple matter?) The quadratic must be a multiple of x(π - x) , and multiplying f by a constant k multiplies both sides of (*) by k^2 , so we may take f(x) = x(π - x) , that is, a = -1 , b = π , c = 0 . Then f'(x) = π - 2x , and with the substitution u = x - fracπ2 (which makes both integrands even), beginaligned int_0^π x^2(π - x)^2\,dx &= int_-π/2^π/2 left( (π^2)/(4) - u^2 right)^2 du = (π^5)/(30), \\ int_0^π (π - 2x)^2\,dx &= int_-π/2^π/2 4u^2\,du = (π^3)/(3). endaligned (For the first: int_-h^h(h^2 - u^2)^2\,du = 2bigl(h^5 - frac23 h^5 + frac15 h^5bigr) = (16)/(15)h^5 with h = fracπ2 .) So (*) says (π^5)/(30) ≤ (π^3)/(3) , that is, π^2 ≤ 10. qed Stage 4 A trigonometric choice For f(x) = psinfrac12 x + qcosfrac12 x + r , what conditions do f(0) = 0 and f(π) = 0 impose on p , q , r ? f(0) = q + r = 0 and f(π) = p + r = 0 . So p = q = -r , and scaling, we take f(x) = sinfrac x2 + cosfrac x2 - 1 . Compute int_0^π f^2 and int_0^π (f')^2 for this function. What inequality for π results? Write s = sinfrac x2 and c = cosfrac x2 . Then (s + c)^2 = 1 + 2sc = 1 + sin x , so f^2 = (s + c)^2 - 2(s + c) + 1 = 2 + sin x - 2sintfrac x2 - 2costfrac x2. Using int_0^π sin x = 2 , int_0^π sinfrac x2 = 2 and int_0^π cosfrac x2 = 2 , int_0^π f^2\,dx = 2π + 2 - 4 - 4 = 2π - 6. And f' = frac12(c - s) , so (f')^2 = frac14(1 - sin x) and int_0^π (f')^2\,dx = frac14(π - 2) . Now (*) gives 2π - 6 ≤ (π - 2)/(4) quadLongrightarrowquad 8π - 24 ≤ π - 2 quadLongrightarrowquad π ≤ (22)/(7). qed Stage 5 Which is better? From π ≤ (22)/(7) we get π^2 ≤ (484)/(49) approx 9.878 , which is better than π^2 ≤ 10 . (The true value is π^2 approx 9.870 .) Notice that this proves (22)/(7) is an upper bound for π ; a quite different integral, in Section 4.3 , shows that it is not equal to π . Looking back A general inequality, a specific function. Choosing a test function turned a statement about all functions into a statement about a number. Scaling. Both sides of (*) scale by the same factor, so we could fix the free constant in each family. Better test functions give better bounds. The closer the test function is to the extreme case sin x , the closer the inequality is to equality, and the better the estimate (Figure 3.7.1). What’s really going on A proof with Fourier series Why is (*) true? At university you will learn that any reasonable function on [0, π] that vanishes at both ends can be written as a Fourier sine series , f(x) = b_1sin x + b_2sin 2x + b_3sin 3x + cdots. Because int_0^π sin mxsin nx\,dx = 0 for m ≠ n , all the cross terms vanish when you square and integrate, giving int_0^π f^2 = fracπ2bigl(b_1^2 + b_2^2 + b_3^2 + cdotsbigr), qquad int_0^π (f')^2 = fracπ2bigl(1^2 b_1^2 + 2^2 b_2^2 + 3^2 b_3^2 + cdotsbigr). Each term on the right is at least the corresponding term on the left, which proves (*) , and shows that equality holds only when f is a multiple of sin x . Part (i) of the question is the single-term case. Vibrating strings and quantum particles The ratio int (f')^2 big/ int f^2 is called a Rayleigh quotient , and (*) says its smallest possible value, for functions pinned at 0 and π , is 1 . This number has physical meaning. For a string fixed at both ends, int (f')^2 measures the stretching energy and int f^2 the size of the displacement, and the minimum value of the ratio determines the lowest note the string can play. In quantum mechanics, the same minimum is the lowest energy of a particle trapped in a box: it cannot be zero, because a wave pinned at both ends must bend. Lord Rayleigh used exactly this trick, guessing a test function and computing the ratio, to estimate the frequencies of vibrating systems; because the extreme case gives the minimum, any guess gives an upper bound on the true lowest frequency, and good guesses give very accurate ones. The calculus of variations Finding the function that minimises a ratio of integrals is a problem in the calculus of variations , where the unknown is a whole function rather than a number. The minimiser here, sin x , satisfies the differential equation f'' + f = 0 , and this is no coincidence: minimising an integral always leads to a differential equation for the minimiser. We return to this idea in Section 4.7 . The thinking skill Test functions An inequality that holds for every function in a class can be applied to a cleverly chosen function to give information about a specific number. The art is in the choice: a test function close to the extreme case gives a nearly sharp result. This idea runs through analysis, physics and engineering, from estimating eigenvalues to the finite element method. Try this next A quartic. Use f(x) = x^2(π - x)^2 in (*) . Show that it gives only π^2 ≤ 12 . Why is this test function worse than the parabola? (Compare its shape with sin x .) Two sine waves. Check (*) directly for f(x) = sin x + sin 2x , computing both sides. A different interval. Show by a substitution that if g(0) = g(L) = 0 then displaystyleint_0^L g^2 ≤ (L^2)/(π^2)int_0^L (g')^2 . What does this say about strings of different lengths? Rayleigh’s method. harder Take f(x) = x(π - x) + λ x^2(π - x)^2 and choose λ to make the bound on π^2 as good as possible. (The algebra is heavy; a computer algebra system helps.) Further reading T. W. Körner, Fourier Analysis (Cambridge University Press). A wonderful, discursive book on Fourier series and their applications, written by a Cambridge analyst. Hardy, Littlewood & Pólya, Inequalities (Cambridge University Press). Chapter 7 discusses Wirtinger’s inequality and its relatives. Richard Feynman, The Feynman Lectures on Physics , Volume II, Chapter 19 (“The principle of least action”). Feynman’s lecture on minimising integrals, with physical intuition throughout. Free online.

title: What We Have Learned
headings: 1. How do you know an argument is correct? 2. How do you prove an inequality? 3. What is a function, really? 4. A toolkit for rigour and inequalities Where next
text: We began with a “proof” that 1 = 2 and three questions: how to know an argument is correct, how to prove inequalities, and what a function really is. Here is what the chapter’s nine questions have taught us. 1. How do you know an argument is correct? Section 3.1 gave us a checklist. At every step, ask three things: is the calculation right? does the step follow logically? what has been assumed without being said? The errors there were typical. Comparing the values at two stationary points says nothing about which is a maximum. Stationary values do not bound a function on an infinite domain. The fundamental theorem of calculus needs a continuous integrand. And an argument can arrive at a “correct-looking” answer by accident. The same vigilance ran through the rest of the chapter. Section 3.7 showed by counterexample that dropping a hypothesis ( f(0) = f(π) = 0 ) breaks an inequality. In Section 3.8 , the assumption that the function is differentiable was essential: without it, Cauchy’s functional equation has wild solutions that nobody can write down. And in Section 3.6 and Section 3.3 , the equality conditions told us whether a bound was best possible, which is the kind of question a careful mathematician always asks. 2. How do you prove an inequality? We met the classical inequalities from several directions, and saw how they are related. Squares are non-negative. The two-number AM–GM is just (a - b)^2 ≥ 0 . Cauchy’s forward–backward induction built the general case from it ( Section 3.2 ). Convexity. A concave curve lies above its chords. That one fact gives Jensen’s inequality, and with the logarithm it gives AM–GM in a line; with sin x it gives a sharp inequality for triangles ( Section 3.3 ). Areas. The area under a curve plus the area beside it covers a rectangle. That gives Young’s inequality, which leads to Hölder and Cauchy–Schwarz ( Section 3.4 ). Shape of a graph. Rewriting a^b versus b^a as a comparison of ( x)/(x) at two points settled π^e versus e^π ( Section 3.5 ). Interpolation and the triangle inequality. Writing the derivative in terms of values, then bounding term by term, gave Markov’s inequality for quadratics ( Section 3.6 ). Test functions. Applying a general inequality to a cleverly chosen function gave π^2 ≤ 10 and π ≤ (22)/(7) ( Section 3.7 ). Choosing among these is a skill that comes with practice. A rough guide: products and sums suggest AM–GM; averages of function values suggest Jensen; a function and its inverse suggest Young; a comparison of two expressions of the same form suggests finding the single function behind them. 3. What is a function, really? The last two sections answered this in two ways. In Section 3.8 , e^kx and tanh kx were not given by formulas at all; they were the only differentiable functions obeying certain addition laws. That is a deeper kind of understanding than a formula: it explains why these functions keep appearing, in compound interest and in Einstein’s velocity addition. In Section 3.9 we went further and invented a function, the inverse of xe^x , because the functions we had were not enough to solve a natural family of equations. Every function on your calculator was once new in the same way. 4. A toolkit for rigour and inequalities Method Where you used it Checking every step and every hypothesis Plausible wrong arguments (3.1) Local versus global behaviour Stationary points and limits at infinity (3.1) Forward–backward induction AM–GM (3.2) Padding with extra terms AM–GM (3.2, 3.3) Jensen’s inequality Triangles; AM–GM (3.3) Comparing areas Young’s inequality (3.4) Separating variables into one function π^e versus e^π (3.5) Triangle inequality, equality cases Markov’s inequality (3.6) Test functions π^2 ≤ 10 (3.7) Functional equations e^x and tanh x (3.8) Inverse functions and substitutions The W function (3.9) Where next The calculus of variations, glimpsed in Section 3.7 , is the subject of Section 4.7 . The geometry behind tanh and its addition law appears in Section 7.6 . Chapter 4 takes the careful attitude of this chapter to integration itself, starting from what an integral actually is. If you want to go further before university J. Michael Steele, The Cauchy–Schwarz Master Class : the best introduction to inequalities, built entirely from problems. Daniel Velleman, How to Prove It : a systematic guide to writing correct proofs. Michael Spivak, Calculus : rigorous calculus from the ground up; many Cambridge students read it the summer before they arrive. E. A. Maxwell, Fallacies in Mathematics : for practice in spotting what has gone wrong. Von Neumann joked that in mathematics you don’t understand things, you just get used to them. There is some truth in it: the precise definitions and careful arguments of this chapter can feel strange at first. But getting used to them is exactly what turns a student who can calculate into a mathematician who can be sure. The proof that 1 = 2 will never fool you again; the aim of a mathematics degree is to make every subtler error just as easy to see.

headings: 4.1 What Is an Integral? 4.2 Building Trigonometry from an Integral 4.3 22/7 Is Bigger Than π 4.4 Wallis, Beta and the Factorial of a Half 4.5 The Sophomore’s Dream 4.6 Integrals With No Formula 4.7 The Calculus of Variations 4.8 Slicing a Spherical Loaf 4.9 Holditch’s Theorem
text: These are brief answers and hints, not full solutions: they give the result and the key step, so that you can check your own work. Try each exercise properly before looking. 4.1 What Is an Integral? The sum is the total area of n rectangles of width frac1n under y = f(x) on [1, 2] . With f(x) = frac1x , frac1nsum(1)/(1 + m/n) = sum(1)/(n + m) → 2 . The second sum is frac1nsum(1)/(1 + (m/n)^2) → int_0^1(dx)/(1 + x^2) = fracπ4 . The upper sum with n strips is frac ansum_r=1^nbigl((ra)/(n)bigr)^2 = (a^3(n + 1)(2n + 1))/(6n^2) , and the lower sum is the same with n - 1 in place of n + 1 in the first factor; both tend to (a^3)/(3) . The terms telescope: r(r + 1)cdots(r + k) - (r - 1)rcdots(r + k - 1) = (k + 1)\,r(r + 1)cdots(r + k - 1) . sum_r=1^nr^5 = (n^2(n + 1)^2(2n^2 + 2n - 1))/(12) . 4.2 Building Trigonometry from an Integral The derivative is -f(a - x)f(x) + f(a - x)f(x) = 0 , so f(a - x)f(x) = f(a) ; put a = x + y . For the cosine, with y fixed let p(x) = c(x + y) - c(x)c(y) + s(x)s(y) and q(x) = s(x + y) - s(x)c(y) - c(x)s(y) . Then p' = -q and q' = p , so p^2 + q^2 is constant, and it is 0 at x = 0 . (dy)/(du) = (1 + u^2)^-3/2 and sqrt1 - y^2 = (1 + u^2)^-1/2 , so fracdysqrt1 - y^2 = (du)/(1 + u^2) . Then S((1)/(sqrt2)) = T(1) , and part (i) with x = 1 gives T(1) = frac12T_∞ . With a = frac12 and x = frac13 , (x + a)/(1 - ax) = 1 , so T(frac13) = T(1) - T(frac12) . (1)/(1 + u^2) ≤ 1 on [0, 1] and ≤ (1)/(u^2) on [1, x] , so for x ≥ 1 , T(x) ≤ 1 + (1 - frac1x) < 2 ; for 0 < x < 1 , T(x) < T(1) ≤ 1 . (The bound 1 + int_1^x u^-2\,du is not valid for x < 1 : at x = frac12 it equals 0 .) T is increasing and bounded, so it has a limit. 4.3 22/7 Is Bigger Than π (22)/(7) - π approx 0.001264 , between (1)/(1260) approx 0.000794 and (1)/(630) approx 0.001587 . ((4!)^2)/(9!) = (576)/(362\,880) = (1)/(630) . (x(1 - x)^2)/(1 + x^2) = x - 2 + (2)/(1 + x^2) , which integrates to frac12 - 2 + fracπ2 . Similarly (x^2(1 - x)^4)/(1 + x^2) = x^4 - 4x^3 + 5x^2 - 4 + (4)/(1 + x^2) , which integrates to frac15 - 1 + frac53 - 4 + π = π - (47)/(15) . Both integrals are positive. The integrands are much larger than (x^4(1 - x)^4)/(1 + x^2) (whose maximum is about 0.003 ), so the errors fracπ2 - frac32 approx 0.07 and π - (47)/(15) approx 0.008 are larger. Polynomial division leaves the remainder (16)/(1 + x^2) , which integrates to 4π ; the integral is 4π - (188684)/(15015) approx 3.6 × 10^-6 , so π approx 3.14159174 . 4.4 Wallis, Beta and the Factorial of a Half u_2m = (1 · 3 cdots (2m - 1))/(2 · 4 cdots 2m)·fracπ2 and u_2m+1 = (2 · 4 cdots 2m)/(3 · 5 cdots (2m + 1)) . Then 1 < fracu_2mu_2m+1 < fracu_2m-1u_2m+1 = (2m + 1)/(2m) , so the ratio tends to 1 , which rearranges to fracπ2 = prod_k ≥ 1((2k)^2)/((2k - 1)(2k + 1)) . Integration by parts gives I_n = (n)/(n + 1)int_0^1x^n+1(1 - x)^n-1\,dx , and writing x^n+1(1 - x)^n-1 = x^n(1 - x)^n-1 - x^n(1 - x)^n together with symmetry leads to I_n = (n)/(2(2n + 1))I_n-1 ; induction gives ((n!)^2)/((2n + 1)!) . With x = sin^2θ , I_1/2 = int_0^π/22sin^2θcos^2θ\,dθ = fracπ8 . The formula suggests bigl((frac12)!bigr)^2/2! = fracπ8 , so (frac12)! = (sqrtπ)/(2) (which is Gamma(frac32) ). Symmetry from x mapsto 1 - x ; the recurrence from x^p = x^p-1 - x^p-1(1 - x) ; and with x = (t)/(1 + t) , 1 - x = (1)/(1 + t) and dx = (dt)/((1 + t)^2) . The integral is b(frac52, frac72) ; using the recurrence and symmetry to reduce to b(frac12, frac12) = π gives (3π)/(256) . From part (i)’s explicit value, u_2m = ((2m)!)/((2^mm!)^2)·fracπ2 = binom2mmfracπ2^2m+1 . Then 2mu_2m^2 → fracπ2 gives binom2mm^2 approx frac4^2mπ m . For m = 10 : binom2010 = 184\,756 , against frac4^10sqrt10π approx 187\,079 (about 1.3\% high). 4.5 The Sophomore’s Dream x^-x = e^-x x = sum_n ≥ 0((-x x)^n)/(n!) , and int_0^1(x^n(- x)^n)/(n!)\,dx = frac1(n + 1)^n+1 (substitute x = e^-u ). So the integral is sum_n ≥ 1n^-n approx 1.2913 . (d)/(dx)x^x = x^x( x + 1) , zero at x = frac1e ; the value is (e^-1)^e^-1 = e^-1/e approx 0.692 . The terms are (1)/(n^n) . Stopping after 7 terms gives error less than (1)/(8^8) approx 6 × 10^-8 , enough; after 6 terms the bound (1)/(7^7) approx 1.2 × 10^-6 is not. So 7 terms. By parts: int_0^1x^2 x\,dx = bigl[(x^3 x)/(3)bigr]_0^1 - int_0^1(x^2)/(3)\,dx = -frac19 . In general int_0^1x^n x\,dx = -(1)/((n + 1)^2) , and ( x)/(1 - x) = sum_n ≥ 0x^n x . 4.6 Integrals With No Formula Differentiate: (d)/(dx)(e^x)/(x + 1) = (xe^x)/((x + 1)^2) , and (d)/(dx)((x - 1)e^x)/(x + 1) = e^xBigl((x - 1)/(x + 1) + (2)/((x + 1)^2)Bigr) = ((x^2 + 1)e^x)/((x + 1)^2) . (d)/(dx)bigl(Pe^-x^2bigr) = (P' - 2xP)e^-x^2 , and P' - 2xP has degree degP + 1 ≥ 1 (for P ≠ 0 ), so it cannot equal 1 . If R = P/Q (in lowest terms) had a pole of order k ≥ 1 at 0 , then R' + R would have a pole of order k + 1 ≥ 2 there, but frac1x has a pole of order 1 . If R has no pole at 0 , neither has R' + R . Either way (Re^x)' ≠ (e^x)/(x) . Differentiating (Pe^x)/(x + 1) gives e^x((x + 1)P' + xP)/((x + 1)^2) . At x = -1 : f(-1) = -P(-1) , and f' = (x + 1)P'' + (x + 1)P' + P gives f'(-1) = P(-1) . For x^3 - 2 : -3 + 3 = 0 ; for x : -1 + 1 = 0 ; for x^2 + 1 : 2 - 2 = 0 . The condition is also sufficient: the map P mapsto (x + 1)P' + xP from polynomials of degree less than d to degree at most d is injective, so its image has dimension d , and it lies inside the d -dimensional space of f with f(-1) + f'(-1) = 0 ; so it is that whole space. 4.7 The Calculus of Variations With y = cos(π x)/(2) , J = (π^2)/(4)int_0^1sin^2 - a^2int_0^1cos^2 = frac12bigl((π^2)/(4) - a^2bigr) < 0 . J(y + εeta) = J(y) + 2εint_0^1(y'eta' - a^2yeta) + ε^2J(eta) ; a minimum at ε = 0 forces the linear term to vanish. Integrating by parts, -y'(0)eta(0) - int_0^1(y'' + a^2y)eta = 0 for every eta with eta(1) = 0 , which forces y'' + a^2y = 0 and y'(0) = 0 . With x = Lu , int_0^Lbigl((y')^2 - a^2y^2bigr)\,dx = frac1Lint_0^1bigl((Y')^2 - (aL)^2Y^2bigr)\,du , so the condition is aL ≤ fracπ2 . (At aL = fracπ2 the integral is still never negative, as in the main text, but y = cos(π x)/(2L) makes it zero; for aL > fracπ2 that same function makes it negative.) The cycloid is x = R(θ - sinθ) , y = R(1 - cosθ) . For the tautochrone, see Section 11.4 : in terms of arc length the motion is exactly simple harmonic. 4.8 Slicing a Spherical Loaf V/A = (frac43π a^3)/(4π a^2) = frac a3 . But a remaining piece of height t has A = 2π at and V = frac13π t^2(3a - t) , so V/A = (t(3a - t))/(6a) , which is largest, (3a)/(8) , at t = frac32a : bigger than frac a3 . The band has height 2Rsin23.4^circ out of the sphere’s 2R , so the fraction is sin23.4^circ approx 0.40 . For y = sqrt x , ysqrt1 + (y')^2 = sqrtx + frac14 , not constant. ysqrt1 + (y')^2 = c gives (y')^2 = (c^2)/(y^2) - 1 , whose solutions are y = c (a cylinder) and the circles (x - x_0)^2 + y^2 = c^2 (spheres). The sphere has volume frac43π a^3 and the cylinder π a^2 · 2a = 2π a^3 ; the ratio is frac23 . 4.9 Holditch’s Theorem frac12int_0^2π(pcos t · qcos t + qsin t · psin t)\,dt = frac12 · 2π pq = π pq . The triangles formed by joining the ends of the two chords are similar (equal angles subtended by the same arcs), so PA · PB = PC · PD . For a circle of radius R with P at distance r from the centre, the diameter through P gives (R - r)(R + r) , so ab = R^2 - r^2 and the ring has area π R^2 - π r^2 = π ab . If a = b then f = π(a - b) = 0 , and the ring’s area is π a^2 = (π L^2)/(4) : the area of the circle with the rod as diameter. Along the two sides through O , x\,dy - y\,dx = 0 . On the third side, parametrised by (x_1, y_1) + s(x_2 - x_1, y_2 - y_1) for 0 ≤ s ≤ 1 , it is (x_1y_2 - x_2y_1)\,ds . So the area is frac12|x_1y_2 - x_2y_1| .

title: Holditch's Theorem
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on The fine print The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2011, Question 5 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/11-s3-q5 The hook Take any oval, any shape at all as long as it is convex, and slide a rod of fixed length round inside it, keeping both ends on the curve. Paint a dot on the rod, dividing it into lengths a and b . As the rod goes once round, the dot traces out a smaller oval. What is the area of the ring between the two curves? The astonishing answer is π ab , whatever the shape of the original curve . A long thin oval, an egg, a rounded triangle: the area of the ring is always the same, and it depends only on where the dot is on the rod. The result was found in 1858 by the Reverend Hamnet Holditch, a fellow of Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, and it is one of the most surprising theorems in elementary geometry. This question proves it with a single formula for area. Before you start Check the theorem in the simplest case. If mathcalC is a circle of radius R , what curve does P trace, and what is the area of the ring? By symmetry, P traces a circle of some radius r with the same centre. The rod AB is a chord of the big circle through P , and the intersecting chords theorem (or “power of a point”) says that for any chord through P , PA × PB = R^2 - r^2 . So ab = R^2 - r^2 , and the ring has area π R^2 - π r^2 = π ab . The theorem says this remains true for every convex curve, not just circles. Working it through Stage 1 Area from coordinates With x = rcosθ and y = rsinθ , all functions of t , compute xdot y - ydot x , where dots denote (d)/(dt) . dot x = dot rcosθ - rsinθ\,dotθ and dot y = dot rsinθ + rcosθ\,dotθ . Then xdot y - ydot x = rcosθ\,(dot rsinθ + rcosθ\,dotθ) - rsinθ\,(dot rcosθ - rsinθ\,dotθ) = r^2dotθ. So frac12int r^2\,dθ = frac12int r^2dotθ\,dt = frac12int (xdot y - ydot x)\,dt . ■ This formula needs no polar coordinates, only the cartesian position as a function of a parameter. When a point goes once anticlockwise round a closed curve enclosing O , it gives the area inside the curve. Stage 2 The ends of the rod The rod points in the direction (cos t, sin t) from A to B , with P a distance a from A and b from B . So A = (x - acos t,\; y - asin t), qquad B = (x + bcos t,\; y + bsin t). Stage 3 The area swept by OA Apply (*) to A . Expand x_Adot y_A - y_Adot x_A and sort the terms by powers of a . With x_A = x - acos t , y_A = y - asin t , we have dot x_A = dot x + asin t and dot y_A = dot y - acos t . Expanding, beginaligned x_Adot y_A - y_Adot x_A &= (x - acos t)(dot y - acos t) - (y - asin t)(dot x + asin t) \\ &= (xdot y - ydot x) + a^2(cos^2 t + sin^2 t) - abigl[(x + dot y)cos t + (y - dot x)sin tbigr]. endaligned Integrating from 0 to 2π and halving: the first term gives [P] , the second gives frac12 a^2 · 2π = π a^2 , and the third gives -af . So [A] = [P] + π a^2 - af. qed Now find [B] . ( Hint: B is obtained from the formula for A by replacing a with what?) B = (x + bcos t, y + bsin t) is the formula for A with a replaced by -b . So [B] = [P] + π b^2 + bf. Stage 4 Eliminating f Both A and B go once round the same curve mathcalC . What does that tell you about [A] and [B] ? Each of A and B travels once anticlockwise round mathcalC as t goes from 0 to 2π , so [A] = [B] = area(mathcalC) . Equating the two expressions, π a^2 - af = π b^2 + bf quadLongrightarrowquad f(a + b) = π(a^2 - b^2) quadLongrightarrowquad f = π(a - b). Since P goes once round mathcalD , [P] = area(mathcalD) , and area(mathcalC) - area(mathcalD) = [A] - [P] = π a^2 - aπ(a - b) = π ab. qed The mysterious quantity f , which depends on the shape of the curve, was never computed: it was eliminated.
