title: Polynomials Whose Roots Are Roots of Unity
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Integer coefficients, and a surprise Irreducibility The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2010, Question 3 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/10-s3-q3 The hook The n th roots of unity, the solutions of z^n = 1 , sit at the vertices of a regular n -gon. But they are not all alike. Among the 12 th roots of unity, for instance, 1 is already a first root of unity, -1 is a square root of unity, i is a fourth root, and only four of the twelve, the primitive ones, need all twelve steps to get back to 1 . Sorting the roots of unity by the number of steps they need, and building a polynomial from each class, produces the cyclotomic polynomials (“circle-dividing”, from the Greek). They are the basic building blocks of z^n - 1 , in the same way that primes are the building blocks of whole numbers, and they lie behind Gauss’s construction of the regular 17 -gon ( Section 6.2 ), the roots-of-unity filter ( Section 5.2 ) and a good deal of modern number theory. Before you start Every n th root of unity satisfies z^n = 1 . But the smallest positive power that gives 1 might be less than n . For each of the four 4th roots of unity, 1 , i , -1 , -i , what is that smallest power? 1^1 = 1 , (-1)^2 = 1 , and i^4 = (-i)^4 = 1 with no smaller power working. So the smallest powers are 1 , 4 , 2 , 4 . This smallest power is called the order of the root of unity, and the primitive n th roots of unity are exactly those of order n . The key fact for the whole question is that every root of unity has exactly one order . Working it through Stage 1 The first few The primitive 4th roots are i and -i , so C_4(x) = (x - i)(x + i) = x^2 + 1 . ■ Which roots of unity have order 1 , 2 , 3 , 5 and 6 ? (Draw the 6 th roots of unity and sort them by order.) Order 1 : just 1 , so C_1(x) = x - 1 . Order 2 : just -1 , so C_2(x) = x + 1 . Order 3 : the cube roots of unity other than 1 , that is, the roots of (x^3 - 1)/(x - 1) . So C_3(x) = x^2 + x + 1 . Order 5 : the fifth roots other than 1 , which are the roots of (x^5 - 1)/(x - 1) , so C_5(x) = x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + x + 1 . Order 6 : of the sixth roots e^kpii/3 , k = 0, ldots, 5 , those with k = 0 , 3 have orders 1 , 2 , and k = 2 , 4 have order 3 . That leaves e^pii/3 , so C_6(x) = (x - e^iπ/3)(x - e^-iπ/3) = x^2 - 2xcostfracπ3 + 1 = x^2 - x + 1. qed Stage 2 Which n gives x^4 + 1 ? The roots of x^4 + 1 = 0 satisfy x^4 = -1 , so x^8 = 1 but x^4 ≠ 1 . Their order divides 8 but not 4 , so it is 8 . Conversely, a root of order 8 satisfies x^8 = 1 , x^4 ≠ 1 , so x^4 = -1 . There are four primitive 8 th roots and four roots of x^4 + 1 , so n = 8 . ■ Stage 3 Primes If p is prime, the order of a p th root of unity divides p , so it is 1 or p . Every p th root except 1 is therefore primitive, and C_p(x) = (x^p - 1)/(x - 1) = x^p-1 + x^p-2 + cdots + x + 1. qed Stage 4 No cyclotomic polynomial is a product of two others Suppose C_q = C_rC_s . Take a root of C_r . What is its order? What does the identity say about its order? What does that force? Every root of C_r (there is at least one, since e^2pii/r is primitive) is a root of C_rC_s = C_q , so it has order q . But it also has order r , and a root of unity has only one order, so r = q . Then C_q = C_q\,C_s , and since C_q is not the zero polynomial, C_s = 1 . That is impossible, because C_s has at least one root, e^2pii/s . So no such q , r , s exist. ■ Looking back Sort by order. Every root of unity has a unique order, and grouping by order splits the roots of z^n - 1 into disjoint classes. Define a polynomial by its roots. Each C_n was pinned down by saying exactly which numbers are its roots. Uniqueness gives impossibility. Part (iv) needed only one idea: a root cannot have two different orders. What’s really going on Factorising x^n - 1 Every n th root of unity has some order d that divides n , and every d th root of unity of order d is an n th root of unity when d mid n . So the roots of x^n - 1 split into classes by order, giving x^n - 1 = prod_d mid nC_d(x). For example x^6 - 1 = C_1C_2C_3C_6 = (x - 1)(x + 1)(x^2 + x + 1)(x^2 - x + 1) . Figure 6.1.1 shows the twelve 12 th roots of unity sorted in this way. The number of primitive n th roots, which is the degree of C_n , is the number of k between 1 and n with no common factor with n : Euler’s totient function varphi(n) . Comparing degrees gives the identity sum_d mid nvarphi(d) = n . Integer coefficients, and a surprise It is not obvious from the definition, but every cyclotomic polynomial has integer coefficients. (Use the factorisation of x^n - 1 and induction: C_n is x^n - 1 divided by a product of earlier cyclotomic polynomials, and long division of integer polynomials by monic integer polynomials keeps the coefficients integers.) For a long time all known examples had coefficients 0 , 1 and -1 . The first exception is C_105 , which contains the term -2x^7 , found by Migotti in 1883; 105 = 3 × 5 × 7 is the smallest number with three distinct odd prime factors. In fact the coefficients of cyclotomic polynomials can be made as large as you like. Irreducibility Part (iv) shows that no cyclotomic polynomial is a product of two others. Something much stronger is true: C_n cannot be factorised at all into polynomials with rational coefficients of lower degree. Gauss proved this for prime n (it follows from Eisenstein’s criterion , which you will meet in a first algebra course), and Kronecker and Dedekind for general n . This irreducibility is what makes the cyclotomic polynomials the “primes” among polynomials related to roots of unity, and it is the starting point for the Galois theory of roots of unity. The thinking skill Classify, then build Sort the objects in a problem into classes with a single, well-defined invariant, and build structure class by class. Here the invariant was the order of a root of unity. Because each root has exactly one order, the classes do not overlap, and x^n - 1 splits as a product over them. The same pattern (a unique invariant giving a disjoint decomposition) underlies prime factorisation and the classification of finite abelian groups. Try this next Check the factorisation. Verify that (x - 1)(x + 1)(x^2 + x + 1)(x^2 - x + 1) = x^6 - 1 , and that x^12 - 1 factorises as in Figure 6.1.1. Twice a prime. Show that if p is an odd prime then C_2p(x) = C_p(-x) . Check this for p = 3 . Totients. Show that varphi(p^k) = p^k - p^k-1 for a prime p , and that C_p^k(x) = C_pbigl(x^p^k-1bigr) . Use this to find C_9 . A longer one. harder Using x^15 - 1 = C_1C_3C_5C_15 , show that C_15(x) = x^8 - x^7 + x^5 - x^4 + x^3 - x + 1 . Further reading Ian Stewart, Galois Theory (CRC Press). The standard undergraduate introduction; cyclotomic polynomials and the regular polygon appear early. Harold Davenport, The Higher Arithmetic (Cambridge University Press). Includes roots of unity and their arithmetic. Marcus du Sautoy, Finding Moonshine (Fourth Estate). A popular account of symmetry and group theory, including the story of Galois.

title: Differentiation from Axioms
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Calculus without limits Automatic differentiation The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 1992, Question 4 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/92-s2-q4 The hook What is differentiation? At school it is defined by a limit, lim_h → 0(f(x+h) - f(x))/(h) , and then you learn rules: the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, the product rule, and so on. This question turns that upside down. Forget limits entirely. Suppose all you know about an operation is that it obeys the sum rule, the product rule and the rule for constants, and that it sends x to 1 . Then, the question shows, it must be differentiation, at least on polynomials. This is the algebraist’s view of calculus: an operation is characterised by the rules it obeys, not by a formula. Operations obeying the product rule are called derivations , and they turn up throughout algebra, geometry and physics. Surprisingly, the same idea is at work inside the software that trains modern machine-learning systems. Before you start Rule (i) is the product rule. How could the product rule tell you anything about a constant? (Think of a constant as a product.) The number 1 equals 1 × 1 . Applying the product rule to 1 × 1 relates lozenge 1 to itself, and that will force it to be zero. In general, the trick with axioms like these is to apply them to cleverly chosen simple inputs. Working it through Stage 1 Constants Apply rule (i) with f = g = 1 . Then use rule (iv) for any other constant. lozenge 1 = lozenge(1 · 1) = 1 · lozenge 1 + 1 · lozenge 1 = 2lozenge 1 , so lozenge 1 = 0 . For any constant λ , rule (iv) gives lozengeλ = lozenge(λ · 1) = λlozenge 1 = 0 . ■ Stage 2 Powers lozenge x^2 = lozenge(x · x) = xlozenge x + xlozenge x = 2x , using rule (iii). Then lozenge x^3 = lozenge(x^2 · x) = xlozenge x^2 + x^2lozenge x = x · 2x + x^2 = 3x^2. Prove by induction that lozenge x^n = nx^n-1 for every positive integer n . The case n = 1 is rule (iii). If lozenge x^n = nx^n-1 , then lozenge x^n+1 = lozenge(x^n · x) = xlozenge x^n + x^nlozenge x = x · nx^n-1 + x^n = (n + 1)x^n. qed Stage 3 All polynomials A general polynomial is h(x) = a_0 + a_1x + cdots + a_mx^m . By rule (ii) (applied repeatedly) and rule (iv), beginaligned lozengeh(x) &= lozenge a_0 + a_1lozenge x + a_2lozenge x^2 + cdots + a_mlozenge x^m \\ &= a_1 + 2a_2x + cdots + ma_mx^m-1 = h'(x). qed endaligned Looking back Axioms determine the operation. Four rules, with no mention of limits, pinned down lozenge completely on polynomials. Generators. Every polynomial is built from constants and x using addition and multiplication. Knowing what lozenge does to the building blocks, and how it interacts with the building operations, determines it everywhere. Induction along the construction. The proof followed the way polynomials are built: powers by repeated multiplication, then sums. What’s really going on Derivations An operation D on an algebraic system that is additive and satisfies the product rule D(fg) = fD(g) + gD(f) is called a derivation . The question shows that on polynomials, a derivation that kills constants is completely determined by D(x) : in fact D(h) = h'(x)\,D(x) , so the only freedom is the choice of the polynomial D(x) . Rule (iii) fixes D(x) = 1 . Derivations appear across mathematics: in geometry, a vector field on a surface can be defined as a derivation on the functions on that surface (it differentiates functions in the direction of the field); in algebra, derivations of a structure measure its “infinitesimal symmetries”; in physics, the commutator [A, B] = AB - BA of quantum mechanics is a derivation in each argument. Calculus without limits The algebraic derivative works in settings where limits make no sense at all. Over a finite field, such as arithmetic modulo a prime p , there are no limits, but the formal derivative of a polynomial is defined by the same rules and still detects repeated roots: a polynomial f has a repeated root exactly when f and f' have a common factor. That is how one shows, for example, that x^n - 1 has no repeated roots when p nmid n , a fact needed to define the cyclotomic polynomials of Section 6.1 over finite fields. The same idea is used in coding theory and cryptography. Automatic differentiation Here is a modern application. Invent a number ε with ε^2 = 0 but ε ≠ 0 , and do arithmetic with dual numbers a + bε . Then (a + bε)(c + dε) = ac + (ad + bc)ε : the ε -part follows exactly the product rule. So for any polynomial, f(x + ε) = f(x) + f'(x)\,ε, and evaluating f at the dual number x + ε computes the value and the derivative at the same time, exactly, with no limits and no rounding error from small differences (Figure 6.5.1). This is called forward-mode automatic differentiation . Its cousin, reverse mode, is the algorithm ( backpropagation ) used to train neural networks with billions of parameters: every time such a system learns, it is applying the product and chain rules, as derivations, step by step. The thinking skill Characterise by properties Describe an operation by the rules it obeys, then show that the rules determine it uniquely. This is the axiomatic method, central to university algebra. Its power is that anything you prove from the axioms applies to every operation that satisfies them, whether it is differentiation of polynomials, of functions on a surface, or something not yet invented. Try this next A different derivation. Suppose lozenge satisfies rules (i), (ii) and (iv), but lozenge x = x instead of 1 . Show that lozengeh(x) = x\,h'(x) . What does lozenge do to x^n ? The quotient rule. Extend lozenge to rational functions f/g , assuming rule (i) still holds. By applying rule (i) to g · (f)/(g) = f , derive the quotient rule. Repeated roots. Show that if (x - a)^2 divides a polynomial f , then x - a divides f' . Use this to show that x^n - 1 has no repeated roots. Dual numbers. Use dual numbers to compute f(2) and f'(2) for f(x) = (x^2 + 1)^3 , and check with the chain rule. Further reading Peter Cameron, Introduction to Algebra (Oxford University Press). Rings, polynomials and fields at first-year level, with the formal derivative. Andreas Griewank & Andrea Walther, Evaluating Derivatives (SIAM). The standard reference on automatic differentiation. Advanced. Michael Nielsen, Neural Networks and Deep Learning (free online). Chapter 2 explains backpropagation clearly.

title: A Polynomial for sqrt2 + sqrt3 + sqrt5
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Doubling the cube Algebraic numbers form a field The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 2023, Question 4 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP II paper in OCR’s download of the 2023 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/707102-2023-past-papers.zip The hook sqrt2 is a root of x^2 - 2 , a polynomial with integer coefficients. So is sqrt3 , of x^2 - 3 . Is sqrt2 + sqrt3 also the root of some polynomial with integer coefficients? What about sqrt2 + sqrt3 + sqrt5 , or sqrt[3]2 + sqrt[3]3 ? Numbers that are roots of polynomials with integer coefficients are called algebraic , and this question shows, by hands-on elimination, that sums of algebraic numbers are algebraic. The degrees that come out, 4 , 8 , 6 , 9 , are not accidents. They measure how “complicated” each number is, and that measurement, the degree of a field extension , is what finally settled the ancient Greek problems of doubling the cube and trisecting the angle. Before you start To find a polynomial with sqrt2 as a root, you square x = sqrt2 to get rid of the square root. How might you get rid of two different square roots, one at a time? Isolate one square root and square, which removes it; then isolate the other and square again. Each squaring may double the degree. That is the whole strategy of the question: eliminate the radicals one at a time. Working it through Stage 1 Two square roots If (x - sqrt2)^2 = 3 , then x^2 - 2sqrt2\,x + 2 = 3 , so x^2 - 1 = 2sqrt2\,x . Squaring removes the remaining square root: (x^2 - 1)^2 = 8x^2 , that is, x^4 - 10x^2 + 1 = 0. qed And x = sqrt2 + sqrt3 satisfies (x - sqrt2)^2 = (sqrt3)^2 = 3 , so f(sqrt2 + sqrt3) = 0 . ■ Stage 2 Three square roots Let x = sqrt2 + sqrt3 + sqrt5 , so x - sqrt5 = sqrt2 + sqrt3 is a root of f . Write f(x - sqrt5) = 0 in the form P(x) + sqrt5\,Q(x) = 0 . How do you then eliminate sqrt5 ? Expand using (x - sqrt5)^2 = x^2 + 5 - 2sqrt5 x and (x - sqrt5)^4 = bigl(x^2 + 5 - 2sqrt5xbigr)^2 = x^4 + 30x^2 + 25 - 4sqrt5\,x(x^2 + 5) : f(x - sqrt5) = bigl(x^4 + 30x^2 + 25bigr) - 4sqrt5\,x(x^2 + 5) - 10bigl(x^2 + 5bigr) + 20sqrt5\,x + 1. Collecting, P(x) = x^4 + 20x^2 - 24 and Q(x) = -4x^3 - 20x + 20x = -4x^3 . So x^4 + 20x^2 - 24 = 4sqrt5\,x^3 . Squaring, bigl(x^4 + 20x^2 - 24bigr)^2 = 80x^6, and expanding gives g(x) = x^8 - 40x^6 + 352x^4 - 960x^2 + 576. qed (Check: (x^4 + 20x^2 - 24)^2 = x^8 + 40x^6 + 352x^4 - 960x^2 + 576 , using 400 - 48 = 352 , and subtracting 80x^6 gives g .) Stage 3 A cubic and a square root If x = a + sqrt2 , then x - sqrt2 is a root of t^3 - 3t + 1 . Substitute, separate the terms with and without sqrt2 , and square. (x - sqrt2)^3 = x^3 - 3sqrt2\,x^2 + 6x - 2sqrt2 , so (x - sqrt2)^3 - 3(x - sqrt2) + 1 = bigl(x^3 + 3x + 1bigr) - sqrt2bigl(3x^2 - 1bigr) = 0. Hence (x^3 + 3x + 1)^2 = 2(3x^2 - 1)^2 . Expanding, x^6 + 6x^4 + 2x^3 + 9x^2 + 6x + 1 = 18x^4 - 12x^2 + 2 , so h(x) = x^6 - 12x^4 + 2x^3 + 21x^2 + 6x - 1. qed The same argument works for b + sqrt2 and c + sqrt2 , since only the fact that a is a root of t^3 - 3t + 1 was used. (The other three roots of h are a - sqrt2 , b - sqrt2 and c - sqrt2 , which came in when we squared.) Stage 4 Two cube roots Let x = sqrt[3]2 + sqrt[3]3 . Cube both sides. Can you write the result in terms of x and a single cube root? Using (u + v)^3 = u^3 + v^3 + 3uv(u + v) with u = sqrt[3]2 , v = sqrt[3]3 : x^3 = 2 + 3 + 3sqrt[3]6\,x, qquadsoqquad x^3 - 5 = 3sqrt[3]6\,x. Cubing again removes the last cube root: (x^3 - 5)^3 = 27 · 6\,x^3 = 162x^3 . Expanding (x^3 - 5)^3 = x^9 - 15x^6 + 75x^3 - 125 , k(x) = x^9 - 15x^6 - 87x^3 - 125. qed Looking back Eliminate one radical at a time. Isolate a radical, raise to the appropriate power, and repeat. Separate rational and irrational parts. Writing an expression as P + sqrt5\,Q and then using P^2 = 5Q^2 is the key move. Squaring adds extra roots. Each squaring brings in “conjugate” roots, such as a - sqrt2 alongside a + sqrt2 . The final polynomial has all of them as roots. What’s really going on Fields and their degrees The set mathbbQ(sqrt2) of all numbers p + qsqrt2 with p , q rational is closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication and division (by non-zero numbers): it is a field . It is a two-dimensional “vector space” over mathbbQ , with basis 1, sqrt2 , so we say it has degree 2 over mathbbQ . Adjoining sqrt3 gives mathbbQ(sqrt2, sqrt3) , with basis 1, sqrt2, sqrt3, sqrt6 and degree 4 ; adjoining sqrt5 as well gives degree 8 (Figure 6.3.1). The tower law says degrees multiply up a tower of fields. The degree of the field generated by a number equals the degree of its minimal polynomial , the lowest-degree polynomial with rational coefficients that it satisfies. One can show that the polynomials f and g in this question are minimal, so sqrt2 + sqrt3 has degree 4 and sqrt2 + sqrt3 + sqrt5 has degree 8 : in fact the single number sqrt2 + sqrt3 + sqrt5 generates the whole degree- 8 field. Doubling the cube Ruler-and-compass constructions can only produce lengths obtained from rational numbers by repeatedly solving linear and quadratic equations. Each such step gives a field extension of degree 1 or 2 , so by the tower law every constructible length lies in a field of degree a power of 2 , and has degree a power of 2 itself. But sqrt[3]2 has minimal polynomial x^3 - 2 , of degree 3 . Since 3 is not a power of 2 , sqrt[3]2 is not constructible, and the Delian problem of doubling the volume of a cube with ruler and compasses, posed around 430 BC, is impossible. Pierre Wantzel proved this in 1837, together with the impossibility of trisecting a general angle and the classification of constructible polygons ( Section 6.2 ). Two thousand years of attempts were ended by an argument about degrees. Algebraic numbers form a field The method of this question shows, in examples, that sums of algebraic numbers are algebraic. In general this is proved with linear algebra: if α and β have degrees m and n , then all the numbers α^iβ^j (with i < m , j < n ) span a space of dimension at most mn , and the mn + 1 powers 1, α + β, (α + β)^2, ldots must be linearly dependent, which gives a polynomial of degree at most mn . Our degrees 4 = 2 × 2 , 6 = 3 × 2 and 9 = 3 × 3 fit this pattern exactly. Numbers that are not algebraic are called transcendental ; e and π are examples (Hermite, 1873, and Lindemann, 1882), and Lindemann’s theorem that π is transcendental proved that squaring the circle is impossible too. The thinking skill Eliminate, then measure To find a polynomial satisfied by an expression in radicals, remove the radicals one at a time by isolating and raising to a power. Then ask what the degree tells you. The degree of the minimal polynomial is an invariant of the number, and comparing degrees is one of the most powerful ways to prove that something is impossible. Try this next A primitive element. Let y = sqrt2 + sqrt3 . Show that y^3 = 11sqrt2 + 9sqrt3 , and deduce that sqrt2 = frac12(y^3 - 9y) . Hence every number p + qsqrt2 + rsqrt3 + ssqrt6 can be written as a polynomial in y . Mixed roots. Find a polynomial of degree 6 with integer coefficients that has sqrt2 + sqrt[3]3 as a root. Irreducibility. Show that x^4 - 10x^2 + 1 has no rational roots and cannot be written as a product of two quadratics with integer coefficients. ( Hint: try (x^2 + ax + b)(x^2 - ax + c) .) Deduce that sqrt2 + sqrt3 has degree 4 . Trisection. Show that cos 3θ = 4cos^3θ - 3cosθ , and deduce that cos 20^circ is a root of 8x^3 - 6x - 1 = 0 . Assuming this cubic has no rational roots (check this), explain why a 60^circ angle cannot be trisected with ruler and compasses. Further reading Ian Stewart, Galois Theory (CRC Press). Field extensions, the tower law and the classical construction problems, written for undergraduates. Richard Courant & Herbert Robbins, What Is Mathematics? (Oxford University Press). Chapter 3 proves the impossibility of the Greek problems with no prerequisites. Robin Hartshorne, Geometry: Euclid and Beyond (Springer). Ruler-and-compass constructions treated with modern algebra.

title: Gauss's 17-gon
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Which polygons can be constructed? The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 1991, Question 4 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/91-s2-q4 The hook On 30 March 1796, an eighteen-year-old student at Göttingen made the first entry in a mathematical diary he would keep for the rest of his life. He had discovered how to construct a regular 17 -sided polygon with ruler and compasses. The Greeks had known how to construct regular polygons with 3 , 4 , 5 and 15 sides, and doubles of these, and for two thousand years nobody had added a single new one. Carl Friedrich Gauss later said that this discovery decided him to become a mathematician rather than a philologist, and he is said to have asked for a 17 -gon to be carved on his tombstone. The heart of the construction is the second half of this question: the sum of four particular cosines equals fracsqrt17 - 14 , a number involving only a square root. Lengths built from square roots can be constructed with ruler and compasses, and with three more steps of the same kind Gauss could construct cos(2π)/(17) itself. Before you start Why does the first part, about cos(2π)/(5) , appear in a question about the 17 -gon? It is a warm-up, using the same idea on a smaller polygon. For the pentagon, the sum cosφ + cos 2φ satisfies a quadratic with rational coefficients, so it can be found by solving a quadratic. For the 17 -gon, the sum z of four cosines will turn out to satisfy a quadratic too. The trick in both cases is to multiply cosines together and use cos Acos B = frac12bigl(cos(A + B) + cos(A - B)bigr) to turn products back into sums of cosines of the same angles. Working it through Stage 1 The pentagon Expand y^2 = (cosφ + cos 2φ)^2 , turn each product into a sum, and use 5φ = 2π to reduce angles like 3φ and 4φ . y^2 = cos^2φ + 2cosφcos2φ + cos^2 2φ = tfrac12(1 + cos 2φ) + (cos 3φ + cosφ) + tfrac12(1 + cos 4φ). Since 5φ = 2π , cos 3φ = cos(2π - 2φ) = cos 2φ and cos 4φ = cosφ . So y^2 = 1 + tfrac12(cosφ + cos2φ) + (cosφ + cos 2φ) = 1 + tfrac32 y, that is, 2y^2 = 3y + 2 . ■ The roots of 2y^2 - 3y - 2 = (2y + 1)(y - 2) = 0 are y = 2 and y = -frac12 . But y = 2 would need both cosines to equal 1 , which they do not, so y = -frac12 . ■ Stage 2 The seventeenth roots of unity sum to zero sum_k=0^16cos kθ is the real part of sum_k=0^16ω^k , where ω = e^iθ is a primitive 17 th root of unity. That geometric series is fracω^17 - 1ω - 1 = 0 . ■ So sum_k=1^16cos kθ = -1 . Since cos(17 - k)θ = cos kθ , the terms pair up, and sum_k=1^8cos kθ = -tfrac12. Stage 3 Splitting the cosines into two groups Let z = cosθ + cos2θ + cos4θ + cos8θ , and let z' be the sum of the other four cosines, cos3θ + cos5θ + cos6θ + cos7θ . What is z + z' ? By Stage 2, z + z' = -frac12 . If we can also find zz' , then z and z' are the roots of a quadratic. Compute zz' . Expand it as 16 products cos aθcos bθ , turn each into a sum of two cosines, and count how often each of cosθ, cos2θ, ldots, cos8θ appears. (Reduce angles using cos kθ = cos(17 - k)θ and cos(-kθ) = cos kθ .) Each product gives cos aθcos bθ = frac12bigl(cos(a + b)θ + cos(a - b)θbigr) , so zz' is frac12 times a sum of 32 cosines. Working through the 16 pairs with a \1, 2, 4, 8\ and b \3, 5, 6, 7\ : for example a = 1 , b = 3 gives cos4θ and cos2θ ; a = 8 , b = 7 gives cos15θ = cos2θ and cosθ . Carrying this out for all sixteen pairs, each of cosθ, ldots, cos8θ appears exactly four times. Therefore zz' = tfrac12 × 4 × sum_k=1^8cos kθ = 2 × left(-tfrac12right) = -1. Stage 4 The quadratic So z and z' are the roots of t^2 + frac12 t - 1 = 0 , that is, 4t^2 + 2t - 4 = 0 , with roots t = frac-1 sqrt174 . Which is z ? Numerically cosθ approx 0.932 , cos2θ approx 0.739 , cos4θ approx 0.092 and cos8θ approx -0.983 , so z approx 0.78 > 0 . Hence z = frac-1 + sqrt174 = -frac1 - sqrt174. qed Looking back Products to sums. The product formula for cosines turned y^2 and zz' into sums of the same cosines, so the algebra closed up. Sum and product give a quadratic. Knowing z + z' and zz' is the same as knowing the quadratic with roots z and z' . The right split matters. Splitting the eight cosines into \1, 2, 4, 8\ and \3, 5, 6, 7\ made every index appear equally often in zz' . A random split would not work. What’s really going on Gauss periods Why \1, 2, 4, 8\ ? Modulo 17 , the powers 3^0, 3^1, 3^2, ldots of 3 run through all the non-zero residues: 1, 3, 9, 10, 13, 5, 15, 11, 16, 14, 8, 7, 4, 12, 2, 6. Taking every other one, 3^0, 3^2, 3^4, ldots , gives 1 , 9 , 13 , 15 , 16 , 8 , 4 , 2 , which are 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 modulo 17 : exactly the angles in z . The other half gives 3, 5, 6, 7 , the angles in z' . Gauss called the sums of ω^k over such classes periods . Because 17 - 1 = 16 = 2^4 , the residues can be halved four times, and at each stage the periods satisfy quadratic equations whose coefficients involve the periods of the previous stage. Four quadratics, so four square roots, lead from the rational numbers down to cos(2π)/(17) : begingathered costfrac2π17 = tfrac116Bigl(-1 + sqrt17 + sqrt34 - 2sqrt17 \\ + 2sqrt17 + 3sqrt17 - sqrt34 - 2sqrt17 - 2sqrt34 + 2sqrt17Bigr). endgathered Every step involves only square roots, and square roots can be constructed with ruler and compasses (using similar triangles or a semicircle), so the 17 -gon is constructible. Which polygons can be constructed? Gauss claimed, and Pierre Wantzel proved in 1837, that a regular n -gon can be constructed with ruler and compasses exactly when n is a power of 2 times a product of distinct Fermat primes , primes of the form 2^2^m + 1 . The known Fermat primes are 3 , 5 , 17 , 257 and 65537 , the Fermat numbers of Section 1.1 . (Fermat guessed that all such numbers are prime, but Euler showed that 2^32 + 1 is divisible by 641 , and no further Fermat primes have ever been found.) So the 257 -gon and the 65537 -gon are constructible; in the nineteenth century Johann Hermes spent about ten years working out the construction of the 65537 -gon, and his manuscript is kept at Göttingen. The 7 -gon and 11 -gon are not constructible, because 7 and 11 are not Fermat primes ( 7 - 1 = 6 and 11 - 1 = 10 are not powers of 2 ), and neither is the 9 -gon, because 9 = 3^2 repeats the Fermat prime 3 . Wantzel’s proof uses the theory of field degrees from Section 6.3 . The thinking skill Find a quadratic by computing sum and product To find a quantity, pair it with a natural partner, compute their sum and their product, and solve the resulting quadratic. The art is in choosing the partner so that both sum and product can be computed. Here the partner came from the symmetry of the residues modulo 17 , and repeating the idea four times gave Gauss his construction. Try this next The heptagon. Try STEP II 1995, Question 6 . It applies Gauss’s idea of grouping roots of unity to the seventh roots, and finds exact values for sums of cosines and sines. Deciding the sign of the sine sum is the subtle step. The pentagon. Show that cos(2π)/(5) = (sqrt5 - 1)/(4) , and use it to describe a ruler-and-compasses construction of a regular pentagon. The other period. Check numerically that z' = cos3θ + cos5θ + cos6θ + cos7θ = frac-1 - sqrt174 . Generators. Show that the powers of 3 modulo 17 give every non-zero residue, but the powers of 2 do not. Which residues do the powers of 2 give? Further reading Ian Stewart, Galois Theory (CRC Press). Chapter on ruler-and-compass constructions and the regular 17 -gon. Richard Courant & Herbert Robbins, What Is Mathematics? (Oxford University Press). Chapter 3 is a beautiful elementary account of constructions, including the 17 -gon. Daniel Kehlmann, Measuring the World (Quercus). A comic novel about Gauss and Alexander von Humboldt, for light relief.

title: Algebra and Structure
headings: Why structure matters What you will meet at university The questions that run through this chapter Ideas in this chapter How to read this chapter
text: Chapter 6 · Introduction From Equations to Structures Mathematics is the art of giving the same name to different things. — Henri Poincaré For most of its history, algebra meant solving equations. The Babylonians solved quadratics four thousand years ago; Italian mathematicians of the sixteenth century solved cubics and quartics; and then, for nearly three hundred years, the quintic resisted every attempt. The resolution, when it came in the 1820s and 1830s, changed algebra completely. Niels Henrik Abel proved that no general formula for the quintic exists, and Évariste Galois explained exactly which equations can be solved, by studying not the equations themselves but the symmetries of their roots . To do so he had to invent a new kind of mathematical object: the group. That shift, from computing answers to studying structures, is the subject of this chapter. Instead of asking “what is the solution?”, modern algebra asks “what kind of object is this, and what operations does it support?” The answers turn out to explain why the old tricks worked, and to settle questions that tricks alone never could. Why structure matters Here are three ancient problems that resisted all attempts for two thousand years: with ruler and compasses, double the volume of a cube; trisect an arbitrary angle; construct a regular 7 -sided polygon. None of them can be done, and the proofs, found in the nineteenth century, are not clever constructions but arguments about structure: about the degree of the field of numbers that ruler and compasses can reach ( Section 6.3 ). The same theory explains why the regular 17 -gon can be constructed ( Section 6.2 ), and why the quartic can be solved but the quintic cannot ( Section 6.4 ). Structures also travel. The axioms for a group are satisfied by the symmetries of a crystal, the permutations of the roots of a polynomial, the rotations of three-dimensional space, the moves of Rubik’s cube and the points of an elliptic curve. A theorem proved once from the axioms holds in all of them. That economy, giving “the same name to different things” as Poincaré put it, is what makes abstract algebra so powerful. What you will meet at university In the first year you will meet groups (sets with an operation satisfying three axioms) and, usually, rings and fields (sets with addition and multiplication). You will prove Lagrange’s theorem, that the size of a subgroup divides the size of the group, and meet permutations, symmetry groups and matrix groups. In the second and third years these lead to Galois theory , which connects fields and groups and answers the classical questions about equations and constructions; to representation theory , which studies groups through matrices; and to algebraic number theory , where the ideas of Section 1.7 are put on a firm footing. The last three sections of this chapter are about groups. Groups are no longer on the STEP syllabus (they were removed in 2019), but the questions are self-contained and each section gives the definitions it needs. The questions that run through this chapter Three big questions What can be built from what? Which numbers can be reached from the rationals by square roots, or by solving equations, and how do we prove something cannot be reached? Why do the formulas for equations work? What is the hidden reason that quadratics, cubics and quartics have formulas, and what changes at degree five? What is gained by abstraction? What happens when we describe objects only by the rules they obey? Ideas in this chapter § Topic Idea 6.1 Cyclotomic polynomials Classify roots of unity by order 6.2 The regular 17 -gon Gauss periods: sums and products give quadratics 6.3 Minimal polynomials Eliminate radicals; degrees multiply 6.4 Solving the quartic Symmetric functions; the resolvent cubic 6.5 Differentiation from axioms An operation determined by its rules 6.6 Unions of subgroups Arguing from the group axioms 6.7 The quaternion group Representing an operation by matrices 6.8 A group of singular matrices Reading definitions literally How to read this chapter Many of these questions can be done by brute force: expand everything, compare coefficients, check every case. Do that first if you need to. Then look back and ask what made the brute force work, and whether there is a structural reason behind it. The structural reason is usually shorter, always more illuminating, and it is what you will need when the brute force becomes impossible.

title: Solving the Quartic
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on The quintic Solving cubics The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2017, Question 3 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/17-s3-q3 The hook Every student learns the formula for solving quadratic equations. Formulas for cubics and quartics exist too; they were found in sixteenth-century Italy amid secret contests and bitter disputes over priority. Gerolamo Cardano published both in his Ars Magna of 1545, the cubic from Niccolò Tartaglia (who had sworn him to secrecy) and the quartic from his own student Lodovico Ferrari. Then, for nearly three hundred years, mathematicians searched in vain for a formula for the quintic. This question shows the trick that solves the quartic, and it is a trick with a deep meaning. Out of the four roots, form three new quantities by pairing the roots up in the three possible ways. Those three quantities satisfy a cubic, which you can solve, and from them the original roots follow. The question why this works, why four roots can be reduced to three quantities but five roots cannot be similarly reduced, is what led Galois to invent group theory. Before you start How many ways are there to split four objects α, β, γ, δ into two pairs? Three: \αβ, γδ\ , \αγ, βδ\ and \αδ, βγ\ (Figure 6.4.1). The three quantities in the question, αβ + γδ and so on, correspond to these three pairings. Any rearrangement of the four roots just shuffles the three pairings among themselves, so any symmetric expression in the three quantities is a symmetric expression in the four roots, and can be written in terms of p , q , r , s . That is why they satisfy a cubic whose coefficients involve only p , q , r , s . Working it through Stage 1 The missing coefficient In a cubic y^3 + Ay^2 + By + C = 0 , what is the sum of the roots in terms of A ? And what is (αβ + γδ) + (αγ + βδ) + (αδ + βγ) in terms of the quartic’s coefficients? The sum of the roots of the cubic is -A . The sum of the three quantities is the sum of all six products of pairs of α, β, γ, δ , which for the quartic x^4 + px^3 + qx^2 + rx + s is q . So A = -q . Stage 2 The specific cubic With p = 0 , q = 3 , r = -6 , s = 10 , the cubic is y^3 - 3y^2 + (0 - 40)y + (120 - 0 - 36) = y^3 - 3y^2 - 40y + 84 = 0. Try small divisors of 84 . y = 2 gives 8 - 12 - 80 + 84 = 0 . Dividing, y^3 - 3y^2 - 40y + 84 = (y - 2)(y^2 - y - 42) = (y - 2)(y - 7)(y + 6) . The largest root is 7 , so αβ + γδ = 7 . ■ Stage 3 Pairs of roots (α + β)(γ + δ) = αγ + αδ + βγ + βδ , which is the sum of all six pair-products minus αβ + γδ , that is, q - 7 = 3 - 7 = -4 . Also αβ · γδ = αβγδ = s = 10 . So αβ and γδ have sum 7 and product 10 : they are the roots of t^2 - 7t + 10 = (t - 2)(t - 5) . With αβ > γδ , αβ = 5 and γδ = 2 . ■ Stage 4 Solving the quartic Find α + β and γ + δ . You know their sum (from p ) and their product (from Stage 3); to decide which is which, use r . α + β + γ + δ = -p = 0 and (α + β)(γ + δ) = -4 , so \α + β, γ + δ\ = \2, -2\ . The coefficient r gives the sum of the four triple products: αβγ + αβδ + αγδ + βγδ = -r = 6 . This can be written as αβ(γ + δ) + γδ(α + β) = 5(γ + δ) + 2(α + β) . If α + β = 2 this is -10 + 4 = -6 ; if α + β = -2 it is 10 - 4 = 6 . So α + β = -2 and γ + δ = 2 . Now α , β are the roots of t^2 + 2t + 5 = 0 , giving -1 2i ; and γ , δ are the roots of t^2 - 2t + 2 = 0 , giving 1 i . The four roots are x = -1 2i, qquad x = 1 i. qed Check: (x^2 + 2x + 5)(x^2 - 2x + 2) = x^4 + 3x^2 - 6x + 10 . Looking back Symmetric functions. Every step used the relations between roots and coefficients: sums and products of roots. Reduce the degree. A quartic problem became a cubic (the resolvent cubic ), and then two quadratics. Use every piece of information. p and q gave the sums and products; s split αβ from γδ ; r decided which pair went with which sum. What’s really going on Why the trick works: permutations of roots In 1770 Joseph-Louis Lagrange asked why the methods for cubics and quartics work, and found the answer in the permutations of the roots. There are 24 ways to rearrange four roots. Under all of them, the three quantities y_1 = αβ + γδ , y_2 = αγ + βδ , y_3 = αδ + βγ are merely shuffled among themselves: each rearrangement of the four roots induces a rearrangement of the three pairings (Figure 6.4.1). So they satisfy a polynomial of degree 3 with coefficients symmetric in the roots. In modern language, there is a group homomorphism from the symmetric group S_4 (all 24 permutations) onto S_3 (the 6 permutations of the pairings), and that is why a quartic can be reduced to a cubic. The quintic For five roots, Lagrange looked for a similar quantity taking only a few values under permutations of the roots, and could not find one that helped. In 1799 Paolo Ruffini, and in 1824 Niels Henrik Abel (completing the proof), showed that there is no general formula for the roots of a quintic using only arithmetic and radicals. A few years later Évariste Galois explained exactly which polynomials can be solved by radicals: those whose group of symmetries of the roots can be broken down in a particular way into simpler pieces. The symmetric group S_4 can be (via S_3 and smaller groups), but S_5 cannot, because it contains a “simple” piece of size 60 that cannot be broken down further. Galois wrote up his theory in a hurry the night before he was killed in a duel in 1832, at the age of twenty. It is now one of the jewels of a mathematics degree, usually met in the third year. Solving cubics The cubic itself can be solved by a similar trick: write a depressed cubic x^3 - 3px + q as a combination of two perfect cubes, which reduces it to a quadratic. That is the method of the 2011 question in the exercises, and it is equivalent to Cardano’s formula. When the cubic has three real roots, the formula still requires complex numbers along the way, the phenomenon that forced mathematicians to take complex numbers seriously (see the introduction to Chapter 5). The thinking skill Symmetry reduces complexity If some quantities built from the roots are only permuted among themselves when the roots are permuted, they satisfy a polynomial of lower degree whose coefficients you can compute. This is the seed of Galois theory: understand an equation by understanding the symmetries of its roots. Try this next Check the cubic. Verify that y_1y_2 + y_2y_3 + y_3y_1 = pr - 4s , where y_1 = αβ + γδ etc. (Expand and use sumα = -p , sumαβγ = -r , αβγδ = s .) The cubic as a sum of cubes. Try STEP III 2011, Question 3 . It solves cubics by writing them as a combination of two cubes, a quite different route from this section’s. Check its answer numerically. Another quartic. Use the method of this section to solve x^4 - 4x^3 + 7x^2 - 6x + 2 = 0 . (One root of the resolvent cubic is a small integer.) Counting permutations. Of the 24 permutations of α, β, γ, δ , find all those that send the pairing \αβ, γδ\ to itself. Show that there are 8 of them. (They form a subgroup of S_4 .) Further reading Mario Livio, The Equation That Couldn’t Be Solved (Simon & Schuster). The story of the quintic and the birth of group theory, for a general reader. Ian Stewart, Why Beauty Is Truth: A History of Symmetry (Basic Books). From Babylonian equations to Galois and beyond. Ian Stewart, Galois Theory (CRC Press). The undergraduate text, with a historical introduction covering exactly this material.

title: The Quaternion Group
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Rotations in three dimensions Four squares The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 1993, Question 5 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/93-s3-q5 The hook On 16 October 1843, walking along the Royal Canal in Dublin with his wife, William Rowan Hamilton had a flash of inspiration that he had been chasing for years. He had been trying to multiply triples of numbers, the way complex numbers multiply pairs, and failing. The answer, he suddenly saw, needed four numbers, and a multiplication in which the order matters: ij ≠ ji . He carved the rules into the stone of Brougham Bridge: i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = ijk = -1. These are the quaternions . The question builds them from pairs of complex numbers, and finds inside them a small group of eight elements with a twisted multiplication. Quaternions are now used to describe rotations in three dimensions in every computer game, flight simulator and spacecraft guidance system. Before you start For the group definitions, see Section 6.6 . Two more words: the order of an element g of a group is the smallest positive n with g^n = e ; and two groups are isomorphic if there is a one-to-one correspondence between them that respects the operations, so that they are “the same group with different labels”. Think of the pair (z_1, z_2) as standing for a “number” z_1 + z_2j , where j is a new symbol with j^2 = -1 and jw = w^*j for complex w . Multiply (z_1 + z_2j)(w_1 + w_2j) using these rules. Do you get the formula for circ ? (z_1 + z_2j)(w_1 + w_2j) = z_1w_1 + z_1w_2j + z_2jw_1 + z_2jw_2j = z_1w_1 + z_1w_2j + z_2w_1^*j + z_2w_2^*j^2 , which is (z_1w_1 - z_2w_2^*) + (z_1w_2 + z_2w_1^*)j . Yes: the operation circ is quaternion multiplication in disguise. Working it through Stage 1 Associativity via matrices Checking (a circ b) circ c = a circ (b circ c) directly is a long calculation. There is a slicker way. Associate to (z_1, z_2) the complex matrix M = beginpmatrix z_1 & z_2 \\ -z_2^* & z_1^* endpmatrix . What is the top row of the matrix product M(z_1, z_2)\,M(w_1, w_2) ? The top row of the product is bigl(z_1w_1 - z_2w_2^*,\ z_1w_2 + z_2w_1^*bigr) , exactly (z_1, z_2)circ(w_1, w_2) , and the bottom row is bigl(-(z_1w_2 + z_2w_1^*)^*,\ (z_1w_1 - z_2w_2^*)^*bigr) , so the product has the same special form. So M(a circ b) = M(a)M(b) . Matrix multiplication is associative, and M is one-to-one (you can read off z_1 , z_2 from the top row), so circ is associative. ■ Stage 2 Not commutative (0, 1)circ(i, 0) = (0 · i - 1 · 0,\ 0 · 0 + 1 · i^*) = (0, -i) , but (i, 0)circ(0, 1) = (0, i) . So circ is not commutative. The four special products follow directly from the definition: beginaligned (z, 0)circ(w, 0) &= (zw, 0), & (z, 0)circ(0, w) &= (0, zw), \\ (0, z)circ(w, 0) &= (0, zw^*), & (0, z)circ(0, w) &= (-zw^*, 0). endaligned Stage 3 The group of eight In quaternion notation, A = 1 , C = i , B = j , D = ij = k , and E, G, F, H are their negatives. Every element of S_1 has the form (u, 0) or (0, u) with u \1, i, -1, -i\ . Use the four special products to show that S_1 is closed. What is the identity? By the four special products, the product of two elements of the form (u, 0) or (0, u) is again of one of these forms, with first or second entry uv , uv^* or -uv^* . Since \1, i, -1, -i\ is closed under multiplication, conjugation and negation, the product is in S_1 . The identity is A = (1, 0) : (1, 0)circ(w_1, w_2) = (w_1, w_2) and (w_1, w_2)circ(1, 0) = (w_1, w_2) . Find the order and inverse of each element. A has order 1 . Ecirc E = (-1, 0)circ(-1, 0) = (1, 0) , so E has order 2 . For C = (i, 0) : Ccirc C = (-1, 0) = E , so C has order 4 and C^-1 = C^3 = Ecirc C = G . For B = (0, 1) : Bcirc B = (-1 · 1^*, 0) = (-1, 0) = E , so B has order 4 and B^-1 = F . Similarly Dcirc D = (-icdoti^*, 0) = (-i·(-i), 0) = (-1, 0) = E , so D has order 4 with inverse H . And G , F , H are the inverses of C , B , D , also of order 4 . In summary: element A B C D E F G H inverse A F G H E B C D order 1 4 4 4 2 4 4 4 With closure, associativity (Stage 1), an identity and inverses, S_1 is a group. ■ It is called the quaternion group Q_8 . Stage 4 A subgroup \A, B, E, F\ = \1, j, -1, -j\ consists of the powers of B : B^1 = B , B^2 = E , B^3 = F , B^4 = A . So it is closed and contains inverses: a subgroup, cyclic of order 4 . The matrix J = beginpmatrix 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 endpmatrix satisfies J^2 = -I , J^3 = -J , J^4 = I , so it generates a cyclic group of order 4 too. Matching B^k leftrightarrow J^k is an isomorphism. ■ (Indeed J is exactly M(0, 1) , the matrix of B .) Looking back Represent by matrices. Associativity, painful to check directly, was inherited from matrix multiplication. Find the structure behind a formula. The strange operation circ was quaternion multiplication, and seeing that made everything easier. Orders and inverses describe a group. The table of orders already shows Q_8 is unusual: one element of order 2 and six of order 4 . What’s really going on Beyond the complex numbers The real numbers form a one-dimensional number system in which you can add, multiply and divide; the complex numbers form a two-dimensional one. Hamilton’s quaternions are four-dimensional, and you can still divide, but multiplication is no longer commutative (Figure 6.7.1). In 1878 Ferdinand Frobenius proved that these three, mathbbR , mathbbC and mathbbH (for Hamilton), are the only finite-dimensional “division algebras” over the reals with associative multiplication. If you give up associativity but keep a size that multiplies, |xy| = |x|\,|y| , as it does for real and complex numbers and quaternions, there is exactly one more: the eight-dimensional octonions , discovered by John Graves and Arthur Cayley in the 1840s. Adolf Hurwitz proved in 1898 that these four are the only such systems. (Without the condition on size there are other, stranger non-associative division algebras, but a deep theorem of 1958, due to Raoul Bott, John Milnor and Michel Kervaire, shows that every finite-dimensional real division algebra has dimension 1 , 2 , 4 or 8 .) Rotations in three dimensions The quaternions of modulus 1 describe rotations of three-dimensional space: the rotation through angle θ about a unit axis u corresponds to q = cosfracθ2 + sinfracθ2(u_1i + u_2j + u_3k) , acting on a vector v (written as v_1i + v_2j + v_3k ) by v mapsto qvq^-1 . Composing rotations is multiplying quaternions. This is more efficient and numerically stable than using matrices or angles, and it avoids “gimbal lock”, a loss of one degree of freedom that the Apollo astronauts had to work around with their gyroscope-based navigation. The half-angle fracθ2 is also a clue to something deep: rotating by 360^circ gives q = -1 , not 1 , a fact that physicists see in the behaviour of electrons (spin). Four squares The modulus of a quaternion is multiplicative, |pq| = |p||q| , just like that of a complex number. Writing it out gives Euler’s four-square identity : a product of two sums of four squares is itself a sum of four squares. That is the key step in Lagrange’s theorem that every positive integer is a sum of four squares, which we prove in Section 7.8 , the four-dimensional cousin of the two-squares result in Section 1.6 . The thinking skill Represent abstract objects concretely If an abstract operation is hard to reason about, find a concrete model, such as matrices, in which it becomes a familiar operation. Properties like associativity then come for free. This idea, studying groups by representing them as matrices, grows into the large and beautiful subject of representation theory . Try this next Hamilton’s rules. Using the pairs, check that Ccirc B = D and Bcirc C = H , that is, ij = k and ji = -k . Only one element of order 2 . Show that E = -1 is the only element of order 2 in Q_8 . Deduce that Q_8 is not isomorphic to the group of symmetries of a square (which has five elements of order 2 ). Four squares. Show that det M(z_1, z_2) = |z_1|^2 + |z_2|^2 . Using det(M_1M_2) = det M_1det M_2 , deduce that a product of two sums of four squares is a sum of four squares. Subgroups. Find all the subgroups of Q_8 . Show that every subgroup contains E unless it is \A\ , and that Q_8 is the union of its three cyclic subgroups of order 4 (compare Section 6.6 ). Further reading John Conway & Derek Smith, On Quaternions and Octonions (A. K. Peters). The geometry and arithmetic of quaternions and octonions. Advanced but fascinating. John Baez, “ The octonions ” , Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 39 (2002); also freely available online. A wonderful survey; the introduction is readable now. Andrew Hanson, Visualizing Quaternions (Morgan Kaufmann). Quaternions for rotations, with applications to graphics.

title: A Group of Singular Matrices
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Abstract and concrete The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 1996, Question 6 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/96-s3-q6 The hook Every student learns that a matrix with zero determinant has no inverse. So a group of matrices, in which every element has an inverse, surely cannot contain any singular matrices? It can. The catch is in the word “inverse”. In a group, the inverse of A is the element that combines with A to give the group’s identity, and nothing says the group’s identity has to be the identity matrix I . This question builds a group in which every matrix is singular, and the identity element is a matrix with determinant zero. It is a lesson in reading definitions literally, and in the difference between an abstract structure and the familiar example you first met it in. Before you start For the definition of a group, see Section 6.6 . In part (i), the identity matrix I is not of the form beginpmatrix a & a \\ a & a endpmatrix . So what could the identity element of S be? It must be some matrix E in S with EX = XE = X for every X in S . That is a condition only on how E acts on matrices of this special form, not on all matrices. Find it by solving the equation. Working it through Stage 1 Closure Write M_a for the matrix with all four entries equal to a . Then M_aM_b = beginpmatrix a & a \\ a & a endpmatrixbeginpmatrix b & b \\ b & b endpmatrix = beginpmatrix 2ab & 2ab \\ 2ab & 2ab endpmatrix = M_2ab, and 2ab ≠ 0 when a, b ≠ 0 . So S is closed. ■ Stage 2 The group axioms Matrix multiplication is associative. For the identity, solve M_eM_a = M_a . For inverses, solve M_aM_b = M_e . Associativity is inherited from matrix multiplication. Identity: M_eM_a = M_2ea = M_a for all a exactly when e = frac12 ; by the symmetry of the formula, M_aM_1/2 = M_a too. So E = beginpmatrix frac12 & frac12 \\ frac12 & frac12 endpmatrix is the identity of S . Inverses: M_aM_b = M_2ab = M_1/2 when b = (1)/(4a) , which is non-zero, so M_1/(4a) is the inverse of M_a in S . So S is a group. ■ Every element has determinant a^2 - a^2 = 0 . Stage 3 Singularity spreads Suppose A G is singular, and let B be any element of G . Write B as a product involving A , and take determinants. Let A^-1 denote the inverse of A in the group G (not necessarily a matrix inverse). Then C = A^-1B is in G , and AC = AA^-1B = EB = B. Taking determinants, detB = detA\,detC = 0 . So every element of G is singular. ■ In particular, if one element of a matrix group is invertible as a matrix, all are; a matrix group is either entirely invertible or entirely singular. Stage 4 A 3 × 3 example Can you generalise part (i) to 3 × 3 matrices? Or find something even simpler, using a matrix that “ignores” two of the three coordinates? Take G = left\beginpmatrix a & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 endpmatrix : a ≠ 0right\. The product of the matrices with corner entries a and b is the one with corner entry ab , so G is closed; multiplication is associative; the identity is the matrix with corner entry 1 ; the inverse of the one with corner a is the one with corner frac1a . So G is a group, and every element has determinant 0 . ■ (Another example: the 3 × 3 matrices with all nine entries equal to a ≠ 0 , whose identity has all entries frac13 .) Looking back Read definitions literally. A group’s identity is whatever element acts as an identity within the group ; it need not be the familiar identity. Solve for the structure. The identity and inverses in S were found by solving equations, not by guessing. Determinants are multiplicative. That one property showed that singularity spreads from one element to all of them. What’s really going on Idempotents and hidden invertibility The identity E of any matrix group satisfies E^2 = E : it is idempotent . Geometrically, an idempotent matrix is a projection : it maps every vector onto a subspace and leaves the vectors in that subspace alone. In part (i), E projects the plane onto the line y = x , and every matrix M_a first projects onto that line and then stretches along it by the factor 2a (Figure 6.8.1). On the line, the group acts by invertible stretches; it simply ignores the direction perpendicular to it. So S is really the group of non-zero real numbers under multiplication (via M_a mapsto 2a ), living on a line inside the plane. This is true in general: every group of matrices is, after a change of basis, a group of invertible matrices acting on the image of its identity element, padded with zeros. Abstract and concrete The first groups people studied were concrete: permutations, symmetries, invertible matrices. The abstract definition (a set with an operation satisfying three axioms) was distilled from them. This question shows the value of the abstract view: S and the group of non-zero reals under multiplication are isomorphic , the same group in different clothing, even though one consists of singular matrices and the other of numbers. Recognising when two different-looking structures are “the same” is one of the central skills of algebra, and the notion of isomorphism is how mathematicians make that precise. The thinking skill Question hidden assumptions about familiar objects When a familiar object appears in an abstract definition, check which of its familiar properties the definition actually requires. “The identity of a group of matrices is I ” sounds obvious but is not part of the definition, and dropping it led to a genuinely new example. Questioning assumptions like this is how many new mathematical structures are found. Try this next An isomorphism. Show that the map M_a mapsto 2a is a one-to-one correspondence from S to the non-zero reals that turns matrix multiplication into multiplication of numbers. Not a group. Show that the set of matrices beginpmatrix a & b \\ 0 & 0 endpmatrix with a ≠ 0 is closed under multiplication but is not a group. ( Hint: look for an identity element. Is there a left identity? A right identity?) Idempotents. Find all 2 × 2 real matrices E with E^2 = E . Describe them geometrically. All entries equal. Show that the n × n matrices with all entries equal to a ≠ 0 form a group under multiplication, and find its identity element. Further reading M. A. Armstrong, Groups and Symmetry (Springer). Matrix groups and isomorphisms, with many geometric examples. Gilbert Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra (Wellesley-Cambridge). Projections and idempotent matrices, clearly explained. Joseph Gallian, Contemporary Abstract Algebra (CRC Press). A friendly first course with many examples of unusual groups.

title: Unions of Subgroups
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on How many subgroups does it take? Vector spaces The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 1988, Question 9 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/88-s2-q9 The hook This is one of the shortest questions in the book, and one of the most characteristic of university mathematics. It is about groups , the mathematical language of symmetry, and it asks something that sounds like a puzzle: can a group be covered by two smaller groups sitting inside it? The answer is no, and the proof is three lines long. But three smaller groups can do it, which is a surprise. Group theory was on the STEP syllabus until 2019 and is now a staple of the first year at university. This question needs only the definitions, which are given below, and it is a perfect first taste of how group theorists think: a short, clever argument that uses nothing but the axioms. Before you start A group is a set G with an operation (written as multiplication, ab ) such that: the operation is associative : (ab)c = a(bc) ; there is an identity element e with ea = ae = a for every a ; every a has an inverse a^-1 with aa^-1 = a^-1a = e . Examples: the integers (positive, negative and zero) under addition; the non-zero real numbers under multiplication; the rotations of a square under composition. A subgroup is a subset K of G that is a group in its own right under the same operation: it contains e , and if a, b K then ab K and a^-1 K . If K is a subgroup and a K , but b notin K , can ab be in K ? No. If ab K , then b = a^-1(ab) would be a product of two elements of K , and so in K . This tiny observation is the whole proof. Working it through Stage 1 Two subgroups cannot cover Suppose, for a contradiction, that G = G_1 cup G_2 but neither G_1 nor G_2 is all of G . Since G_1 ≠ G , there is an element not in G_1 . Where must it be? Similarly for G_2 . Now multiply the two elements together. Choose a G with a notin G_1 ; since every element is in G_1 or G_2 , a G_2 . Choose b G with b notin G_2 ; then b G_1 . Consider the product ab . It lies in G_1 or in G_2 . If ab G_1 : since b G_1 , a = (ab)b^-1 G_1 . Contradiction. If ab G_2 : since a G_2 , b = a^-1(ab) G_2 . Contradiction. Either way we reach a contradiction, so G_1 = G or G_2 = G . ■ Notice that we never used the fact that G is finite. The result holds for every group. Stage 2 Three subgroups can Find a group that is the union of three subgroups, none of them the whole group. ( Hint: try a small group in which every element is its own inverse.) Take the Klein four-group V = \e, a, b, c\ , with the rules a^2 = b^2 = c^2 = e and ab = ba = c , bc = cb = a , ca = ac = b . (Concretely: the four symmetries of a non-square rectangle, namely doing nothing, rotating by 180^circ , and reflecting in either axis. Or the pairs (x, y) of bits 0 , 1 under addition modulo 2 .) Its three subgroups H_1 = \e, a\, qquad H_2 = \e, b\, qquad H_3 = \e, c\ each have two elements, none is the whole group, and together they contain every element of V (Figure 6.6.1). ■ Looking back Pick witnesses and combine them. The proof chose an element outside each subgroup and multiplied them. This “take one from each and combine” move is extremely common in algebra. Closure is powerful. The only property of subgroups used was that they are closed under multiplication and inverses. Check the hypotheses you need. Finiteness was given but not used. Noticing that a hypothesis is unnecessary is part of understanding a proof. What’s really going on The language of symmetry Groups arose in the nineteenth century from several directions at once: Galois’s study of permutations of the roots of polynomials ( Section 6.4 ), Cauchy’s work on permutations, and the study of symmetries in geometry and crystallography. The abstract definition above, in which a group is anything satisfying the three axioms, was settled by the end of the century. Its power is generality: a theorem proved from the axioms, like the one in this question, holds simultaneously for groups of numbers, of matrices, of symmetries and of permutations. Today groups are everywhere: in particle physics (the standard model is built on symmetry groups), in chemistry (molecular symmetry determines spectra), in cryptography (elliptic curve groups, Section 1.9 ) and in the solution of Rubik’s cube. How many subgroups does it take? The question suggests a natural problem: what is the smallest number of proper subgroups whose union is the whole group? It is never 2 , by the question. In 1926 Gaetano Scorza showed that a group is the union of three proper subgroups exactly when it has the Klein four-group as a “quotient”. In 1994 J. H. E. Cohn studied the general problem and conjectured several results, and in 1997 M. J. Tomkinson proved that there is no group for which this smallest number is seven, although every number from 3 to 6 occurs. Questions like this, simple to state and surprisingly subtle, are typical of group theory. Vector spaces A similar argument shows that a vector space over the real numbers (such as the plane, or three-dimensional space) can never be the union of finitely many proper subspaces: a plane is not the union of finitely many lines through the origin. But over a finite field it can be: the plane over the field with two elements, which is just the Klein four-group again, is the union of its three lines. The thinking skill Argue from the axioms In abstract algebra, you often know nothing about the objects except the axioms they satisfy. The proof must use only those axioms. This forces arguments to be short and clean, like the one here, and it makes them universally applicable. It takes some getting used to, and it is one of the most distinctive experiences of a first-year algebra course. Try this next Check the group. Write out the multiplication table of the Klein four-group and check the group axioms. Show that it is not the same as the group \1, i, -1, -i\ under multiplication. ( Hint: which elements are their own inverses?) Cyclic groups. A group is cyclic if every element is a power of a single element g . Show that a cyclic group is never the union of proper subgroups, however many. ( Hint: which subgroup contains g ?) The whole numbers. Show directly that (mathbbZ, +) is not the union of the subgroups 2mathbbZ (even numbers) and 3mathbbZ (multiples of 3 ). Is it the union of any two proper subgroups? Lines in the plane. harder Show that the plane mathbbR^2 is not the union of finitely many lines through the origin. ( Hint: each line contains at most one point of the parabola y = x^2 other than the origin.) Further reading M. A. Armstrong, Groups and Symmetry (Springer). A beautifully illustrated first course, driven by geometric examples. Nathan Carter, Visual Group Theory (Mathematical Association of America). Groups through pictures, ideal before university. Peter Neumann, Gabrielle Stoy & Edward Thompson, Groups and Geometry (Oxford University Press). A classic Oxford first-year text.

title: What We Have Learned
headings: 1. What can be built from what? 2. Why do the formulas for equations work? 3. What is gained by abstraction? 4. A toolkit for algebra Where next
text: We began with the shift in algebra from solving equations to studying structures, and with three questions: what can be built from what, why the formulas for equations work, and what is gained by abstraction. Here is what the chapter’s eight questions showed. 1. What can be built from what? In Section 6.3 we eliminated radicals one at a time to find polynomials satisfied by sqrt2 + sqrt3 , sqrt2 + sqrt3 + sqrt5 and sqrt[3]2 + sqrt[3]3 , of degrees 4 , 8 and 9 . Those degrees are invariants: the degree of the field a number generates. Because degrees multiply up a tower of fields, numbers reachable by square roots have degrees that are powers of 2 . That single fact proves that the cube cannot be doubled ( sqrt[3]2 has degree 3 ) and that a 60^circ angle cannot be trisected. In the other direction, Section 6.2 showed how something can be built. Splitting the 17 th roots of unity into Gauss’s periods, the sum cos(2π)/(17) + cos(4π)/(17) + cos(8π)/(17) + cos(16π)/(17) satisfied a quadratic, with root frac-1 + sqrt174 ; three more quadratics lead to cos(2π)/(17) , and so to the construction of the regular 17 -gon. Underneath both sections were the cyclotomic polynomials of Section 6.1 , the building blocks of x^n - 1 , obtained by sorting the roots of unity by their order. 2. Why do the formulas for equations work? Section 6.4 showed the secret of the quartic: from four roots, form the three quantities αβ + γδ , αγ + βδ , αδ + βγ , one for each way of pairing the roots. Any rearrangement of the roots merely shuffles these three, so they satisfy a cubic whose coefficients are known. Solving the cubic, then two quadratics, gave the roots. Lagrange saw that this works because of how permutations of four objects act on the three pairings; Galois saw that it fails for five roots because the group of permutations of five objects contains a piece that cannot be broken down. The formulas are shadows of group structure. 3. What is gained by abstraction? The last four sections described objects by the rules they obey. In Section 6.5 , four rules (additivity, the product rule, constants, lozenge x = 1 ) forced an operation to be differentiation, with no limits in sight. The same rules power automatic differentiation in modern software. In Section 6.6 , a three-line argument from the group axioms showed that no group is the union of two proper subgroups, for every group at once. In Section 6.7 , a strange operation on pairs of complex numbers turned out to be Hamilton’s quaternion multiplication, and representing it by matrices made associativity automatic. In Section 6.8 , reading the definition of a group literally produced a group of singular matrices whose identity is not the identity matrix, and which is “really” the group of non-zero real numbers in disguise. In each case, the abstract view explained something that calculation alone would have obscured. 4. A toolkit for algebra Method Where you used it Classifying by a unique invariant Roots of unity by order (6.1) Sum and product give a quadratic Gauss periods (6.2); the quartic (6.4) Product-to-sum formulas The 17 -gon (6.2) Eliminating radicals Minimal polynomials (6.3) Degrees and the tower law Impossibility of constructions (6.3) Symmetric functions of roots The resolvent cubic (6.4) Determining an operation by its axioms Derivations (6.5) Arguing from group axioms Unions of subgroups (6.6) Matrix representations Quaternions (6.7) Isomorphism Singular matrix groups (6.8) Where next Quaternions lead to Lagrange’s four-square theorem in Section 7.8 . Matrices as algebraic objects, with their own rules, are the subject of Chapter 7. The arithmetic of number systems like the Gaussian integers, where factorisation can fail, was the theme of Section 1.7 . If you want to go further before university Mario Livio, The Equation That Couldn’t Be Solved : the quintic, Galois and the birth of group theory. Nathan Carter, Visual Group Theory : groups through pictures, the ideal first look. M. A. Armstrong, Groups and Symmetry : a first university course, built on geometry. Ian Stewart, Galois Theory : for when you are ready for the full story. Galois died at twenty, after a duel, leaving a few dozen pages that took the mathematical world decades to understand. What he saw was that an equation’s deepest secrets are not in its coefficients but in the symmetries of its solutions. That insight, giving the same name to different things and studying the structure they share, now runs through all of mathematics. You have seen it at work in polynomials, polygons, quaternions and matrices; at university you will see it almost everywhere.

headings: 7.1 Rules That Fail for Matrices 7.2 Stretching Without Turning 7.3 What Makes a Determinant 7.4 Matrices That Return to the Start 7.5 Rotating in Three Dimensions 7.6 Hyperbolic Rotations and Relativity 7.7 Quantities That Never Change 7.8 Four Squares 7.9 Only Five Platonic Solids
text: These are brief answers and hints, not full solutions: they give the result and the key step, so that you can check your own work. Try each exercise properly before looking. 7.1 Rules That Fail for Matrices Comparing XP and PX with X = beginpmatrix a & b \\ c & d endpmatrix forces c = 0 and a = d : the matrices beginpmatrix a & b \\ 0 & a endpmatrix . Cayley–Hamilton gives N^2 = tN - dI , so tN = dI . If t ≠ 0 then N is a multiple of I , and N^2 = 0 forces N = 0 , contradicting t ≠ 0 . So t = 0 , and then d = 0 . The answer: beginpmatrix a & b \\ c & -a endpmatrix with a^2 + bc = 0 . The diagonal entries of the square are cos^2θ + sin^2θ = 1 and the off-diagonal ones are 0 . The fixed vector is (cosfracθ2, sinfracθ2) , so it reflects in the line through the origin at angle fracθ2 . With M = beginpmatrix a & b \\ c & d endpmatrix , M^2 = beginpmatrix a^2 + bc & b(a + d) \\ c(a + d) & d^2 + bc endpmatrix ; subtract (a + d)M and add (ad - bc)I to get 0 . 7.2 Stretching Without Turning Mu = lambdau with u ≠ 0 needs det(M - lambdaI) = 0 , which is the quadratic. Here the trace is 6 and the determinant is (4)/(25)(54 - 4) = 8 , so λ^2 - 6λ + 8 = 0 : λ = 2 (for (1, 2) ) and 4 (for (2, -1) ). v · Mu = λ\,v · u , and since M is symmetric, v · Mu = Mv · u = μ\,v · u . So (λ - μ)\,u · v = 0 . The characteristic equation λ^2 - 2λcosθ + 1 = 0 has discriminant -4sin^2θ , negative unless θ is a multiple of π . The eigenvalues are e^pmiθ . (1, 0) = frac15(1, 2) + frac25(2, -1) , so T^n(1, 0) = (2^n)/(5)(1, 2) + (2 · 4^n)/(5)(2, -1) = frac15bigl(2^n + 4^n+1,\ 2^n+1 - 2 · 4^nbigr) . For n = 1 this is ((18)/(5), -frac45) , as it should be. 7.3 What Makes a Determinant (detMN)^3 = (detM)^3(detN)^3 , and (detJ)^3 = -1 ≠ 1 . The function |detM| is multiplicative, but |detJ| = 1 . beginpmatrix a & λ a \\ c & λ c endpmatrix = beginpmatrix a & 0 \\ c & 0 endpmatrixbeginpmatrix 1 & λ \\ 0 & 0 endpmatrix , and the second factor has second row 0 times its first, so f of it is 0 . beginpmatrix k & 0 \\ 0 & 1 endpmatrix = JK_kJ , so its value is f(J)^2f(K_k) = f(K_k) . And K_kK_l = K_kl . Row reduction writes any invertible matrix as a product of elementary matrices: row swaps ( J ), row scalings ( K_k or JK_kJ ), and shears ( beginpmatrix 1 & t \\ 0 & 1 endpmatrix or its conjugate by J ). Shears have f = 1 (as in part (iv), using K^-1PK ). Also J is a product of shears and K_-1 , so f(K_-1) = f(J) = -1 . Hence f(M) = g(detM) where g(k) = f(K_k) ; for singular M , f(M) = 0 by part (iii). 7.4 Matrices That Return to the Start |1 + e^iφ|^2 = 2 + 2cosφ = 1 gives φ = (2π)/(3) , so R^3 = I . For S : its eigenvalues are cube roots of 1 . If both were 1 , then, since x^3 - 1 has distinct roots, S would be diagonalisable and equal to I . Non-real eigenvalues of a real matrix come in conjugate pairs, so they are e^2pii/3 : detS = 1 and trS = -1 . The eigenvalues must be the primitive sixth roots e^pmiπ/3 (any other choice of sixth roots, paired with conjugates, gives M^2 = I or M^3 = I ). So trM = 1 and detM = 1 . The eigenvalues are roots of unity with product 1 , so they are e^pmiθ (or both 1 ), and the trace 2cosθ is an integer in [-2, 2] . Example of order 6 : beginpmatrix 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 endpmatrix . M^3 = (t^2 - d)M - tdI and M^4 = (t^3 - 2td)M - d(t^2 - d)I . For M^4 = -I ( M cannot be a multiple of I ), t(t^2 - 2d) = 0 and d(t^2 - d) = 1 . t = 0 gives -d^2 = 1 , impossible; so t^2 = 2d , d^2 = 1 , and d = 1 , t^2 = 2 . 7.5 Rotating in Three Dimensions z mapsto a + e^iθ(z - a) . The composite is z mapsto e^i(θ + φ)z + k with k = e^iφa(1 - e^iθ) + b(1 - e^iφ) ; if e^i(θ+φ) ≠ 1 it has the fixed point c = frack1 - e^i(θ+φ) . If θ + φ = 2π it is the translation by (b - a)(1 - e^-iθ) . beginpmatrix 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 endpmatrix : it fixes (1, 1, 1) , has trace 0 = 1 + 2cos120^circ , and sends i → j → k → i . K^2r = n × (n × r) = (n.r)n - r , and then K^3r = n × bigl((n.r)n - rbigr) = -Kr . In the series, the odd powers give (θ - (θ^3)/(3!) + cdots)K = sinθ\,K and the even powers (from K^2 on) give ((θ^2)/(2!) - (θ^4)/(4!) + cdots)K^2 = (1 - cosθ)K^2 . The composite fixes every point of the line of intersection, and has determinant (-1)^2 = 1 . In each plane perpendicular to that line it is the product of two reflections in lines at angle α , which is a rotation by 2α . 7.6 Hyperbolic Rotations and Relativity The entries of T(u)T(w) are cosh ucosh w + sinh usinh w = cosh(u + w) and sinh ucosh w + cosh usinh w = sinh(u + w) . So T(u)^-1 = T(-u) . tanh u = 0.8 gives u = frac12(1.8)/(0.2) = 3 approx 1.099 and cosh u = frac12(3 + frac13) = frac53 . On the ship, 10 × frac35 = 6 years pass. The area is frac12oint(x\,dy - y\,dx) . The straight sides contribute nothing, and along the hyperbola, with x = cosh s , y = sinh s , the integrand is (cosh^2s - sinh^2s)\,ds = ds , giving frac v2 . T has determinant cosh^2u - sinh^2u = 1 , so it preserves area; it maps the hyperbola to itself and moves the point with parameter v to v + u . x' + y' = (cosh u + sinh u)(x + y) = e^up and x' - y' = e^-uq ; also x^2 - y^2 = pq . In these coordinates T is a squeeze: a stretch by e^u along the asymptote y = x and a compression by e^-u along y = -x , which slides points along each hyperbola pq = constant. 7.7 Quantities That Never Change dot a = -Ct = -tc , dot d = Ct = tc , dot c = 0 , and dot b = (A - D)t - Ct^3 = t(a - d) , matching MN - NM = tbeginpmatrix -c & a - d \\ 0 & c endpmatrix . dotM = -S^-1dotSS^-1M_0S + S^-1M_0dotS = -NM + MN , using dotS = SN . N = M^-1dotM = beginpmatrix 2 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 endpmatrix , and detM = 2t - t = t , whose derivative is 1 = trN . (d)/(dt)tr(M^k) = sum_jtr(M^jdotMM^k-1-j) = ktr(M^k-1dotM) by cycling, and tr(M^k-1(MN - NM)) = tr(M^kN) - tr(M^k-1NM) = 0 , again by cycling. 7.8 Four Squares (L_1, L_2, L_3, L_4) = (1, 4, 4, 4) , and 1 + 16 + 16 + 16 = 49 . This is a different representation from 7^2 + 0^2 + 0^2 + 0^2 . With c = d = r = s = 0 : L_1 = ap - bq , L_2 = aq + bp , L_3 = L_4 = 0 , which is (a^2 + b^2)(p^2 + q^2) = (ap - bq)^2 + (aq + bp)^2 . Squares are 0 , 1 or 4 modulo 8 . Sums of three of these give 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 modulo 8 , never 7 . 2 = (1)^2 + (1)^2 + 0^2 + 0^2 : choose the two non-zero places ( 6 ways) and their signs ( 4 ways), giving 24 . Since 2 is not divisible by 4 , Jacobi’s formula gives 8σ(2) = 8 × 3 = 24 . 7.9 Only Five Platonic Solids With h = 2m + 2n - mn , V = (4m)/(h) , E = (2mn)/(h) and F = (4n)/(h) ; swapping m and n swaps V and F . The cube and octahedron are dual, as are the dodecahedron and icosahedron; the tetrahedron is self-dual. F = 32 , E = frac12(12 · 5 + 20 · 6) = 90 and V = frac13(180) = 60 , and 60 - 90 + 32 = 2 . In general, with P pentagons and H hexagons, E = frac12(5P + 6H) and V = frac13(5P + 6H) , so V - E + F = -frac16(5P + 6H) + P + H = frac P6 . This equals 2 , so P = 12 . Divide the top and bottom (which have holes) into four trapezia each. Then V = 16 , F = 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 and E = 12 + 12 + 8 = 32 , so V - E + F = 0 . 180^circ n(1 - frac2m) < 360^circ is n(m - 2) < 2m , that is, mn - 2m - 2n < 0 , or (m - 2)(n - 2) < 4 . With m, n ≥ 3 the solutions are (3, 3) , (3, 4) , (4, 3) , (3, 5) and (5, 3) .

title: What Makes a Determinant
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on The determinant as area Determinants in higher dimensions The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 2019, Question 8 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP II paper in OCR’s download of the 2019 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/696590-2019-past-papers.zip The hook The determinant of a 2 × 2 matrix is ad - bc . Where does that formula come from, and why is it so important? One answer is that it is the factor by which the matrix scales areas. Another, which this question explores, is that the determinant is essentially the only function on matrices that turns matrix multiplication into ordinary multiplication: det(MN) = detMdetN . The question gives you an unknown function f with that one property (plus two mild conditions to rule out trivial cases), and asks you to deduce, step by step, how it must behave. Like the derivations of Section 6.5 , it is an exercise in pinning an object down by its properties alone. By the end, f has been forced to change sign when rows are swapped, vanish on singular matrices and equal 1 on shears: exactly the behaviour of the determinant. Before you start What does each special matrix in the question do? Work out JM , MJ , KM and PM for a general M = beginpmatrix a & b \\ c & d endpmatrix . JM swaps the rows of M ; MJ swaps its columns. KM multiplies the second row by k . PM adds the second row to the first. These are the elementary row operations of Gaussian elimination. Since f turns products into products, knowing f on these special matrices tells you how f responds to each row operation. Working it through Stage 1 The identity f(M) = f(MI) = f(M)\,f(I) . Since f(M) ≠ 0 , divide to get f(I) = 1 . ■ Stage 2 Swapping J^2 = I , so f(J)^2 = f(I) = 1 , giving f(J) = 1 . Since f(J) ≠ 1 , f(J) = -1 . Now beginpmatrix c & d \\ a & b endpmatrix = JM , so its value is f(J)f(M) = -f(M) . And beginpmatrix d & c \\ b & a endpmatrix = JMJ (swap rows, then columns), so its value is f(J)^2f(M) = f(M) . ■ Stage 3 Dependent rows First consider a matrix B with two equal rows. What is JB ? What does that say about f(B) ? If both rows of B are (a, b) , swapping them changes nothing: JB = B . So f(B) = f(J)f(B) = -f(B) , which forces f(B) = 0 .
