Now if A has rows (a, b) and k(a, b) , then A = KB , where B has both rows equal to (a, b) . So f(A) = f(K)f(B) = 0 . ■ (This includes k = 0 , where the second row is zero.) Stage 4 The shear Compute P^2 and K^-1PK . Choose k to make them equal. What does that give for f(P) ? P^2 = beginpmatrix 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 endpmatrix and, for k ≠ 0 , K^-1PK = beginpmatrix 1 & 0 \\ 0 & frac1k endpmatrixbeginpmatrix 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 endpmatrixbeginpmatrix 1 & 0 \\ 0 & k endpmatrix = beginpmatrix 1 & k \\ 0 & 1 endpmatrix. With k = 2 , K^-1PK = P^2 . Taking f of both sides, and using f(K^-1)f(K) = f(I) = 1 , f(P) = f(P)^2, so f(P) = 0 or 1 . But P is invertible, and f(P)f(P^-1) = f(I) = 1 , so f(P) ≠ 0 . Therefore f(P) = 1 . ■ Looking back Special elements reveal the function. Applying the multiplicative property to I , J , K and P gave the value of f on each, and its effect on each row operation. An element equal to its own transform. A matrix with equal rows is unchanged by a row swap, which changes the sign of f ; so f must be zero there. Conjugation preserves f . f(K^-1PK) = f(P) , a fact used again and again in algebra. What’s really going on Every multiplicative function is a function of the determinant The question stops at f(P) = 1 , but the argument can be completed. Every invertible matrix is a product of elementary matrices (row swaps, row scalings and shears), and the question shows how f behaves on each. It follows that f(M) = φ(detM) for some function φ of a single real number with φ(xy) = φ(x)φ(y) . The determinant itself is the case φ(x) = x , but φ(x) = x^3 , or φ(x) = |x|^1/2\,sign(x) , work too. In other words, the determinant is the only fundamentally new multiplicative function on matrices . In the language of group theory, the determinant captures everything about the group of invertible matrices that can be seen by a commutative group. The determinant as area Geometrically, a 2 × 2 matrix sends the unit square to a parallelogram, and detM is its signed area : positive if the orientation is preserved, negative if it is reversed (Figure 7.3.1). The multiplicative property then has an obvious meaning: doing two transformations in turn multiplies their area scale factors. A row swap reverses orientation, which is why detJ = -1 ; a shear slides the square into a parallelogram of the same area, which is why detP = 1 ; and a matrix with dependent rows squashes the square flat, which is why its determinant is zero. Every step of the question has a picture. Determinants in higher dimensions For n × n matrices the determinant is the signed volume scale factor, and it is characterised by three properties: it is linear in each row, it changes sign when two rows are swapped, and it equals 1 on the identity. From these alone you can derive the familiar expansion formulas, and Gaussian elimination gives an efficient way to compute it. The determinant appears in the change-of-variables formula for multiple integrals (the Jacobian ), in the formula for the inverse of a matrix, and, as we saw in Section 5.4 , in the discriminant of a polynomial. The thinking skill Probe an unknown function with special inputs When a function is known only through a property, apply the property to the simplest special inputs you can think of, and see what it forces. Here the identity, a swap, a scaling and a shear were enough to determine almost everything. Choosing inputs that are their own squares, inverses or conjugates is particularly effective. Try this next Other examples. Show that f(M) = (detM)^3 satisfies all the conditions of the question, and that f(M) = |detM| satisfies the multiplicative property but not f(J) ≠ 1 . Column operations. Show that f is also zero on any matrix whose second column is a multiple of the first. Scalings. Let K_k = beginpmatrix 1 & 0 \\ 0 & k endpmatrix . Show that fbeginpmatrix k & 0 \\ 0 & 1 endpmatrix = f(K_k) , and that f(K_k)f(K_l) = f(K_kl) . Reduction to the determinant. harder Show that every invertible 2 × 2 matrix can be written as a product of matrices of the forms J , K_k and beginpmatrix 1 & t \\ 0 & 1 endpmatrix . Deduce that f(M) depends only on detM . Further reading Sheldon Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right (Springer; free online). Defines the determinant from its properties, in the spirit of this question. Gilbert Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra (Wellesley-Cambridge). Chapter 5 develops determinants from three rules. 3Blue1Brown, “ The determinant ” (video, free online). The area interpretation, beautifully animated.

title: Stretching Without Turning
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Eigenvectors everywhere The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 1990, Question 6 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/90-s3-q6 The hook A matrix transformation usually moves every vector to a new direction. But many matrices have a few special directions they do not turn at all, only stretching or shrinking along them. These are their eigenvectors (from the German eigen , “own” or “characteristic”), and the stretch factors are their eigenvalues . When there are enough of them, as there always are for a symmetric matrix like the one in this question, the transformation becomes transparent: in the right coordinates it is just a stretch along two axes. This question finds the eigenvectors of a particular matrix and uses them to understand what it does to a circle. Eigenvectors are one of the most useful ideas in all of applied mathematics. They describe the natural vibrations of a bridge, the principal axes of a spinning object, the energy levels of an atom, the most important directions in a cloud of data, and the ranking of web pages by Google’s original PageRank algorithm. Before you start What does it mean for T to leave a vector “unchanged in direction but multiplied by a scalar”? Write it as an equation. It means Tv = lambdav for some number λ : v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ . Notice that the two vectors in the question, (1, 2) and (2, -1) , are perpendicular. That is not a coincidence: the matrix is symmetric , and symmetric matrices always have perpendicular eigenvectors. Working it through Stage 1 The eigenvectors Tbeginpmatrix 1 \\ 2 endpmatrix = frac25beginpmatrix 9 - 4 \\ -2 + 12 endpmatrix = frac25beginpmatrix 5 \\ 10 endpmatrix = 2beginpmatrix 1 \\ 2 endpmatrix, qquad Tbeginpmatrix 2 \\ -1 endpmatrix = frac25beginpmatrix 20 \\ -10 endpmatrix = 4beginpmatrix 2 \\ -1 endpmatrix. So (1, 2) is stretched by 2 and (2, -1) by 4 . ■ Stage 2 The image of the circle To find the equation of E , express x and y in terms of X and Y (invert the matrix), and substitute into x^2 + y^2 = 1 . The matrix frac25beginpmatrix 9 & -2 \\ -2 & 6 endpmatrix has determinant (4)/(25)(54 - 4) = 8 , and its inverse is (1)/(20)beginpmatrix 6 & 2 \\ 2 & 9 endpmatrix . So x = (6X + 2Y)/(20) and y = (2X + 9Y)/(20) , and x^2 + y^2 = 1 becomes (6X + 2Y)^2 + (2X + 9Y)^2 = 400 quadLongrightarrowquad 40X^2 + 60XY + 85Y^2 = 400, which, divided by 5 , is 8X^2 + 12XY + 17Y^2 = 80 . ■ What shape is E , and what is its area? Use the eigenvectors. The unit circle has radius 1 in every direction. In the direction of (2, -1) it is stretched by 4 , and in the perpendicular direction (1, 2) by 2 . So E is an ellipse with semi-axes 4 and 2 , along the eigenvector directions (Figure 7.2.1), and its area is π × 4 × 2 = 8π . (Equivalently, any linear map multiplies areas by |det T| = 8 , and the circle has area π .) Stage 3 The greatest value of X On C , X = frac25(9x - 2y) . How large can 9x - 2y be when x^2 + y^2 = 1 ? 9x - 2y is the dot product of (9, -2) with the unit vector (x, y) , so its largest value is |(9, -2)| = sqrt85 , attained when (x, y) points along (9, -2) . Hence the greatest value of X is frac25sqrt85 = 2sqrt(85)/(25) = 2sqrt(17)/(5) . ■ Stage 4 A tangent The point frac15(3, 4) on C has tangent line 3x + 4y = 5 . A linear map sends tangent lines to tangent lines. Use this to find the tangent to E . Substituting x = (6X + 2Y)/(20) , y = (2X + 9Y)/(20) into 3x + 4y = 5 : (3(6X + 2Y) + 4(2X + 9Y))/(20) = 5 quadLongrightarrowquad 26X + 42Y = 100, that is, 13X + 21Y = 50 . ■ (Check: the point itself is Tbigl(frac35, frac45bigr) = bigl((38)/(25), (36)/(25)bigr) , and 13 · (38)/(25) + 21 · (36)/(25) = (494 + 756)/(25) = 50 .) Looking back Eigenvectors are the natural axes. In the coordinates given by the eigenvectors, T is just a stretch by 4 and by 2 , and its effect on a circle is obvious. Determinants measure area. The area of E is |det T| times the area of C . Linear maps preserve tangency. Transforming the circle’s tangent gave the ellipse’s tangent with almost no calculation. What’s really going on The spectral theorem Every real symmetric matrix has a full set of perpendicular eigenvectors, with real eigenvalues. This is the spectral theorem , one of the central results of a first linear algebra course. It says that every symmetric linear map is, in suitable perpendicular coordinates, just a stretch along each axis. Equivalently, every quadratic form like 8X^2 + 12XY + 17Y^2 can be rotated into the form λ_1 u^2 + λ_2 v^2 , which is why every central conic is an ellipse or hyperbola with perpendicular axes (the principal axis theorem ). The idea goes back to Cauchy in the 1820s, who used it to find the principal axes of quadric surfaces and of the stress in a solid body. Symmetry is what makes this work. A matrix that is not symmetric need not be so obliging: a rotation through 90^circ turns every direction, so it has no real eigenvectors at all, and the shear beginpmatrix 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 endpmatrix has only one eigenvector direction, so it is not a stretch along any pair of axes. Eigenvectors everywhere Here are a few of the places eigenvectors appear. Vibrations. A system of masses and springs vibrates in normal modes , patterns in which every part moves in step at a single frequency. These are eigenvectors of a matrix, and the frequencies come from the eigenvalues ( Section 11.2 ). Data. The directions in which a cloud of data points is most spread out are the eigenvectors of its covariance matrix. Finding them is principal component analysis , one of the basic tools of statistics and machine learning ( Section 13.7 ). Quantum mechanics. The possible results of measuring a quantity are the eigenvalues of a matrix (or operator), and the energy levels of an atom are eigenvalues. Web search. Google’s PageRank, the original idea behind the search engine, ranks pages by the entries of the eigenvector, with eigenvalue 1 , of a huge matrix describing the links between pages. The thinking skill Choose coordinates adapted to the transformation To understand a linear transformation, find the directions it does not rotate. In those coordinates it becomes simple. This is the same idea as choosing the Fermat point as origin in Section 5.6 , or changing variables to simplify a map in Section 2.8 : the right coordinates make the structure obvious. Try this next Finding eigenvalues. Show that the eigenvalues of beginpmatrix a & b \\ c & d endpmatrix are the roots of λ^2 - (a + d)λ + (ad - bc) = 0 , and check that the matrix in the question gives λ = 2 and 4 . Perpendicular eigenvectors. Show that if M is symmetric and Mu = lambdau , Mv = muv with λ ≠ μ , then u · v = 0 . ( Hint: compute v · Mu in two ways.) A rotation. Show that the rotation matrix beginpmatrix cosθ & -sinθ \\ sinθ & cosθ endpmatrix has no real eigenvectors unless θ is a multiple of π . What are its complex eigenvalues? Powers. Using the eigenvectors, find T^nbeginpmatrix 1 \\ 0 endpmatrix . ( Hint: write (1, 0) as a combination of (1, 2) and (2, -1) .) Further reading Gilbert Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra (Wellesley-Cambridge). Chapter 6 is an excellent introduction to eigenvalues and their applications. Kurt Bryan & Tanya Leise, “ The $25 , 000 , 000 , 000 eigenvector: the linear algebra behind Google ” , SIAM Review 48 (2006). Readable and freely available. 3Blue1Brown, Essence of Linear Algebra (video series, free online). Beautiful animations of exactly the geometric ideas in this section.

title: Matrices That Return to the Start
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Why crystals have no five-fold symmetry The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 2020, Question 6 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP II paper in OCR’s download of the 2020 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/696589-2020-past-papers.zip The hook Some transformations, repeated enough times, bring everything back to where it started. A rotation by 90^circ does it in four steps, a reflection in two. Which 2 × 2 matrices have this property, M^n = I for some n , and how can you tell? The surprise of this question is that two numbers, the trace and the determinant , are enough to decide. You do not need to know the four entries, only a + d and ad - bc . And the answer has a striking consequence for the physical world: it explains why crystals can have 2 -, 3 -, 4 - and 6 -fold symmetry but never 5 -fold, a “law” of crystallography that held for two centuries until a discovery in 1982 won a Nobel Prize. Before you start Every 2 × 2 matrix satisfies M^2 - (trM)M + (detM)I = 0 (the Cayley–Hamilton theorem; check it by multiplying out). How could that help with questions about M^2 ? It expresses M^2 in terms of M and I : M^2 = tM - dI , where t = trM and d = detM . So a condition on M^2 becomes a condition linking M , t and d . That is the key to the whole question. Working it through Stage 1 The trace of the square M^2 = beginpmatrix a^2 + bc & ab + bd \\ ac + cd & bc + d^2 endpmatrix , so tr(M^2) = a^2 + 2bc + d^2 = (a + d)^2 - 2(ad - bc) . ■ Stage 2 Square roots of pmI Suppose M^2 = I . Substitute into M^2 = tM - dI . If t ≠ 0 , what does that say about M ? If M^2 = I , then I = tM - dI , so tM = (1 + d)I . If t ≠ 0 , then M is a multiple of I , say cI , and c^2 = 1 , so M = pmI , which is excluded. Hence t = 0 , and then (1 + d)I = 0 , so d = -1 . Conversely, if t = 0 and d = -1 , then M^2 = tM - dI = I , and M ≠ pmI because tr(pmI) = 2 ≠ 0 . ■ For M^2 = -I : substituting gives tM = (d - 1)I . If t ≠ 0 then M = cI with c^2 = -1 , impossible for real c . So t = 0 and d = 1 . Conversely, t = 0 and d = 1 give M^2 = -I . ■ Stage 3 Fourth roots Let N = M^2 , so M^4 = I means N^2 = I . By part (ii), either N = pmI or trN = 0 and detN = -1 . Why is the second case impossible? detN = det(M^2) = (detM)^2 ≥ 0 , so detN ≠ -1 . Hence N = M^2 = pmI . The converse is clear. ■ For M^4 = -I : by part (ii) applied to N = M^2 , this holds exactly when tr(M^2) = 0 and det(M^2) = 1 , that is, t^2 - 2d = 0 and d^2 = 1 . Since t^2 = 2d ≥ 0 , we need d = 1 , and then t^2 = 2 . So M^4 = -I iff detM = 1 and trM = sqrt2. qed Stage 4 An eighth root of I that is not a rotation Any matrix with M^4 = -I has M^8 = I . A rotation by 45^circ has trace sqrt2 and determinant 1 ; we want another matrix with the same trace and determinant that is not a rotation. Take M = beginpmatrix sqrt2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 endpmatrix, qquad trM = sqrt2, quad detM = 1. By Stage 3, M^4 = -I , so M^8 = I . But M is not a rotation or reflection, because those preserve lengths, and Mbeginpmatrix 1 \\ 0 endpmatrix = beginpmatrix sqrt2 \\ 1 endpmatrix has length sqrt3 ≠ 1 . ■ Looking back Cayley–Hamilton turns powers into linear combinations. Every power of a 2 × 2 matrix is a combination of M and I , with coefficients depending only on trace and determinant. Determinants of squares are non-negative. That simple fact ruled out a whole case in part (iii). Trace and determinant are invariants. Two matrices with the same trace and determinant (and not multiples of I ) behave alike under powers, whether or not they look alike. What’s really going on Similar matrices Why is M in Stage 4 “a rotation in disguise”? Two matrices M and R are similar if M = SRS^-1 for some invertible S : they represent the same transformation in different coordinates. Similar matrices have the same trace and determinant, and (for 2 × 2 matrices that are not multiples of I ) the converse holds too. So any real matrix with trace sqrt2 and determinant 1 is similar to the rotation by 45^circ , and in the skewed coordinates given by S it simply rotates (Figure 7.4.1). In general, a real 2 × 2 matrix with M^n = I is always similar to a rotation or a reflection. Why crystals have no five-fold symmetry A crystal is a regular, repeating arrangement of atoms. A rotational symmetry of the crystal sends the lattice of atoms to itself, so in coordinates based on the lattice it is given by a matrix with integer entries. Its trace is therefore an integer. But a rotation by angle θ has trace 2cosθ in any coordinates, and 2cosθ is an integer only when it is -2, -1, 0, 1 or 2 , that is, for rotations of order 2 , 3 , 4 and 6 (and 1 ). Five-fold symmetry would need 2cos72^circ = (sqrt5 - 1)/(2) , which is not an integer. This is the crystallographic restriction theorem . In 1982 Dan Shechtman observed an alloy with apparent five-fold symmetry and was at first ridiculed; it turned out to be a quasicrystal , ordered but not periodic, like the Penrose tilings, and so not covered by the theorem. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2011. The thinking skill Look for invariants that capture the essential behaviour When a question is about an object with many parameters, ask whether a few combinations of them, invariant under a change of viewpoint, are enough. Here four entries reduced to two invariants, the trace and the determinant, because the question (“does M^n = I ?”) does not depend on the coordinates. Finding the right invariants is often the key to classification problems. Try this next Rotations of order three. Try STEP II 2021, Question 7 (in OCR’s download of the 2021 papers, a zip file). It starts from a rotation matrix with an unusual property and ends with a fact about every real 2 × 2 matrix whose cube is the identity. Order six. Find a condition on the trace and determinant for M^6 = I but M^2 ≠ I and M^3 ≠ I . The crystallographic restriction. Show that if M has integer entries, detM = 1 and M^n = I for some n , then trM \-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\ . Find an integer matrix of order 6 . Cayley–Hamilton for powers. Use M^2 = tM - dI to express M^3 and M^4 in the form pM + qI , and use this to rederive the condition for M^4 = -I . Further reading M. A. Armstrong, Groups and Symmetry (Springer). Includes the crystallographic restriction and the classification of wallpaper patterns. Marjorie Senechal, Quasicrystals and Geometry (Cambridge University Press). The mathematics of quasicrystals and aperiodic order. Gilbert Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra (Wellesley-Cambridge). Similar matrices and the Cayley–Hamilton theorem.

title: Four Squares
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Two, three, four Waring’s problem The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 1994, Question 8 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/94-s3-q8 The hook 7 is not a sum of two squares, or of three. But it is a sum of four: 7 = 4 + 1 + 1 + 1 . In 1770 Joseph-Louis Lagrange proved that every positive whole number is a sum of four squares (allowing 0^2 ). The theorem had been conjectured by Bachet in 1621 and claimed by Fermat, who as usual left no proof; Euler worked on it for forty years without quite finishing. The key tool, found by Euler in 1748, is in this question: a product of two sums of four squares is itself a sum of four squares. It means you only need to prove Lagrange’s theorem for prime numbers, and the rest follows by multiplying. The question derives the identity in a few lines from determinants of complex matrices, which are the quaternions of Section 6.7 in disguise. Before you start Recall the two-square version: (a^2 + b^2)(p^2 + q^2) is a sum of two squares because |z|^2|w|^2 = |zw|^2 for complex numbers z = a + bi , w = p + qi . How could matrices extend this to four squares? The idea is to find a kind of “number” made from four real numbers whose “size squared” is a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 and which is multiplicative. Matrices are multiplicative under determinants: det(AB) = detAdetB . So we want a matrix built from a, b, c, d whose determinant is a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 , and such that products of such matrices are again of the same form. Working it through Stage 1 The determinant is a sum of four squares What is the determinant of beginpmatrix z_1 & z_2 \\ -z_2^* & z_1^* endpmatrix ? If z_1 = a + bi and z_2 = c + di , what is it in terms of a, b, c, d ? det = z_1z_1^* + z_2z_2^* = |z_1|^2 + |z_2|^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 . Similarly with z_3 = p + qi and z_4 = r + si , the second matrix has determinant p^2 + q^2 + r^2 + s^2 . Stage 2 The product has the same form Multiplying, beginpmatrix z_1 & z_2 \\ -z_2^* & z_1^* endpmatrixbeginpmatrix z_3 & z_4 \\ -z_4^* & z_3^* endpmatrix = beginpmatrix z_1z_3 - z_2z_4^* & z_1z_4 + z_2z_3^* \\ -z_2^*z_3 - z_1^*z_4^* & -z_2^*z_4 + z_1^*z_3^* endpmatrix. Writing w_1 = z_1z_3 - z_2z_4^* and w_2 = z_1z_4 + z_2z_3^* , the bottom row is (-w_2^*, w_1^*) , so the product is beginpmatrix w_1 & w_2 \\ -w_2^* & w_1^* endpmatrix , of the same form. Its determinant is |w_1|^2 + |w_2|^2 , and since determinants multiply, (a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2)(p^2 + q^2 + r^2 + s^2) = |w_1|^2 + |w_2|^2. Stage 3 Reading off the four squares Expand w_1 = (a + bi)(p + qi) - (c + di)(r - si) and w_2 = (a + bi)(r + si) + (c + di)(p - qi) into real and imaginary parts. w_1 = (ap - bq - cr - ds) + i(aq + bp + cs - dr), w_2 = (ar - bs + cp + dq) + i(as + br - cq + dp). So beginaligned L_1 &= ap - bq - cr - ds, & L_2 &= aq + bp + cs - dr, \\ L_3 &= ar - bs + cp + dq, & L_4 &= as + br - cq + dp, endaligned each linear in a, b, c, d and in p, q, r, s , with (a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2)(p^2 + q^2 + r^2 + s^2) = L_1^2 + L_2^2 + L_3^2 + L_4^2 . ■ For example, 7 = 2^2 + 1^2 + 1^2 + 1^2 and 3 = 1^2 + 1^2 + 1^2 + 0^2 . With (a, b, c, d) = (2, 1, 1, 1) and (p, q, r, s) = (1, 1, 1, 0) the formulas give (L_1, L_2, L_3, L_4) = (0, 2, 4, 1) , and indeed 0^2 + 2^2 + 4^2 + 1^2 = 21 = 7 × 3 . Looking back Multiplicativity does the work. The identity came from det(AB) = detAdetB , exactly as the two-square identity comes from |zw| = |z||w| . Closure under multiplication. The special form beginpmatrix z_1 & z_2 \\ -z_2^* & z_1^* endpmatrix is preserved by products, which is what makes the result another sum of four squares. Bookkeeping matters. The final step is routine but error-prone; signs and conjugates must be handled carefully. What’s really going on Lagrange’s four-square theorem Here is the shape of Lagrange’s proof. By Euler’s identity, it is enough to show every prime p is a sum of four squares. A counting argument shows that some multiple mp , with m < p , is a sum of four squares. A clever “descent” then shows that if mp is a sum of four squares with 1 < m < p , so is m'p for some smaller m' ; repeating, we reach m = 1 . (Compare Fermat’s descent in Section 1.5 .) In 1834 Jacobi went much further and found the exact number of ways to write n as a sum of four squares: 8 times the sum of the divisors of n that are not multiples of 4 . For example, 1 can be written in 8 ways ( 1 in any of four positions). Two, three, four The pattern across dimensions is subtle. Sums of two squares come from complex numbers, and a number is a sum of two squares exactly when its primes of the form 4k + 3 appear to even powers ( Section 1.6 ). Sums of four squares come from quaternions, and every number is one. But sums of three squares have no multiplication identity at all (there is no three-dimensional number system with a multiplicative size; that is why Hamilton failed with triples, Section 6.7 ), and the theorem is harder: Legendre and Gauss showed that n is a sum of three squares unless n = 4^k(8m + 7) (Figure 7.8.1). Beyond four, the eight-dimensional octonions give an eight-square identity, found by Degen and Graves, and Hurwitz proved in 1898 that identities of this kind exist only for 1 , 2 , 4 and 8 squares. Waring’s problem Lagrange’s theorem is the first case of a question asked by Edward Waring in 1770: is there, for each k , a number g(k) such that every positive integer is a sum of at most g(k) k th powers? David Hilbert proved in 1909 that there is. We now know g(2) = 4 , g(3) = 9 (for example 23 = 2 · 2^3 + 7 · 1^3 needs nine cubes) and g(4) = 19 . The thinking skill Find a multiplicative structure To show a property is preserved under multiplication, find an algebraic structure (complex numbers, quaternions, matrices) in which the property is the “size” of an object and size is multiplicative. Once such a structure is found, a product identity comes for free, and a problem about all numbers reduces to a problem about primes. Try this next A worked example. Use the formulas for L_1, ldots, L_4 with (a, b, c, d) = (p, q, r, s) = (2, 1, 1, 1) to write 49 = 7 × 7 as a sum of four squares, and check your answer. Is it the same as the obvious 49 = 7^2 + 0^2 + 0^2 + 0^2 ? Two squares inside four. Show that if c = d = r = s = 0 , the identity reduces to the two-square identity of Section 1.6 . Numbers needing four squares. Show that no number of the form 8m + 7 is a sum of three squares, by considering squares modulo 8 . Jacobi’s formula. Count the representations of 2 as a sum of four squares (with order and signs mattering), and check that the answer is 8 × (1 + 2) = 24 . Further reading Harold Davenport, The Higher Arithmetic (Cambridge University Press). Chapter V proves Lagrange’s four-square theorem. John Conway & Derek Smith, On Quaternions and Octonions (A. K. Peters). The arithmetic of quaternions, including a proof of the four-square theorem via quaternion integers. Aigner & Ziegler, Proofs from THE BOOK , chapter “Representing numbers as sums of two squares”. The two-square companion to this section.

title: Hyperbolic Rotations and Relativity
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on What the question means physically The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 1991, Question 6 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/91-s3-q6 The hook A rotation matrix beginpmatrix cos u & -sin u \\ sin u & cos u endpmatrix moves points round the circle x^2 + y^2 = 1 , and rotating by u then by w is rotating by u + w . Replace cos and sin by cosh and sinh , adjust a sign, and you get the matrix in this question. It moves points along the hyperbola x^2 - y^2 = 1 instead, and it too adds its “angles”. It is a hyperbolic rotation . This is not just a curiosity. With x standing for time and y for distance (in units where the speed of light is 1 ), the matrix is a Lorentz boost : the transformation, discovered in Einstein’s special relativity, between the measurements of two observers moving at constant velocity relative to each other. The “hyperbolic angle” u is the rapidity , and the fact that rapidities add explains the strange velocity-addition law we met in Section 3.8 . Before you start What identity do cosh u and sinh u satisfy, analogous to cos^2u + sin^2u = 1 ? And what are the addition formulas for cosh(u + v) and sinh(u + v) ? cosh^2u - sinh^2u = 1 , and beginaligned cosh(u + v) &= cosh ucosh v + sinh usinh v, \\ sinh(u + v) &= sinh ucosh v + cosh usinh v. endaligned You can check these from the definitions cosh u = frac12(e^u + e^-u) and sinh u = frac12(e^u - e^-u) . The point (cosh v, sinh v) lies on the hyperbola x^2 - y^2 = 1 , just as (cos v, sin v) lies on the circle. Working it through Stage 1 The hyperbola is invariant beginaligned x'^2 - y'^2 &= (xcosh u + ysinh u)^2 - (xsinh u + ycosh u)^2 \\ &= (x^2 - y^2)(cosh^2u - sinh^2u) = x^2 - y^2, endaligned since the cross terms 2xycosh usinh u cancel. So T preserves x^2 - y^2 , and in particular maps the hyperbola x^2 - y^2 = 1 to itself. ■ Which lines through the origin are mapped to themselves? (Look for eigenvectors.) Tbeginpmatrix 1 \\ 1 endpmatrix = (cosh u + sinh u)beginpmatrix 1 \\ 1 endpmatrix = e^ubeginpmatrix 1 \\ 1 endpmatrix and Tbeginpmatrix 1 \\ -1 endpmatrix = e^-ubeginpmatrix 1 \\ -1 endpmatrix . So the lines y = x and y = -x are each mapped to themselves: one is stretched by e^u , the other shrunk by e^-u . These are the asymptotes of the hyperbola. ■ Stage 2 Adding hyperbolic angles A line with gradient tanh v has direction vector (cosh v, sinh v) . Its image has direction Tbeginpmatrix cosh v \\ sinh v endpmatrix = beginpmatrix cosh ucosh v + sinh usinh v \\ sinh ucosh v + cosh usinh v endpmatrix = beginpmatrix cosh(u + v) \\ sinh(u + v) endpmatrix, which has gradient tanh(u + v) . A linear map sends parallel lines to parallel lines, so this holds whether or not the line passes through the origin. Hence v' = v + u . ■ Stage 3 When are angles preserved? The angle psi between two lines with gradients m_1 , m_2 satisfies tanpsi = left|(m_1 - m_2)/(1 + m_1m_2)right| . Simplify this when m_i = tanh v_i . ( Hint: put everything over cosh v_1cosh v_2 .) Using tanh v_1 - tanh v_2 = (sinh(v_1 - v_2))/(cosh v_1cosh v_2) and 1 + tanh v_1tanh v_2 = (cosh(v_1 + v_2))/(cosh v_1cosh v_2) , tanpsi = left|(sinh(v_1 - v_2))/(cosh(v_1 + v_2))right|. After the transformation, v_1 - v_2 is unchanged and v_1 + v_2 becomes v_1 + v_2 + 2u . When is cosh(v_1 + v_2) = cosh(v_1 + v_2 + 2u) ? Assuming the lines are not parallel ( v_1 ≠ v_2 ), the angles are equal exactly when cosh(v_1 + v_2) = cosh(v_1 + v_2 + 2u) . Since cosh is even and strictly increasing on [0, ∞) , this means v_1 + v_2 = (v_1 + v_2 + 2u) . The plus sign gives u = 0 , which is excluded, so v_1 + v_2 = -u. qed Stage 4 The picture When v_1 + v_2 = -u , the transformed angles are v_1' = v_1 + u = -v_2 and v_2' = v_2 + u = -v_1 . So the image of ell_1 has gradient -tanh v_2 : it is the reflection of ell_2 in the x -axis, and the image of ell_2 is the reflection of ell_1 . For lines through the origin, the transformation swaps the two lines and reflects them, which explains why the angle between them is unchanged (Figure 7.6.1). Looking back An invariant quadratic form. T preserves x^2 - y^2 , just as a rotation preserves x^2 + y^2 . Eigenvectors are the asymptotes. The lines left invariant are y = x , stretched and shrunk by e^ u . Hyperbolic angles add. Parametrising directions by tanh v turned the action of T into simple addition, v mapsto v + u . What’s really going on Special relativity In Einstein’s special relativity (1905), different observers moving at constant velocity relative to each other disagree about time and distance, but they all agree on the quantity t^2 - x^2 (with the speed of light c = 1 ), the spacetime interval . The transformations preserving it are the Lorentz transformations , and in one space dimension they are exactly the matrices in this question, with x as time and y as distance. An observer moving with velocity v = tanh u uses coordinates related to ours by this matrix, with cosh u = frac1sqrt1 - v^2 , the famous factor γ of time dilation. Hermann Minkowski saw in 1908 that this makes spacetime a four-dimensional geometry with a “distance” that has a minus sign in it: “Henceforth space by itself, and time by itself, are doomed to fade away into mere shadows.” What the question means physically The invariant lines y = x are the paths of light rays. They are the same for every observer: the speed of light is the same for everyone, the founding principle of relativity. The hyperbola x^2 - y^2 = 1 is the set of events one unit of “proper time” from the origin, as measured by observers moving at all possible constant velocities. Adding rapidities. A line of gradient tanh v through the origin is the path of an object moving at velocity tanh v . A boost by rapidity u changes its velocity to tanh(v + u) = (tanh v + tanh u)/(1 + tanh vtanh u) , which is Einstein’s velocity-addition formula from Section 3.8 . Velocities do not add; rapidities do. And in Section 5.8 we saw the same addition formula as the distance rule in the Poincaré disc: the set of possible velocities in relativity, measured with rapidity, is a hyperbolic space. The thinking skill Find the right parametrisation Describe your objects by a parameter in which the transformation becomes simple. Describing directions by their gradient, T acts by a messy formula; describing them by v with gradient tanh v , it simply adds u . The same idea made rotations simple with angles, and made the map x mapsto x^2 - 2 simple in Section 2.8 . Try this next Composing boosts. Show that T(u)T(w) = T(u + w) , where T(u) is the matrix in the question. What is T(u)^-1 ? Time dilation. A spaceship travels at 0.8 times the speed of light. Find its rapidity u and cosh u . If 10 years pass on Earth, how much time passes on the ship? (Use t_ship = t_Earth/cosh u .) Hyperbolic area. Show that the area enclosed by the hyperbola x^2 - y^2 = 1 , the x -axis and the line from the origin to (cosh v, sinh v) is frac v2 , just as the corresponding area for a circle is fracθ2 . Why must T preserve such areas? Squeeze. Change coordinates to p = x + y , q = x - y . Show that T becomes p mapsto e^up , q mapsto e^-uq , and that the hyperbola becomes pq = 1 . Describe the transformation geometrically in these coordinates. Further reading Edwin Taylor & John Wheeler, Spacetime Physics (W. H. Freeman). Special relativity with rapidity and spacetime diagrams, for students with A-level mathematics. Tevian Dray, The Geometry of Special Relativity (CRC Press). Relativity as hyperbolic trigonometry, in exactly the spirit of this section. Albert Einstein, Relativity: The Special and the General Theory (various editions). Einstein’s own popular account, still very readable.

title: Linear Algebra and Geometry
headings: Why linear algebra matters What you will meet at university The questions that run through this chapter Ideas in this chapter How to read this chapter
text: Chapter 7 · Introduction Transformations of Space We think basis-free, we write basis-free, but when the chips are down we close the office door and compute with matrices like fury. — Irving Kaplansky, on his and Paul Halmos’s approach to linear algebra At school, a matrix usually appears as a tool for solving simultaneous equations, or as a recipe for transforming points: multiply the matrix by a column vector and read off the new coordinates. Both are useful, but they hide what makes matrices one of the most important ideas in mathematics. A matrix is a linear transformation : a way of stretching, rotating, reflecting and shearing space, and matrices can be added, multiplied, raised to powers and differentiated, just like numbers. Except that they are not like numbers. Their multiplication depends on the order, they can multiply to zero, and they have hidden invariants (trace, determinant, eigenvalues) that capture their essential behaviour regardless of how they are written down. Why linear algebra matters Linear algebra is probably the most widely used branch of mathematics. Every computer graphics engine, from video games to film animation, is a machine for multiplying matrices: every rotation of a character, every camera angle, every perspective projection is a matrix. The search engines and recommendation systems of the internet are built on eigenvectors. Engineers find the vibration frequencies of bridges and buildings from eigenvalues; statisticians find the main patterns in data with them; quantum mechanics is written entirely in the language of linear algebra. And modern machine learning, at its core, is very large amounts of matrix multiplication. There is a reason for this ubiquity. Linear problems are the ones we can solve completely, and almost every non-linear problem looks linear if you zoom in close enough. That is the idea of calculus, and it means that linear algebra is the language in which the local behaviour of almost everything is described. What you will meet at university Linear algebra is one of the two pillars of the first year, alongside analysis. You will meet vector spaces (sets where you can add and scale, of which the plane and three-dimensional space are just the first examples) and linear maps between them, and learn that matrices are simply linear maps written in coordinates. You will study determinants, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and the spectral theorem , which says that symmetric matrices can be diagonalised by a rotation. Later courses use this everywhere: in differential equations (Chapter 8), in geometry (where rotations and reflections form groups), in the theory of Lie groups , which describe continuous symmetries, and in functional analysis, which is linear algebra in infinitely many dimensions. The questions that run through this chapter Three big questions How are matrices like numbers, and how are they different? Which rules of arithmetic survive, and which fail? What does a matrix really do? How can we see the geometry of a transformation, and which numbers capture it independently of coordinates? What stays the same? Which quantities are preserved by transformations, or by motion, and what do they tell us? The chapter starts with the rules of matrix algebra ( Section 7.1 ), then turns to the geometry of transformations: eigenvectors, determinants, matrices of finite order, rotations in three dimensions and the hyperbolic rotations of special relativity. It continues with conserved quantities of evolving matrices, the four-square identity from determinants, and ends with a counting argument, Euler’s formula, that classifies the Platonic solids. Ideas in this chapter § Topic Idea 7.1 Rules that fail Non-commutativity; zero divisors 7.2 Eigenvectors Directions a transformation does not rotate 7.3 The determinant Characterised by multiplicativity; signed area 7.4 Matrices of finite order Trace, determinant and Cayley–Hamilton 7.5 Rotations in 3D Rodrigues’ formula from the cross product 7.6 Lorentz boosts Hyperbolic angles add 7.7 Conserved quantities The trace of a commutator is zero 7.8 Four squares Multiplicative determinants 7.9 Platonic solids Double counting and Euler’s formula How to read this chapter For every matrix in this chapter, draw what it does. Take the unit square, or the unit circle, or a few vectors, and sketch their images. A two-minute sketch will often show you the answer (an eigenvector, a counterexample, an invariant line) before you start calculating, and it will help you check the calculation afterwards.

title: Quantities That Never Change
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Isospectral flows Jacobi’s formula The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2024, Question 5 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP III paper in OCR’s download of the 2024 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/725753-2024-past-papers.zip The hook Some of the deepest facts in physics are conservation laws : energy, momentum and angular momentum stay the same however complicated the motion. When a system has enough conserved quantities, its motion can be solved exactly; when it has too few, it can be chaotic. This question shows a remarkable way of manufacturing conserved quantities. If a matrix changes in time according to (dM)/(dt) = MN - NM , then however wildly its entries vary, its trace and determinant, and hence its eigenvalues, never change. Such a pair (M, N) is called a Lax pair , after Peter Lax, who introduced the idea in 1968 to explain the astonishing behaviour of solitons , solitary waves that pass through each other unchanged. Before you start The expression MN - NM is called the commutator of M and N . When is it zero? What is its trace, given part (i)? It is zero exactly when M and N commute. And by part (i) its trace is tr(MN) - tr(NM) = 0 , always. That single fact is the beginning of every conservation law in the question. Working it through Stage 1 The trace With M = beginpmatrix a & b \\ c & d endpmatrix and N = beginpmatrix p & q \\ r & s endpmatrix , the diagonal entries of MN are ap + br and cq + ds , so tr(MN) = ap + br + cq + ds . Swapping the roles of M and N gives pa + qc + rb + sd , the same. Clearly tr(M + N) = trM + trN . ■ Stage 2 The derivative of a determinant Differentiate detM = ad - bc by the product rule. Then compute M^-1(dM)/(dt) and its trace, using M^-1 = (1)/(detM)beginpmatrix d & -b \\ -c & a endpmatrix . Writing dots for derivatives, (d)/(dt)detM = dot ad + adot d - dot bc - bdot c . And M^-1dotM = (1)/(detM)beginpmatrix d & -b \\ -c & a endpmatrixbeginpmatrix dot a & dot b \\ dot c & dot d endpmatrix has diagonal entries (ddot a - bdot c)/(detM) and (-cdot b + adot d)/(detM) . Their sum is (1)/(detM)(d)/(dt)detM . ■ Stage 3 Three conserved quantities Take the trace of dotM = MN - NM . For the determinant, use part (ii): what is M^-1(MN - NM) ? Trace: (d)/(dt)trM = trdotM = tr(MN) - tr(NM) = 0 . Determinant: by part (ii), (1)/(detM)(d)/(dt)detM = trbigl(M^-1(MN - NM)bigr) = trN - tr(M^-1NM) = trN - trN = 0, using part (i) in the form trbigl(M^-1(NM)bigr) = trbigl((NM)M^-1bigr) = trN . Trace of the square: tr(M^2) = (trM)^2 - 2detM (see Section 7.4 ), which is constant because both terms are. ■ Stage 4 An explicit solution With N = tI + tE , where E = beginpmatrix 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 endpmatrix , compute MN - NM and write down the differential equations for a , b , c , d . Solve them in the order c , then a and d , then b . The part tI commutes with everything, so MN - NM = t(ME - EM) . Now ME = beginpmatrix 0 & a \\ 0 & c endpmatrix and EM = beginpmatrix c & d \\ 0 & 0 endpmatrix , so dot a = -tc, qquad dot b = t(a - d), qquad dot c = 0, qquad dot d = tc. So c = C is constant; then a = A - frac12Ct^2 and d = D + frac12Ct^2 ; then dot b = t(A - D - Ct^2) , so b = B + frac12(A - D)t^2 - frac14Ct^4 . Therefore M = beginpmatrix A - frac12Ct^2 & B + frac12(A - D)t^2 - frac14Ct^4 \ 0.5ex] C & D + frac12Ct^2 endpmatrix. qed Check: the trace is A + D , and the determinant is (A - frac12Ct^2)(D + frac12Ct^2) - Cbigl(B + frac12(A - D)t^2 - frac14Ct^4bigr) = AD - BC , constant as promised (Figure 7.7.1). Stage 5 A different equation If dotM = MN , then N = M^-1dotM , and by part (ii) trN is the logarithmic derivative of detM . Can the trace of M stay constant while its determinant changes? Certainly. Take M = beginpmatrix 1 & t \\ t & 1 endpmatrix for |t| < 1 (where detM = 1 - t^2 ≠ 0 ). Its trace is constantly 2 . Define N = M^-1dotM , so that dotM = MN : N = (1)/(1 - t^2)beginpmatrix 1 & -t \\ -t & 1 endpmatrixbeginpmatrix 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 endpmatrix = (1)/(1 - t^2)beginpmatrix -t & 1 \\ 1 & -t endpmatrix, which is non-singular, with trN = (-2t)/(1 - t^2) ≠ 0 for t ≠ 0 . So no , trN need not be zero. ■ Looking back The trace of a commutator is zero. From tr(MN) = tr(NM) , every conservation law followed. Logarithmic derivatives. Part (ii) turned the derivative of a determinant into a trace, which is linear and easy to handle. Check conservation in the explicit solution. The formula for M(t) was checked by confirming that its trace and determinant are constant. What’s really going on Solitons and Lax pairs In 1834 the Scottish engineer John Scott Russell followed, on horseback, a solitary wave travelling along the Union Canal near Edinburgh for over a mile without losing its shape. Such waves are described by the Korteweg–de Vries (KdV) equation , and in the 1960s computer experiments by Norman Zabusky and Martin Kruskal showed that two of these “solitons” can collide and emerge unchanged, as if they were particles. Explaining this needed infinitely many conserved quantities. Peter Lax showed in 1968 that the KdV equation can be written as dot L = LP - PL for a pair of differential operators L and P ; then, exactly as in this question, the eigenvalues of L are conserved, and they provide the infinitely many conservation laws. Systems with a Lax pair are called integrable , and they are among the few nonlinear systems that can be solved exactly. Isospectral flows Since the trace and determinant of M determine its characteristic polynomial λ^2 - (trM)λ + detM , the eigenvalues of M do not change with time. The flow dotM = [M, N] moves M around inside the set of matrices with fixed eigenvalues. In fact, the solution is always of the form M(t) = S(t)^-1M(0)S(t) for some invertible S(t) : the matrix stays similar to its starting value. The same idea runs through physics: in quantum mechanics, an observable A evolves by (dA)/(dt) = (i)/(hbar)[H, A] , where H is the energy, so anything that commutes with the energy is conserved. Jacobi’s formula Part (ii) holds for invertible matrices of any size and is called Jacobi’s formula . It is safest written without the logarithm, as (d)/(dt)detM = detM\,trbigl(M^-1dotMbigr) , because detM may be negative; the logarithmic form (d)/(dt)detM = trbigl(M^-1dotMbigr) needs detM > 0 (or |detM| in general). A consequence: if dotM = AM for a constant matrix A , then detM(t) = e^ttrAdetM(0) . In the study of differential equations this tells you how volumes in phase space grow or shrink; for the equations of classical mechanics the trace is zero and volume is preserved, a result known as Liouville’s theorem . The thinking skill Find what does not change When something evolves, look for quantities built from it that stay constant. They constrain the motion and often reveal its structure. Here the trace and determinant were conserved because the rate of change was a commutator. In mechanics, conserved quantities come from symmetries (Noether’s theorem), and finding them is often the first step in solving a problem. Try this next Check the solution. Verify by differentiating that the matrix M(t) in Stage 4 satisfies dotM = MN - NM . Similarity. Show that if M(t) = S^-1M_0S , where M_0 is constant and S(t) satisfies dotS = SN , then dotM = MN - NM . ( Hint: (d)/(dt)S^-1 = -S^-1dotSS^-1 .) Volume growth. Let M(t) = beginpmatrix e^2t & 0 \\ 0 & e^-t endpmatrix . Find N with dotM = MN , and check that (d)/(dt)detM = trN . Higher powers. Show directly that (d)/(dt)tr(M^k) = 0 for every positive integer k when dotM = MN - NM . Further reading P. G. Drazin & R. S. Johnson, Solitons: An Introduction (Cambridge University Press). The standard undergraduate introduction, including Lax pairs. Thierry Dauxois & Michel Peyrard, Physics of Solitons (Cambridge University Press). Includes the story of Scott Russell’s wave. Dwight Neuenschwander, Emmy Noether’s Wonderful Theorem (Johns Hopkins University Press). How symmetries give conservation laws.

title: Rules That Fail for Matrices
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Infinitely many square roots Non-commutativity in physics The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 1993, Question 6 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/93-s2-q6 The hook Matrices can be added and multiplied, so it is tempting to treat them like numbers. This question tests that temptation with four “rules” that are true for numbers, and asks which survive for matrices. Most of them fail, and the way they fail is instructive. Matrix multiplication is not commutative; there are non-zero matrices whose product is zero; and a quadratic equation for matrices can have infinitely many solutions. These failures are not defects. They are the reason matrices are useful: they describe transformations of space, and doing two transformations in different orders genuinely gives different results. In 1925 Werner Heisenberg discovered that the quantities of quantum mechanics behave like matrices rather than numbers, and that the failure of AB = BA is the mathematical form of the uncertainty principle. Before you start For real numbers, why is it true that ab = 0 implies a = 0 or b = 0 ? Which property of numbers does the argument use, and does it hold for matrices? If ab = 0 and a ≠ 0 , divide by a to get b = 0 . The argument needs every non-zero number to have an inverse. Non-zero matrices need not have inverses (those with determinant zero do not), so the argument breaks down. Keep the geometric picture in mind too: a matrix is a transformation of the plane, and a product AB means “do B , then A ”. Working it through Stage 1 Can AB = 0 but BA ≠ 0 ? Think geometrically. You want B to send everything into a line that A then squashes to zero. But in the other order, A should not squash everything that B then kills. Let A = beginpmatrix 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 endpmatrix , which projects onto the x -axis (killing the y -axis), and B = beginpmatrix 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 endpmatrix , which sends (x, y) to (0, x) , into the y -axis. Then AB = beginpmatrix 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 endpmatrixbeginpmatrix 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 endpmatrix = beginpmatrix 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 endpmatrix, qquad BA = beginpmatrix 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 endpmatrix ≠ 0. The assertion is false (Figure 7.1.1). ■ Stage 2 The difference of two squares Expanding carefully, keeping the order of every product: (A - B)(A + B) = A^2 + AB - BA - B^2. This equals A^2 - B^2 exactly when AB = BA . With the matrices of Stage 1, AB - BA = -BA ≠ 0 , so the assertion is false . ■ Stage 3 Non-zero solutions of AX = 0 If detA ≠ 0 , what can you do to AX = 0 ? If detA = 0 , can you find a non-zero column vector v with Av = 0 ? If detA ≠ 0 , then A^-1 exists and X = A^-1AX = 0 : no non-zero solution. If detA = 0 , write A = beginpmatrix a & b \\ c & d endpmatrix with ad = bc . The vectors beginpmatrix b \\ -a endpmatrix and beginpmatrix d \\ -c endpmatrix satisfy Abeginpmatrix b \\ -a endpmatrix = beginpmatrix ab - ba \\ cb - da endpmatrix = 0 , and similarly for the other. Since A ≠ 0 , at least one of them is non-zero; call it v . Then the matrix X whose two columns are both v is non-zero and AX = 0 . So the assertion is true . ■ Stage 4 How many square roots? Find non-zero A and B for which X^2 + AX + B = 0 has infinitely many solutions. ( Hint: make the left-hand side a perfect square, (X - I)^2 , and think about matrices whose square is zero.) Take A = -2I and B = I , both non-zero. The equation becomes (X - I)^2 = 0 . Any matrix N with N^2 = 0 gives a solution X = I + N , and there are infinitely many such N : N = beginpmatrix 0 & t \\ 0 & 0 endpmatrix, qquad N^2 = 0 for every real t. So X = beginpmatrix 1 & t \\ 0 & 1 endpmatrix is a solution for every t , and the assertion is false . ■ Looking back Order matters. Every expansion must keep products in order; AB and BA are usually different. Zero divisors. Non-zero matrices can multiply to zero, which breaks the argument behind “a quadratic has at most two roots”. Think of transformations. Each counterexample was easy to find by picturing what the matrices do to the plane. What’s really going on Matrices as an algebra Arthur Cayley introduced matrix algebra in 1858, treating matrices as single objects that can be added and multiplied, rather than just as tables of coefficients. He noticed at once that multiplication is not commutative, and he proved the Cayley–Hamilton theorem : every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic equation. For a 2 × 2 matrix with trace t and determinant d , this says M^2 - tM + dI = 0 , a fact we use repeatedly in this chapter ( Section 7.4 ). The 2 × 2 real matrices form a ring : you can add, subtract and multiply, but multiplication is not commutative, and there are zero divisors , non-zero elements whose product is zero. Infinitely many square roots Stage 4 can be made even more striking. The equation X^2 = I has the obvious solutions pmI , but also every reflection of the plane in a line through the origin, X = beginpmatrix cosθ & sinθ \\ sinθ & -cosθ endpmatrix , since reflecting twice does nothing. That is a whole circle of square roots of I . A polynomial of degree n with number coefficients has at most n roots because numbers have no zero divisors; matrices do, and the count fails. Non-commutativity in physics In classical mechanics, position x and momentum p are numbers and xp = px . In quantum mechanics they become operators (infinite matrices) with xp - px = ihbar , where hbar is Planck’s constant divided by 2π . This single non-commutation relation implies Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle: position and momentum cannot both be known exactly. When Heisenberg discovered the rules of quantum mechanics in 1925 he did not know what matrices were; Max Born recognised that the strange multiplication rule Heisenberg had invented was matrix multiplication. The thinking skill Test familiar rules in a new setting When you meet a new kind of object, check which familiar rules still hold, and find out exactly which property each rule depends on. The rule “ ab = 0 implies a = 0 or b = 0 ” depends on division; “ (a - b)(a + b) = a^2 - b^2 ” depends on commutativity. Knowing what each rule rests on tells you when you can still use it. Try this next When do they commute? Find all 2 × 2 matrices that commute with beginpmatrix 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 endpmatrix . Square roots of zero. Find all 2 × 2 real matrices N with N^2 = 0 . ( Hint: use the Cayley–Hamilton theorem to show trN = detN = 0 .) Reflections. Show that every reflection matrix beginpmatrix cosθ & sinθ \\ sinθ & -cosθ endpmatrix squares to I , and find the line it reflects in. Cayley–Hamilton. Prove that every 2 × 2 matrix satisfies M^2 - (trM)M + (detM)I = 0 by direct calculation. Further reading Gilbert Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra (Wellesley-Cambridge). The most popular first linear algebra text, with an emphasis on understanding. Sheldon Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right (Springer; free online). A more abstract approach, centred on linear maps rather than matrices. Jim Baggott, The Quantum Story (Oxford University Press). The history of quantum mechanics, including Heisenberg’s matrix mechanics.

title: Only Five Platonic Solids
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Beyond the sphere Symmetry groups The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 1999, Question 4 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/99-s3-q4 The hook There are infinitely many regular polygons: triangles, squares, pentagons, and so on for every number of sides. You might expect infinitely many regular polyhedra too. There are exactly five: the tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron. Plato associated four of them with the elements (fire, earth, air, water) and the fifth with the cosmos; Euclid’s Elements , the most influential mathematics book ever written, ends with a proof that there are no others; Kepler built a model of the solar system from them. This question proves the classification in a few lines, from a single remarkable formula found by Euler in 1750: for any convex polyhedron, V - E + F = 2 . A formula about counting turns into a theorem about shapes, and the number 2 turns out to be a fingerprint of the sphere. Before you start Check Euler’s formula on a cube: how many vertices, edges and faces does it have? And on a square-based pyramid? The cube has V = 8 , E = 12 , F = 6 , and 8 - 12 + 6 = 2 . The square-based pyramid has 5 vertices, 8 edges and 5 faces, and 5 - 8 + 5 = 2 . The formula holds for any polyhedron without holes, however irregular. In a regular polyhedron, each face has m edges and each edge borders two faces. What equation does that give between E and F ? Similarly, between E and V ? Counting edge–face incidences in two ways: each of the F faces has m edges, and each edge is counted twice (once for each of its two faces), so mF = 2E . Similarly each vertex has n edges and each edge has two ends, so nV = 2E . This “count the same thing in two ways” trick is called double counting . Working it through Stage 1 A formula for F From mF = 2E and nV = 2E , we have E = (mF)/(2) and V = (mF)/(n) . Substituting into Euler’s formula, (mF)/(n) - (mF)/(2) + F = 2 quadLongrightarrowquad F\,(2m - mn + 2n)/(2n) = 2 quadLongrightarrowquad F = (4n)/(2m + 2n - mn). And 4 - (n - 2)(m - 2) = 4 - (mn - 2m - 2n + 4) = 2m + 2n - mn = h . So F = (4n)/(h) . ■ Stage 2 Which values of m and n are possible? What is the smallest possible value of m (sides of a face) and of n (faces at a vertex)? And since F > 0 , what sign must h have? A polygon needs at least 3 sides, so m ≥ 3 , and at least 3 faces must meet at each vertex of a solid, so n ≥ 3 . Since F > 0 , we need h > 0 , that is, (n - 2)(m - 2) < 4 . With both factors at least 1 , the only possibilities for (m - 2, n - 2) are (1, 1) , (1, 2) , (2, 1) , (1, 3) and (3, 1) . For each of the five possibilities, compute h , then F , then E = (mF)/(2) and V = (mF)/(n) . Identify each solid. m n h F E V solid 3 3 3 4 6 4 tetrahedron 3 4 2 8 12 6 octahedron 4 3 2 6 12 8 cube 3 5 1 20 30 12 icosahedron 5 3 1 12 30 20 dodecahedron These are the only possibilities, so there are at most five regular polyhedra; and all five exist (Euclid shows how to construct each of them). ■ Looking back Double counting. Counting edge–face and edge–vertex incidences in two ways gave mF = 2E and nV = 2E . An inequality from positivity. The simple requirement F > 0 cut infinitely many candidates down to five. Existence is separate. The argument shows there are at most five; that each actually exists has to be checked by constructing it. What’s really going on Euler’s formula and topology Euler stated V - E + F = 2 in 1750, but his proof had gaps, and the formula has a fascinating history of attempted proofs, counterexamples and repairs. A “picture frame” polyhedron, with a square hole through the middle, has V - E + F = 0 ; a polyhedron made of two cubes joined at a vertex has V - E + F = 3 . Imre Lakatos turned this history into a famous book, Proofs and Refutations , about how mathematical concepts are sharpened by counterexamples. The resolution is that V - E + F depends only on the shape of the surface in the loose sense of topology: it is 2 for any surface that can be deformed into a sphere, 0 for a torus (a doughnut), and 2 - 2g for a surface with g holes. This number, the Euler characteristic , was one of the first ideas of topology, the study of properties unchanged by stretching and bending. Beyond the sphere What happens when h = 0 or h < 0 ? When (m - 2)(n - 2) = 4 , there are three solutions, (3, 6) , (4, 4) and (6, 3) : six triangles, four squares or three hexagons meet at a point with angles adding up to exactly 360^circ . These are the three regular tilings of the flat plane, the patterns of bathroom floors and honeycombs. And when (m - 2)(n - 2) > 4 , the angles at a vertex add up to more than 360^circ , which is impossible in the flat plane but perfectly possible in the hyperbolic plane of Section 5.8 . There are infinitely many regular tilings of the hyperbolic plane, one for every point above the curve in Figure 7.9.1; Escher’s Circle Limit woodcuts are drawings of some of them. So the classification of Platonic solids is really the first case of a trichotomy (sphere, plane, hyperbolic plane) that runs through all of geometry. Symmetry groups The symmetries of the Platonic solids form groups: 12 rotations for the tetrahedron, 24 for the cube and octahedron (which are dual: swap faces and vertices, m leftrightarrow n ), and 60 for the dodecahedron and icosahedron. The icosahedral group of order 60 is the “simple” group that, as we mentioned in Section 6.4 , prevents the quintic from being solved by radicals. Felix Klein wrote a whole book, Lectures on the Icosahedron (1884), connecting the icosahedron to the solution of quintic equations. The thinking skill Double counting Count the same collection in two different ways and equate the results. Here the collection was the set of (edge, face) pairs with the edge on the face. Double counting is one of the most powerful tools in combinatorics, and it reappears throughout Chapter 9. Try this next Duality. Show that swapping m and n swaps V and F and leaves E unchanged. Which pairs of Platonic solids are dual to each other? Which is self-dual? A football. A traditional football is made of 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons, with three faces meeting at each vertex. Use double counting and Euler’s formula to check that V - E + F = 2 . Show more generally that any such polyhedron made of pentagons and hexagons, three at each vertex, has exactly 12 pentagons. A torus. Make a “picture frame” polyhedron (a square block with a square hole) and count V , E and F . Check that V - E + F = 0 . Angles at a vertex. The interior angle of a regular m -gon is 180^circ(1 - frac2m) . Show that n of them fit round a vertex of a convex solid (total less than 360^circ ) exactly when (m - 2)(n - 2) < 4 , giving a second proof of the classification. Further reading David Richeson, Euler’s Gem (Princeton University Press). The history of V - E + F = 2 and how it led to topology. Excellent for a sixth-former. Imre Lakatos, Proofs and Refutations (Cambridge University Press). A dialogue about Euler’s formula and the nature of proof. H. S. M. Coxeter, Regular Polytopes (Dover). The classic book on regular polyhedra and their higher-dimensional cousins.

title: Rotating in Three Dimensions
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Rotations do not commute The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2022, Question 7 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP III paper in OCR’s download of the 2022 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/696587-2022-past-papers.zip The hook In two dimensions, rotating a point is easy: multiply by e^iθ . In three dimensions it is much harder. There is no single complex number to multiply by, rotations about different axes do not commute, and writing down the matrix for “rotate by 37^circ about the axis through (1, 2, 2) ” looks daunting. This question builds that matrix, for any axis and any angle, out of the cross product. The result is Rodrigues’ rotation formula , published by Olinde Rodrigues in 1840. It is used every day in robotics, computer graphics and spacecraft navigation, and it reveals a lovely fact: crossing with n is “rotation by 90^circ about n ”, and every rotation about n is built from it, just as e^iθ = cosθ + isinθ is built from multiplication by i . Before you start What does n × r look like geometrically, when r is perpendicular to n ? And when r is parallel to n ? If r parallel n , then n × r = 0 . If r perp n , then n × r has the same length as r (since |n| = 1 and the angle is 90^circ ), is perpendicular to both, and by the right-hand rule is r rotated by 90^circ anticlockwise about n (looking down n ). So f kills the component of r along n and rotates the perpendicular component by 90^circ . That picture explains the whole question. Working it through Stage 1 Crossing twice f(r) = n × r = (bz - cy,\ cx - az,\ ay - bx) . Crossing again with n = (a, b, c) , the x -component of f(f(r)) is b(ay - bx) - c(cx - az) = -x(b^2 + c^2) + aby + acz. qed Since a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 1 , this is -x(1 - a^2) + aby + acz = a(ax + by + cz) - x , which is the x -component of (n.r)n - r . The other components follow by symmetry, so f(f(r)) = (n.r)n - r . ■ Write r = r_parallel + r_perp , where r_parallel = (n.r)n is the component along n . What is f(f(r)) in terms of these? f(f(r)) = r_parallel - r = -r_perp . Applying f twice kills the parallel part and rotates the perpendicular part by 180^circ about n , which simply reverses it (Figure 7.5.1). This is the analogue of i^2 = -1 . Stage 2 The rotation Compute g(n) . Then compute g(r) for r perp n , using f(f(r)) = -r for such r . f(n) = n × n = 0 , so g(n) = n : the axis is fixed. If r perp n , then f(f(r)) = -r and g(r) = r + sinθ\,(n × r) - (1 - cosθ)r = cosθ\,r + sinθ\,(n × r). Since n × r is r turned through 90^circ about n , with the same length, this is r rotated through θ about n , exactly like (cosθ + isinθ)z in the plane. Since g is linear and every vector is a sum of a multiple of n and a vector perpendicular to n , g is the rotation through angle θ about the axis through the origin in the direction n (anticlockwise when viewed from the tip of n ). ■ Stage 3 The reflection Simplify h(s) = -s - 2f(f(s)) using part (i). What does it do to vectors along n , and to vectors perpendicular to n ? h(s) = -s - 2bigl((n.s)n - sbigr) = s - 2(n.s)n . Vectors perpendicular to n are unchanged, and h(n) = -n . So h is the reflection in the plane through the origin perpendicular to n . ■ Looking back Decompose into parallel and perpendicular parts. Every step became clear once r was split into its components along and across n . Linearity reduces the work. To identify a linear map, it is enough to know what it does to a few well-chosen vectors. An analogue of complex numbers. On vectors perpendicular to n , f behaves like multiplication by i : f^2 = -1 , and g = cosθ + sinθ\,f . What’s really going on Euler’s rotation theorem Every rotation of three-dimensional space that fixes the origin is a rotation about some axis through the origin. Euler proved this in 1775. In matrix terms, every 3 × 3 rotation matrix has an eigenvector with eigenvalue 1 , the axis. Rodrigues’ formula gives the converse: for every axis n and angle θ , the rotation matrix is R = I + sinθ\,K + (1 - cosθ)\,K^2, qquad K = beginpmatrix 0 & -c & b \\ c & 0 & -a \\ -b & a & 0 endpmatrix, where K is the matrix of r mapsto n × r . Since K^3 = -K , the exponential series e^thetaK = I + thetaK + (θ^2)/(2!)K^2 + cdots collapses to exactly this formula, the three-dimensional version of e^iθ = cosθ + isinθ . This connection between rotations and exponentials of “infinitesimal rotations” K is the starting point of the theory of Lie groups . Rotations do not commute Hold a book flat, rotate it 90^circ about a vertical axis and then 90^circ about a horizontal axis; then start again and do the two rotations in the other order. The book ends up in different positions. Composition of rotations in three dimensions is not commutative, unlike in two dimensions. This is one reason the quaternions of Section 6.7 are useful: the rotation by θ about n corresponds to the quaternion cosfracθ2 + sinfracθ2(ai + bj + ck) , and composing rotations is multiplying quaternions, with the non-commutativity built in. Rodrigues himself, in his 1840 paper, found the composition formula for rotations three years before Hamilton invented quaternions. The thinking skill Split into invariant parts To understand a transformation, split space into pieces it treats simply: here, the axis (left alone) and the plane perpendicular to it (rotated). This is the same idea as eigenvectors in Section 7.2 : find subspaces the transformation preserves, and study it on each piece. Try this next Rotations in the plane. Try STEP III 2017, Question 2 . Using complex numbers, it shows that two rotations of the plane combine to give a rotation, with one exception. Find the exception, and what the combination is then. A specific rotation. Find the matrix of the rotation by 120^circ about the axis in the direction (1, 1, 1) . Show that it permutes the coordinate axes cyclically. Powers of K . Show that K^2r = (n.r)n - r and K^3 = -K , and deduce Rodrigues’ formula from the exponential series. Two reflections make a rotation. Show that reflecting in two planes through the origin, at angle α to each other, is a rotation by 2α about their line of intersection. Further reading Simon Altmann, Rotations, Quaternions, and Double Groups (Dover). The definitive account of three-dimensional rotations, including Rodrigues’ contribution. Simon Altmann, “ Hamilton, Rodrigues, and the quaternion scandal ” , Mathematics Magazine 62 (1989). A short, lively history. John Stillwell, Naive Lie Theory (Springer). Rotations, quaternions and Lie groups for undergraduates.

title: What We Have Learned
headings: 1. How are matrices like numbers, and how are they different? 2. What does a matrix really do? 3. What stays the same? 4. A toolkit for linear algebra Where next
text: We began by saying that a matrix is a transformation of space with a life of its own, and asked three questions: how matrices are like numbers and how they differ, what a matrix really does, and what stays the same. Here is what the chapter’s nine questions showed. 1. How are matrices like numbers, and how are they different? Matrices can be added and multiplied, but Section 7.1 showed which familiar rules fail. Multiplication is not commutative, so (A - B)(A + B) need not be A^2 - B^2 ; there are zero divisors, so AB = 0 does not force BA = 0 ; and a quadratic matrix equation can have infinitely many roots. Each failure had a geometric explanation, in terms of what the matrices do to the plane. What survives, crucially, is that determinants multiply, det(AB) = detAdetB . Section 7.3 showed that this property essentially characterises the determinant, and Section 7.8 used it to prove Euler’s four-square identity, the key step in Lagrange’s theorem that every whole number is a sum of four squares. 2. What does a matrix really do? Several sections answered this by finding the right point of view. Eigenvectors ( Section 7.2 ) are the directions a matrix does not turn. In their coordinates a symmetric matrix is just a stretch, and the image of a circle is an ellipse whose axes and area can be read off. The determinant ( Section 7.3 ) is the signed area scale factor: shears preserve area, swaps reverse orientation, singular matrices squash the plane flat. Trace and determinant ( Section 7.4 ) decide, via the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, whether a matrix returns to the identity after a few steps. A matrix with M^8 = I need not be a rotation; it is a rotation seen in skewed coordinates. And because traces of integer matrices are integers, crystals cannot have five-fold symmetry. Rotations in three dimensions ( Section 7.5 ) are built from the cross product by Rodrigues’ formula, the three-dimensional analogue of e^iθ = cosθ + isinθ . Hyperbolic rotations ( Section 7.6 ) move points along a hyperbola and add their hyperbolic angles. They are the Lorentz boosts of special relativity, and their invariant lines are the paths of light. 3. What stays the same? Invariants were everywhere. Rotations preserve x^2 + y^2 , Lorentz boosts preserve x^2 - y^2 , and similar matrices share their trace and determinant. In Section 7.7 , a matrix evolving by dotM = MN - NM kept its trace and determinant, and so its eigenvalues, constant, however much its entries changed: the mechanism behind the conservation laws of solitons. And in Section 7.9 , the invariant was a number, V - E + F = 2 , which holds for every convex polyhedron and pins the regular ones down to just five. That number, the Euler characteristic, was one of the first invariants of topology. 4. A toolkit for linear algebra Method Where you used it Geometric counterexamples Rules that fail (7.1) Eigenvectors as natural axes The ellipse (7.2); boosts (7.6) Probing with special matrices The determinant (7.3) Cayley–Hamilton Finite order (7.4) Splitting into parallel and perpendicular parts Rodrigues’ formula (7.5) Choosing the right parameter Rapidity (7.6) tr(MN) = tr(NM) Conserved quantities (7.7) Multiplicativity of determinants Four squares (7.8) Double counting Platonic solids (7.9) Where next Eigenvalues and eigenvectors govern the vibrations of systems of springs and masses in Section 11.2 . The eigenvectors of a covariance matrix appear in statistics in Section 13.7 . Differential equations and dynamical systems are the subject of Chapter 8. If you want to go further before university 3Blue1Brown, Essence of Linear Algebra : a free video series that shows what matrices do. Watch it first. Gilbert Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra : the classic first course, with a strong emphasis on understanding and applications. Sheldon Axler, Linear Algebra Done Right : a more abstract approach, centred on linear maps; free online. David Richeson, Euler’s Gem : Euler’s formula and the birth of topology. Kaplansky joked that he and Halmos thought without coordinates but computed with matrices “like fury” behind closed doors. That captures what this chapter has tried to show: matrices are concrete and computable, but behind every calculation there is geometry (a stretch, a rotation, a projection, a boost) and an invariant that does not depend on how you write it down. Learning to move between the two views is one of the most valuable skills a mathematician can have.

The formula breaks down: tanfracπ2 is infinite, matching the fact that there is no turning at all. 8.6 The Quantum Oscillator This is a direct (if tedious) differentiation; alternatively, it follows from Exercise 4. With 2λ = ω , int y_0y_2 = int(2ω x^2 - 1)e^-ω x^2\,dx = 2ω · (1)/(2ω)sqrtfracπω - sqrtfracπω = 0 . y'' = (4λ^2x^2 - 2λ)y , so the equation needs 4λ^2 = ω^2 and 2λ = (2 + 1)ω . With λ = fracω2 > 0 (for decay), = 0 . (d)/(dx)(y_my_n' - y_ny_m') = y_my_n'' - y_ny_m'' = (m^2 - n^2)y_my_n . Integrate from 0 to π : the left side gives 0 because y_m and y_n vanish at both ends, and m^2 ≠ n^2 . Write c = (2n + 1)ω , so y_n'' = (ω^2x^2 - c)y_n . Differentiating z = ω xy_n - y_n' twice and using this (and its derivative) gives z'' - ω^2x^2z = -(c + 2ω)z , and c + 2ω = (2n + 3)ω . From y_0 = e^-ω x^2/2 : 2ω xe^-ω x^2/2 , then 2ω(2ω x^2 - 1)e^-ω x^2/2 , which are multiples of y_1 and y_2 . 8.7 Chaos You Can Solve (i) By induction: if 0 < x < 1 then 0 < x(1 - x) ≤ frac14 , so 0 < kx(1 - x) < 1 . (ii) a = ka(1 - a) gives k = (1)/(1 - a) . (iii) With x_1 = ka(1 - a) = ab , the condition x_2 = a is kab(1 - ab) = a ; using k = (b)/(1 - a) this becomes ab^3 - b^2 + 1 - a = 0 . The root b = 1 is the fixed point ( x_1 = a ), so factor it out: ab^2 + (a - 1)b + (a - 1) = 0 ; solving for b gives k = (b)/(1 - a) . Equivalently, the two points of a 2 -cycle are the roots of k^2x^2 - k(k + 1)x + (k + 1) = 0 , whose discriminant k^2(k + 1)(k - 3) is positive only when k > 3 . p = -1 , q = 0 , r = -2 : 4pr = 8 = 8 + 2q - q^2 . Matching coefficients gives α = frac4p = -4 and β = (q - 4)/(2p) = 2 , so v_n = 2 - 4sin^2(2^nθ) = 2cos(2^n+1θ) , which is 2cos(2^nφ) with φ = 2θ . u_3 = u_0 needs sin^2 8θ = sin^2θ , so 8θ = θ + kπ . With θ = fracπ7 : the cycle sin^2fracπ7 → sin^2(2π)/(7) → sin^2(4π)/(7) → sin^2(8π)/(7) = sin^2fracπ7 . With θ = fracπ9 : sin^2fracπ9 , sin^2frac2π9 , sin^2(4π)/(9) . The map u mapsto u_3 has 2^3 = 8 fixed points; two of them ( 0 and frac34 ) are fixed points of the map itself, leaving 6 points of period exactly 3 : two 3 -cycles. Each step doubles θ , which loses one binary digit of accuracy, so after roughly 50 steps the computed values bear no relation to the true ones. They are not useless: the computed sequence stays close to a true orbit from a slightly different starting point (the shadowing property), so its statistics are still right. 8.8 Period Three Implies Chaos With a , b , c > 0 and d < 0 : b = 7 - 2a , c = 7 - 2b , d = 7 - 2c , a = 7 + 2d . Solving gives 17a = 49 , so the cycle is (49)/(17) → (21)/(17) → (77)/(17) → -(35)/(17) → (49)/(17) , with three points in I_2 = [1, 5] and one in I_1 = [-3, 1] . The point found has itinerary I_2, I_2, ldots, I_2, I_1 (with n - 1 ≥ 3 steps in I_2 ). The cycle 1 → 5 → -3 cannot follow this: -3 is not in I_2 , so neither 1 (whose second image is -3 ) nor 5 (whose first image is -3 ) nor -3 itself can be the point. The covering diagram is [1, 2] → [3, 4], [4, 5] ; [2, 3] → [4, 5] ; [3, 4] → [2, 3], [3, 4] ; [4, 5] → [1, 2] . The only loop of length 3 is [3, 4] → [3, 4] → [3, 4] , which gives the fixed point, not a 3 -cycle. With x = 14y - 7 , (f(x) + 7)/(14) = 1 - |2y - 1| , the tent map. Doubling shifts the binary digits left; if the digit shifted out was 1 , the result is 2 - 2y , which flips the remaining digits. The 3 -cycles are frac27 → frac47 → frac67 and frac29 → frac49 → frac89 (that is, x = -3, 1, 5 and x = -(35)/(9), -frac79, (49)/(9) ); in binary frac27 = 0.overline010 and frac29 = 0.overline001110 .

title: Bounding Without Solving
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Energy in physics and engineering The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2013, Question 7 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/13-s3-q7 The hook Most differential equations cannot be solved. There is no formula for the solution of y'' + y^3 = 0 in terms of familiar functions, let alone for the monster in part (iii). Yet we can still say a great deal about the solutions: that they stay bounded, that they oscillate, that they settle down. The trick is to find a quantity, built from the solution and its derivative, that never increases. Then the solution is trapped. In physics, that quantity is usually energy . A ball rolling in a bowl cannot climb higher than its starting height, because energy is conserved, or, with friction, decreases. This question applies the same reasoning to three equations, the last of them chosen so that you have to invent the “energy” yourself. The method, due to Aleksandr Lyapunov in 1892, is one of the most important tools in the study of differential equations. Before you start For part (i), think of y as the position of a particle and x as time. Then y'' = -y^3 is Newton’s law with force -y^3 . What are the kinetic and potential energies? The kinetic energy is frac12(y')^2 (taking mass 1 ), and the force -y^3 comes from the potential V(y) = frac14y^4 , since force is -V'(y) . The total energy is frac12(y')^2 + frac14y^4 , which is half of E . Conservation of energy is exactly the statement that E is constant. Working it through Stage 1 Conservation By the chain rule, (dE)/(dx) = 2y'y'' + 2y^3y' = 2y'bigl(y'' + y^3bigr) = 0. So E is constant, equal to its value at x = 0 : E = 0 + frac12 = frac12 . Since (y')^2 ≥ 0 , we get frac12y^4 ≤ frac12 , so y^4 ≤ 1 and |y| ≤ 1 . ■ The solution oscillates between -1 and 1 , tracing the closed curve (y')^2 + frac12y^4 = frac12 in the (y, y') plane (Figure 8.2.1). Stage 2 Dissipation Differentiate E = (v')^2 + 2cosh v . Use the differential equation to replace v'' . What sign does the result have? (dE)/(dx) = 2v'v'' + 2sinh v\,v' = 2v'bigl(v'' + sinh vbigr) = 2v'bigl(-xv'bigr) = -2x(v')^2 ≤ 0 quadfor x ≥ 0. The term xv' acts like friction, and it removes energy. So E(x) ≤ E(0) for x ≥ 0 . At x = 0 , cosh( 3) = (3 + frac13)/(2) = frac53 , so E(0) = (10)/(3) . Hence 2cosh v ≤ (v')^2 + 2cosh v = E(x) ≤ tfrac103, qquadsoqquad cosh v(x) ≤ tfrac53. qed Stage 3 Inventing the energy Part (iii) gives no hint. We need a function E = (w')^2 + F(w) that does not increase. If E = (w')^2 + F(w) , then E' = 2w'w'' + F'(w)w' . What should F'(w) be, so that the equation can be used to replace w'' and leave only a multiple of (w')^2 ? We want E' = 2w'bigl(w'' + wcosh w + 2sinh wbigr) , so we need F'(w) = 2(wcosh w + 2sinh w) . Since (d)/(dw)(wsinh w) = sinh w + wcosh w , we can take F(w) = 2wsinh w + 2cosh w, qquad E = (w')^2 + 2wsinh w + 2cosh w. Then, using the equation, (dE)/(dx) = -2(5cosh x - 4sinh x - 3)(w')^2. Show that 5cosh x - 4sinh x - 3 ≥ 0 for all x . (Write it in terms of e^x and look for a perfect square.)
