Andrew Pontzen, The Universe in a Box (Riverhead). How gravity, collapse and simulation explain the structure of the universe.

title: The Stacked-Ball Effect
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on The basketball and the tennis ball Gravitational slingshots The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 2010, Question 10 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/10-s2-q10 The hook Hold a tennis ball on top of a basketball and drop them together. The basketball bounces off the floor, and the tennis ball shoots up to several times the height you dropped it from, sometimes high enough to hit the ceiling. Try it outdoors. Part (i) of the question shows that a single collision has a speed limit: however heavy the ball that hits it, a stationary ball cannot be sent off at more than twice the speed of the incoming one. Part (ii) shows how to break the limit: pass the motion down a chain of ever-lighter balls, and the speed multiplies at every step. The same idea sends space probes to the outer planets, and has been suggested as part of the mechanism of a supernova. Before you start From Section 10.1 : if a mass M moving at speed u hits a stationary mass m elastically, what is the speed of m afterwards? The result there (with the roles of the masses swapped) gives the speed of the struck particle as (2M)/(M + m)u . Another way to remember it: in an elastic collision the relative velocity is reversed. If the heavy ball barely slows down, the light ball must leave at about u more than the heavy ball’s speed, that is about 2u . Working it through Stage 1 The speed limit With M = bm , the speed of A after the collision is v_A = (2bm)/(bm + m)\,u = (2b)/(b + 1)\,u. How does (2b)/(b+1) compare with 2 ? What happens as b → ∞ ? Since (2b)/(b + 1) = 2 - (2)/(b + 1) < 2 for every b , the speed of A is always less than 2u , however heavy B is. It approaches 2u as b → ∞ : an infinitely heavy ball would bounce A off as if from a moving wall. ■ Stage 2 Passing it along a chain In part (ii), each particle is λ times as heavy as the next one. What does part (i) say about each collision in the chain? B_1 (mass λ^n m ) hits B_2 (mass λ^n-1m ), which is λ times lighter. By part (i) with b = λ , B_2 moves off at (2λ)/(λ + 1)u . Then B_2 hits B_3 , which is again λ times lighter, and B_3 moves off at bigl((2λ)/(λ + 1)bigr)^2u . After n such collisions, the last one being B_n hitting A , v_A = Bigl((2λ)/(λ + 1)Bigr)^nu. (Later collisions between the B s can only push A further; they cannot slow it, since nothing ever hits A from in front.) Is (2λ)/(λ + 1) bigger or smaller than 1 ? Since λ > 1 , 2λ > λ + 1 , so the ratio r = (2λ)/(λ + 1) exceeds 1 , and r^n → ∞ as n → ∞ . So by taking n large enough, A can be made to move as fast as we like. ■ Stage 3 Twenty times as fast With λ = 4 , r = frac85 = 1.6 , and we need 1.6^n > 20 . Taking logarithms to base 10 , log_101.6 = log_1016 - 1 = 4log_102 - 1 approx 0.20412, qquad log_1020 = 1 + log_102 approx 1.30103, so we need n > (1.30103)/(0.20412) approx 6.37 . The least value is n = 7 . (Indeed 1.6^6 approx 16.8 and 1.6^7 approx 26.8 .) ■ Looking back Iterate a single result. Part (i) was used n times in part (ii), turning a bounded gain into an unbounded one. A limit that is never reached. The bound 2u is approached but never attained, so the right statement is a strict inequality. Logarithms turn powers into products. The question of how many steps are needed became a division. What’s really going on The basketball and the tennis ball Let the two balls fall together from height H , reaching the floor at speed U = sqrt2gH . Suppose everything is perfectly elastic and the basketball is much heavier. It bounces off the floor with speed U upwards, and immediately meets the tennis ball, still moving down at speed U . In the basketball’s frame, the tennis ball approaches at 2U and, bouncing off a very heavy object, leaves at 2U . Back in the ground frame, that is 2U + U = 3U upwards (Figure 10.2.1). Since height is proportional to the square of the launch speed, the tennis ball rises to 9H . Real balls are not perfectly elastic. With coefficient of restitution e and mass ratio M/m , the tennis ball leaves at speed (Me(2 + e) - m)/(M + m)U . STEP I 2014 Q10, in the exercises, uses a measured height to work backwards to the mass ratio. Gravitational slingshots A space probe flying past a planet does not touch it, but gravity acts like a very soft elastic collision with a very heavy object. In the planet’s frame, the probe swings round and leaves with the same speed it arrived with. If the planet is moving towards the probe at speed V , then in the Sun’s frame the probe can gain up to 2V , exactly as the tennis ball does. The two Voyager probes, launched in 1977, used a rare alignment of the outer planets to pass from Jupiter to Saturn (and, for Voyager 2 , on to Uranus and Neptune), gaining speed at each encounter. Without these gravity assists, the journey to Neptune would have taken about thirty years instead of twelve. The energy comes from the planet, which slows down by an immeasurably small amount. Superballs and supernovae In 1968 W. R. Mellen described in the American Journal of Physics a “superball rebound projectile” made by stacking several balls of decreasing size, and noted that the top ball can be launched at many times the impact speed. Astrophysicists have pointed out a loose analogy with a core-collapse supernova: the infalling outer layers of a star rebound off the stiff, dense core, and a shock wave carries momentum outwards into ever less dense material, accelerating it to enormous speeds. Demonstrations of the stacked-ball effect are used to explain the idea to students, though real supernovae involve much more physics, including neutrinos, than bouncing balls. The thinking skill Iterate a single result When a process is a repetition of one simple step, solve the step once and compose it. A gain factor less than 2 per step becomes unbounded after many steps, because the factors multiply. At university this is the idea behind transfer matrices, multi-stage amplifiers and multi-stage rockets ( Section 10.3 ): the gain of a chain is the product of the gains of its links. Try this next The real thing. Try STEP I 2014, Question 10 : the stacked-ball problem with real numbers and imperfect bounces. An inelastic chain. Try STEP I 2017, Question 10 . It sends a collision along a chain of particles whose masses grow geometrically. When is each particle involved in exactly two collisions? Three balls. Three perfectly elastic balls are stacked, each much lighter than the one below. Show that the top ball leaves at 7U and rises to 49H . With k balls, show that the top one leaves at (2^k - 1)U . Where does the energy come from? In part (ii), show that the total kinetic energy is conserved even though A ’s speed is unbounded. What happens to the heavy particles? Further reading David Morin, Introduction to Classical Mechanics (Cambridge University Press), Chapter 5, which includes the stacked-ball problem. W. R. Mellen, “ Superball rebound projectiles ” , American Journal of Physics 36 (1968). Short and fun. Gary Flandro, “Fast reconnaissance missions to the outer solar system utilizing energy derived from the gravitational field of Jupiter” , Astronautica Acta 12 (1966). The paper that proposed the Voyager “grand tour”.

title: Three Stars in a Triangle
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Kepler’s law in disguise Lagrange points Stability The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP I 1999, Question 11 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/99-s1-q11 The hook Two bodies attracting each other by gravity can be solved completely, as Newton showed and as Section 10.6 explained: each moves on a conic about their common centre of mass, an ellipse if they are bound together, or a parabola or hyperbola if they have enough energy to escape each other. Add a third body and everything changes. The three-body problem has no general solution in terms of familiar functions, and in 1890 Henri Poincaré discovered that its solutions can be chaotic, the first appearance of chaos in mathematics. Yet some special solutions are perfectly simple. In 1772 Joseph-Louis Lagrange found that three bodies at the corners of an equilateral triangle can rotate rigidly, the triangle turning like a wheel. This question finds that solution for equal masses. Lagrange’s triangle is not just a curiosity: the Sun, Jupiter and thousands of “Trojan” asteroids form exactly this configuration, and space telescopes are parked at similar points today. Before you start For a star to move in a circle of radius R with angular velocity ω , what must the total force on it be? It must have magnitude mω^2R and point towards the centre of the circle. So we need to check that the total gravitational force on each star points at the centre of the triangle, and find the ω that makes its size right. Working it through Stage 1 The geometry How far is each corner of an equilateral triangle of side a from its centre? The centre lies on each median, two-thirds of the way from the corner. A median has length asin 60^circ = (sqrt3)/(2)a , so the distance from each corner to the centre is R = frac23·(sqrt3)/(2)a = (a)/(sqrt3). By symmetry the centre of the triangle is the centre of mass of three equal stars. Stage 2 The force on one star Each of the other two stars pulls with force (γ m^2)/(a^2) . What is the angle between the two pulls? What is their resultant, and in which direction does it point? The two pulls point along the two sides of the triangle that meet at the star, so the angle between them is 60^circ . By symmetry their resultant lies along the bisector of that angle, which passes through the centre. Each pull makes 30^circ with the bisector, so the resultant has magnitude 2·(γ m^2)/(a^2)cos 30^circ = (sqrt3\,γ m^2)/(a^2), pointing at the centre (Figure 10.8.1). Stage 3 The angular velocity Setting the resultant equal to mω^2R : mω^2(a)/(sqrt3) = (sqrt3\,γ m^2)/(a^2), qquadsoqquad ω^2 = (3γ m)/(a^3). With this angular velocity, the same calculation applies to each star (by symmetry), so all three move round the centre in circles, keeping the triangle rigid. ■ Stage 4 A fourth star at the centre A star of mass λ m at the centre is at distance (a)/(sqrt3) from each corner. What extra force does it exert on each corner star? Does the centre of mass move? Does the central star feel any net force? The central star does not change the centre of mass, and by symmetry the three pulls on it cancel, so it stays at rest. It pulls each corner star towards the centre with force (γλ m^2)/((a/sqrt3)^2) = (3γλ m^2)/(a^2) . The total inward force on a corner star is now (sqrt3 + 3λ)(γ m^2)/(a^2) , so mω^2(a)/(sqrt3) = (sqrt3 + 3λ)(γ m^2)/(a^2), qquad ω^2 = ((3 + 3sqrt3\,λ)γ m)/(a^3) = (3γ m)/(a^3)bigl(1 + sqrt3\,λbigr). qed Looking back Guess a symmetric solution. We did not solve the three-body problem; we guessed a highly symmetric motion and checked that Newton’s laws allow it. Symmetry fixes directions. The resultant force had to lie along the bisector, so only its size needed calculating. Check every body. By symmetry, verifying one star verified all three; the central star needed a separate (easy) check. What’s really going on Kepler’s law in disguise Write the answer as ω^2a^3 = γ(3m) . For two bodies in circular orbit a distance a apart, Kepler’s third law (an exercise in Section 10.6 ) says ω^2a^3 = γ(m_1 + m_2) , the total mass. The three stars obey the same law, with the total mass 3m . In fact Lagrange showed that the equilateral solution exists for any three masses, not just equal ones: the triangle rotates about the centre of mass with ω^2a^3 = γ(m_1 + m_2 + m_3) . Euler had found a second family a few years earlier, with the three bodies on a rotating straight line. These five configurations (three collinear, two triangular, up to labelling) are the only ones in which three bodies keep the same shape. Lagrange points Take m_1 to be the Sun, m_2 a planet, and m_3 a tiny asteroid. The equilateral solution says the asteroid can sit at the third corner of an equilateral triangle with the Sun and the planet, ahead of or behind the planet in its orbit. These are the Lagrange points L_4 and L_5 ; Euler’s collinear solutions give L_1 , L_2 and L_3 . Jupiter has over ten thousand known “Trojan” asteroids clustered around its L_4 and L_5 points. The James Webb Space Telescope orbits near the Sun–Earth L_2 point, 1.5 million km beyond the Earth, where it can keep the Sun, Earth and Moon all behind its sunshield. Stability Would the Starmakers’ triangle last? For equal masses, no: the slightest disturbance grows, and the stars fly apart or collide. Edward Routh showed in 1875 that Lagrange’s triangle is stable only if one mass dominates, precisely when 27(m_1m_2 + m_2m_3 + m_3m_1) < (m_1 + m_2 + m_3)^2. For the Sun and Jupiter this holds comfortably, which is why the Trojans survive. For three equal masses, 27 × 3m^2 > 9m^2 , so the configuration is unstable. Poincaré’s mistake and the figure eight In 1887 King Oscar II of Sweden offered a prize for a solution of the many-body problem. Henri Poincaré won it in 1889 with a long memoir on the three-body problem, but while the memoir was being printed an editor found a gap. In correcting it, Poincaré discovered that some solutions behave with “a complexity so astonishing that I cannot even attempt to draw it”: the first glimpse of chaos. The printed copies were recalled and destroyed, at Poincaré’s expense. New special solutions are still being found: in 1993 Cristopher Moore discovered numerically, and in 2000 Alain Chenciner and Richard Montgomery proved, that three equal masses can chase each other round a figure-eight curve. Thousands more periodic orbits have since been found by computer. The thinking skill Guess a symmetric solution and verify it When a problem is too hard to solve in general, look for solutions with as much symmetry as possible. A symmetric guess reduces many unknowns to one or two, and checking it is often easy. This is a powerful strategy in mathematics and physics: symmetric equilibria, steady states, travelling waves and rigidly rotating configurations are often the first solutions found, and the starting points for studying the rest. The next question is always whether the symmetric solution is stable. Try this next Four stars in a square. Four stars of mass m are placed at the corners of a square of side a . Show that they can rotate rigidly about the centre with ω^2 = ((4 + sqrt2)γ m)/(2a^3) . Two equal stars and a planet. Two stars of mass M orbit their centre of mass, a distance a apart. A planet of negligible mass sits at the centre. Is it in equilibrium? Is it stable to small displacements along the line joining the stars? Perpendicular to it? Unequal masses. Three stars of masses m_1 , m_2 , m_3 are at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side a , rotating about their centre of mass G . Show that the gravitational force on m_1 is (γ m_1(m_1 + m_2 + m_3))/(a^3)\,overrightarrowP_1G , where P_1 is its position. ( Hint: write the forces as vectors and use the definition of the centre of mass.) Deduce Lagrange’s result. n stars. n equal stars sit at the corners of a regular n -gon inscribed in a circle of radius R . Find ω^2 for rigid rotation as a sum over k of (1)/(sin(kπ/n)) . Further reading June Barrow-Green, Poincaré and the Three Body Problem (American Mathematical Society). The story of the prize and Poincaré’s discovery of chaos. Richard Montgomery, “ A new solution to the three-body problem ” , Notices of the American Mathematical Society 48 (2001). The figure eight, explained by one of its discoverers; free online. Florin Diacu & Philip Holmes, Celestial Encounters (Princeton University Press). A popular history of the three-body problem and chaos.

title: Two Bodies Become One
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Why z^2 is quadratic The two-body problem The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2004, Question 11 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/04-s3-q11 The hook Two bodies attract or repel each other: the Earth and the Moon, two stars, a proton and an electron. Each body’s motion depends on where the other one is, so the equations are coupled, and it looks as if both motions must be found at once. Newton’s great simplification was to change variables. Instead of the two positions, use the centre of mass , which moves as if no forces acted at all, and the separation , which moves like a single particle with a modified mass. One hard problem becomes two easy ones. This question carries out that separation for two particles on a line. Along the way there is a small miracle: the separation turns out to be the square root of a quadratic in t , for a reason that has nothing to do with the question as set and everything to do with motion in a plane. Before you start Write down Newton’s second law for each particle. In which direction does each force act? The force is repulsive, so it pushes P (on the left) to the left and Q (on the right) to the right: 2ddot x_1 = -(2)/(z^3), qquad 1 · ddot x_2 = +(2)/(z^3). These are coupled, because each involves z = x_2 - x_1 . Working it through Stage 1 The separation Which combination of the two equations involves only z ? Subtract: ddot z = ddot x_2 - ddot x_1 = (2)/(z^3) + (1)/(z^3) = (3)/(z^3) . ■ The separation behaves like a single particle of mass frac23 pushed by the force (2)/(z^3) . The number frac23 = (2 × 1)/(2 + 1) is the reduced mass (m_1m_2)/(m_1 + m_2) . Stage 2 Energy for the separation With ddot z = v(dv)/(dz) , separate the variables and integrate. What are the initial values of z and v = dot z ? From v(dv)/(dz) = (3)/(z^3) , integrating gives frac12v^2 = -(3)/(2z^2) + C . Initially z = 1 and dot z = dot x_2 - dot x_1 = 0 - 1 = -1 , so frac12 = -frac32 + C , giving C = 2 : v^2 = 4 - (3)/(z^2). (This is conservation of energy for the separation: kinetic energy plus potential energy (3)/(2z^2) per unit reduced mass is constant.) Stage 3 A surprisingly simple solution The answer to show is z^2 = 4t^2 - 2t + 1 . So look at w = z^2 instead of z . What is dot w^2 in terms of w ? With w = z^2 , dot w = 2zdot z , so dot w^2 = 4z^2dot z^2 = 4z^2Bigl(4 - (3)/(z^2)Bigr) = 16w - 12. Differentiating, 2dot wddot w = 16dot w , so (whenever dot w ≠ 0 ) ddot w = 8 . Hence w is a quadratic in t : w = 4t^2 + α t + β . Initially w = 1 and dot w = 2zdot z = -2 , so β = 1 and α = -2 : z = sqrt4t^2 - 2t + 1. qed (You can check directly: dot w^2 = (8t - 2)^2 = 64t^2 - 32t + 4 = 16(4t^2 - 2t + 1) - 12 .) The particles come closest at t = frac14 , when z = (sqrt3)/(2) , and then separate for ever. Stage 4 The centre of mass What equation does 2x_1 + x_2 satisfy? Why is it the natural combination to look at? Adding the two equations of motion, 2ddot x_1 + ddot x_2 = -(2)/(z^3) + (2)/(z^3) = 0 . The forces are equal and opposite (Newton’s third law), so the total momentum 2dot x_1 + dot x_2 is constant. It starts at 2 × 1 + 0 = 2 , and 2x_1 + x_2 starts at 1 , so 2x_1 + x_2 = 1 + 2t. The centre of mass, at (2x_1 + x_2)/(3) , moves steadily at speed frac23 . Combining with x_2 - x_1 = z , x_1 = frac1 + 2t - sqrt4t^2 - 2t + 13, qquad x_2 = frac1 + 2t + 2sqrt4t^2 - 2t + 13. qed Looking back Decouple by changing variables. The difference of the equations involved only z ; the weighted sum involved only the centre of mass. Energy integral. Writing ddot z = v(dv)/(dz) turned a second-order equation into a first-order one: conservation of energy. Change the unknown. The equation for z was awkward; the equation for z^2 was trivial. What’s really going on Why z^2 is quadratic For any force law of the form ddot z = k/z^3 , the same calculation gives (d^2)/(dt^2)(z^2) = 2dot z^2 + 2zddot z = 2dot z^2 + (2k)/(z^2) = constant, since frac12dot z^2 + (k)/(2z^2) is the conserved energy. So z^2 is always a quadratic in t . Why? Here is the hidden reason. Think of a particle moving freely, in a straight line at constant speed, in a plane . Its distance r from the origin satisfies r^2 = (a quadratic in t) , since r^2 = (x_0 + at)^2 + (y_0 + bt)^2 . And in polar coordinates its radial equation of motion is ddot r - rdotθ^2 = 0 ; with the angular momentum h = r^2dotθ constant, that becomes ddot r = (h^2)/(r^3). The inverse-cube repulsion is exactly the centrifugal effect of the hidden angular motion. In our problem, z^2 = 4t^2 - 2t + 1 = (2t - frac12)^2 + frac34 is the squared distance from the origin of a point moving at speed 2 along a straight line that passes the origin at distance (sqrt3)/(2) . The one-dimensional repelling particles are the shadow of free motion in two dimensions. The two-body problem The method of this question works for any force between two bodies that depends only on their separation and acts along the line between them, in three dimensions as well as one. The centre of mass moves uniformly, and the separation vector r obeys μddotr = F(r) , with μ = (m_1m_2)/(m_1 + m_2) . For gravity this is the Kepler problem , solved by Newton in the Principia : the separation traces an ellipse, parabola or hyperbola. The Earth and the Sun both orbit their common centre of mass, which lies inside the Sun; the Earth and the Moon orbit a point about 4700 km from the Earth’s centre, inside the Earth but well away from its centre, which is why the Earth wobbles monthly. Astronomers find planets round other stars by detecting exactly this wobble in the star. Integrable systems In 1969 Francesco Calogero studied many particles on a line repelling each other with inverse-square potentials (that is, inverse-cube forces), and found that, remarkably, the system can be solved exactly for any number of particles. Jürgen Moser explained the reason in 1975, using a matrix whose eigenvalues stay constant as it evolves: the Lax pairs of Section 7.7 . The Calogero–Moser system is now a central example of an integrable system , a system with enough conserved quantities to be solved completely, and it connects mechanics with random matrices, quantum field theory and the theory of solitons. The thinking skill Choose coordinates that decouple When two quantities are coupled, look for combinations that are not. Sums and differences, weighted by the right constants, often separate a problem into independent pieces. Centre of mass and relative coordinates are the first example. At university the same idea appears as diagonalising a matrix (normal modes, Section 11.2 ), as separation of variables for partial differential equations, and in quantum mechanics. Try this next Two masses on a string. Try STEP III 2023, Question 9 (in OCR’s download of the 2023 papers, a zip file). It follows two particles joined by a string, using the centre of mass to separate the motion. Look for when one particle moves backwards. Attraction. Repeat the question with an attractive force (2)/(z^3) . Show that z^2 is still a quadratic in t , and find when the particles collide. The hidden plane. For the motion in the question, find the straight line in the plane whose distance from the origin is z(t) , and the angle θ(t) swept out. Check that z^2dotθ is constant and that (z^2dotθ)^2 = 3 . Kepler’s third law. Two stars of masses m_1 and m_2 move in circles about their centre of mass, a distance a apart, under gravity. Show that the period T satisfies T^2 = (4π^2a^3)/(G(m_1 + m_2)) . Further reading John Taylor, Classical Mechanics (University Science Books), Chapter 8. The two-body problem, reduced mass and orbits. Daniel Kleppner & Robert Kolenkow, An Introduction to Mechanics (Cambridge University Press), Chapter 10, on central forces. Francesco Calogero, Classical Many-Body Problems Amenable to Exact Treatments (Springer). For the ambitious: the world of exactly solvable systems.

title: What We Have Learned
headings: 1. What can conservation laws decide on their own? 2. How do small steps add up? 3. How do we tame many bodies? 4. A toolkit for mechanics Where next
text: We began by saying that some things never change, and that knowing which ones is half of physics. We asked three questions: what conservation laws can decide on their own, how small steps add up, and how to tame many bodies. Here is what the chapter’s eight questions showed. 1. What can conservation laws decide on their own? For two bodies colliding elastically in a line, momentum and energy determine the outcome completely, and that single result was used again and again. For more bodies, they do not. In Section 10.1 , a row of marbles had many outcomes consistent with both laws, and it took a further physical fact (marbles cannot pass through each other) to rule some out. The square of the momentum minus the energy gave a sum of cross terms that had to vanish, an inequality argument that proved certain motions impossible. And the familiar behaviour of Newton’s cradle turned out to depend on details beyond the conservation laws: how the shock travels through the balls. Conservation laws also exposed hidden assumptions. In Section 10.3 , firing guns all at once gave more speed than firing them one at a time, but only because it used more energy; holding the right quantity fixed reversed the conclusion. 2. How do small steps add up? Several sections repeated one simple step. In Section 10.2 , a collision that can at most double a speed became, through a chain of lighter and lighter balls, unlimited gain: the principle behind the basketball and tennis ball and behind gravitational slingshots. In Section 10.3 , many small firings became an integral, and Tsiolkovsky’s logarithm, which explains why rockets are mostly fuel and why they have stages. In Section 10.4 , each bounce off a moving piston added 2u to a molecule’s speed, and an exact recurrence revealed that speed times length stays almost constant: an adiabatic invariant, and the reason compressed gases heat up. And in Section 10.5 , infinitely many bounces took a finite time, because the times formed a convergent geometric series. 3. How do we tame many bodies? By choosing coordinates and exploiting symmetry. In Section 10.6 , the centre of mass moved uniformly and the separation behaved like a single particle with the reduced mass; a hidden plane even explained why the separation squared was a quadratic in time. In Section 10.7 , symmetry and integration showed that a spherical shell exerts no gravity inside and acts as a point mass outside, which let a collapsing cloud of dust be treated as a single equation, with a free-fall time that sets the pace of star formation. And in Section 10.8 , a symmetric guess solved a special case of the unsolvable three-body problem: Lagrange’s rotating triangle, realised in the Trojan asteroids. 4. A toolkit for mechanics Method Where you used it Conservation laws as constraints Newton’s cradle (10.1) Change of frame Collisions (10.2); piston (10.4) Iterating one result Stacked balls (10.2) Momentum for variable mass Rockets (10.3) Sum to integral Rocket equation (10.3); shell (10.7) Recurrence and telescoping Piston (10.4) Geometric series Wedge (10.5) Centre of mass and reduced mass Two bodies (10.6) Energy integral v\,dv/dz Two bodies (10.6); collapse (10.7) Symmetric guess Three stars (10.8) Where next Chapter 11 turns from conservation to oscillation and rotation: resonance, normal modes, the real pendulum, and motion in accelerating and rotating frames. The energy method of Section 8.2 and the limit cycles of Section 8.4 are the differential-equation side of the same ideas. The chaos Poincaré found in the three-body problem is the subject of Section 8.7 . If you want to go further before university Daniel Kleppner & Robert Kolenkow, An Introduction to Mechanics : the classic first-year text; demanding but rewarding. David Morin, Introduction to Classical Mechanics : hundreds of problems, many of them as surprising as the ones in this chapter. Richard Feynman, The Character of Physical Law : lectures for a general audience on conservation laws, symmetry and gravity. Dwight Neuenschwander, Emmy Noether’s Wonderful Theorem : why symmetry implies conservation. Feynman said that there is no known exception to the conservation of energy. This chapter has tried to show how much they can do: rule out impossible outcomes, reveal hidden invariants, and turn hopelessly complicated systems into ones we can understand. But it has also shown their limits. They constrain, but they do not always decide; and where they stop, the details of forces, symmetries and frames must take over.

title: Infinitely Many Bounces in Finite Time
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on When θ ≥ 60^circ Bouncing balls and inelastic collapse The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2002, Question 11 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/02-s3-q11 The hook Zeno of Elea argued that you can never reach a wall: first you must cover half the distance, then half of what remains, and so on for ever. The resolution, that infinitely many steps can take a finite total time, is an infinite series that converges. This question is Zeno’s paradox made real: a puck sliding into the corner of a wedge bounces off the walls infinitely many times, yet arrives at the corner after a finite time. Nature does this too. A ball bouncing on the floor with a coefficient of restitution less than 1 bounces infinitely often in a finite time and then comes to rest. In computer simulations of granular materials (sand, grain, snow) this “inelastic collapse” is a real difficulty: the computer is asked to handle infinitely many collisions in a finite time. Before you start When a particle hits a smooth wall with coefficient of restitution e , what happens to the component of velocity along the wall? And the component perpendicular to it? A smooth wall exerts no force along itself, so the component of velocity parallel to the wall is unchanged. The perpendicular component is reversed and multiplied by e . So if the particle arrives at angle α to the wall and leaves at angle β , then tanβ = etanα, and since the parallel component is unchanged, (speed in) cosα = (speed out) cosβ . Working it through Stage 1 The angle of departure The particle arrives at M_1 at angle θ to the wall OA (measured on the side away from O ). At what angle varphi to OA does it leave? Use the triangle OM_1N_1 to find varphi in terms of θ . The particle leaves M_1 heading towards O ’s side, at angle varphi to the wall, so the angle OM_1N_1 is varphi . In triangle OM_1N_1 , the angle at O is 30^circ . At N_1 , the angle M_1N_1B is θ and O , N_1 , B lie on a line, so the angle ON_1M_1 is 180^circ - θ . The angles of the triangle add to 180^circ : 30^circ + varphi + (180^circ - θ) = 180^circ, qquadsoqquad varphi = θ - 30^circ. (In particular, θ > 30^circ .) The restitution law tanvarphi = etanθ then gives e = (tan(θ - 30^circ))/(tanθ), and conservation of the parallel component, u_1cosθ = v_1cosvarphi , gives (v_1)/(u_1) = (cosθ)/(cos(θ - 30^circ)). qed Stage 2 The pattern repeats At N_1 , the particle arrives at angle θ to the wall OB , measured on the side away from O . Compare this with its arrival at M_1 . What happens next? The situation at N_1 is the mirror image of the situation at M_1 : the particle meets a wall at angle θ , on the side away from O . So it leaves at angle θ - 30^circ and meets OA again at angle θ , and so on for ever. Every bounce is a scaled copy of the first. Each triangle OM_kN_k , ON_kM_k+1 , … is similar to the one before (Figure 10.5.1), and the speed is multiplied by the same factor at every bounce. Stage 3 Two ratios By what factor rho does the distance from O shrink from one bounce to the next? By what factor k does the speed shrink? So by what factor does the time for each leg shrink? The sine rule in triangle OM_1N_1 gives rho = (ON_1)/(OM_1) = (sinvarphi)/(sin(180^circ - θ)) = (sin(θ - 30^circ))/(sinθ). All lengths in the next triangle are rho times those in this one, so each leg of the path is rho times as long as the previous leg. The speed is multiplied by k = (cosθ)/(cos(θ - 30^circ)) at each bounce. Time is length divided by speed, so each leg takes (rho)/(k) = (sin(θ - 30^circ)cos(θ - 30^circ))/(sinθcosθ) = (sin(2θ - 60^circ))/(sin 2θ) times as long as the previous one. Stage 4 A geometric series The total time is T_1(1 + r + r^2 + cdots) , where T_1 is the time for the first leg and r = (sin(2θ - 60^circ))/(sin 2θ) . This is finite if 0 < r < 1 . When is sin(2θ - 60^circ) < sin 2θ ? Use the identity sin X - sin Y = 2costfrac12(X + Y)sintfrac12(X - Y) . sin 2θ - sin(2θ - 60^circ) = 2cos(2θ - 30^circ)sin 30^circ = cos(2θ - 30^circ), which is positive when 2θ - 30^circ < 90^circ , that is, when θ < 60^circ . And r > 0 since θ > 30^circ . So for 30^circ < θ < 60^circ the series converges: the particle makes infinitely many bounces, its distance from O shrinks by the factor rho < 1 each time, and it reaches O after the finite time (T_1)/(1 - r) . ■ Looking back Self-similarity. Once one bounce was understood, every later bounce was a scaled copy, so the whole infinite process reduced to two ratios. Combine ratios correctly. Distance shrinks by rho and speed by k , so time shrinks by rho/k . Infinitely many events, finite total. A geometric series with ratio less than 1 converges. What’s really going on When θ ≥ 60^circ At θ = 60^circ , the ratio is exactly 1 : every leg takes the same time, and the particle never reaches O , although it gets ever closer. (The speed and the leg lengths both shrink by the same factor.) For θ > 60^circ , the legs take longer and longer. In every case the particle approaches O and makes infinitely many bounces; only for θ < 60^circ does it get there in finite time. The value e = tan 30^circ/tan 60^circ = frac13 is the dividing line. Bouncing balls and inelastic collapse The simplest example of the same phenomenon: a ball dropped onto a floor rises to height e^2H , then e^4H , and so on. The time between bounces is proportional to the speed at each bounce, which shrinks by the factor e , so the total time is a geometric series: with T_0 = sqrt2H/g the time of the first fall, the ball stops bouncing after T_0 + 2eT_0 + 2e^2T_0 + cdots = T_0\,(1 + e)/(1 - e). Infinitely many bounces, and then rest. In 1992 Sean McNamara and William Young showed that the same thing happens in simulations of many inelastic particles in a line: a group of them can undergo infinitely many collisions in a finite time, an “inelastic collapse”. Simulations of sand and granular flows must include special rules to avoid it, and the phenomenon helps explain why granular gases spontaneously form clusters. Zeno and convergence Zeno’s paradoxes, from around 450 BC, troubled philosophers for two thousand years. The mathematical resolution, that an infinite sum can have a finite value, was made precise only in the nineteenth century, when Cauchy, Weierstrass and others defined convergence by means of limits (the subject of Chapter 2). The surprising feature of this question is that the process is physically infinite: there really are infinitely many collisions, in a finite time. Mathematicians studying billiards in polygons and the motion of colliding particles call such behaviour a Zeno phenomenon , and it is one of the subtleties in proving that systems of colliding hard spheres have well-defined motions for all time. The thinking skill Sum an infinite process When a process repeats with a constant scale factor, the total of any additive quantity (time, distance, energy) is a geometric series. Decide convergence from the ratio. Here the key was to find the right ratio: not the ratio of distances, nor of speeds, but of times. At university, the same reasoning governs the convergence of iterative methods, the theory of fractals, and the analysis of algorithms that repeatedly halve a problem. Try this next The total distance. Show that the total distance travelled from M_1 to O is finite for every θ between 30^circ and 90^circ , and find it in terms of OM_1 and θ . Other wedges. Repeat the question for a wedge of angle α instead of 30^circ . Show that varphi = θ - α , and find the condition on θ for the particle to reach O in a finite time. Elastic walls. If e = 1 , can the particle ever reach O ? ( Hint: reflect the wedge repeatedly in its walls, so that the path becomes a straight line. How many copies of a 30^circ wedge fit round O ?) The bouncing ball. A ball is dropped from height 1 m with e = 0.8 . How long does it bounce for, and how far does it travel in total? (Take g = 9.8 m s ^-2 .) Further reading David Morin, Introduction to Classical Mechanics (Cambridge University Press), Chapter 5. Includes several problems on bouncing balls and infinite sequences of collisions. Sean McNamara & William Young, “ Inelastic collapse and clumping in a one-dimensional granular medium ” , Physics of Fluids A 4 (1992). Serge Tabachnikov, Geometry and Billiards (American Mathematical Society; free online). The mathematics of billiards, including the unfolding trick in the exercises.

title: Gravity in an Accelerating Train
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Fictitious forces The equivalence principle The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 2021, Question 10 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP II paper in OCR’s download of the 2021 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/696588-2021-past-papers.zip The hook When a train pulls out of a station, you feel pressed back into your seat; a cup of coffee on the table tilts its surface; a ball on the floor rolls towards the back. From inside the train it looks exactly as if gravity had tilted, pointing slightly backwards as well as down. Einstein called the realisation that this is more than an analogy “the happiest thought of my life”: gravity and acceleration are, locally, indistinguishable. This question puts a bead on a curved wire in an accelerating train. Seen from the train, the bead behaves exactly as if it were in a gravitational field tilted by the angle whose tangent is a/g . The bottom of the wire is no longer the lowest point, and the bead oscillates about a new equilibrium. Before you start The train accelerates westwards (in the negative x direction) at a . For an observer in the train, what “fictitious” force appears to act on a mass m ? In the train’s frame, Newton’s second law holds if we add a fictitious force -m × (acceleration of the frame) . The frame accelerates at -a in the x direction, so the fictitious force is +ma , pointing east. Together with gravity, the bead feels an effective gravity of (a, -g) per unit mass: tilted towards the east. Working it through Stage 1 No rest at the origin At the origin the wire ky = x^2 is horizontal. The normal reaction is vertical there, so it cannot cancel the eastward fictitious force ma . The net force along the wire is ma ≠ 0 , so the bead cannot stay at rest relative to the train. ■ Stage 2 An energy equation Write Newton’s law in the train’s frame, including the normal reaction N . Then take the dot product with the velocity (dot x, dot y) . Why does N disappear? In the train’s frame, m(ddot x, ddot y) = N + (ma, -mg). The wire is smooth, so N is perpendicular to the wire, and hence to the velocity (dot x, dot y) , which is along the wire. Taking the dot product with the velocity kills N : mdot xddot x + mdot yddot y = madot x - mgdot y, qquadsoqquad dot x(ddot x - a) + dot y(ddot y + g) = 0. qed The left side is the derivative of frac12(dot x^2 + dot y^2) - ax + gy , which is therefore constant. ■ This is conservation of energy in the train’s frame, with a potential energy -ax + gy per unit mass that includes the fictitious force. Stage 3 How high? The constant is 0 , since the bead starts at rest at the origin. At the highest point the bead is momentarily at rest. What equation does that give? At rest, frac12(dot x^2 + dot y^2) = 0 , so ax = gy . With y = (x^2)/(k) , this gives ax = (gx^2)/(k) , so (apart from the starting point x = 0 ) x = (ak)/(g) , and b = (a^2k)/(g^2). qed The bead swings east and up the wire to the point bigl((ak)/(g), (a^2k)/(g^2)bigr) , then back to the origin, and so on. Stage 4 The fastest point Write the speed squared as a function of x alone. Where is it greatest? The speed squared is 2(ax - gy) = 2bigl(ax - (gx^2)/(k)bigr) , a quadratic in x that is greatest at x = (ak)/(2g) , halfway between the turning points. There the speed squared is 2bigl((a^2k)/(2g) - (a^2k)/(4g)bigr) = (a^2k)/(2g) , so the maximum speed is asqrt(k)/(2g). qed Find the gradient of the wire at x = (ak)/(2g) . How does it relate to the direction of the effective gravity (a, -g) ? The gradient is (2x)/(k) = frac ag . So at this point the wire is perpendicular to the effective gravity: it is the “lowest” point of the wire in the tilted field, and the bead oscillates about it (Figure 11.5.1). Looking back Work in the convenient frame, and add the fictitious force. In the train’s frame the wire is fixed, and the only price is an extra constant force. Dot with the velocity. This removes constraint forces and gives an energy equation. Interpret the answer. The turning point and the fastest point have a geometric meaning: effective gravity is tilted. What’s really going on Fictitious forces Newton’s laws hold in inertial frames, those that are not accelerating. In an accelerating frame they can be rescued by adding fictitious forces: -mA for a frame with acceleration A , and, in a rotating frame, the centrifugal and Coriolis forces. They are called fictitious because no object exerts them; they are artefacts of the frame. But they are perfectly real to anyone inside it. The centrifugal force flattens the Earth at the poles, and the Coriolis force sets the direction in which hurricanes spin (anticlockwise in the northern hemisphere) and deflects long-range artillery shells. The equivalence principle A constant fictitious force -mA is proportional to mass, exactly like gravity. No experiment in a closed box can tell the difference between the box resting on a planet and the box accelerating in empty space: this is the equivalence principle . Einstein took it as the starting point of general relativity. Since light travelling across an accelerating box appears to bend, light must bend in a gravitational field too; and since clocks at the front and back of an accelerating rocket run at different rates, clocks at different heights in a gravitational field must too. Both predictions have been confirmed, and the second must be corrected for in every GPS satellite, whose clocks run faster than clocks on the ground by about 45 microseconds a day from this effect alone. Einstein’s happiest thought In 1907, working at the patent office in Bern, Einstein was writing a review article on special relativity when, as he later recalled, “the happiest thought of my life” came to him: a person falling freely from a roof would not feel their own weight. Gravity could be “transformed away” by choosing a falling frame. It took him eight more years, and a great deal of new mathematics (the differential geometry of curved spaces, developed by Gauss and Riemann), to turn the thought into the general theory of relativity of 1915. The thinking skill Find a conserved quantity in a moving frame In a frame with constant acceleration, a constant fictitious force acts. It can be included in a potential energy, and energy is conserved in that frame. The trick of dotting the equation of motion with the velocity to eliminate constraint forces works in any frame. At university it becomes a general principle: a system whose equations do not depend explicitly on time has a conserved energy. Try this next A cannon on a train. Try STEP I 2000, Question 9 : a projectile fired inside an accelerating carriage, where the acceleration acts like a tilt in gravity. A headwind. Try STEP II 2006, Question 11 : a projectile against a constant wind, which can blow it back towards you before it lands. Coffee in a train. Show that the surface of a cup of coffee in the accelerating train is a plane tilted at angle arctan(a/g) to the horizontal. Small oscillations. Find the period of small oscillations of the bead about x = (ak)/(2g) . ( Hint: near the new bottom the wire is approximately a circle of radius equal to its radius of curvature.) Further reading Daniel Kleppner & Robert Kolenkow, An Introduction to Mechanics (Cambridge University Press), the chapter on non-inertial frames and fictitious forces. Albert Einstein, Relativity: The Special and the General Theory (various editions). Einstein’s own popular account, including the accelerating box. Pedro Ferreira, The Perfect Theory (Little, Brown). A biography of general relativity.

The second plough faces snow of depth k × (gap); while this is deeper than the snow the first plough met at the same place, it falls further behind. frac1α(dt_3)/(dy) = t_3 - t_2(y) . Writing t_3 = t_2 + g gives g = e^α ybigl(T - α Ty + (α^2hy^2)/(2k)bigr) . If kT ≥ 2h , this vanishes at y = (k)/(α h)bigl(T - sqrtT^2 - 2hT/kbigr) , before the second plough catches the first; if kT < 2h , the second catches the first first. 11.14 Parabola, Not Catenary Yes. The horizontal tension H is still constant, the middle segment has slope 0 , and the slopes then go up in steps of frac wH . With x measured from the middle of the horizontal segment, the k th joint is at x = (k - frac12)h and height (wh)/(2H)k(k - 1) above the lowest joints, which is (w)/(2Hh)bigl(x^2 - (h^2)/(4)bigr) : a parabola. The tension is sqrtH^2 + V^2 , greatest where the vertical component V is greatest: in the end segments, where V supports half the load, ((2n + 1)w)/(2) . So T_max = sqrtH^2 + frac14(2n + 1)^2w^2 . y' = sinhfrac xc and y'' = frac1ccoshfrac xc = frac1csqrt1 + sinh^2frac xc . The length is int_0^Xcoshfrac xc\,dx = csinhfrac Xc . For a shallow curve with sag s , both the catenary and the parabola have length about 2d + (4s^2)/(3d) , so both give s approx sqrtfrac32d(L - d) ; they differ only at order s^4 . For a nearly taut chain, the difference is far smaller than anything Galileo could have measured.

title: Backspin
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on A conserved quantity Snooker, bowling and tennis The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 1997, Question 10 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/97-s3-q10 The hook Press down on the back of a marble with your finger so that it squirts forwards while spinning backwards. It slides away from you, slows, stops, and then, as if it had changed its mind, rolls back. Snooker players use the same effect in the “screw” or “draw” shot, hitting the cue ball low so that it spins backwards, stops on hitting the object ball, and comes back. The question asks for the exact amount of backspin that makes the marble stop dead, and the amount that makes it return at one-seventh of its starting speed. The calculation tracks two quantities, linear and angular velocity, both changed by the same frictional force. Behind it there is a beautiful shortcut: one combination of the two is not changed by friction at all. A note on the syllabus Rotational dynamics was removed from the STEP specification in 2019. All you need here is: a solid sphere of mass m and radius a has moment of inertia I = frac25ma^2 about a diameter, and a torque tau changes its angular velocity according to Idotω = tau , the rotational version of mdot v = F . Before you start The marble moves forwards at v and spins backwards at ω . How fast is the bottom point of the marble moving over the table? Which way does friction act? The bottom point moves at v due to the marble’s motion, plus aω due to the backward spin (a backward spin carries the bottom point forwards). So it slides forwards at v + aω , and friction acts backwards, opposing the sliding. The marble rolls without slipping only when v + aω = 0 . Working it through Stage 1 What friction does Let the friction force be F , backwards. What does it do to v ? Its torque about the centre is Fa : does it increase or decrease the backspin? Friction decelerates the marble: mdot v = -F , so v = v_0 - frac Fm t . Acting backwards at the bottom of the marble, it also exerts a torque Fa that opposes the backspin: Idotω = -Fa , so with I = frac25ma^2 , ω = ω_0 - (5F)/(2ma)t. Both v and ω decrease steadily while the marble slides. Stage 2 Stopping dead For the marble to stop completely, v and ω must reach zero at the same moment. When does each reach zero? v = 0 at t = (mv_0)/(F) , and ω = 0 at t = (2maω_0)/(5F) . These are equal when v_0 = frac25aω_0 , that is, (v_0)/(aω_0) = frac25. qed At that moment the marble has no linear or angular velocity, and friction (which only acts while there is sliding) switches off: it stays put. Stage 3 Coming back If the backspin is larger, v reaches zero while ω is still positive. The bottom point is still sliding forwards, so friction still acts backwards. What happens next, and when does sliding stop? Friction continues to push the marble backwards, so v becomes negative, while ω keeps decreasing. Sliding stops when v + aω = 0 : v_0 + aω_0 - Bigl(frac Fm + (5F)/(2m)Bigr)t = 0, qquad t^* = (2m(v_0 + aω_0))/(7F). At that moment, v = v_0 - (2(v_0 + aω_0))/(7) = (5v_0 - 2aω_0)/(7). From then on the marble rolls without slipping, friction stops acting, and v stays constant. For it to roll back at speed (v_0)/(7) we need 5v_0 - 2aω_0 = -v_0 , so (v_0)/(aω_0) = frac13. qed Looking back Track two quantities. Friction changed both v and ω , at rates in a fixed ratio. Know when a force switches off. Sliding friction acts only while there is sliding; once the marble rolls, it stops. The sliding speed is the key variable. It decreased linearly, and its zero marked the change from sliding to rolling. What’s really going on A conserved quantity There is a quicker way to the final speed. Consider the angular momentum of the marble about the point of contact with the table. Friction acts at that point, so it has no moment about it, and the normal reaction and gravity both act along the vertical through it. So this angular momentum is conserved while the marble slides. It is mva (from the motion of the centre) minus Iω (the backspin counts negatively): L = mav - tfrac25ma^2ω. When rolling at speed V , with aω = -V , it is maV + frac25maV = frac75maV . Equating with the initial value, tfrac75maV = mav_0 - tfrac25ma^2ω_0, qquad V = (5v_0 - 2aω_0)/(7), the same answer with no reference to the size of the friction force, or even to whether it is constant. The final speed is determined by conservation alone; friction only decides how long it takes to get there. Snooker, bowling and tennis The same analysis explains many sports. A snooker ball struck centrally slides at first and then starts to roll, finishing at frac57 of its initial speed (set ω_0 = 0 in the formula). A ten-pin bowling ball thrown with sidespin skids down the lane and then “hooks” when it starts to roll. A tennis ball hit with topspin dips sharply, though there the main effect is aerodynamic: a spinning ball deflects the air around it, the Magnus effect . Coriolis and billiards Gaspard-Gustave Coriolis, now remembered for the fictitious force in rotating frames ( Section 11.5 ), wrote in 1835 a whole book on the mathematics of billiards, Théorie mathématique des effets du jeu de billard . He showed, among other things, that a ball struck with spin follows a parabola while it slides before rolling straight, and analysed exactly the screw shot of this question. The book is still cited by physicists who study the game. The thinking skill Track two quantities changed by one force When a single force affects several quantities, write down how it changes each, and look for a combination it does not change at all. Here friction changed v and ω but not the angular momentum about the contact point. At university, finding such combinations is a recurring theme: choosing the point about which to take moments so that unknown forces drop out is the rotational version of choosing a frame. Try this next Topspin. If the marble starts with forward spin ω_0 instead of backspin, find its final rolling speed. For what value of v_0/(aω_0) does it speed up? A snooker ball. A ball struck centrally starts sliding at v_0 with no spin. Show that it ends up rolling at frac57v_0 , and find the fraction of kinetic energy lost. (The kinetic energy of rolling is frac12mV^2 + frac12Iω^2 .) A hoop. Repeat the question for a thin hoop rolling in its own plane, with I = ma^2 . What ratio v_0/(aω_0) now makes it return at (v_0)/(7) ? The draw shot. Where must a snooker cue strike the ball (at what height above the centre, in terms of a ) for the ball to roll without sliding from the start? ( Hint: take angular momentum about the contact point during the impulse.) Further reading David Morin, Introduction to Classical Mechanics (Cambridge University Press), Chapter 8, on angular momentum and rolling with slipping. Daniel Kleppner & Robert Kolenkow, An Introduction to Mechanics (Cambridge University Press), the chapters on rigid body motion. David Alciatore, The Illustrated Principles of Pool and Billiards (Sterling). The physics of the game, with many diagrams.

title: Parabola, Not Catenary
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Parabola or catenary? Upside-down chains and arches The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP I 1991, Question 10 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/91-s1-q10 The hook Hold a chain by its two ends and it hangs in a curve called the catenary (from the Latin for chain). Galileo thought it was a parabola; it is not, as the teenage Huygens showed in 1646. But hang a heavy roadway from the chain by evenly spaced struts, as in a suspension bridge, and the chain does form a parabola. The difference is in how the weight is spread: along the curved chain itself for the catenary, evenly along the horizontal for the bridge. This question proves the parabola with nothing more than resolving forces at each joint. The key is that the horizontal component of tension is the same all the way along, so each segment’s slope is proportional to the weight it supports. The result is a beautiful pattern: the drops between successive joints go up in the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7, ldots , whose partial sums are the perfect squares. Before you start At each joint A_i , three forces act: the tensions in the two neighbouring segments, and the weight w hanging from the strut. Which component of tension can the weight not affect? The weight is vertical, so at each joint the horizontal components of the two tensions must balance. So the horizontal component of tension, H say, is the same in every segment of the chain. Working it through Stage 1 The equations at each joint Let segment A_i-1A_i make angle φ_i below the horizontal (going from A_i-1 towards the middle), so its tension T_i has horizontal component T_icosφ_i and vertical component T_isinφ_i . Resolving at A_i for 1 ≤ i ≤ n : T_icosφ_i = T_i+1cosφ_i+1 = H, qquad T_isinφ_i - T_i+1sinφ_i+1 = w. (The segment on the outer side pulls up and out with the larger vertical component; the inner segment pulls in and slightly down; the difference supports the strut.) What happens at the middle joint A_n+1 ? Use the symmetry of the bridge. By symmetry, the two segments meeting at A_n+1 are mirror images, so each supports half of its strut: T_n+1sinφ_n+1 = frac12w . Stage 2 Slopes from weights Working outwards from the middle, the vertical components are T_n+1sinφ_n+1 = tfrac12w, quad T_nsinφ_n = tfrac32w, quadldots,quad T_1sinφ_1 = tfrac2n+12w. Dividing each by H , the slopes are tanφ_i = ((2(n + 1 - i) + 1)w)/(2H) . The slope of segment A_i-1A_i is also fracy_i-1 - y_ih , so fracy_n - y_n+1h = (w)/(2H), qquad fracy_n-1 - y_nh = (3w)/(2H), qquadldots,qquad (y_0 - y_1)/(h) = ((2n + 1)w)/(2H). Inverting and multiplying by the odd numbers, each of frachy_n - y_n+1 , frac3hy_n-1 - y_n , …, ((2n + 1)h)/(y_0 - y_1) equals (2H)/(w) . ■ Stage 3 The parabola Let j count joints outwards from the middle, so that A_n+1-j is at horizontal distance jh from A_n+1 . How far is it above A_n+1 ? Adding the drops, with c = (wh)/(2H) : y_n+1-j - y_n+1 = cbigl(1 + 3 + 5 + cdots + (2j - 1)bigr) = cj^2. With x measured from the middle, x = jh , so the height above the lowest joint is (c)/(h^2)x^2 = (w)/(2Hh)x^2 . By symmetry the same holds on the other side, and the supports ( j = n + 1 ) fit the same formula. So all the points lie on the parabola y = y_n+1 + (w)/(2Hh)(x - x_n+1)^2. qed Looking back Find what is constant. With only vertical loads, the horizontal tension is the same everywhere. Accumulate from the middle. Each segment supports all the weight between it and the middle, so the vertical components grow in steps of w . Odd numbers sum to squares. 1 + 3 + cdots + (2j - 1) = j^2 turned a list of slopes into a parabola. What’s really going on Parabola or catenary? The continuous version of the argument explains both curves. For a chain y(x) under constant horizontal tension H , the vertical component of tension is Hy' , and over a short stretch it changes by the load carried there: H\,dy' = dW . If the load is spread evenly horizontally (a heavy roadway, weight rho per unit length of road), then Hy'' = rho , so y is a quadratic: a parabola. If the load is the chain’s own weight, spread evenly along the chain ( rho per unit length of chain), then Hy'' = rhosqrt1 + y'^2 , whose solution is the catenary y = ccoshfrac xc , with c = H/rho . Near the bottom, where the chain is nearly horizontal, the two are almost the same; they differ near the supports, where the chain is steep and a given horizontal distance contains more chain. Real suspension bridges, whose deck is much heavier than their cables, are very close to parabolas. Upside-down chains and arches A chain is in pure tension; turn its shape upside down and you have an arch in pure compression, with no tendency to bend. Robert Hooke published this in 1675 as an anagram, which decoded reads: “As hangs the flexible line, so but inverted will stand the rigid arch.” Christopher Wren and Hooke used the idea for the dome of St Paul’s Cathedral, and Antoni Gaudí designed the Sagrada Família in Barcelona by hanging weighted strings from the ceiling and photographing them upside down. The Gateway Arch in St Louis is a (weighted) inverted catenary. The catenary challenge In 1690 Jakob Bernoulli challenged mathematicians to find the shape of a hanging chain. Within a year, solutions were published by his brother Johann, by Leibniz and by Huygens. Johann Bernoulli later recalled with glee that his brother, who had set the problem, had failed to solve it. The catenary was one of the first triumphs of the new calculus, and it led to the hyperbolic functions cosh and sinh , studied systematically by Vincenzo Riccati and Johann Heinrich Lambert in the eighteenth century. The thinking skill Resolve forces at every joint For a structure made of joints and straight members, balance forces at each joint. Constant components and accumulating loads often reveal the shape. At university this becomes the analysis of trusses and frameworks in engineering, and, in the continuous limit, the differential equations of cables, beams and membranes. The step from a discrete chain to a continuous one is the same move from sums to integrals seen in Section 10.3 . Try this next An even number of struts. Repeat the question with 2n struts, so that the lowest point of the chain is a horizontal segment in the middle. Do the joints still lie on a parabola? The tension. Find the greatest tension in the chain, in terms of H , w and n . Where is it? The catenary. Verify that y = ccoshfrac xc satisfies y'' = frac1csqrt1 + y'^2 . Show that the length of the catenary from x = 0 to x = X is csinhfrac Xc . Galileo’s error. A chain of length 2L hangs between two supports at distance 2d apart. For L only slightly larger than d , show that the sag of the catenary is approximately the same as that of a parabola. Why did Galileo’s experiments not reveal the difference? Further reading E. H. Lockwood, A Book of Curves (Cambridge University Press). The catenary, the parabola and their relatives. Jacques Heyman, The Stone Skeleton (Cambridge University Press). How masonry arches and domes stand up, from Hooke’s chain onwards. David Billington, The Tower and the Bridge (Princeton University Press). The art and engineering of bridges.

title: A Ball That Comes Back Towards You
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on A geometric view Monotonicity is not automatic The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 2019, Question 9 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP II paper in OCR’s download of the 2019 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/696590-2019-past-papers.zip The hook Throw a ball forwards and it moves away from you until it lands. Obviously. Throw it straight up and it comes back. Somewhere in between, something must change: there must be angles at which the ball moves away, then comes closer , then moves away again before landing. This question finds the exact threshold, sinα = (2sqrt2)/(3) , or about 70.5^circ . The result is a nice example of a common situation in mathematics: a quantity everyone assumes is monotonic, which is not. It also shows a standard technique, used constantly at university: to find out whether a distance is increasing, differentiate its square , which avoids square roots. Before you start Why is it easier to work with OP^2 than with OP ? Is “ OP is increasing” the same as “ OP^2 is increasing”? OP^2 = x^2 + y^2 is a polynomial in t , while OP involves a square root. Since OP ≥ 0 , and squaring is increasing on non-negative numbers, OP increases exactly when OP^2 does. Working it through Stage 1 The squared distance With x = utcosα and y = utsinα - frac12gt^2 , OP^2 = u^2t^2cos^2α + u^2t^2sin^2α - ugt^3sinα + tfrac14g^2t^4 = u^2t^2 - ugt^3sinα + tfrac14g^2t^4. Differentiate with respect to t . After taking out a factor of t , what is left? When is it positive for all t ? (d)/(dt)OP^2 = 2u^2t - 3ugt^2sinα + g^2t^3 = tbigl(g^2t^2 - 3ugsinα\,t + 2u^2bigr). For t > 0 , the sign is that of the quadratic g^2t^2 - 3ugsinα\,t + 2u^2 . This quadratic has positive leading coefficient, so it is positive for every t if its discriminant is negative: 9u^2g^2sin^2α - 8u^2g^2 < 0 quadLongleftrightarrowquad sin^2α < frac89 quadLongleftrightarrowquad sinα < (2sqrt2)/(3). In that case OP is increasing throughout the flight. ■ Stage 2 Steeper throws If sinα > (2sqrt2)/(3) , the quadratic has two real roots. Are they positive? Is the smaller one before the particle lands? The roots have sum (3usinα)/(g) > 0 and product (2u^2)/(g^2) > 0 , so both are positive, and between them the quadratic, and so (d)/(dt)OP^2 , is negative. The particle lands at T = (2usinα)/(g) . The smaller root is t_1 = (u)/(2g)bigl(3sinα - sqrt9sin^2α - 8bigr) < (u)/(2g)·3sinα < (2usinα)/(g) = T. So just after t_1 (and before landing) OP is decreasing. ■ Stage 3 A moving observer Q moves away from O along the ground in the opposite direction, at speed v . Measured from Q , the horizontal separation is x + vt . What does that do to the calculation? The separation QP has horizontal component (ucosα + v)t and vertical component utsinα - frac12gt^2 . So QP^2 = bigl((ucosα + v)^2 + u^2sin^2αbigr)t^2 - ugt^3sinα + tfrac14g^2t^4, the same as before with u^2 replaced by w^2 = (ucosα + v)^2 + u^2sin^2α in the first term. The derivative is tbigl(g^2t^2 - 3ugsinα\,t + 2w^2bigr) , and the condition for it to be positive for all t > 0 is 9u^2sin^2α < 8w^2 quadLongleftrightarrowquad u^2sin^2α < 8(ucosα + v)^2, after cancelling 8u^2sin^2α from both sides. Taking square roots (both usinα and ucosα + v are positive), this is usinα < 2sqrt2(ucosα + v) , which rearranges to 2sqrt2\,v > (sinα - 2sqrt2cosα)u. qed (This is sufficient for QP to increase throughout the flight, since the derivative is then positive for all t > 0 .) Looking back Differentiate the square. Squared distances are polynomials, and their derivatives have the same sign as the derivative of the distance. A quadratic that is always positive. The condition “increasing for all time” became a discriminant condition. A new problem as an old one. The moving observer only changed one coefficient, so the earlier analysis applied directly. What’s really going on A geometric view OP decreases exactly when the velocity of P points “inwards”, making an obtuse angle with the vector overrightarrowOP , that is, when overrightarrowOPcdotv < 0 . For a steep throw, near the top of the flight the particle is high above and slightly in front of the thrower, moving almost horizontally away, but starting to fall; once the downward part of its velocity outweighs the outward part, relative to the direction of overrightarrowOP , it comes closer. For shallow throws the particle is always far enough in front that its velocity never points back towards O . The critical case is when the velocity is perpendicular to overrightarrowOP at exactly one instant, the moment when the distance pauses in Figure 11.10.1. Monotonicity is not automatic Many quantities that “obviously” increase do not. The distance of the Moon from the Earth oscillates; the distance between two cars on a winding road can decrease even when one is always ahead; the population of a predator can fall while its prey multiplies. Proving that a quantity is monotonic usually means showing that a derivative has a fixed sign, and the technique here (reduce to a polynomial, then check its roots or discriminant) is the standard way to do it. In analysis, monotonicity is often the key to proving convergence: a bounded monotonic sequence converges, as you saw in Chapter 2. The thinking skill Check monotonicity through a derivative To decide whether a quantity always increases, differentiate it (or a convenient function of it, such as its square) and ask whether the derivative can change sign. At university, sign arguments of this kind are used to prove inequalities, to locate maxima and minima, and to study the stability of solutions of differential equations, where a quantity that always decreases (as in Section 8.2 ) proves that a system settles down. Try this next How close? For α = 80^circ , find the times at which OP has its local maximum and minimum, and the distances there, in units of u^2/g . On a slope. Repeat part (i) for a ball thrown up a plane inclined at angle β to the horizontal, landing on the plane. Does the critical angle (measured from the plane) change? With air resistance. Suppose the ball also experiences a resistance proportional to its velocity. Without calculating, would you expect the critical angle to be larger or smaller than 70.5^circ ? Why? Throwing from a height. If the ball is thrown from the top of a cliff and lands far below, show that OP eventually increases for any angle, and find whether there are angles for which it decreases at some stage. Further reading James Walker, The Flying Circus of Physics (Wiley). Hundreds of surprising everyday physics puzzles. David Morin, Introduction to Classical Mechanics (Cambridge University Press), Chapter 3, on projectiles, with several counter-intuitive problems. J. M. Steele, The Cauchy–Schwarz Master Class (Cambridge University Press). The art of proving that one thing is always bigger than another.

title: How Fielders Catch
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Optical acceleration cancellation What fielders really do The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 1998, Question 11 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/98-s2-q11 The hook A ball is struck high into the outfield. A good fielder sets off at once and arrives just as it comes down. How? Nobody can solve the equations of projectile motion in their head in a fraction of a second, and in any case the fielder does not know the ball’s speed or angle. Yet fielders, and dogs catching frisbees, do it routinely. In 1968 the physicist Seville Chapman proposed an answer, and this question proves it. If the fielder watches the angle of elevation θ of the ball, and moves so that tanθ increases at a constant rate , she will arrive exactly where the ball lands. She needs no knowledge of physics, only the ability to notice whether the ball seems to be rising faster or slower than steadily. A hard prediction problem is replaced by a simple feedback rule. Before you start Put the batsman at the origin and the fielder at distance D . If the ball is at (x, y) , what is tanθ ? The ball is at height y above the fielder’s eye, and at horizontal distance D - x in front of her (it is coming towards her). So tanθ = (y)/(D - x) . Working it through Stage 1 The perfectly placed fielder Let the ball have horizontal speed U and initial vertical speed W , and let it land (at eye level) at time T . Write x , y and D in terms of U , W , T , g and t . Can you factorise y ? We have x = Ut and y = Wt - frac12gt^2 , and the ball returns to eye level at T = (2W)/(g) , where the fielder is: D = UT . Since W = frac12gT , y = tfrac12gt(T - t), qquad D - x = U(T - t). The factor T - t cancels: tanθ = (frac12gt(T - t))/(U(T - t)) = (g)/(2U)\,t. So (d)/(dt)tanθ = (g)/(2U) , a constant. ■ Stage 2 The running fielder Now the fielder starts at distance D_0 and runs towards the batsman at speed v , so her position is D_0 - vt . She catches the ball at time T . What is D_0 ? Repeat the calculation. To catch the ball at time T , she must be where it lands: D_0 - vT = UT , so D_0 = (U + v)T . Her horizontal distance from the ball is D_0 - vt - Ut = (U + v)(T - t) , and again the factor cancels: tanθ = (frac12gt(T - t))/((U + v)(T - t)) = (g)/(2(U + v))\,t. So if she is running at the right speed, tanθ increases at a constant rate. The question asks for the converse: if she runs so that (d)/(dt)tanθ is constant, will she catch the ball? Suppose she runs at speed v and tanθ = (frac12gt(T - t))/(D_0 - (U + v)t) increases at a constant rate c , so tanθ = ct (it is 0 at t = 0 ). Then tfrac12g(T - t) = cbigl(D_0 - (U + v)tbigr) quadfor all t. Comparing the coefficients of t and the constant terms: frac12g = c(U + v) and frac12gT = cD_0 . Dividing, D_0 = (U + v)T : exactly the condition to be at the landing point at time T . So she should choose v to keep tanθ rising steadily, and then she catches the ball. ■ Looking back Look for a common factor. Both the height and the horizontal distance contained T - t , and cancelling it made tanθ linear. Prove the converse. Showing that the rule works (it leads to the catch) needed the reverse argument, comparing coefficients. An invariant that is easy to perceive. A steady rise in tanθ can be judged by eye; the landing point cannot. What’s really going on Optical acceleration cancellation Chapman’s rule is now called optical acceleration cancellation : the fielder moves so as to keep the “optical acceleration” (d^2)/(dt^2)tanθ at zero. If the ball’s image accelerates upwards, the ball will go over her head, so she backs away; if it decelerates, the ball will fall short, so she runs in (Figure 11.11.1). The strategy does not tell her where the ball will land, but it gets her there. It is a feedback control law, like the ones that steer guided missiles: missiles use proportional navigation , keeping the line-of-sight angle to the target constant, which is the sideways version of the same idea. What fielders really do Do real fielders use Chapman’s rule? Experiments in the 1990s, with cameras mounted on the heads of baseball outfielders, gave mixed results. Michael McBeath and colleagues argued in Science in 1995 that, for balls hit to one side, fielders run along curved paths that keep the ball’s image moving in a straight line across their field of view (a “linear optical trajectory”), which also leads them to the catch. Later work has suggested that both strategies, and a mixture of them, are used, and that fielders often do not run at constant speed. A 2004 study found that dogs catching frisbees follow paths consistent with the same optical rules. Whatever the details, the remarkable conclusion stands: catching does not require prediction, only the right feedback. Chapman’s paper Seville Chapman’s “Catching a baseball”, published in the American Journal of Physics in 1968, is three pages long and contains essentially the calculation in this question. He noted that the strategy works only without air resistance, and that a real baseball’s trajectory is distorted by drag and spin, which would complicate things. Nevertheless, the idea that the brain uses simple invariants of the visual field to solve complicated control problems has become important in psychology and robotics. The thinking skill Find an invariant that is easy to observe When a quantity is hard to predict, look for a related quantity that can be observed directly and that behaves simply exactly when things are on track. Here the landing point was hard to predict, but the rate of change of tanθ was easy to monitor. At university this is the idea of feedback control, and of choosing an observable that encodes the information you need. Try this next Running backwards. If the ball will land behind the fielder’s starting position, show that she should run away from the batsman, and that the same rule applies. Not θ itself. Show that, for a perfectly placed fielder, (dθ)/(dt) is not constant. Why is tanθ the right quantity to watch? Eye level. If the ball is struck from a height h below the fielder’s eye level, is tanθ still linear in t for a well-placed fielder? (Assume she catches it at eye level.) Air resistance. With linear air resistance, the horizontal velocity decays exponentially. Is tanθ still linear in t for a well-placed fielder? Further reading Seville Chapman, “ Catching a baseball ” , American Journal of Physics 36 (1968). Michael McBeath, Dennis Shaffer & Mary Kaiser, “ How baseball outfielders determine where to run to catch fly balls ” , Science 268 (1995). Dennis Shaffer et al., “ How dogs navigate to catch Frisbees ” , Psychological Science 15 (2004).

title: Oscillations, Rotation and Moving Frames
headings: Why this matters What you will meet at university The questions that run through this chapter Ideas in this chapter How to read this chapter
text: Chapter 11 · Introduction Motion, Seen Clearly The career of a young theoretical physicist consists of treating the harmonic oscillator in ever-increasing levels of abstraction. — Attributed to Sidney Coleman The previous chapter used conservation laws to understand collisions and gravity. This one turns to the other great themes of a first course in dynamics: things that oscillate, things that rotate, and the art of describing motion from the most useful point of view. Oscillation is everywhere. Pendulums and springs are the textbook examples, but the same mathematics describes the vibrations of molecules, the swaying of buildings, the circuits in a radio and, in quantum mechanics, the behaviour of light itself. The reason is that almost anything near a stable equilibrium behaves like a spring: pull it a little way and the restoring force is proportional to the displacement. So the simple harmonic oscillator is the first approximation to almost every physical system, and much of physics consists of understanding what happens when the approximation is not quite right. Why this matters Engineers must know the natural frequencies of every structure they build, to keep them away from the frequencies of wind, traffic and earthquakes. Chemists identify molecules by their vibrations. Timekeeping, from Huygens’s pendulum clocks to quartz watches and atomic clocks, is the art of making a perfect oscillator. Rotation governs everything from the spin of a snooker ball to the stability of satellites. And the question of which frames of reference are “natural” led, through the equivalence of gravity and acceleration, to Einstein’s general relativity. The chapter ends with six questions grouped as surprising trajectories : projectiles, ants, fielders and snowploughs whose behaviour is not what intuition predicts. They are short, elegant problems, and each has a proper mathematical idea at its centre: envelopes, monotonicity, feedback, divergence, linear differential equations and the difference between a parabola and a catenary. What you will meet at university A first-year dynamics course covers simple, damped and forced harmonic motion, resonance, and coupled oscillators and their normal modes (where linear algebra and mechanics meet). It treats rigid bodies, moments of inertia and rolling, and motion in accelerating and rotating frames, with the centrifugal and Coriolis forces. Later courses develop all of this into Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics, where the choice of coordinates becomes a central theme, and into the theory of waves, which are oscillations spread out in space. Nonlinear oscillations, like the large-amplitude pendulum, lead to elliptic functions and to the dynamical systems of Chapter 8. The questions that run through this chapter Three big questions When is motion simple? When does a system oscillate with a single, fixed frequency, and what happens when it does not? What is the right point of view? Which coordinates, which variables and which frame of reference make a problem easy? Can intuition be trusted? Where does everyday intuition about motion go wrong, and how does mathematics correct it? The chapter begins with oscillations: resonance ( Section 11.1 ), normal modes, the real pendulum and the tautochrone. It then turns to frames and rigid bodies: an accelerating train, a spinning marble, a rod that behaves like three particles, and a solid that can rest at three different tilts. The last six sections are the surprising trajectories.
