Ideas in this chapter § Topic Idea 11.1 Forced oscillations Resonance and beats 11.2 Coupled oscillators Normal modes are eigenvectors 11.3 The real pendulum Elliptic integrals; the AGM 11.4 The tautochrone Simple harmonic in arc length 11.5 Moving frames Fictitious forces; equivalence principle 11.6 Rolling and sliding A conserved angular momentum 11.7 Moments of inertia Dynamical equivalence; Simpson’s rule 11.8 Stability Normals through the centre of mass 11.9 Projectiles The envelope of trajectories 11.10 Projectiles Distance need not increase 11.11 Catching A feedback rule 11.12 Stretching ropes Fractions and the harmonic series 11.13 Snowploughs Time as a function of distance 11.14 Suspension bridges Parabola, not catenary Two sections, Section 11.6 and Section 11.7 , use rotational dynamics and moments of inertia, which were removed from the STEP specification in 2019. They are included because they are excellent questions; each gives the facts it needs. How to read this chapter Before you start any calculation, ask which variable the problem wants. Arc length for the tautochrone, x y for coupled springs, the fraction of the rope for the ant, time as a function of distance for the snowplough: in each case, the right choice turns a difficult problem into a familiar one.

title: Normal Modes
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Normal modes are eigenvectors Coming close without arriving The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2014, Question 10 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/14-s3-q10 The hook One mass on a spring bounces up and down in a simple, regular way. Join two masses with springs and the motion looks complicated: each mass jerks about irregularly, energy sloshing from one to the other. But hidden inside the complication are two perfectly simple motions, the normal modes , in which the masses move together or exactly opposite, each mode oscillating at its own frequency. Every motion of the system is a combination of the two. This question finds the normal modes of two masses between three springs, and then proves something striking: started from rest with one mass displaced, the system never returns to its starting position. The reason is that the ratio of the two frequencies is sqrt3 , and sqrt3 is irrational. Before you start With X at distance a + x from P and Y at distance a + y from Q , how long is the middle spring XY ? Which springs are stretched and which compressed when x and y are positive? The three lengths add up to 3a , so XY = 3a - (a + x) - (a + y) = a - x - y . When x, y > 0 , the outer springs are stretched (by x and y ) and the middle one is compressed (by x + y ). Working it through Stage 1 The equations of motion Measure x in the direction from P towards Q . The spring PX has extension x , so its tension (λ x)/(a) pulls X back towards P . The spring XY has extension -(x + y) , so its tension -(λ(x + y))/(a) pulls X towards Y (a negative tension is a push). So mddot x = -(λ x)/(a) - (λ(x + y))/(a) = -(λ)/(a)(2x + y). qed By symmetry (swap the roles of X and Y , P and Q ), mddot y = -(λ)/(a)(2y + x). Stage 2 Decoupling Each equation involves both x and y . Which combinations of the two equations involve only one combination of x and y ? Subtracting and adding, m(ddot x - ddot y) = -(λ)/(a)(x - y), qquad m(ddot x + ddot y) = -(3λ)/(a)(x + y). Each is the equation of simple harmonic motion: x - y oscillates with ω^2 = (λ)/(ma) , and x + y with 3ω^2 . Stage 3 The initial conditions Initially XP = a and YQ = frac12a , so x = 0 and y = -frac12a , and both particles are at rest. So x - y = frac12a and x + y = -frac12a at t = 0 , with zero rates of change, giving x - y = tfrac12acosω t, qquad x + y = -tfrac12acossqrt3\,ω t. So A = frac12a and B = 0 . ■ Stage 4 Never returning Write y in terms of t . For Y to be back at its initial position, y = -frac12a . What must both cosines be? Subtracting, y = frac12bigl((x + y) - (x - y)bigr) = -frac14abigl(cossqrt3\,ω t + cosω tbigr) . For y = -frac12a we need cossqrt3\,ω t + cosω t = 2 , and since each cosine is at most 1 , both must equal 1 : ω t = 2π k, qquad sqrt3\,ω t = 2π j for integers k and j . For t > 0 , k ≥ 1 , and dividing, sqrt3 = frac jk , which is impossible because sqrt3 is irrational. So Y never returns to its initial position. ■ Looking back Find the combinations that decouple. x - y and x + y each satisfied an equation of their own. Symmetry suggests them. The system is symmetric under swapping the two sides, so symmetric and antisymmetric combinations are natural. Irrationality has physical consequences. The motion is not periodic because a frequency ratio is irrational. What’s really going on Normal modes are eigenvectors Write the equations as a matrix equation: mbeginpmatrixddot x \\ ddot yendpmatrix = -(λ)/(a)beginpmatrix2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2endpmatrixbeginpmatrixx \\ yendpmatrix. The combinations that decouple are the eigenvectors of the matrix: (1, -1) with eigenvalue 1 , and (1, 1) with eigenvalue 3 ( Section 7.2 ). In the first mode, x = -y : both particles move the same way along the line (remember that x and y are measured from opposite ends), and the middle spring keeps its length. In the second, x = y : they move in opposite directions, squeezing and stretching the middle spring, which makes the frequency higher. The squares of the frequencies are the eigenvalues, multiplied by (λ)/(ma) . This works for any number of masses and springs. A system of N coupled oscillators has N normal modes, given by the eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix, and the spectral theorem guarantees that they always exist and are perpendicular. Molecules vibrate in normal modes, which is how chemists identify them by the infrared light they absorb. Buildings and bridges have normal modes, which engineers must keep away from the frequencies of wind and earthquakes. And as the number of masses tends to infinity, the normal modes become the harmonics of a vibrating string, the starting point of Fourier analysis. Coming close without arriving Although Y never returns exactly, it comes as close as you like. The reason is a theorem of Kronecker: if α is irrational, the multiples α, 2α, 3α, ldots , taken modulo 1 , come arbitrarily close to every number in [0, 1] . So we can find times when ω t is a multiple of 2π and sqrt3\,ω t is within any tolerance of one. The motion is quasi-periodic : it winds round a torus (one angle for each mode) without ever closing up. The same distinction, between rational and irrational frequency ratios, is at the heart of the KAM theorem on the stability of the solar system. The thinking skill Change variables to decouple equations When equations are coupled, look for combinations of the variables that evolve independently. In linear problems, these are the eigenvectors. This is the same idea as the centre of mass and relative coordinates of Section 10.6 . At university it becomes diagonalisation: choose a basis in which the matrix is diagonal, and a system of coupled equations falls apart into independent ones. Try this next Energy. Show that the total energy frac12m(dot x^2 + dot y^2) + (λ)/(2a)bigl(x^2 + y^2 + (x + y)^2bigr) is constant, and that it splits into a sum of two terms, one for each normal mode, each of which is separately constant. Pure modes. How should the particles be started so that the motion is periodic, with period (2π)/(ω) ? With period (2π)/(sqrt3\,ω) ? A stiffer middle spring. If the middle spring has modulus μ instead of λ , find the two normal-mode frequencies. For which values of μ/λ is every motion periodic? Three masses. Three equal masses are connected in a line by four identical springs between two fixed points. Find the matrix and its eigenvalues ( 2 - sqrt2 , 2 , 2 + sqrt2 ), and describe the three normal modes. Further reading A. P. French, Vibrations and Waves (MIT Introductory Physics Series), Chapter 5, on coupled oscillators and normal modes. Gilbert Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra (Wellesley-Cambridge), the chapter on eigenvalues, which includes springs and masses as a main example. Steven Strogatz, Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos (CRC Press), Chapter 8, on quasi-periodic motion on a torus.

title: The Real Pendulum
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Elliptic integrals Gauss’s remarkable formula The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 1998, Question 11 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/98-s3-q11 The hook Every physics student learns that a pendulum’s period is 2πsqrtl/g , independent of the size of the swing. Galileo believed this, supposedly after timing a swinging lamp in Pisa cathedral against his pulse, and it is the reason pendulum clocks work. But it is not quite true. The formula comes from the approximation sinθ approx θ , and a pendulum swinging through a wide arc takes longer. At 90^circ the period is 18\% longer; a pendulum released from almost upside down can take as long as you like. This question finds the exact period as an integral, and then the first correction for moderate swings. The integral cannot be evaluated in elementary functions: it is an elliptic integral , and the story of how such integrals were tamed runs from Gauss’s arithmetic–geometric mean to the theory of elliptic curves. Before you start The bob moves on a circle of radius l . What are its speed and its height (relative to the lowest point) in terms of θ and dotθ ? The speed is ldotθ , and the height above the lowest point is l(1 - cosθ) . Since the string does no work (its tension is always perpendicular to the motion), energy is conserved. Working it through Stage 1 Energy At the extreme angle γ the bob is momentarily at rest. Conservation of energy gives tfrac12ml^2dotθ^2 + mgl(1 - cosθ) = mgl(1 - cosγ), and dividing by ml , frac12ldotθ^2 = g(cosθ - cosγ) . ■ Stage 2 The period as an integral How can you write cosθ - cosγ in terms of half-angles? And how much of the period is spent going from θ = 0 to θ = γ ? Using cosθ = 1 - 2sin^2fracθ2 , we have cosθ - cosγ = 2bigl(sin^2fracγ2 - sin^2fracθ2bigr) , so dotθ = 2sqrtfrac gl\,Bigl(sin^2fracγ2 - sin^2fracθ2Bigr)^1/2. By symmetry the swing from 0 to γ takes a quarter of the period, so P = 4int_0^γ(dθ)/(dotθ) = 2sqrtfrac lgint_0^γBigl(sin^2fracγ2 - sin^2fracθ2Bigr)^-1/2dθ. qed Stage 3 Removing the singularity The integrand becomes infinite at θ = γ . Write k = sinfracγ2 and substitute sinfracθ2 = ksinφ . What range of φ corresponds to 0 ≤ θ ≤ γ ? What happens to the integrand? As θ goes from 0 to γ , φ goes from 0 to fracπ2 . Differentiating, frac12cosfracθ2\,dθ = kcosφ\,dφ , so dθ = (2kcosφ\,dφ)/(cosfracθ2) = frac2kcosφ\,dφsqrt1 - k^2sin^2φ. Meanwhile sin^2fracγ2 - sin^2fracθ2 = k^2(1 - sin^2φ) = k^2cos^2φ . The awkward factors cancel: P = 2sqrtfrac lgint_0^π/2(1)/(kcosφ)·frac2kcosφsqrt1 - k^2sin^2φ\,dφ = 4sqrtfrac lgint_0^π/2fracdφsqrt1 - k^2sin^2φ. The new integrand is perfectly well behaved, since k < 1 . Stage 4 The first correction For small k , expand (1 - k^2sin^2φ)^-1/2 by the binomial theorem. What is int_0^π/2sin^2φ\,dφ ? To first order, (1 - k^2sin^2φ)^-1/2 approx 1 + frac12k^2sin^2φ , and int_0^π/2sin^2φ\,dφ = fracπ4 . So P approx 4sqrtfrac lgBigl(fracπ2 + (k^2)/(2)·fracπ4Bigr) = 2πsqrtfrac lgBigl(1 + (k^2)/(4)Bigr). For small γ , k = sinfracγ2 approx fracγ2 , so k^2 approx (γ^2)/(4) and P approx 2πsqrtfrac lgBigl(1 + (γ^2)/(16)Bigr). qed For a swing of 20^circ ( γ approx 0.35 ) the correction is less than 1\% ; at 60^circ it is about 7\% (Figure 11.3.1). Looking back Energy gives a first integral. A second-order equation became a first-order one, and the period became an integral. A substitution tames a singularity. The integrand blew up at the turning point; the substitution sinfracθ2 = ksinφ removed the problem. Exact first, then approximate. We found an exact formula and expanded it, which also tells us how good the approximation is. What’s really going on Elliptic integrals The integral K(k) = int_0^π/2fracdφsqrt1 - k^2sin^2φ is the complete elliptic integral of the first kind , so called because a close relative gives the perimeter of an ellipse. The exact period is P = 4sqrtl/g\,Kbigl(sinfracγ2bigr) . Expanding the integrand fully and integrating term by term using the Wallis integrals int_0^π/2sin^2nφ\,dφ of Section 4.4 , one finds P = 2πsqrtfrac lgBigl(1 + bigl(tfrac12bigr)^2k^2 + bigl(tfrac1·32·4bigr)^2k^4 + bigl(tfrac1·3·52·4·6bigr)^2k^6 + cdotsBigr). No finite combination of familiar functions gives K(k) ; it is a genuinely new function. Gauss’s remarkable formula There is a far better way to compute K . In Section 2.6 you met the arithmetic–geometric mean : start with a and b , and repeatedly replace them by their arithmetic and geometric means. Gauss discovered in 1799 that K(k) = fracπ2\,AGMbigl(1, sqrt1 - k^2bigr), so the period of a pendulum with amplitude γ is exactly P = frac2πsqrtl/gAGMbigl(1, cosfracγ2bigr). The AGM converges so fast that, for swings of up to about 160^circ , three or four steps give the period to ten significant figures, and the values in Figure 11.3.1 were computed this way. Nearer 180^circ the two starting values, 1 and cosfracγ2 , are far apart and it takes a step or two more, but five steps suffice even at 179^circ . Gauss wrote in his diary that this discovery “opens an entirely new field of analysis”, and he was right: inverting elliptic integrals led Abel and Jacobi to elliptic functions , and those led to elliptic curves , which are now central to number theory (they were the key to the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem) and to the cryptography that secures the internet. Galileo’s lamp and Huygens’s clock Galileo’s claim that a pendulum’s period does not depend on its amplitude, made around 1602, was a good approximation for the small swings he studied. Christiaan Huygens realised that it was not exact, and in 1659 found the curve along which the period really is independent of amplitude: the cycloid, the subject of Section 11.4 . His pendulum clocks, made from 1656 onwards, improved timekeeping from errors of about a quarter of an hour a day to about fifteen seconds. Marine chronometers, which solved the problem of finding longitude at sea, later abandoned the pendulum altogether, but pendulum clocks remained the most accurate timekeepers in the world until the 1920s. The thinking skill From an exact integral to a series approximation When a quantity is given by an integral that cannot be evaluated, transform it into a well-behaved form, then expand the integrand and integrate term by term. This is how physicists find corrections to idealised results, and it is the start of perturbation theory . At university you will learn when term-by-term integration is justified (uniform convergence), and how to estimate the error made by stopping. Try this next A tethered particle. Try STEP III 2015, Question 9 : an oscillator whose period depends on its amplitude even for small oscillations. Why does it, when a pendulum’s does not? The next term. Carry the binomial expansion one term further and show that P approx 2πsqrtfrac lgbigl(1 + (γ^2)/(16) + (11γ^4)/(3072)bigr) . The AGM by hand. Use three steps of the AGM to estimate the period of a pendulum with amplitude 90^circ , and compare with the value 1.1803 in the figure. Clocks. A pendulum clock is regulated to keep perfect time with an amplitude of 4^circ . If its amplitude increases to 5^circ , how many seconds a day does it lose? Further reading David Morin, Introduction to Classical Mechanics (Cambridge University Press), Chapter 4, which treats the large-amplitude pendulum. Jonathan Borwein & Peter Borwein, Pi and the AGM (Wiley). Gauss’s discovery and its uses, including the fastest ways to compute π . Dava Sobel, Longitude (Fourth Estate). The story of timekeeping at sea, beyond the pendulum.

title: Resonance
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on The resonance limit Damping and the resonance curve The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 1991, Question 12 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/91-s2-q12 The hook Push a child on a swing at just the right moments and small pushes build into large swings. Push at the wrong rhythm and nothing much happens. Every oscillating system has a natural frequency , and driving it at that frequency produces a response out of all proportion to the effort. This is resonance . It is why a singer can shatter a wine glass, why soldiers break step when crossing a bridge, and why a radio can pick out one station from thousands. This question shakes the top of an elastic string and asks when the string stays taut. The answer contains the factor (1)/(n - p) , which blows up as the driving frequency p approaches the natural frequency n : a gentle shake near resonance is enough to make the string go slack. Before you start The particle hangs in equilibrium with extension c . If the string has modulus λ , what is the relation between λ , a , c , m and g ? What is the extension when the top has moved down by bsin pt and the particle by x ? In equilibrium, tension equals weight: (λ c)/(a) = mg . When the top is displaced down by bsin pt and the particle by x , the string’s length increases by x - bsin pt , so the extension is c + x - bsin pt . Working it through Stage 1 The equation of motion Taking downwards as positive, the forces on the particle are its weight mg and the tension (λ)/(a)(c + x - bsin pt) upwards: mddot x = mg - (λ)/(a)(c + x - bsin pt) = -(λ)/(a)(x - bsin pt), using (λ c)/(a) = mg . Since (λ)/(ma) = (g)/(c) = n^2 , this is ddot x = -n^2(x - bsin pt) . ■ The particle is pulled towards the moving point bsin pt with a spring force. Without the driving, it would oscillate with angular frequency n , its natural frequency. Stage 2 Solving The equation is ddot x + n^2x = n^2bsin pt . Try a particular solution of the form x = Csin pt . Then add the general solution of ddot x + n^2x = 0 . Which initial conditions does the particle satisfy? Substituting x = Csin pt gives (-p^2 + n^2)C = n^2b , so C = (n^2b)/(n^2 - p^2) (we need p ≠ n ). The complementary function is Dcos nt + Esin nt . The particle starts at rest in equilibrium: x(0) = 0 forces D = 0 , and dot x(0) = 0 gives Cp + En = 0 , so E = -(nbp)/(n^2 - p^2) . Altogether, x(t) = (bn)/(n^2 - p^2)(nsin pt - psin nt). qed Stage 3 Staying taut The string is taut exactly when its extension is positive. Write the extension c + x - bsin pt in terms of t . Subtracting bsin pt from x(t) , beginaligned x - bsin pt &= (b)/(n^2 - p^2)bigl(n^2sin pt - npsin nt - (n^2 - p^2)sin ptbigr) \\ &= (bp)/(n^2 - p^2)(psin pt - nsin nt). endaligned So the string remains taut throughout if and only if c + (bp)/(n^2 - p^2)(psin pt - nsin nt) ≥ 0 qquadfor all t ≥ 0. How negative can psin pt - nsin nt possibly be? Since |sin| ≤ 1 , we have psin pt - nsin nt ≥ -(p + n) . So the extension is at least c - (bp(n + p))/(n^2 - p^2) = c - (bp)/(n - p), which is positive if pb < (n - p)c . ■ What happens to this condition as p approaches n ? How small must the shaking amplitude b be when p = 0.9n ? When p = 0.99n ? Looking back Measure from equilibrium. Using the equilibrium extension c removed gravity from the equation. Particular plus complementary. The forced response at frequency p plus the free oscillation at frequency n , with constants fixed by the initial conditions. Bound, do not solve. We did not find the minimum extension exactly; a crude bound on the sines was enough for a sufficient condition. What’s really going on The resonance limit Let p → n in the solution. Both the numerator and the denominator tend to zero, and a limit calculation (or l’Hôpital’s rule, differentiating with respect to p ) gives x(t) → (b)/(2)(sin nt - ntcos nt). The term ntcos nt grows without limit: driving exactly at the natural frequency makes the amplitude increase linearly in time, each push adding to the motion in step with it. Just below resonance, the two frequencies drift in and out of step, producing beats : the amplitude swells and dies away with the slow frequency n - p (Figure 11.1.1). The same beats are heard when two guitar strings are almost in tune. Damping and the resonance curve Real systems lose energy, through friction or air resistance, and that limits the growth. With damping, the steady response to a driving force at frequency p has an amplitude that peaks near the natural frequency; the sharper the peak, the less damping there is. Engineers describe this by the quality factor Q : roughly, the number of oscillations a system makes before losing most of its energy. A wine glass has Q in the thousands, which is why a sustained note at exactly its natural frequency can break it. A car’s suspension is deliberately given a low Q , so that bumps do not set it bouncing. Bridges that move In 1831 a column of soldiers marching in step over the Broughton Suspension Bridge near Manchester set it vibrating until it collapsed; since then, troops have been ordered to break step on bridges. The London Millennium Bridge, opened in June 2000, began to sway sideways as soon as crowds crossed it: pedestrians unconsciously adjusted their steps to the sway, feeding it energy in step, and the bridge closed for two years while dampers were fitted. The famous collapse of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in 1940 is often described as resonance, but it was a different phenomenon, aeroelastic flutter , in which the wind’s force depends on the bridge’s own motion. Its analysis needs the ideas of self-excited oscillation and limit cycles ( Section 8.4 ). The thinking skill Superpose a forced response and a free response For a linear equation driven by a periodic force, the solution is the response at the driving frequency plus a free oscillation at the natural frequency, chosen to fit the starting conditions. Linearity makes this work: solutions can be added. At university, the same principle, applied to sums of many driving frequencies, leads to Fourier analysis, transfer functions in engineering, and Green’s functions in physics. Try this next A falling lift. Try STEP II 1996, Question 11 : a mass on an elastic string in a lift that starts and then stops accelerating. Watch how the final amplitude depends on how long the acceleration lasts. At resonance. Solve ddot x + n^2x = n^2bsin nt with x(0) = dot x(0) = 0 directly, by trying a particular solution x = Ctcos nt . Check that it agrees with the limit above. Beats. Show that nsin pt - psin nt can be written as a sum of two terms, one of which is approximately 2ncos((n+p)t)/(2)sin((p-n)t)/(2) when p is close to n . Hence explain the beat period (2π)/(n - p) . Damped resonance. For ddot x + 2kdot x + n^2x = Fcos pt with small k > 0 , find the steady-state amplitude, and show that it is greatest when p^2 = n^2 - 2k^2 . Further reading A. P. French, Vibrations and Waves (MIT Introductory Physics Series). Chapter 4 on forced oscillations and resonance is the classic account. Steven Strogatz, Sync (Penguin). How things fall into step, from fireflies to the Millennium Bridge. Henry Petroski, To Engineer Is Human (Vintage). Engineering failures, including the bridges in the history box.

title: The Ant on the Rubber Rope
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on The harmonic series version Light in an expanding universe The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 2018, Question 10 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/18-s2-q10 The hook An ant sets off along a rubber rope one kilometre long, walking at one centimetre per second. Every second, the rope is stretched uniformly by another kilometre. The far end races away at a thousand metres per second, a hundred thousand times faster than the ant. Does the ant ever reach the end? Astonishingly, yes. The stretching carries the ant along with it, and although the ant’s progress as a fraction of the rope shrinks, the fractions add up like the harmonic series, which diverges ( Section 2.3 ). The ant arrives, though only after a time that dwarfs the age of the universe. This question solves the continuous version exactly, and finds that the time grows exponentially with the ratio of the speeds. Before you start The string is stretched uniformly: every piece is stretched by the same factor. At time t its length is a + ut . If the point at distance x from the peg is a fraction (x)/(a + ut) of the way along, how fast does it move? Each point on the string keeps the same fraction f of the length, so its distance from the peg is f(a + ut) , and its speed is fu = (ux)/(a + ut) . Points near the peg barely move; the far end moves at u . Working it through Stage 1 The ant’s equation The ant moves at v relative to the string, plus the speed of the string beneath it: (dx)/(dt) = v + (ux)/(a + ut). Differentiate (x)/(a + ut) by the quotient rule and use the equation for dot x . (d)/(dt)Bigl((x)/(a + ut)Bigr) = (dot x)/(a + ut) - (ux)/((a + ut)^2) = (1)/(a + ut)Bigl(v + (ux)/(a + ut)Bigr) - (ux)/((a + ut)^2) = (v)/(a + ut). qed The fraction of the string the ant has covered increases at the rate (v)/(a + ut) : its own speed divided by the current length. The stretching drops out completely, because it does not change anyone’s fraction. Stage 2 Reaching the end Integrate from 0 to t . When does the fraction reach 1 ? The ant starts at the peg, so (x)/(a + ut) = int_0^t(v\,ds)/(a + us) = frac vu(a + ut)/(a). The ant reaches the end when the fraction is 1 : (a + uT)/(a) = frac uv = k , so a + uT = ae^k , that is uT = a(e^k - 1). qed The logarithm grows without limit, so the ant always arrives, however fast the rope is stretched. Stage 3 The way back Walking back, the ant’s speed relative to the string is -v . What is the rate of change of its fraction now? It starts at fraction 1 at time T . The same calculation with -v gives (d)/(dt)bigl((x)/(a + ut)bigr) = -(v)/(a + ut) , so (x)/(a + ut) = 1 - frac vu(a + ut)/(a + uT). The fraction reaches 0 when a + ut = (a + uT)e^k . Since a + uT = ae^k , the return time is t - T = ((a + uT)(e^k - 1))/(u) = (ae^k· uT/a)/(u) = Te^k. qed The journey back takes e^k times as long as the journey out: by the time the ant turns round, the string is e^k times longer than at the start. Looking back Use the right variable. The fraction of the rope covered was the natural quantity: the stretching does not change it. Integrating factor in disguise. Multiplying by (1)/(a + ut) turned a linear differential equation into an exact derivative. Divergence beats speed. The fraction grew like a logarithm, which is unbounded, so the ant always arrives. What’s really going on The harmonic series version The puzzle is usually told with discrete stretches. A rope is 1 km long; the ant walks 1 cm in the first second; then the rope is stretched by 1 km; then the ant walks another centimetre, and so on. In the n th second, the ant covers 1 cm of a rope n km long: a fraction (1)/(100\,000\,n) . Stretching does not change its fraction, so after N seconds it has covered (1)/(100\,000)Bigl(1 + frac12 + frac13 + cdots + frac1NBigr) approx ( N + 0.577)/(100\,000) of the rope. It arrives when H_N approx 100\,000 , after about e^100\,000 seconds, a number with over 43\,000 digits. (For comparison, the universe is about 4 × 10^17 seconds old.) Our continuous answer agrees: k = frac uv = 100\,000 , and T approx frac aue^k . Light in an expanding universe The ant on the rope is a model of light crossing an expanding universe. Distant galaxies recede from us, carried by the expansion of space itself, and light from them travels towards us at speed c through the expanding space, as the ant walks along the stretching rope. Whether light from a distant galaxy ever reaches us depends on how the expansion rate changes with time. In a universe expanding at a steady rate, like the rope, light always arrives eventually. In a universe whose expansion accelerates, as ours appears to, there are galaxies whose light will never reach us: there is a cosmic event horizon . The analogue for the ant is a rope stretched exponentially, so that the end’s speed grows in proportion to the length (try it in the exercises). Gardner’s ant The puzzle seems to have been invented by the French mathematician Denys Wilquin in 1972, as a worm on an elastic band, and was popularised by Martin Gardner in his Scientific American column and in his book Time Travel and Other Mathematical Bewilderments . It is one of the best-known examples of a result that contradicts intuition and is nevertheless easy to prove, and it is a favourite illustration of the divergence of the harmonic series. The thinking skill Find the quantity the complication does not affect When part of a problem changes everything (here, the stretching), look for a quantity it leaves alone. Stretching changes every distance but no fraction. Working with the fraction removed the stretching from the problem. At university, this idea appears as comoving coordinates in cosmology and fluid mechanics, and more generally as the search for invariants under a transformation. Try this next Halfway. When is the ant halfway along the rope? Is that before or after time frac T2 ? Exponential stretching. Suppose instead the rope’s length is ae^λ t . Show that the ant reaches the end only if v > λ a . (This is the cosmic event horizon.) An accelerating rope. If the length is a + frac12bt^2 , does the ant always arrive? The discrete puzzle. In the discrete version, how many seconds does the ant need to cover 1\% of the rope? Use H_N approx N + 0.577 . Further reading Martin Gardner, Time Travel and Other Mathematical Bewilderments (W. H. Freeman). Includes the ant on the rubber rope. Julian Havil, Gamma: Exploring Euler’s Constant (Princeton University Press). The harmonic series, and the ant. Barbara Ryden, Introduction to Cosmology (Cambridge University Press). Expanding space, horizons and comoving coordinates, at undergraduate level.

title: The Safety Parabola
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Envelopes The focus The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 2014, Question 10 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/14-s2-q10 The hook A fountain sprays water at the same speed in every direction. The jets form a glittering dome with a sharp outer edge: inside, water passes through every point; outside, none reaches. That edge is a parabola, called the parabola of safety , because a target outside it cannot be hit by a cannon of the given muzzle speed, whatever the angle. The surprising thing is that the boundary is not itself one of the trajectories. It is the envelope of the whole family, a curve that touches every trajectory once, exactly like the line y = 0 touching the family of parabolas in Section 8.1 . This question finds it with nothing more than the discriminant of a quadratic. Before you start Write x and y in terms of t , and eliminate t . How can you write sec^2θ in terms of λ = tanθ ? With x = utcosθ and y = utsinθ - frac12gt^2 , substitute t = (x)/(ucosθ) : y = xtanθ - (gx^2)/(2u^2cos^2θ) = λ x - (gx^2)/(2u^2)(1 + λ^2), using sec^2θ = 1 + tan^2θ . Working it through Stage 1 Fix x , vary the angle For a fixed x > 0 , think of y as a function of λ . What kind of function is it? Which values does it take as λ ranges over all real numbers? For fixed x , y is a quadratic in λ with negative leading coefficient -(gx^2)/(2u^2) : a downward parabola in λ . It has a maximum, and as λ → ∞ , y → -∞ . Since it is continuous, it takes every value up to its maximum. The maximum is where (dy)/(dλ) = x - (gx^2)/(u^2)λ = 0 , that is λ = (u^2)/(gx) , and there Y = (u^2)/(gx)\,x - (gx^2)/(2u^2)Bigl(1 + (u^4)/(g^2x^2)Bigr) = (u^2)/(2g) - (gx^2)/(2u^2). qed (Equivalently: the point (x, y) can be reached exactly when the quadratic (gx^2)/(2u^2)λ^2 - xλ + (gx^2)/(2u^2) + y = 0 has a real root λ , and the discriminant condition gives y ≤ Y .) Stage 2 The region The curve Y = (u^2)/(2g) - (gx^2)/(2u^2) is a downward parabola with its vertex at bigl(0, (u^2)/(2g)bigr) , the height reached by firing straight up, crossing the ground at x = (u^2)/(g) , the maximum range. Every point on or below it (and above the ground) can be reached, and no point above it can (Figure 11.9.1). Through a point strictly below the curve, how many trajectories pass? And through a point on it? A point below the curve corresponds to a quadratic in λ with two real roots: two angles of projection, one high and one low. A point on the curve corresponds to a repeated root: exactly one trajectory, which touches the curve there. Stage 3 The furthest point The furthest reachable point from O (on or above the ground) lies on the boundary. Write the squared distance x^2 + Y^2 as a function of x^2 . Is it increasing or decreasing? Let X = x^2 . Then x^2 + Y^2 = X + Bigl((u^2)/(2g) - (gX)/(2u^2)Bigr)^2, qquad (d)/(dX)(x^2 + Y^2) = 1 - (g)/(u^2)Bigl((u^2)/(2g) - (gX)/(2u^2)Bigr) = frac12 + (g^2X)/(2u^4) > 0. So the distance increases as we move out along the boundary, and the furthest point is where the boundary meets the ground, at x = (u^2)/(g) . The furthest distance is (u^2)/(g), achieved by the ordinary maximum-range shot at 45^circ . ■ Looking back Turn the question around. Instead of asking where a given trajectory goes, ask which trajectories pass through a given point. A quadratic in the parameter. For each point, the equation for λ = tanθ is a quadratic, and its discriminant decides whether the point can be reached. Two, one or none. Two angles reach a point inside, one reaches a point on the boundary, none reaches a point outside. What’s really going on Envelopes A one-parameter family of curves F(x, y, λ) = 0 often has an envelope : a curve touching every member of the family. It is found by solving F = 0 and (partialF)/(partialλ) = 0 together, which is exactly what we did by maximising y over λ . Envelopes appear throughout science. The bright curve of light on the surface of a cup of coffee is the envelope of reflected rays, a caustic . A supersonic aircraft’s sonic boom is carried by the envelope of the sound waves it emits, the Mach cone . And in Section 8.1 , the envelope of a family of solutions of a differential equation was itself a solution, a “singular” one. The focus The parabola of safety has a remarkable property: its focus is the launch point O . (A parabola y = c - (x^2)/(4c) has its focus at the origin; here c = (u^2)/(2g) .) Every trajectory, too, is a parabola, and the foci of all the trajectories lie on a circle of radius (u^2)/(2g) about O . There is an energy explanation: the speed of the projectile at height y is sqrtu^2 - 2gy , which is zero at the height (u^2)/(2g) of the directrix, and parabolas whose directrix is the same line and which pass through O have their foci on that circle. Torricelli’s parabola Galileo showed around 1609 that projectiles move along parabolas, and that the maximum range on level ground is at 45^circ . His student Evangelista Torricelli, better known for inventing the barometer, found the parabola of safety in 1644, in his De motu gravium . For gunners it answered a practical question: which targets are within range at all? Torricelli also showed that the trajectories through a given point come in pairs with angles symmetric about the direction of the point and the vertical, the high and low shots of the question. The thinking skill Envelopes of families of curves To find the boundary of the region covered by a family of curves, fix a point and ask for which parameter values a curve passes through it. The boundary is where the number of solutions changes. The same idea, counting solutions as a point moves, is the basis of the study of caustics in optics, of bifurcations in dynamical systems, and of catastrophe theory, which classifies how the number of solutions of an equation can change. Try this next An exploding firework. Try STEP II 2023, Question 10 (in OCR’s download of the 2023 papers, a zip file). It views the particles from an explosion as a sphere whose centre falls freely, and finds a particle that runs along the paraboloid of safety. Firing up a slope. Find the maximum range of a projectile with speed u up a plane inclined at angle β . ( Hint: where does the line y = xtanβ meet the parabola of safety?) Show that the best angle bisects the angle between the slope and the vertical. Two angles. Show that the two angles that reach a point P are symmetric about the bisector of the angle between OP and the vertical. The foci. Show that the trajectory with angle θ has its focus at bigl((u^2)/(2g)sin2θ, -(u^2)/(2g)cos2θbigr) , and hence that the foci lie on a circle about O . Further reading David Morin, Introduction to Classical Mechanics (Cambridge University Press), Chapter 3, which discusses the envelope of trajectories. J. W. Bruce, P. J. Giblin & C. G. Gibson, “ On caustics of plane curves ” , American Mathematical Monthly 88 (1981). Envelopes and caustics in geometry. E. H. Lockwood, A Book of Curves (Cambridge University Press). Envelopes, caustics and many classical curves, with constructions.

title: Simpson's Rule in a Rod
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Simpson’s rule Gaussian quadrature and the inertia tensor The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 1989, Question 13 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/89-s2-q13 The hook How does a uniform rod respond to being pushed and spun? It turns out that, for every purpose in mechanics, a rod behaves exactly like three point masses: one-sixth of its mass at each end and two-thirds at the middle. Nothing you can do to the rod (push it, spin it about any axis) distinguishes it from the three particles. The numbers frac16 , frac23 , frac16 may look familiar. They are the weights in Simpson’s rule , int_-a^af approx 2abigl(frac16f(-a) + frac23f(0) + frac16f(a)bigr) , the numerical integration method you may have met at A level. This is no coincidence: a dynamically equivalent system and a numerical integration rule are solving the same problem. A note on the syllabus Moments of inertia were removed from the STEP specification in 2019. The moment of inertia of a body about an axis is sum m_id_i^2 , the sum of each mass times the square of its distance from the axis (an integral for a continuous body). A uniform rod of mass m and length 2a has moment of inertia frac13ma^2 about a perpendicular axis through its centre. The parallel axis theorem says that the moment of inertia about any axis is the moment about the parallel axis through the centre of mass plus md^2 , where d is the distance between the axes. Before you start Two systems have the same mass, the same centre of mass, and the same moment of inertia about every axis through it. Why does the parallel axis theorem then give the same moment of inertia about every other axis too? For any axis, both moments of inertia equal (moment about the parallel axis through O ) + md^2 . The first terms agree by assumption, and m and d are the same for both systems. ■ Working it through Stage 1 The rod Put masses p at each end and q at the middle. By symmetry the centre of mass is right. What do the total mass and the moment of inertia about a perpendicular axis through the centre require? We need 2p + q = m , and the moment of inertia about a perpendicular axis through the middle must be frac13ma^2 : 2pa^2 = frac13ma^2 . So p = frac16m and q = frac23m . Does this work for every axis through the centre, not just the perpendicular one? For an axis through the centre at angle psi to the rod, a point at distance r along the rod is at distance rsinpsi from the axis. So every moment of inertia (rod or particles) is sin^2psi times the value for the perpendicular axis, and the two agree for all psi . (Axes not in a plane containing the rod work the same way: only the distance of each point from the axis matters, and for points on a line through O this is proportional to r .) So the rod is dynamically equivalent to masses frac16m , frac23m , frac16m . ■ Stage 2 The rectangle Cut the lamina into thin strips parallel to one side. Replace each strip by its three equivalent particles. What do you get, and what can you do next? Each thin strip is a rod, equivalent to frac16 , frac23 , frac16 of its mass on the left edge, the centre line and the right edge. Adding over all the strips, the lamina is equivalent to three uniform rods (along the left edge, the middle and the right edge) with masses frac16M , frac23M , frac16M . Now replace each of these rods by three particles in the same ratio. The mass at each point is a product of two fractions (Figure 11.7.1): corners: tfrac16 · tfrac16 = tfrac136, qquad edge midpoints: tfrac16 · tfrac23 = tfrac19, qquad centre: tfrac23 · tfrac23 = tfrac49, all times M . ■ (Strictly, each replacement must preserve the moment of inertia about every axis through the centre of the whole lamina, which it does: each replacement keeps the mass, the centre of mass and the moments of inertia about axes through the centre of mass of the piece, and the parallel axis theorem does the rest.) Stage 3 The square about its diagonal For a square of side 2a , the diagonal passes through two corners and the centre, which contribute nothing. The other two corners are at distance sqrt2a from it, and the four edge midpoints at distance (a)/(sqrt2) . So I = 2 · tfrac136M · 2a^2 + 4 · tfrac19M · tfraca^22 = tfrac19Ma^2 + tfrac29Ma^2 = tfrac13Ma^2. qed This is the same as the moment of inertia about an axis through the centre parallel to a side. (That is no accident: for a square, all axes through the centre in its plane give the same answer, by a symmetry argument in the exercises.) Stage 4 A non-uniform rod Let the rod have length L and density (2mx)/(L^2) at distance x from one end. Put masses p_0 , p_1 , p_2 at x = 0 , frac L2 , L . Matching the total mass, the centre of mass and the moment of inertia about the end gives three equations. What are they? The rod has total mass m , first moment int_0^L x · (2mx)/(L^2)\,dx = frac23mL and second moment int_0^L x^2·(2mx)/(L^2)\,dx = frac12mL^2 about the light end. Matching these: p_0 + p_1 + p_2 = m, qquad tfrac12Lp_1 + Lp_2 = tfrac23mL, qquad tfrac14L^2p_1 + L^2p_2 = tfrac12mL^2. Subtracting the third (divided by L^2 ) from the second (divided by L ) gives frac14p_1 = frac16m , so p_1 = frac23m , then p_2 = frac13m and p_0 = 0 . Only two particles are needed: frac23m at the midpoint and frac13m at the heavy end. ■ Looking back Match moments. Dynamical equivalence means matching the zeroth, first and second moments of the mass distribution. Build up dimension by dimension. A rectangle is a rod of rods, so its weights are products. Count equations and unknowns. Three moments to match, three unknown masses; and sometimes a solution happens to have a zero. What’s really going on Simpson’s rule Matching moments of a mass distribution is the same problem as designing a numerical integration rule. A rule int_-a^af(x)\,dx approx w_0f(-a) + w_1f(0) + w_2f(a) that is exact for f = 1, x, x^2 must satisfy w_0 + w_1 + w_2 = 2a, qquad -aw_0 + aw_2 = 0, qquad a^2w_0 + a^2w_2 = tfrac23a^3, exactly the conditions for the rod (with f = 1, x, x^2 playing the roles of mass, first moment and moment of inertia). The solution is w = 2a(frac16, frac23, frac16) : Simpson’s rule. A bonus comes from symmetry: the rule is also exact for f = x^3 , since both sides vanish, so Simpson’s rule integrates cubics exactly, and its error for smooth functions is proportional to the fourth derivative. A rod therefore matches its three particles not just in mass, centre and moment of inertia, but in the third moment too. Gaussian quadrature and the inertia tensor If the positions as well as the masses are free, two particles suffice: half the mass at each of the points (a)/(sqrt3) . Check: 2 · frac12m · (a^2)/(3) = frac13ma^2 . This is the two-point Gauss–Legendre rule , int_-a^af approx abigl(f(-(a)/(sqrt3)) + f((a)/(sqrt3))bigr) , which is also exact for cubics. Carl Friedrich Gauss showed in 1814 that n cleverly placed points can integrate polynomials of degree 2n - 1 exactly, and Gaussian quadrature is now a standard method of numerical analysis. In mechanics, the moments of inertia of a body about all axes through its centre are encoded in a symmetric 3 × 3 matrix, the inertia tensor . Two bodies with the same mass, centre of mass and inertia tensor respond identically to all forces, which is why engineers can replace a complicated part by a few point masses in a simulation. The eigenvectors of the inertia tensor are the principal axes , the axes about which a body can spin steadily. The thinking skill Replace a system by an equivalent one If two systems agree in every quantity that matters for the problem, replace the complicated one by the simple one. Here only three moments mattered, so a continuous rod could be replaced by three particles. At university, this idea appears as Gaussian quadrature, as multipole expansions in electromagnetism and gravitation (far away, only a few moments of a charge or mass distribution matter), and as the method of moments in statistics. Try this next Simpson’s rule. Use Simpson’s rule with a single interval to estimate int_0^1(dx)/(1 + x^2) , and compare with fracπ4 . Check that the rule is exact for int_-1^1x^3\,dx and int_-1^1x^2\,dx but not for int_-1^1x^4\,dx . All axes alike. Show that the moment of inertia of a square lamina about any axis through its centre in its plane is frac13Ma^2 . ( Hint: the nine equivalent particles are symmetric under rotation by 90^circ ; what does that say about a quadratic expression in cospsi and sinpsi ?) A triangle. Show that a uniform triangular lamina of mass M is dynamically equivalent to three particles of mass frac13M at the midpoints of its sides. A solid cube. Find a dynamically equivalent system of 27 particles for a uniform solid cube, and use it to find the moment of inertia of a cube of side 2a about an edge. Further reading Daniel Kleppner & Robert Kolenkow, An Introduction to Mechanics (Cambridge University Press), the chapter on rigid bodies and moments of inertia. Endre Süli & David Mayers, An Introduction to Numerical Analysis (Cambridge University Press), the chapters on numerical integration, including Simpson’s rule and Gaussian quadrature. Philip Davis & Philip Rabinowitz, Methods of Numerical Integration (Dover). The classic reference.

title: The Snowplough Problem
meta: Chapter 11 · STEP III Specimen paper Question 11
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Agnew’s snowplough Information that travels The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III Specimen paper, Question 11 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/spec-s3-q11 The hook Snow is falling steadily. A snowplough sets off down a road, slowing down as the snow it meets gets deeper. A second plough follows a little later along the cleared road. It meets only the snow that has fallen since the first plough passed, which is shallower, so it travels faster, and eventually it catches up. When? This is a version of a famous problem published by Ralph Agnew in 1942, which became one of the best-known puzzles in differential equations. Its charm is that the second plough’s speed depends on when the first plough passed each point , so the solution to part (i) feeds into the equation for part (ii). And the equation is cleverest when written “upside down”, with time as a function of distance. Before you start The first plough meets snow of depth h + kt at time t . What is its speed? Is it easier to find x as a function of t , or t as a function of x ? Its speed is (dx)/(dt) = (k)/(α(h + kt)) . This separates neatly. Turning it over, (dt)/(dx) = (α(h + kt))/(k) , which is a simple linear equation for t as a function of x . Either way works for the first plough; for the second, the upside-down form is essential. Working it through Stage 1 The first plough From (dt)/(dx) = αbigl(frac hk + tbigr) , the quantity frac hk + t grows exponentially in x : frac hk + t = Ce^α x . At x = 0 , t = 0 , so C = frac hk and t_1(x) = frac hkbigl(e^α x - 1bigr). qed The first plough slows down exponentially: equal distances take exponentially increasing times. Stage 2 The second plough’s equation The second plough reaches position y at time t . How deep is the snow there? (What was the depth just after the first plough passed?) The first plough cleared all the snow at position y at time t_1(y) . Since then, snow has accumulated at rate k , so the depth at time t is z = kbigl(t - t_1(y)bigr) . The second plough’s speed is therefore (dy)/(dt) = (k)/(α kbigl(t - t_1(y)bigr)) = (1)/(αbigl(t - t_1(y)bigr)), and turning it over, frac1α(dt)/(dy) = t - frac hkbigl(e^α y - 1bigr). qed Stage 3 Solving This is linear in t : (dt)/(dy) - α t = -(α h)/(k)(e^α y - 1) . What integrating factor works? What is the starting condition? Multiplying by e^-α y , (d)/(dy)bigl(te^-α ybigr) = -(α h)/(k)bigl(1 - e^-α ybigr), qquad te^-α y = -(α h)/(k)y - frac hke^-α y + C. The second plough starts at y = 0 at t = T , so T = -frac hk + C , giving C = T + frac hk . Multiplying back by e^α y and rearranging, t_2(y) = frac hkbigl(e^α y - 1bigr) + Bigl(T - (α hy)/(k)Bigr)e^α y. qed (To verify, as the question asks: differentiate and substitute; the terms combine to αbigl(t - t_1(y)bigr) .) Stage 4 The collision The ploughs collide when both reach the same point at the same time. Compare t_2(y) with t_1(y) . The difference is t_2(y) - t_1(y) = bigl(T - (α hy)/(k)bigr)e^α y , the time gap between the two ploughs at position y . It shrinks to zero when y = (kT)/(α h). qed At that point the second plough reaches the first: the snow in front of it has zero depth, and in the model its speed becomes infinite (Figure 11.13.1). Looking back Turn the equation upside down. With t as a function of position, both equations were linear. One solution feeds the next. The first plough’s timetable t_1(y) appeared in the second plough’s equation. Compare, do not solve twice. The collision condition came from the difference t_2 - t_1 , which had a simple factor. What’s really going on Agnew’s snowplough In Ralph Palmer Agnew’s version, from his 1942 textbook Differential Equations , it starts snowing heavily and steadily one morning; a snowplough sets out at noon and covers 2 miles in the first hour and 1 mile in the second; when did it start snowing? The plough’s speed is inversely proportional to the depth, which is proportional to the time since the snow started. The answer (an exercise below) involves the golden ratio: it started snowing about 37 minutes before noon. Versions with two ploughs, like this question, followed. Information that travels The second plough’s motion depends on the history recorded in the road: the time at which each point was last cleared. This is a simple example of a system with memory , in which the state at one place depends on what happened there earlier. Traffic flow, the motion of glaciers and the spreading of a forest fire all have this character, and their mathematics, the theory of first-order partial differential equations and their characteristics , is a standard second-year topic. The idea of writing time as a function of position (“when does the front arrive here?”) is exactly the method of arrival times used for such problems. The thinking skill Choose the independent variable A differential equation may be much simpler with the roles of the variables reversed. If the rate depends on the time at which something happened at a place, write time as a function of place. Both equations here became linear when written for t(y) . At university, the freedom to choose which variable is independent (and to change it when convenient) is used constantly, from the hodograph method in fluid mechanics to the use of arc length as a parameter in geometry. Try this next Agnew’s problem. Snow starts falling at a steady rate at an unknown time before noon. A snowplough whose speed is inversely proportional to the depth starts at noon and goes 2 miles in the first hour and 1 mile in the second. Show that if it started snowing t_0 hours before noon, then bigl(1 + (2)/(t_0)bigr)^2 = bigl(1 + (1)/(t_0)bigr)^3 , deduce that (1)/(t_0) is the golden ratio, and find when it started snowing. Verification. Verify by differentiation that t_2(y) satisfies the differential equation of part (ii). The time gap. Show that if kT > h , the time gap t_2(y) - t_1(y) first increases and then decreases to zero, and find where it is greatest. What happens if kT ≤ h ? Interpret this. Three ploughs. A third plough starts at time 2T . Write down the equation for its motion. Does it catch the second plough before or after the second catches the first? Further reading Ralph Palmer Agnew, Differential Equations (McGraw-Hill, 1942). The original snowplough problem. George Simmons, Differential Equations with Applications and Historical Notes (CRC Press), which discusses the snowplough problem among many others. Richard Haberman, Mathematical Models (SIAM). Traffic flow and characteristics, at an accessible level.

title: The Tautochrone
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Why the cycloid? The brachistochrone The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 1994, Question 9 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/94-s3-q9 The hook Release two marbles at the same moment inside a bowl, one from near the rim and one from just above the bottom. Which reaches the bottom first? In an ordinary bowl, the one starting lower usually wins. But there is a bowl in which they always arrive together, wherever they start. It is the tautochrone (Greek for “same time”), and its cross-section is a cycloid , the curve traced by a point on the rim of a rolling wheel. Huygens discovered this in 1659 and used it to design a pendulum clock whose period would not depend on its swing, correcting the flaw found in Section 11.3 . This question proves the tautochrone property in a few lines, by choosing the right variable: distance along the curve, rather than horizontal position. Before you start The bowl is smooth. Which forces act on the particle, and which of them does work? Gravity and the normal reaction. The normal reaction is perpendicular to the surface, and so to the motion, so it does no work. Only gravity does work, and energy is conserved. Working it through Stage 1 Energy along the curve The speed of the particle along the surface is bigl|(ds)/(dt)bigr| , since s is arc length. Conservation of energy gives frac12mdot s^2 + mgy = constant, so dot s^2 + 2gy is constant. ■ Stage 2 Simple harmonic motion in s Use s = 2sqrtky to replace y by a function of s . What kind of motion does the resulting equation describe? Since y = (s^2)/(4k) , the energy equation becomes dot s^2 + (g)/(2k)s^2 = constant = (g)/(2k)s_0^2, where s_0 = 2sqrtkh is the starting arc length (the particle starts at rest). Differentiating, 2dot sddot s + frac gk sdot s = 0 , so ddot s = -(g)/(2k)\,s. This is simple harmonic motion in the variable s , with ω^2 = (g)/(2k) , whatever the amplitude: s = s_0cosω t . Stage 3 The time to the bottom The particle reaches V (where s = 0 ) after a quarter of a period: (π)/(2ω) = fracπ2sqrt(2k)/(g) = πsqrt(k)/(2g), which does not depend on h . ■ Why does this work? The “restoring force” along the curve is g times the slope, g(dy)/(ds) = (g)/(2k)s : exactly proportional to the distance from the bottom, measured along the curve. That is the defining property of simple harmonic motion. A particle starting higher has further to go, but is pushed proportionally harder. Stage 4 Two particles When do the particles reach V , and how fast are they moving? Who has more momentum? Both reach V at the same time T = πsqrtk/(2g) , from opposite sides. The speed at V is ω times the amplitude in s , which is proportional to sqrtheight . Let the heavier particle, released from h , have speed U at V ; the lighter one, released from α^2h , has speed α U . Their momenta are α m · U and m · α U in opposite directions: equal and opposite. The total momentum at the collision is zero. With total momentum zero and coefficient of restitution α , what are the velocities just after the collision? The momentum stays zero, so after the collision the particles again move in opposite directions with momenta of equal size, and their relative speed is α times the approach speed α U + U . If the lighter particle (mass α m ) now moves at speed w , the heavier (mass m ) moves at speed α w , and w + α w = α(1 + α)U , so w = α U . Each particle bounces back with its speed multiplied by α : the particle of mass α m leaves at α U , and the one of mass m at α^2U . Stage 5 The whole motion Each particle now climbs back up its own side, to a height reduced by the factor α^2 (since height is proportional to speed squared): the particle of mass α m to α^2h and the particle of mass m to α^4h . By the tautochrone property, both return to V at exactly the same moment, a time 2T later, with momenta again equal and opposite. The same collision happens again, with all speeds scaled by α . So: the particles always collide at V , at times T, 3T, 5T, ldots ; after the n th collision they rise to heights α^2nh and α^2n+2h ; the motion dies away geometrically but never stops: there are infinitely many collisions, and they continue for ever. ■ Looking back Choose the natural variable. In terms of arc length s , the motion is exactly simple harmonic. In terms of x or y it is a mess. Energy gives the equation. Differentiating the energy equation produced the equation of motion directly. Symmetry in time. Because every journey to the bottom takes the same time, the two particles were synchronised for ever, and the collisions repeated exactly. What’s really going on Why the cycloid? A wheel of radius R rolling under a line traces the cycloid x = R(t + sin t) , y = R(1 - cos t) . Then (dx)/(dt) = R(1 + cos t) and (dy)/(dt) = Rsin t , so the speed along the curve is Rsqrt2 + 2cos t = 2Rcosfrac t2 . Integrating, the arc length from the bottom is s = 4Rsinfrac t2 , while y = 2Rsin^2frac t2 . Hence s^2 = 8Ry : the cycloid is exactly the curve with s = 2sqrtky , with k = 2R . Conversely, the requirement that the restoring force be proportional to s forces the curve to be a cycloid. The brachistochrone In 1696 Johann Bernoulli challenged the mathematicians of Europe: along what curve does a bead slide from one point to a lower point (not directly below it) in the shortest time? The answer, the brachistochrone , is again a cycloid. Newton is said to have solved the problem in a single evening after receiving it; he published his solution anonymously, but Bernoulli recognised the author, “as the lion by its claw”. The problem is the founding example of the calculus of variations , which you met in Section 4.7 : finding the curve that minimises a quantity defined by an integral. Huygens’s cycloidal clock Huygens knew that a simple pendulum keeps imperfect time because its period depends on its amplitude. In his Horologium Oscillatorium (1673) he showed how to make the bob move along a cycloid: hang the string between two curved “cheeks” shaped as cycloids, and the string wraps round them in such a way that the bob traces a cycloid itself (the involute of a cycloid is another cycloid). In practice the cheeks caused more error through friction than they removed, and clockmakers instead kept the swings small. But Huygens’s analysis invented the theory of evolutes and involutes, and his book was one of the great works of seventeenth-century mechanics. The thinking skill Find the variable in which the motion is simple Motion along a curve is often simplest in terms of the distance along the curve. Look for the variable that makes the equation linear. At university this becomes the idea of generalised coordinates in Lagrangian mechanics: any variables that describe the configuration can be used, and choosing them well can make a problem solvable. Try this next Different heights. A particle is released from height h in the tautochrone bowl. Show that its speed at V is sqrt2gh , as it must be by energy conservation, and check that this agrees with ω s_0 . An ordinary bowl. In a hemispherical bowl of radius R , compare the time taken to reach the bottom from a small height with the time from the rim. Which is longer? (Use the result of Section 11.3 .) Equal masses. Repeat the second part of the question with two particles of equal mass m , released from heights h_1 and h_2 , and coefficient of restitution e . Do they still always collide at V ? Cycloid arc length. Show that one arch of a cycloid has length 8R , and that the area under it is 3π R^2 , three times the area of the rolling circle. Further reading George Simmons, Differential Equations with Applications and Historical Notes (CRC Press). Includes the tautochrone and the brachistochrone, with their history. E. A. Whitman, “ Some historical notes on the cycloid ” , American Mathematical Monthly 50 (1943). Why the cycloid was called “the Helen of geometers”. Paul Nahin, When Least Is Best (Princeton University Press). The brachistochrone and other optimisation problems, told with history.

title: Tilted Equilibria
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Equilibria as critical points The Gömböc The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2025, Question 9 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP III paper in OCR’s download of the 2025 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/750486-2025-past-papers.zip The hook Put a rugby ball on a table and it settles on its side; stand it on its end and, with great care, it balances there too, but the slightest nudge topples it. Every rigid body resting on a table has a set of equilibrium positions, some stable and some unstable, and which ones exist depends only on its shape and its centre of mass. How many can a body have? How few? This question builds a solid, shaped like a spinning top with a domed upper half and a pointed lower half, and shows that besides resting upright or upside down it can rest at three different tilts. The key idea is a single geometric condition: a body rests on a point of its surface exactly when the normal to the surface at that point passes through the centre of mass. Behind it lies a recent discovery: a convex shape, the Gömböc, with only one stable and one unstable position. Before you start A solid rests on a table, touching at a single point X of its curved surface. The forces on it are its weight (acting at the centre of mass G ) and the reaction at X . When are these in equilibrium? The table is tangent to the surface at X , and the reaction acts at X , perpendicular to the table: along the normal to the surface. The weight acts vertically through G . Two forces balance only if they act along the same line, so the vertical through X , which is the normal at X , must pass through G . So: the body can rest touching at X exactly when the normal at X passes through G . Working it through Stage 1 The centre of mass Slice the solid into thin cylindrical shells of radius x , thickness δ x and height y . What is the volume of a shell, and where is its centre of mass? With y = fracr^n - x^nr^n-1 , a shell has volume 2π xy\,δ x and its centre of mass at height frac y2 . So V = int_0^r 2π xy\,dx = frac2πr^n-1Bigl(fracr^n+22 - fracr^n+2n + 2Bigr) = (nπ r^3)/(n + 2), and the moment about the base is beginaligned int_0^r 2π x·(y^2)/(2)\,dx &= fracπr^2n-2int_0^r x(r^n - x^n)^2\,dx \\ &= π r^4Bigl(frac12 - (2)/(n + 2) + (1)/(2n + 2)Bigr) = (n^2π r^4)/(2(n + 1)(n + 2)). endaligned (The bracket simplifies because (n + 1)(n + 2) - 4(n + 1) + (n + 2) = n^2 .) Dividing, bar y = (nr)/(2(n + 1)). qed For n = 2 (a paraboloid) this is frac r3 , the familiar result; as n → ∞ the solid becomes a cylinder and bar y → frac r2 . Stage 2 Where normals meet the axis The gradient of the curve at x = rp is -fracnx^n-1r^n-1 = -np^n-1 , so the normal has gradient frac1np^n-1 . Moving along the normal from bigl(rp, r(1 - p^n)bigr) to the y -axis, x decreases by rp and y by fracrpnp^n-1 = fracrnp^n-2 . So Y = rBigl(1 - p^n - frac1np^n-2Bigr). qed For n = 4 , Y = rbigl(1 - p^4 - (1)/(4p^2)bigr) . Where is it greatest? What happens as p → 0 , and at p = 1 ? (dY)/(dp) = rbigl(-4p^3 + (1)/(2p^3)bigr) = 0 when p^6 = frac18 , that is p^2 = frac12 . Then Y = rbigl(1 - frac14 - frac12bigr) = frac14r . ■ As p → 0 , Y → -∞ (near the top the dome is very flat, and its normals are almost vertical, meeting the axis far below); at p = 1 , Y = -frac14r . So as p runs from 0 to 1 , Y rises from -∞ to frac14r and falls back to -frac14r . Stage 3 The spinning top The solid in part (iii) is a dome ( n = 4 ) on top of an upside-down paraboloid ( n = 2 ). Where is its centre of mass? From Stage 1, the dome has volume (2π r^3)/(3) and centre of mass at (2r)/(5) ; the paraboloid has volume (π r^3)/(2) and, being upside down, centre of mass at -frac r3 . So bar y = (frac23·frac25 - frac12·frac13)/(frac23 + frac12)\,r = frac(4)/(15) - frac16frac76\,r = (3r)/(35). G is at bigl(0, (3r)/(35)bigr) , slightly above the widest point. Stage 4 Counting equilibria A tilted equilibrium needs a point (not A or B ) whose normal passes through G . On each part of the surface, how many points have normals meeting the axis at height (3r)/(35) ? The dome. Its normals meet the axis at heights Y which rise from -∞ to frac14r and fall to -frac14r . Since -frac14r < (3r)/(35) < frac14r , by the intermediate value theorem the value (3r)/(35) is taken once on the rising part and once on the falling part: two points. The pointed base. By part (ii) with n = 2 , reflected in the x -axis, the normal at the point with parameter p meets the axis at -rbigl(1 - p^2 - frac12bigr) = rbigl(p^2 - frac12bigr) , which increases from -frac12r to frac12r . It equals (3r)/(35) exactly once, at p^2 = (41)/(70) . Each of these three points gives an equilibrium, and the three normals make different angles with the axis, so overrightarrowAB makes three different non-zero angles with the vertical (Figure 11.8.1). ■ Looking back Turn a physical condition into geometry. Equilibrium became “the normal passes through G ”. Existence without solving. We never found the angles. The intermediate value theorem, with the shape of the function Y(p) , showed how many there are. Reuse a general result. Part (ii) for general n handled both pieces of the surface in part (iii). What’s really going on Equilibria as critical points When the solid rests on the point X , the height of G above the table is the distance from G to the tangent plane at X , which for a convex body is |GX| when GX is along the normal. In general, the equilibria are the critical points of the distance from G to the surface: a point X where |GX| is stationary is exactly a point whose normal passes through G . Stable equilibria are local minima of this distance ( G as low as possible), and unstable ones are local maxima or saddle points. Going round the cross-section from A to B , the distance from G is: large at A (a maximum: balanced on its point, unstable), smaller at the tilted point on the base (a minimum, stable), larger at the rim, smaller at the lower tilted point of the dome (stable), larger at the upper one (unstable), and smaller at B (stable: resting on the top of the dome). Minima and maxima must alternate, as the figure shows. (In fact there is one more equilibrium that the question does not count: the solid can balance, unstably, on its sharp rim, where the surface has no single normal.) The Gömböc How few equilibria can a convex body have? Any body has at least one stable and one unstable position: the nearest and furthest points of the surface from G . A two-dimensional convex shape of uniform density always has at least four (two minima and two maxima of distance, alternating). In 1995 Vladimir Arnold asked whether a three-dimensional convex body of uniform density could have just two: one stable, one unstable. In 2006 Gábor Domokos and Péter Várkonyi constructed one, the Gömböc : put it down in any position, and it rolls and rocks until it reaches its single stable position. Domokos later noticed that some tortoises have shells close to this shape, which helps them right themselves when turned over. Archimedes and floating bodies The study of the stability of bodies goes back to Archimedes, who in On Floating Bodies analysed when a floating paraboloid (a model of a ship’s hull) is stable upright and when it capsizes, in terms of its shape and density. His answer, worked out with geometry alone, involves exactly the kind of centre-of-mass and normal calculations used here. Naval architects still use his ideas, in the form of the metacentre : a ship is stable if the point where the vertical through the centre of buoyancy meets the ship’s axis lies above the centre of mass. The thinking skill Potential energy landscapes Equilibria are the stationary points of potential energy, and stable equilibria are its minima. Count stationary points instead of solving for them. Here the potential energy was proportional to the height of G , the distance from G to the surface. At university this viewpoint runs through mechanics, chemistry (molecules settle into minima of energy) and topology, where Morse theory shows that the numbers of minima, maxima and saddles of any function on a surface are constrained by the surface’s shape. Try this next A self-righting toy. Try STEP II 1996, Question 9 : when does a cone on a hemisphere right itself? ( Hint: where must G be relative to the centre of the hemisphere?) A sphere. For a uniform solid sphere, every normal passes through the centre. What does that say about its equilibria? What if the sphere’s centre of mass is displaced slightly from its centre? An ellipse. Show that an elliptical disc rolling in its own plane on a line has exactly four equilibria, and identify which are stable. Two paraboloids. Replace the dome in part (iii) by a paraboloid ry = r^2 - x^2 , so that the solid is symmetric about the x -axis. Show that G is at the origin, find the tilted equilibria, and explain why they come in pairs with equal tilts. Further reading Péter Várkonyi & Gábor Domokos, “ Static equilibria of rigid bodies: dice, pebbles, and the Poincaré–Hopf theorem ” , Journal of Nonlinear Science 16 (2006). The Gömböc paper. Daniel Kleppner & Robert Kolenkow, An Introduction to Mechanics (Cambridge University Press), on equilibrium and stability. Chris Rorres, “ Completing Book II of Archimedes’s On Floating Bodies ” , Mathematical Intelligencer 26 (2004). Archimedes’ stability analysis, with modern pictures.

title: What We Have Learned
headings: 1. When is motion simple? 2. What is the right point of view? 3. Can intuition be trusted? 4. A toolkit for oscillations and frames Where next
text: We began with things that swing, things that spin, and things seen from somewhere that moves. We asked three questions: when is motion simple, what is the right point of view, and can intuition be trusted? Here is what the chapter’s fourteen questions showed. 1. When is motion simple? Simple harmonic motion, with a single frequency independent of amplitude, is the ideal. Driving it at its natural frequency produced resonance ( Section 11.1 ), with beats just off resonance and unlimited growth exactly on it. Two coupled oscillators turned out to be two independent simple oscillators in disguise ( Section 11.2 ), but with frequencies in the irrational ratio sqrt3 , so the combined motion never repeats. The real pendulum is not simple at all ( Section 11.3 ): its period grows with amplitude, through an elliptic integral that Gauss’s arithmetic–geometric mean computes with astonishing speed. And the tautochrone ( Section 11.4 ) showed how to make motion exactly simple again, by bending the track into a cycloid. 2. What is the right point of view? Almost every question was solved by choosing the right variable or the right frame. Coordinates. Arc length made the tautochrone simple; the combinations x y decoupled the springs; the fraction of the rope removed the stretching from the ant’s problem ( Section 11.12 ); writing time as a function of distance made the snowploughs’ equations linear ( Section 11.13 ). Frames. In the accelerating train ( Section 11.5 ), a fictitious force tilted gravity, and the bead oscillated about a new lowest point. Einstein turned this observation into general relativity. Points to take moments about. For the spinning marble ( Section 11.6 ), angular momentum about the contact point was conserved, because friction acts there, giving the final speed without knowing the friction. Equivalent systems. A rod behaves exactly like three particles ( Section 11.7 ), with the weights of Simpson’s rule; and the equilibria of a solid are where its normals pass through the centre of mass ( Section 11.8 ). 3. Can intuition be trusted? Often not. The boundary of the region a cannon can reach is not a trajectory but their envelope ( Section 11.9 ). A ball thrown steeply enough comes back towards you before it lands ( Section 11.10 ). A fielder can catch a ball without predicting where it will land, by keeping its image rising steadily ( Section 11.11 ). An ant walking slowly along a rope stretched a hundred thousand times faster still reaches the end ( Section 11.12 ). A hanging chain is not a parabola, but a chain carrying a bridge is ( Section 11.14 ). In each case, a short calculation replaced a confident but wrong intuition with a precise statement, and usually with an explanation. 4. A toolkit for oscillations and frames Method Where you used it Particular plus complementary solution Resonance (11.1) Decoupling by eigenvectors Normal modes (11.2) Energy integral and substitution Pendulum (11.3) The natural variable Tautochrone (11.4); ant (11.12) Fictitious forces Train (11.5) Angular momentum about a point Backspin (11.6) Matching moments Simpson’s rod (11.7) Counting stationary points Tilted equilibria (11.8) Discriminants and envelopes Safety parabola (11.9) Sign of a derivative Coming back (11.10) Comparing coefficients Fielders (11.11) Integrating factors Ant (11.12); snowplough (11.13) Resolving at joints Bridge (11.14) Where next The next two chapters turn to probability and statistics, starting with Section 12.1 . Normal modes are eigenvectors ( Section 7.2 ), and the quantum harmonic oscillator of Section 8.6 is the oscillator of this chapter in quantum mechanics. Limit cycles ( Section 8.4 ) are oscillations that sustain themselves, and chaos ( Section 8.7 ) is what nonlinear oscillators can do when driven. If you want to go further before university A. P. French, Vibrations and Waves : the classic introduction to oscillations, resonance and normal modes. David Morin, Introduction to Classical Mechanics : rotation, frames and many surprising problems. Steven Strogatz, Sync : how oscillators fall into step, from fireflies to bridges. George Simmons, Differential Equations with Applications and Historical Notes : the tautochrone, the brachistochrone and the snowplough, with their history. Coleman joked that a physicist’s career consists of treating the harmonic oscillator in ever more abstract ways. This chapter has tried to show why: the oscillator is the simplest motion there is, and almost everything looks like one if you choose the right point of view. Learning to find that point of view, a variable, a frame or a combination, is the most useful skill that mechanics teaches.

title: The Last Passenger's Seat
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Symmetry arguments How many passengers are displaced? The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 2021, Question 11 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP II paper in OCR’s download of the 2021 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/696588-2021-past-papers.zip The hook A hundred passengers board a full plane. The first has lost their boarding card and sits anywhere. Each later passenger takes their own seat if it is free, and otherwise a random free seat. What is the probability that the last passenger gets their own seat? The chaos might cascade through the whole plane, so you might expect a small probability; or perhaps most passengers are unaffected and it should be close to 1 . The answer is exactly frac12 , for any number of passengers. This question proves it with a recurrence and induction. But there is also a beautiful one-line argument by symmetry, which explains why the answer is frac12 and lets you write down the answer for any passenger at once. Before you start Work out P_2 and P_3 by listing what can happen. With two seats, T_1 takes S_1 (then T_2 gets S_2 ) or S_2 , each with probability frac12 : P_2 = frac12 . With three seats: if T_1 takes S_1 (probability frac13 ), everyone is fine; if T_1 takes S_3 , T_3 loses; if T_1 takes S_2 , then T_2 chooses between S_1 and S_3 at random, and T_3 is fine only if T_2 chooses S_1 . So P_3 = frac13 + frac13·frac12 = frac12 . Working it through Stage 1 The recurrence Suppose T_1 sits in S_k , with 2 ≤ k ≤ n - 1 . What happens to passengers T_2, ldots, T_k-1 ? When T_k arrives, which seats are free, and how does the situation compare with a smaller train? Passengers T_2, ldots, T_k-1 find their seats free and sit in them. When T_k arrives, the free seats are S_1 and S_k+1, ldots, S_n : there are n - k + 1 of them. T_k chooses one at random, and from then on each passenger takes their own seat if free and a random one if not. This is exactly the original problem with n - k + 1 seats, T_k playing the role of the first passenger and S_1 playing the role of T_k ’s “own” seat (the one that, if taken, sorts everything out). So the conditional probability that T_n gets S_n is P_n-k+1 . Now condition on T_1 ’s seat, each with probability frac1n : S_1 gives success for sure, S_n gives certain failure, and S_k gives P_n-k+1 . So P_n = frac1nBigl(1 + 0 + sum_k=2^n-1P_n-k+1Bigr) = frac1nBigl(1 + sum_r=2^n-1P_rBigr). qed Stage 2 The answer P_2 = P_3 = frac12 . Guess P_n and prove it by strong induction. Claim: P_n = frac12 for all n ≥ 2 . It holds for n = 2 . If P_r = frac12 for 2 ≤ r ≤ n - 1 , then P_n = frac1nBigl(1 + (n - 2)/(2)Bigr) = frac1n·frac n2 = frac12. qed Stage 3 The penultimate passenger Try to find a slicker argument. At the end, which seat is left for T_n ? Could it be S_2 ? The last seat left for T_n is either S_1 or S_n . It cannot be S_k for 2 ≤ k ≤ n - 1 , because T_k would have taken it.
