And every random choice made before then treats S_1 and S_n symmetrically: whenever a displaced passenger chooses, S_1 and S_n are equally likely to be picked. The first of the two to be chosen decides the outcome, so each is equally likely to be the one left: P_n = frac12 . The same argument works for any passenger T_k , k ≥ 2 . T_k loses their seat only if some earlier passenger took it. The displacement continues until someone picks S_1 ; among the seats S_1, S_k, S_k+1, ldots, S_n , which are all treated alike by the choosers before T_k arrives, the first to be chosen is equally likely to be any of these n - k + 2 seats, and T_k loses only if it is S_k . So P(T_k sits in S_k) = (n - k + 1)/(n - k + 2). For k = n - 1 (with n ≥ 3 ) this gives Q_n = frac23 ; and Q_2 = frac12 , since then T_n-1 = T_1 , who sits in S_1 with probability frac12 . ■ Looking back Reduce to a smaller copy. After T_1 sat in S_k , the rest of the problem was the same problem with fewer seats. Strong induction. The recurrence involved all smaller cases, so the induction assumed the result for all of them. Find the symmetry. The seats S_1 and S_n are interchangeable throughout, which explains the frac12 without any algebra. What’s really going on Symmetry arguments The second proof is an example of a powerful idea in probability: if two outcomes are related by a symmetry of the random process, they have the same probability. The process here does not distinguish between S_1 and S_n until one of them is chosen, so they must be equally likely to be the survivor. Symmetry arguments often replace long calculations with a single observation. The next few sections are full of them: an extra coin toss in Section 12.6 , a knockout draw in Section 12.7 . How many passengers are displaced? The number of displaced passengers (those who do not get their own seat) is also nicely behaved. T_1 is displaced unless they choose S_1 , and T_k (for k ≥ 2 ) is displaced with probability (1)/(n - k + 2) . Adding, the expected number of displaced passengers is Bigl(1 - frac1nBigr) + Bigl(frac1n + (1)/(n - 1) + cdots + frac12Bigr) = H_n - frac1n, roughly n : even in a plane of 300 the chaos affects only about six passengers on average. The harmonic numbers, again ( Section 9.11 ). The thinking skill Look for a symmetry If the random process cannot tell two outcomes apart, they are equally likely. Find the moment at which they first become distinguishable. At university, symmetry arguments appear throughout probability, from the reflection principle ( Section 9.10 ) to exchangeability, the property that a sequence of random variables has the same distribution in any order, which is the basis of much of modern statistics. Try this next Two forgetful passengers. If the first two passengers both choose at random, what is the probability that the last gets their own seat? Displaced passengers. Verify the expected number of displaced passengers for n = 3 by listing the possibilities. An indirect route. Show, using the recurrence, that sum_r=2^n-1P_r = (n - 2)/(2) is consistent with the symmetry argument. The last seat. Show that, conditional on the last passenger not getting their own seat, the last passenger gets S_1 with probability 1 . Why? Further reading Peter Winkler, Mathematical Puzzles: A Connoisseur’s Collection (A K Peters). Includes the airline seat puzzle and many others solved by symmetry. Frederick Mosteller, Fifty Challenging Problems in Probability (Dover). A classic collection. Joseph Blitzstein & Jessica Hwang, Introduction to Probability (CRC Press; free online).

text: These are brief answers and hints, not full solutions: they give the result and the key step, so that you can check your own work. Try each exercise properly before looking. 12.1 Precise Conditioning In both (iv) and (v), the other k - 1 discs are a random selection from the remaining b + n - 1 , of which n - 1 are numbered, so both equal frac(n - 1)binombk-2binomb+n-1k-1 . Answer (vi) is fracbinom n2binombk-2binomb+nk - binom bk . With N = b + n , the two agree only when (2N - nk)binomN-1k-1 = 2kbinom bk . That happens only in odd cases, such as (b, n, k) = (2, 4, 3) , (3, 3, 4) or (6, 11, 3) , or trivially when n = 2 and every disc is drawn. It does not hold for the question’s values. Of the 14^2 = 196 equally likely (sex, day) pairs for the two children, 196 - 13^2 = 27 include at least one Tuesday boy. Of those, 7^2 - 6^2 = 13 have two boys. So the probability is (13)/(27) . You pick door 1. If the car is behind door 1 (probability frac13 ), switching loses; if it is behind door 2 or 3, the host must open the other goat door, and switching wins: frac23 . If the host opens a door at random and it happens to show a goat, the outcomes “car behind your door” and “car behind the other closed door” are equally likely given what you saw: frac12 . P(≥2 mid ≥1) = (1 - P(0) - P(1))/(1 - P(0)) approx 0.370 , but P(≥2 mid ace of spades) = 1 - binom4812big/binom5112 approx 0.561 . Knowing which ace makes a second ace more likely. 12.2 The Base-Rate Fallacy Both say “body” with probability pq if it is there and (1 - p)(1 - q) if not. With prior odds 1 : 1 , the posterior is (pq)/(pq + (1 - p)(1 - q)) = (pq)/(1 - p - q + 2pq) . For the second part, “ A is there” is true in two of the three equally likely cases, so P(both mid both say A) = (pq)/(2pq + (1 - p)(1 - q)) . We need 0.9π > (1)/(11)(1 - π) , that is, π > (10)/(109) approx 9.2\% . Each positive AL result multiplies the odds by (0.9)/(1/11) = 9.9 . From prior odds (1)/(99) : after one positive, odds 0.1 (probability (1)/(11) ); after two, odds 0.99 (probability about 0.497 ); after three, odds 9.8 (probability about 0.907 ). Of the 100 people with the condition, 99 test positive; of the 999\,900 without it, about 9999 do. So about 10\,100 people are told they may have it, and only 99 of them (about 1\% ) actually do. 12.3 What Does "Random" Mean? title: The Base-Rate Fallacy
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Odds and evidence The prosecutor’s fallacy The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 1998, Question 12 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/98-s2-q12 The hook A test for a disease is 90\% accurate on people who have it and gives few false alarms. Frankie tests positive. How worried should Frankie be? Most people, including, in many studies, most doctors, say “about 90\% ”. The true answer in this question is (1)/(11) , about 9\% . Ten times smaller. The mistake is to ignore the base rate : the disease is rare, so even a small false-positive rate among the many healthy people produces far more false alarms than there are true cases. This base-rate fallacy matters in medicine, in law (where it is called the prosecutor’s fallacy), in security screening and in machine learning. Bayes’ theorem is the cure. Before you start Imagine 1000 people. How many have the disease? How many of them test positive? How many of the healthy people test positive? Of 1000 people, 10 have the disease and 9 of them test positive. Of the 990 healthy people, (1)/(11) test positive: 90 false positives. So 99 people test positive, of whom only 9 are ill. Working it through Stage 1 Bayes’ theorem Write D for “Frankie has the disease” and + for “AL is positive”. You know P(+ mid D) and want P(D mid +) . How are they related? By the definition of conditional probability, P(D mid +) = (P(D cap +))/(P(+)) , and P(+) splits according to whether Frankie has the disease: beginaligned P(D mid +) &= (P(+ mid D)P(D))/(P(+ mid D)P(D) + P(+ mid bar D)P(bar D)) \\ &= frac0.9 × 0.010.9 × 0.01 + (1)/(11) × 0.99 = (0.009)/(0.009 + 0.09) = (1)/(11). qed endaligned This is the (9)/(99) of the thousand people. Stage 2 A second test The second test is given only to those who tested positive on AL. What is the proportion of sufferers in that group? Use it as the new “base rate”. Among those positive on AL, a fraction (1)/(11) are sufferers and (10)/(11) are not. Applying Bayes’ theorem again, with these as the prior probabilities, P(D mid both positive) = frac0.9 × (1)/(11)0.9 × (1)/(11) + p × (10)/(11) = (0.9)/(0.9 + 10p). Setting this equal to frac12 gives 10p = 0.9 , so p = 0.09 . ■ (Assuming, as the question implicitly does, that the two tests’ errors are independent given whether Frankie is ill.) With p = 0.09 , STEP’s false-positive rate is about the same as AL’s, yet a second positive result raises the probability from (1)/(11) to frac12 . Why does the same quality of test have a much bigger effect the second time? Looking back Natural frequencies. Imagining 1000 people made the answer obvious and easy to check. Prior times likelihood. The posterior probability depends on both the test’s accuracy and the base rate. Updating in stages. Yesterday’s posterior is today’s prior: the second test started from (1)/(11) , not (1)/(100) . What’s really going on Odds and evidence Bayes’ theorem is clearest in terms of odds . The odds of D are P(D) : P(bar D) . A piece of evidence E multiplies the odds by the likelihood ratio (P(E mid D))/(P(E mid bar D)) : posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio. Here the prior odds are 1 : 99 , and AL’s likelihood ratio is 0.9 div (1)/(11) = 9.9 , giving posterior odds 9.9 : 99 = 1 : 10 , that is, probability (1)/(11) . A second independent test with likelihood ratio 10 (as STEP with p = 0.09 has) brings the odds to 1 : 1 . Taking logarithms, evidence adds : each independent test contributes the logarithm of its likelihood ratio. Alan Turing used exactly this, measuring evidence in “bans” and “decibans”, to break Enigma messages at Bletchley Park. The prosecutor’s fallacy In 1999 the solicitor Sally Clark was convicted of murdering her two baby sons, partly on the strength of evidence that the chance of two cot deaths in one family was “1 in 73 million”. Quite apart from the error in that number (it assumed the two deaths were independent, ignoring genetic and environmental factors), the reasoning confused P(evidence mid innocent) with P(innocent mid evidence) . Double murder by a mother is also extremely rare, and the relevant comparison is between the two explanations. The Royal Statistical Society wrote publicly to point out the error, and her conviction was overturned in 2003. The mathematics is exactly that of this question. Gigerenzer and natural frequencies In the 1990s the psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer showed that doctors who were given test statistics as conditional probabilities mostly got questions like this one badly wrong, but that when the same information was presented as natural frequencies (“of 1000 women, 10 have breast cancer; of these, 8 test positive…”) most got them right. His work has changed how medical risks are communicated to patients in many countries. The thinking skill Reverse a conditional with Bayes’ theorem P(A mid B) and P(B mid A) are different numbers. To get from one to the other you need the base rate P(A) . Bayesian reasoning, updating beliefs in the light of evidence, is the foundation of modern statistics and machine learning, from spam filters to medical diagnosis. At university you will meet it as Bayesian inference, with prior and posterior distributions instead of single probabilities. Try this next A body in the fridge. Try STEP II 1987, Question 16 : Bayes’ theorem with two witnesses of different reliability, in one of STEP’s more memorable settings. How rare? For a test with sensitivity 0.9 and false-positive rate (1)/(11) , how common must a disease be for a positive result to mean a better than even chance of having it? Repeat the test. If AL itself is repeated, and the results are independent given the person’s true state, what is the probability of disease after two positive AL results? After three? Screening. A screening programme tests a million people for a condition with prevalence 1 in 10\,000 , using a test with sensitivity 99\% and false-positive rate 1\% . How many people will be told they may have the condition, and how many of them actually do? Further reading Gerd Gigerenzer, Reckoning with Risk (Penguin). Natural frequencies, medical tests and the courtroom. David Spiegelhalter, The Art of Statistics (Pelican). Includes medical screening and the Sally Clark case. Sharon Bertsch McGrayne, The Theory That Would Not Die (Yale University Press). The history of Bayes’ theorem, including Turing’s use of it.

title: What Does "Random" Mean?

text: The question STEP III 2022, Question 12 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP III paper in OCR’s download of the 2022 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/696587-2022-past-papers.zip The hook “Choose a chord of a circle at random. What is its expected length?” The question sounds as if it has an answer. It does not, until you say what “at random” means. Pick two random points on the circle and join them, and the expected length is (4a)/(π) approx 1.27a . Pick a random point inside the circle and a random direction through it, and the answer is (16a)/(3π) approx 1.70a . Both are perfectly reasonable ways to choose “a random chord”. This is Bertrand’s paradox , published by Joseph Bertrand in 1889 as a warning. Probability is only well defined once the random experiment is specified. The paradox helped to push mathematicians towards the rigorous foundations of probability built in the twentieth century, in which every probability lives on a precisely defined space of outcomes. Before you start If the angle AOB is θ , what is the length of the chord AB ? (Drop a perpendicular from O .) The perpendicular from O bisects the chord and the angle, so AB = 2asinfracθ2 . Working it through Stage 1 Two points on the circle E(AB) = (1)/(2π)int_0^2π2asinfracθ2\,dθ = (a)/(π)Bigl[-2cosfracθ2Bigr]_0^2π = (a)/(π)· 4 = (4a)/(π). qed Stage 2 A random point inside What is P(R ≤ r) for 0 ≤ r ≤ a ? Differentiate to get the density. P(R ≤ r) is the area of the disc of radius r divided by the area of the whole disc, (r^2)/(a^2) . So R has density (2r)/(a^2) on [0, a] . (Points are more likely to be far from the centre, because there is more area there.) A chord through C makes angle t with OC . How far is the chord from O ? The distance from O to the line is Rsin t , so the chord has length 2sqrta^2 - R^2sin^2t . Stage 3 Averaging over C With s = sin t , beginaligned L(t) &= int_0^a 2sqrta^2 - r^2s^2·(2r)/(a^2)\,dr = (4)/(a^2)Bigl[-frac(a^2 - r^2s^2)^3/23s^2Bigr]_0^a \\ &= (4)/(a^2)·fraca^3 - a^3(1 - s^2)^3/23s^2 = (4a(1 - cos^3t))/(3sin^2t). qed endaligned Factorise 1 - cos^3t and sin^2t = 1 - cos^2t . What cancels? With c = cos t , (1 - c^3)/(1 - c^2) = ((1 - c)(1 + c + c^2))/((1 - c)(1 + c)) = (1 + c + c^2)/(1 + c) = c + (1)/(1 + c) , and 1 + cos t = 2cos^2frac t2 . So L(t) = (4a)/(3)Bigl(cos t + tfrac12sec^2tfrac t2Bigr). qed Stage 4 A random direction too beginaligned Ebigl(L(T)bigr) &= frac2πint_0^π/2(4a)/(3)Bigl(cos t + tfrac12sec^2tfrac t2Bigr)dt \\ &= (8a)/(3π)Bigl[sin t + tantfrac t2Bigr]_0^π/2 = (8a)/(3π)(1 + 1) = (16a)/(3π). qed endaligned Looking back Specify the experiment. “A random chord” became a precise procedure in each part, and each procedure gave a different answer. Densities from areas. P(R ≤ r) came directly from geometry; differentiating gave the density. Average in stages. First over the position of C (with t fixed), then over t . What’s really going on Bertrand’s three answers Bertrand’s own question was: what is the probability that a random chord is longer than the side of the inscribed equilateral triangle, sqrt3a ? He gave three methods and three answers. Random endpoints: fix one endpoint; the chord is long if the other lies in the middle third of the circle. Probability frac13 . Random radius and a random point on it as the midpoint: the chord is long if its distance from O is less than frac a2 . Probability frac12 . Random midpoint anywhere in the disc: the chord is long if the midpoint lies within frac a2 of O . Probability frac14 . Each method is a different probability distribution on the set of chords, and there is no contradiction: they answer different questions. The lesson is that “uniformly at random” only makes sense relative to a chosen parametrisation, and for continuous sets there is usually no single natural one. Is there a right answer? In 1973 the physicist Edwin Jaynes argued that the second method is the “right” one, on the grounds that the answer should not change if the circle is moved or rescaled slightly: a random chord should be like a straw thrown onto a circle drawn on the floor. Only the distribution with uniform distance from the centre has this invariance, and experiments throwing straws confirm frac12 . The same idea, that the right distribution is the one that respects the symmetries of the situation, underlies integral geometry , the mathematics of random lines, which also explains Buffon’s needle in Section 12.20 . From paradox to axioms Bertrand published his chord paradox in Calcul des probabilités (1889), partly to mock what he saw as careless uses of “geometric probability”. Henri Poincaré discussed it too. In 1900 David Hilbert listed the axiomatisation of probability among his famous problems for the new century, and Andrey Kolmogorov solved it in 1933: probability is a measure on a space of outcomes, and every question about “random” objects must first say which space and which measure. Bertrand’s paradox is the standard example of why this is necessary. The thinking skill Define the random experiment Before calculating a probability, describe exactly how the random object is generated. Different descriptions can give different answers. At university, every probability calculation starts from a sample space and a probability measure. In statistics and physics, choosing the right model of randomness, often by symmetry, is a large part of the work. Try this next Bertrand’s probabilities. Verify the three probabilities frac13 , frac12 , frac14 above. The other mean. Show that if the chord’s midpoint is chosen uniformly in the disc (the right-hand picture), the expected length is (4a)/(3) . ( Hint: this is L(fracπ2) . Why?) Random distance. If the distance of the chord from O is uniform on [0, a] , show that the expected length is (π a)/(2) . Three methods, three distributions. For each of the three methods, find the probability density of the chord’s length ell on [0, 2a] . Further reading Edwin Jaynes, “ The well-posed problem ” , Foundations of Physics 3 (1973). The invariance argument, readable and provocative. Gábor Székely, Paradoxes in Probability Theory and Mathematical Statistics (Reidel). Bertrand’s paradox and many others. Daniel Klain & Gian-Carlo Rota, Introduction to Geometric Probability (Cambridge University Press). Integral geometry, for later.

title: Extinction or Explosion
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on The probability of extinction The critical threshold The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 2003, Question 12 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/03-s2-q12 The hook In 1873 Francis Galton posed a question in the Educational Times : why do aristocratic family names die out so often? Each man has some random number of sons, each of whom passes on the name. Even if each man has on average more than one son, will the name survive for ever? The question founded the theory of branching processes , which now models nuclear chain reactions, the spread of epidemics, the growth of cell populations and the survival of mutations. This question sets up the simplest model: each particle splits into 0 , 1 or 2 particles. The expected population grows or shrinks geometrically. But expectation is not the whole story. Even when the expected population explodes, there is a positive chance that the line dies out completely, and a beautiful fixed-point argument finds it. Before you start If there are two particles at one stage, what is the distribution of the number at the next stage? Each of the two particles independently produces a B(2, p) number of offspring, so the total is B(4, p) : four independent “chances” each succeeding with probability p . Working it through Stage 1 Two, then two P(X_1 = 2) = p^2 , and then P(X_2 = 2 mid X_1 = 2) = binom42p^2q^2 = 6p^2q^2 . So P(X_1 = 2, X_2 = 2) = 6p^4q^2. qed Stage 2 Reasoning backwards In how many ways can X_2 = 2 happen? (What can X_1 be?) X_2 = 2 needs X_1 = 1 (probability 2pq ) followed by 2 offspring ( p^2 ), or X_1 = 2 followed by 2 from B(4, p) . ( X_1 = 0 leaves nothing.) So P(X_2 = 2) = 2p^3q + 6p^4q^2 , and P(X_1 = 2 mid X_2 = 2) = (6p^4q^2)/(2p^3q + 6p^4q^2) = (3pq)/(1 + 3pq). Setting this equal to (9)/(25) : 75pq = 9 + 27pq , so pq = (3)/(16) , that is p(1 - p) = (3)/(16) , giving p = frac14 or p = frac34 . ■ Stage 3 The expected population If there are k particles at stage n - 1 , what is the expected number at stage n ? Then average over k . Each particle has on average E(X) = 2p offspring, so k particles have 2pk on average: E(X_n mid X_n-1 = k) = 2pk . Averaging over k , E(X_n) = 2p\,E(X_n-1) . With E(X_0) = 1 , E(X_n) = (2p)^n. For p = frac14 , (2p)^n = 2^-n → 0 ; for p = frac34 , (2p)^n = bigl(frac32bigr)^n → ∞ . ■ Looking back Sums of independent binomials. k particles each giving B(2, p) give B(2k, p) in total. Bayes’ theorem in time. P(X_1 = 2 mid X_2 = 2) reasoned backwards from a later observation to an earlier state. Conditional expectation. Conditioning on the previous generation turned the expectation into a geometric sequence. What’s really going on The probability of extinction For p = frac34 , the expected population grows without limit. Does that mean the population survives? Not necessarily: if the first particle has no offspring (probability q^2 = (1)/(16) ), the line ends at once. Let e be the probability of eventual extinction. The first particle has k offspring, and each of their lines dies out independently with probability e , so e = q^2 + 2pq\,e + p^2e^2 = (q + pe)^2 = G(e), where G(s) = (q + ps)^2 is the probability generating function of the offspring number. The extinction probability is a fixed point of G : in fact the smallest non-negative one. For p = frac34 , (1 + 3e)^2 = 16e gives 9e^2 - 10e + 1 = 0 , so e = frac19 or 1 , and the extinction probability is frac19 . For p = frac14 , the only fixed point in [0, 1] is e = 1 : extinction is certain (Figure 12.15.1). The critical threshold In general, a branching process dies out with certainty if the mean number of offspring is less than 1 , and also if it equals 1 , except in the trivial case where every individual has exactly one offspring (when the family line simply continues for ever, one at a time); it survives with positive probability if the mean is greater than 1 . The mean offspring number is the reproduction number R of epidemiology: an epidemic with R > 1 may take off, but even then an early outbreak can fizzle out by chance, with probability given by exactly the fixed-point equation above. In nuclear physics, a chain reaction is critical when each fission causes on average exactly one more, and the art of running a reactor is to keep it there. Galton, Watson and Bienaymé Galton’s question was answered, partly incorrectly, by the Reverend Henry William Watson in 1874: he found the fixed-point equation but concluded that every family name dies out eventually, missing the second root. The correct analysis had in fact been given in 1845 by the French statistician Irénée-Jules Bienaymé, whose work was forgotten until the 1970s. The model is now called the Galton–Watson process (sometimes Bienaymé–Galton–Watson), and is a central example in every course on random processes. The thinking skill Condition on the first generation A process that renews itself (each offspring starts an independent copy of the whole process) satisfies an equation obtained by conditioning on the first step. The equation e = G(e) is a fixed-point problem, the same kind met in Section 2.2 and Section 8.7 . At university, generating functions and fixed points are the main tools for branching processes, random trees and random networks. Try this next Extinction in general. For offspring distribution B(2, p) , show that the extinction probability is 1 if p ≤ frac12 and bigl(frac qpbigr)^2 if p > frac12 . The variance. Show that Var(X_n) satisfies Var(X_n) = (2p)^2Var(X_n-1) + 2pq\,E(X_n-1) , and find it for p = frac12 . Extinction by generation n . Let e_n = P(X_n = 0) . Show that e_n = G(e_n-1) , and compute e_1 , e_2 , e_3 for p = frac34 . Do they approach frac19 ? Surnames. If each man has 0 , 1 , 2 or 3 sons with probabilities frac14 each, what is the probability that his surname eventually dies out? Further reading Geoffrey Grimmett & David Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes (Oxford University Press), the section on branching processes. Adam Kucharski, The Rules of Contagion (Profile). Reproduction numbers and outbreaks, for a general reader. David Kendall, “ Branching processes since 1873 ” , Journal of the London Mathematical Society 41 (1966). The history, including Bienaymé.

title: Breaking a Stick
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on The classic broken stick How you break the stick matters The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 1990, Question 16 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/90-s3-q16 The hook Break a stick at two random points. Can the three pieces form a triangle? The famous answer is: with probability frac14 . And if they do, is the triangle acute or obtuse? Obtuse, usually: only about a third of the triangles formed are acute. Questions like these, about random shapes, have entertained probabilists since the nineteenth century, and they are a perfect training ground for working with continuous probability: a random point in a region, a condition defining a sub-region, and an integral for its area. This question takes two different ways of breaking the stick, and in each case asks how likely an obtuse angle is. The answers, 3 - 2sqrt2 and 3 - 42 , are unexpected numbers that come from simple geometry. Before you start Three lengths form a triangle if and only if each is less than the sum of the other two. If the lengths add up to L , what does this say about the longest one? When is the angle opposite side c obtuse? c < a + b with a + b + c = L means c < frac L2 ; so three pieces form a triangle exactly when every piece is shorter than half the total. By the cosine rule, the angle opposite c is obtuse exactly when c^2 > a^2 + b^2 . Working it through Stage 1 One cut, then halve The pieces are X , (1 - X)/(2) , (1 - X)/(2) . The two equal pieces are always less than frac12 , so a triangle forms if and only if X < frac12 . The triangle is isosceles; the equal angles are acute, so it is obtuse only if the angle opposite X is obtuse: X^2 > 2Bigl((1 - X)/(2)Bigr)^2 = ((1 - X)^2)/(2), qquadthat isqquad sqrt2X > 1 - X, quad X > (1)/(1 + sqrt2) = sqrt2 - 1. Given X < frac12 , X is uniform on [0, frac12] , so P(obtuse mid triangle) = (frac12 - (sqrt2 - 1))/(frac12) = 3 - 2sqrt2 approx 0.172. qed Stage 2 The second construction Check the three triangle inequalities for sides x , y and 2 - x - y , for (x, y) in the triangle with vertices (1, 0) , (1, 1) , (0, 1) . The region is \x ≤ 1, y ≤ 1, x + y ≥ 1\ . The inequalities are: x + y ≥ 2 - x - y , i.e. x + y ≥ 1 ; x + (2 - x - y) ≥ y , i.e. y ≤ 1 ; and y + (2 - x - y) ≥ x , i.e. x ≤ 1 . All hold in the region (with equality on its edges, where the triangle is degenerate). ■ The angle at B is opposite the side CA = y . Write the condition y^2 > x^2 + (2 - x - y)^2 as an inequality for y . Expanding, y^2 > x^2 + 4 + x^2 + y^2 - 4x - 4y + 2xy , so 4y - 2xy > 2x^2 - 4x + 4 , that is 2y(2 - x) > 2(x^2 - 2x + 2) . Since 2 - x > 0 , angle ABC obtuse iff y > (x^2 - 2x + 2)/(2 - x). qed Stage 3 The area Divide x^2 - 2x + 2 by 2 - x . Then find the area of the part of the region above the curve, and divide by the region’s area, frac12 . Since x^2 - 2x + 2 = -x(2 - x) + 2 , the curve is y = -x + (2)/(2 - x) . It runs from (0, 1) to (1, 1) , and lies above the line y = 1 - x and below y = 1 for 0 < x < 1 (Figure 12.21.1). The obtuse region lies between the curve and y = 1 , with area int_0^1Bigl(1 + x - (2)/(2 - x)Bigr)dx = 1 + frac12 + bigl[2(2 - x)bigr]_0^1 = frac32 - 22. Dividing by frac12 : P(angle ABC obtuse) = 3 - 42 approx 0.227 . ■ Looking back Translate geometry into inequalities. “Forms a triangle” and “is obtuse” both became inequalities between the lengths. Conditional probability for continuous variables. Given X < frac12 , X was uniform on the smaller interval. Probability as a ratio of areas. For a uniform point in a region, probability is area divided by total area. What’s really going on The classic broken stick Break a stick at two independent uniform points U and V . The pair (U, V) is uniform on the unit square, and the three pieces form a triangle exactly when each is less than frac12 : that cuts out four small triangles of total area frac34 , leaving probability frac14 . Given that a triangle forms, the probability that it is acute is 32 - 2 approx 0.079 out of frac14 , that is about 32\% . The pieces are an example of a uniform random partition , and their joint distribution is the Dirichlet distribution , which appears in Bayesian statistics and in models of how a resource is shared out at random. How you break the stick matters Notice that the two methods in the question give different answers, 3 - 2sqrt2 and 3 - 42 , to similar-sounding questions, and both differ from the classic method. As with Bertrand’s chords ( Section 12.3 ), “random” means nothing until the procedure is specified. Random triangles Problems about random triangles were popular Victorian puzzles. Lewis Carroll’s Pillow Problems (1893) asks for the probability that a triangle chosen “at random” is obtuse, and his answer, like those in this section, depends entirely on the model of randomness he chose. Problems about random triangles have continued to produce surprises: for instance, the probability that three uniformly random points in a square form an obtuse triangle is about 0.725 , computed exactly only in the twentieth century. The thinking skill Geometry of the sample space Represent the random outcome as a point in a region, the event as a sub-region, and compute probability as a ratio of areas (or an integral of a density). At university, this picture is the foundation of multivariate probability, and of the change-of-variables formula, which tells you how densities transform when the coordinates are changed. Try this next The classic. Show that if a stick is broken at two independent uniform points, the probability that the pieces form a triangle is frac14 . Break the longer piece. Break a stick at a uniform point, then break the longer piece at a uniform point. Show that the probability that the three pieces form a triangle is 22 - 1 approx 0.386 . Acute or obtuse. In part (ii), find the probability that the triangle ABC has an obtuse angle at C (opposite AB = 2 - x - y ). Hence find the probability that it has an obtuse angle somewhere. Expected longest piece. For the classic broken stick, show that the expected length of the longest piece is (11)/(18) . Further reading Martin Gardner, The Colossal Book of Mathematics (Norton), which includes the broken-stick problem. Frederick Mosteller, Fifty Challenging Problems in Probability (Dover). Lewis Carroll, Pillow Problems (Dover, with A Tangled Tale ). Victorian puzzles, including random triangles.

title: Buffon's Needle
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Buffon’s noodle Estimating π , and how not to The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP I 1993, Question 16 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/93-s1-q16 The hook Drop a needle onto a floor of parallel floorboards. The chance that it lies across a crack involves π , even though there is no circle anywhere in sight. Count the crossings in many throws and you can estimate π by experiment. This is Buffon’s needle , posed by Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon, in 1733 and solved by him in 1777: the first problem in geometric probability , and the ancestor of every Monte Carlo method. The π comes from the angle: the needle’s direction is uniform on a half-turn, and averaging the length of its “shadow” across the lines over all directions gives a factor frac2π . The question does the calculation with an integral of cos^-1 . Before you start The pin’s centre is at distance x from the nearest line, and the pin makes angle y with the perpendicular to the lines. How far does the pin reach towards the line? Each half of the pin has length a , and its component perpendicular to the lines is acos y . So the pin crosses the nearest line exactly when acos y ≥ x . (Since a < b , it cannot reach any other line.) Working it through Stage 1 The integral With t = cos y , as t goes from 0 to 1 , y = cos^-1t goes from fracπ2 to 0 , and dt = -sin y\,dy . So int_0^1cos^-1t\,dt = int_0^π/2ysin y\,dy = bigl[-ycos ybigr]_0^π/2 + int_0^π/2cos y\,dy = 0 + 1 = 1. qed (Or: the integral is the area between the graph of cos^-1 and the axes, which is the same as the area under y = cos x from 0 to fracπ2 , reflected in y = x .) Stage 2 Given the position For fixed x , which angles y give a crossing? What is their probability? If x ≥ a , the pin cannot reach the line. If x < a , a crossing needs cos y ≥ frac xa , that is y ≤ cos^-1frac xa . Since Y is uniform on [0, fracπ2] , P(cross mid X = x) = (2)/(π)cos^-1frac xa qquad (0 ≤ x < a). qed Stage 3 Averaging over the position X is uniform on [0, b] , with density frac1b , so P(cross) = frac1bint_0^afrac2πcos^-1frac xa\,dx = (2a)/(π b)int_0^1cos^-1t\,dt = (2a)/(π b), qed substituting x = at . With a needle exactly as long as the half-spacing ( a = (b)/(2) , so the needle’s length 2a equals b ), the crossing probability is frac1π . How many throws would you need to estimate π to two decimal places? Looking back Two independent coordinates. The pin’s position and angle were independent and uniform, so the probability was a double integral that could be done one variable at a time. Condition, then average. First fix x and average over the angle; then average over x . A substitution reveals the constant. Scaling x = at reduced the answer to a single universal integral. What’s really going on Buffon’s noodle Here is a way to see the answer with almost no calculation. Bend the needle into any shape, a “noodle”, and let C be the number of times it crosses a line. By linearity of expectation, the expected number of crossings of a curve is the sum over its small pieces, so it is proportional to the length: E(C) = kappa L for some constant kappa . To find kappa , take the noodle to be a circle of diameter equal to the line spacing 2b : it always crosses exactly twice, and its length is 2π b . So kappa · 2π b = 2 , giving kappa = (1)/(π b) . For a straight needle of length 2a < 2b , which crosses at most once, P(cross) = E(C) = (2a)/(π b) . This argument is due to Joseph-Émile Barbier (1860), and it is a gem of probabilistic reasoning: the π comes from the circle that was chosen to calibrate the constant. Estimating π , and how not to If n needles are thrown and c cross, then frac cn approx (2a)/(π b) and π approx (2an)/(bc) . The error shrinks only like (1)/(sqrt n) , so to get π to three decimal places needs about a million throws. In 1901 the Italian mathematician Mario Lazzarini claimed to have obtained π approx (355)/(113) = 3.1415929ldots (correct to six decimal places) from 3408 throws. Statisticians have pointed out that the result is far too good to be true: with 3408 throws and a carefully chosen needle, (355)/(113) arises from exactly 1808 crossings, and stopping the experiment at the right moment would produce it. It is a classic cautionary tale about selective reporting. Buffon Buffon was a naturalist, director of the royal botanical garden in Paris and author of a 36 -volume natural history. He presented the needle problem (and a version with square tiles, the “franc-carreau” game) to the Académie des Sciences in 1733, and published the solution in 1777. His aim was to show that geometry, not just arithmetic, could be used in probability. Integral geometry, the theory of random lines and their intersections with curves and surfaces, grew from it, and is now used in stereology, the science of estimating the size and shape of three-dimensional structures (such as cells in a tissue) from two-dimensional slices. The thinking skill Probability as an integral over a region When an outcome depends on several independent continuous random variables, the probability of an event is the integral of the joint density over the region where the event occurs. At university this becomes the foundation of continuous probability: joint densities, marginal distributions and changes of variable, all of which reappear in Section 12.21 and Section 12.22 . Try this next A long needle. If a > b , the needle may cross more than one line. Show that the expected number of crossings is still (2a)/(π b) . The noodle. Bend a needle of length 2a into a right angle (two arms of length a ). What is the expected number of crossings? Square tiles. A coin of radius r is tossed onto a floor of square tiles of side s > 2r . Find the probability that it lies entirely within one tile. Lazzarini’s needle. With a = frac56b (so that (2a)/(π b) = (5)/(3π) ), show that 3408 throws with 1808 crossings give the estimate π approx (355)/(113) . Further reading Daniel Klain & Gian-Carlo Rota, Introduction to Geometric Probability (Cambridge University Press), which starts from Buffon’s needle. Lee Badger, “ Lazzarini’s lucky approximation of π ” , Mathematics Magazine 67 (1994). The statistics of a suspicious experiment. Paul Nahin, Digital Dice (Princeton University Press). Monte Carlo methods for probability problems.

title: A Distribution With No Mean
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on No mean Where Cauchy variables come from The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 1995, Question 12 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/95-s3-q12 The hook Take the average of many measurements, and the random errors cancel out: the average settles down to the true value. This law of large numbers is the foundation of all statistics. But it has a hidden assumption: the measurements must have a finite mean. This question constructs a perfectly natural random variable, the ratio of two independent standard normal variables, which has no mean at all. Its averages never settle down; in fact the average of a million of them has exactly the same distribution as a single one. This is the Cauchy distribution . Its density looks like a harmless bell, but its tails are so heavy that occasional enormous values dominate any average. The question finds it with a lovely geometric argument: a ratio of coordinates is the slope of a line, and radial symmetry makes the angle of that line uniform. Before you start If (U, V) is a random point whose density depends only on its distance from the origin, what can you say about the angle Theta that the line from the origin to the point makes with an axis? Rotating the plane does not change the density, so every direction is equally likely: the angle Theta is uniform on [0, 2π) . And frac UV depends only on the direction, not the distance. Working it through Stage 1 The joint density Since X and Y are independent, their joint density is the product of their densities: f(x, y) = frac1sqrt2πe^-x^2/2·frac1sqrt2πe^-y^2/2 = (1)/(2π)e^-frac12(x^2 + y^2). It depends on x and y only through x^2 + y^2 , the square of the distance from the origin: the density is constant on circles centred at the origin. That is what “radially symmetrical” means. Stage 2 Using the symmetry frac UV < k happens in two ways, according to the sign of V . How are they related by the rotation through 180^circ , (u, v) mapsto (-u, -v) ? frac UV < k means: either V > 0 and U < kV , or V < 0 and U > kV . The rotation (u, v) mapsto (-u, -v) maps the first region onto the second, and preserves the density. So the two have the same probability, and PBigl(frac UV < kBigr) = 2P(U < kV, V > 0). qed Stage 3 An angle Draw the region \V > 0, U < kV\ in the plane with u horizontal and v vertical. It is a wedge with its vertex at the origin. What is its angle? The region V > 0 is the upper half-plane. The line u = kv through the origin makes angle arctan k with the positive v -axis (towards the positive u side when k > 0 ). The part of the upper half-plane to the left of this line is a wedge of angle fracπ2 + arctan k . By radial symmetry, the probability of a wedge is its angle divided by 2π , so PBigl(frac UV < kBigr) = 2·(fracπ2 + arctan k)/(2π) = frac12 + frac1πarctan k. Differentiating with respect to k gives the density g(k) = (1)/(π(1 + k^2)). qed Looking back Independent normals are radially symmetric. The product of two normal densities depends only on distance. Ratio means direction. frac UV depends only on the angle of the point, which is uniform. Probabilities of wedges. With radial symmetry, the probability of a wedge is proportional to its angle. What’s really going on No mean The mean of the Cauchy distribution would be int_-∞^∞(k)/(π(1 + k^2))\,dk , but int_0^K(k)/(1 + k^2)\,dk = frac12(1 + K^2) → ∞ : the integral does not converge, and the mean does not exist. (Symmetry might suggest the answer is 0 , but the positive and negative parts are both infinite, and ∞ - ∞ has no value.) The variance is infinite too. Worse, the average of n independent Cauchy variables is again Cauchy, with exactly the same distribution. (One way to see this uses the characteristic function E(e^itX) = e^-|t| .) So averaging does not help at all: the average of a million measurements is no more reliable than one. Figure 12.22.1 shows what happens: the running average of normal samples settles down, while that of Cauchy samples lurches about for ever, jolted by occasional huge values. Where Cauchy variables come from Shine a torch, pointing in a uniformly random direction, at a wall: the position of the spot on the wall is Cauchy distributed. In physics the same density, called the Lorentzian , describes the shape of spectral lines and resonance peaks (compare Section 11.1 ). In finance, heavy-tailed distributions like the Cauchy are used to model the occasional crashes that normal models wildly underestimate. The lesson for statistics is serious: methods based on averages and variances fail for heavy-tailed data, and robust methods, such as using the median (which for the Cauchy distribution is perfectly well behaved), are needed. Poisson, Cauchy and a dispute The distribution was studied by Siméon Denis Poisson in 1824, who noticed that it violates the law of large numbers. Augustin-Louis Cauchy met it in 1853 during a public dispute with Irénée-Jules Bienaymé over the method of least squares: Cauchy used it to show that least squares can be a poor method when errors are heavy-tailed. The name stuck to Cauchy, an example of what Stephen Stigler calls “Stigler’s law of eponymy”: no scientific discovery is named after its original discoverer. The thinking skill Check that expectations exist Before using a mean or variance, make sure the integral defining it converges. Symmetry does not make a divergent integral zero. At university, integrability conditions are part of every theorem in probability: the law of large numbers needs a finite mean, the central limit theorem ( Section 12.24 ) a finite variance. The Cauchy distribution is the standard counterexample when they fail. Try this next The torch. A torch at distance 1 from a long straight wall points in a direction making angle Theta with the perpendicular, where Theta is uniform on (-fracπ2, fracπ2) . Show that the spot’s position tanTheta has the Cauchy distribution. The reciprocal. Show that if C is Cauchy, so is frac1C . ( Hint: frac UV and frac VU .) The median works. Show that the median of the Cauchy distribution is 0 and its quartiles are 1 . Radius and angle. For X , Y independent standard normals, show by changing to polar coordinates that R^2 = X^2 + Y^2 is exponential with mean 2 and is independent of the angle. (This is the basis of the Box–Muller method for generating normal random numbers.) Further reading Geoffrey Grimmett & Dominic Welsh, Probability: An Introduction (Oxford University Press), on transformations of random variables. Nassim Nicholas Taleb, The Black Swan (Penguin). Heavy tails and why they matter, for a general reader. Stephen Stigler, The History of Statistics (Harvard University Press). Includes the Cauchy–Bienaymé dispute.

title: The Central Limit Theorem
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on The general theorem How fast? The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2008, Question 12 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/08-s3-q12 The hook Add up many small independent random effects, whatever their individual distribution, and the total follows the bell-shaped normal curve. This is the central limit theorem , perhaps the most important theorem in probability. It explains why heights, measurement errors and exam marks are roughly normal, and why statisticians can say how reliable an average is without knowing anything about the underlying distribution, provided it has a finite variance (compare Section 12.22 ). This question proves the theorem in a special case. A frog makes random jumps with a two-sided exponential distribution, whose density has a sharp peak, nothing like a bell. After many jumps, his total displacement is normal. The tool is the moment generating function , which turns sums of independent variables into products, and products into sums by taking logarithms. A note on the syllabus Moment generating functions were removed from the STEP specification in 2019. The moment generating function of a random variable X is M_X(θ) = E(e^θ X) . Its derivatives at 0 give the moments: M'(0) = E(X) , M''(0) = E(X^2) . For independent X and Y , M_X+Y = M_XM_Y , and M_cX(θ) = M_X(cθ) . If moment generating functions converge, so (in a suitable sense) do the distributions. Before you start The density frac12e^-|x| is symmetric. What does it look like? What is its mean? It is a tent-shaped curve with a sharp peak of height frac12 at 0 , decaying exponentially on both sides (Figure 12.24.1). By symmetry the mean is 0 . Working it through Stage 1 The moment generating function For |θ| < 1 , splitting the integral at 0 , M_X(θ) = frac12int_-∞^0e^(1 + θ)x\,dx + frac12int_0^∞ e^-(1 - θ)x\,dx = frac12Bigl((1)/(1 + θ) + (1)/(1 - θ)Bigr) = (1)/(1 - θ^2). qed Expanding, M_X(θ) = 1 + θ^2 + θ^4 + cdots , so E(X) = 0 and E(X^2) = 2 (the coefficient of (θ^2)/(2!) ). The variance is 2 . Stage 2 The frog’s displacement What is the moment generating function of Y = X_1 + cdots + X_n ? Of Y/sqrt2n ? By independence M_Y(θ) = (1 - θ^2)^-n , and scaling, M_Y/sqrt2n(θ) = M_YBigl(fracθsqrt2nBigr) = Bigl(1 - (θ^2)/(2n)Bigr)^-n. (The scaling by sqrt2n , the standard deviation of Y , makes the variance 1 .) Stage 3 The limit Take the logarithm and use (1 - u) approx -u for small u . lnM_Y/sqrt2n(θ) = -nbigl(1 - (θ^2)/(2n)bigr) = -nbigl(-(θ^2)/(2n) - (θ^4)/(8n^2) - cdotsbigr) → (θ^2)/(2) , so M_Y/sqrt2n(θ) → e^θ^2/2, qed the moment generating function of the standard normal distribution. Stage 4 The frog’s chances For large n , Y is approximately N(0, 2n) . When is P(|Y| ≥ 25) = 0.05 ? For a standard normal Z , P(|Z| ≥ 1.96) = 0.05 . So we need frac25sqrt2n = 1.96 , giving 2n = bigl((25)/(1.96)bigr)^2 approx 162.7 and n approx 81.3 . Since the chance of landing far away grows with n , the least number of jumps giving at least a 5\% chance is about 82 . ■ Looking back Transforms turn sums into products. The moment generating function of a sum of independent variables is the product of theirs. Logarithms turn products into sums. bigl(1 - (θ^2)/(2n)bigr)^-n became a sum whose limit was easy. Standardise. Dividing by the standard deviation sqrt2n kept the variance at 1 , so the limit was neither 0 nor infinite. What’s really going on The general theorem The same argument works for any distribution with mean 0 and finite variance σ^2 (and a moment generating function, though this can be avoided). Then M(θ) = 1 + frac12σ^2θ^2 + o(θ^2) , and Bigl(MBigl((θ)/(σsqrt n)Bigr)Bigr)^n = Bigl(1 + (θ^2)/(2n) + oBigl(frac1nBigr)Bigr)^n → e^θ^2/2. Only the variance survives the limit: the shape of the original distribution is forgotten. That is why the normal distribution is universal. At university the theorem is proved with the characteristic function E(e^iθ X) , which always exists, and the convergence of distributions is made precise by Lévy’s continuity theorem. How fast? The central limit theorem says what happens in the limit, not how quickly. The Berry–Esseen theorem bounds the error by a constant times (E|X|^3)/(σ^3sqrt n) . For a symmetric distribution like the frog’s, the approximation is good after a few dozen jumps. For skewed distributions, or in the extreme tails, it can be poor even for large n : the normal approximation underestimates the chance of very rare events, a fact with consequences for insurance and finance. From de Moivre to Lindeberg De Moivre found the normal approximation to the binomial in 1733 ( Section 12.23 ), and Laplace extended it to sums of more general variables in 1810, coining the idea that errors of measurement are sums of many small effects. Rigorous proofs came much later: Aleksandr Lyapunov in 1901, and Jarl Lindeberg in 1922, who found essentially the weakest conditions under which the theorem holds. The name “central limit theorem” was given by George Pólya in 1920, meaning that the theorem is central to probability theory. The thinking skill Transform, simplify, transform back A hard operation (adding independent random variables, which convolves their densities) becomes an easy one (multiplication) after a transform. Do the work there, and interpret the result. The same strategy underlies generating functions ( Section 9.4 ), Fourier and Laplace transforms in analysis and engineering, and logarithms, which turn multiplication into addition. Try this next Exact for two jumps. Show that Y = X_1 + X_2 has density frac14(1 + |y|)e^-|y| , and check its variance is 4 . Binomial to normal. For X sim B(1, frac12) shifted to have mean 0 (taking values frac12 ), find M_X(θ) = coshfracθ2 , and show that the moment generating function of a standardised sum of n such variables tends to e^θ^2/2 . The frog, exactly. Use a computer (or the exact density for n = 2 as a check) to see how accurate the normal approximation is for n = 82 . Why not Cauchy? The Cauchy distribution ( Section 12.22 ) has no moment generating function. Which step of the argument fails, and what happens to the average of n Cauchy variables? Further reading Geoffrey Grimmett & Dominic Welsh, Probability: An Introduction (Oxford University Press), the chapter on generating functions and limit theorems. Hans Fischer, A History of the Central Limit Theorem (Springer). From Laplace to Lindeberg. David Spiegelhalter, The Art of Statistics (Pelican), on why the normal distribution is everywhere.

title: Precise Conditioning
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on The boy-or-girl puzzle Monty Hall The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP I 2007, Question 13 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/07-s1-q13 The hook “Given that” is the most dangerous phrase in probability. The last four parts of this question sound almost identical: the disc numbered 3 is taken first; the disc numbered 3 is taken; a numbered disc is taken first; a numbered disc is taken. Three of them give the answer frac12 . The fourth does not. The difference is exactly the one behind the famous “boy or girl” puzzle (a family has two children, at least one is a boy; what is the chance both are boys?), which has tripped up generations of students and a fair number of professional mathematicians. The lesson is that a condition is a precise statement about which outcomes remain possible, and the way information was obtained matters as much as the information itself. Before you start Four discs are taken from eleven. Does the order of drawing matter for the event “all four are numbered”? How many equally likely sets of four discs are there? Every set of four discs is equally likely to be the set drawn, so we can ignore order: there are binom114 = 330 equally likely sets. Working it through Stage 1 No condition There are binom54 = 5 sets of four numbered discs, so P(all four numbered) = (5)/(330) = (1)/(66). Stage 2 The 3 comes first Once the disc numbered 3 has been drawn first, what are the remaining three draws? The other three discs form a random set of three from the remaining ten (four numbered, six blank), all binom103 = 120 sets equally likely. So (ii)quad (binom43)/(120) = (4)/(120) = (1)/(30), qquad (iii)quad (binom41binom62)/(120) = (4 × 15)/(120) = frac12, since in (iii) exactly one of the other three must be numbered. Stage 3 The 3 is taken (at some point) Does it matter when the disc numbered 3 was drawn? Given that 3 is among the four, what can you say about the other three? By symmetry, given that the set of four contains the 3, the other three discs are a random set of three from the remaining ten, exactly as in Stage 2. So (iv) is also frac12 . Stage 4 A numbered disc comes first Given that the first disc is numbered (whichever number it is), the other three are again a random set of three from the remaining ten discs, of which four are numbered and six blank. So (v) is frac12 too. Stage 5 A numbered disc is taken Now the condition is “at least one of the four is numbered”. Is that the same as any of the previous conditions? How many of the 330 sets satisfy it? This condition is different: it does not single out any particular disc. Only binom64 = 15 sets have no numbered disc, so 315 satisfy the condition. Of these, binom52binom62 = 10 × 15 = 150 contain exactly two numbered discs. So (vi)quad (150)/(315) = (10)/(21). qed Why is (vi) different from (v)? In (v) we know which disc is numbered (the first), and the other three are unconstrained. In (vi) we only know that some disc is numbered. Sets with three or four numbered discs satisfy “some disc is numbered” in more ways, so they are not under-represented the way they are in (v). Looking back A condition restricts the sample space. P(A mid B) is the proportion of outcomes in B that are also in A . Symmetry saves work. Whether the 3 was drawn first or at some point made no difference, because all positions are alike. “A specific one” is not “at least one”. Conditions that sound alike can select quite different sets of outcomes. What’s really going on The boy-or-girl puzzle Martin Gardner posed this in 1959: Mr Smith has two children, at least one of whom is a boy; what is the probability that both are boys? Listing the equally likely families BB, BG, GB, GG and removing GG leaves three, of which one is BB: the answer is frac13 . But if we know that the elder child is a boy, the answer is frac12 . These are parts (vi) and (v) of our question in miniature. Gardner later admitted that the question as he first posed it was ambiguous: it depends on how we came to know that there is a boy. If we met one of the children at random and he was a boy, the answer is frac12 ; if we asked “do you have at least one son?” and were told yes, it is frac13 . Probability depends on the process that produced the information, not just the information. Monty Hall The same lesson underlies the most argued-about puzzle in probability. On a game show, a car is behind one of three doors. You pick door 1. The host, who knows where the car is, always opens one of the other two doors to reveal a goat, and always offers you the chance to switch; when the car is behind your door, so that he has a choice, he picks between the other two at random. He opens door 3, and offers you door 2. Should you switch? Yes: switching wins with probability frac23 . The host’s choice of door is not random; it depends on where the car is, and that carries information. The precise rules matter. If the host always opens door 3 whenever he can, then seeing door 3 open makes doors 1 and 2 equally likely, and switching wins with probability only frac12 ; yet a contestant who decides in advance always to switch still wins frac23 of the time, because switching wins exactly when the first choice was wrong. When Marilyn vos Savant gave this answer in a magazine column in 1990, she received thousands of letters telling her she was wrong, some from mathematicians. A computer simulation, or a careful list of the equally likely cases, settles it. Bayes and Laplace Conditional probability was put on a systematic footing by Thomas Bayes, whose essay was published after his death in 1763, and by Pierre-Simon Laplace, who in 1774 stated the rule now called Bayes’ theorem in its general form. Andrey Kolmogorov’s axioms of 1933, which every university course now starts from, define P(A mid B) = P(A cap B)/P(B) , and the rest of probability theory is built on that definition. The next section, Section 12.2 , shows what Bayes’ theorem does in practice. The thinking skill Be precise about the condition Before computing a conditional probability, write down exactly which outcomes satisfy the condition. Ask how the information was obtained. At university, conditional probability and conditional expectation are among the most important tools in probability and statistics, and the most frequent source of errors. Writing out the sample space, at least for a small case, is the best defence. Try this next Generalise. With b blank and n numbered discs, and k drawn, show that the answers to (iv) and (v) are always equal, and find when (vi) equals them. Boys born on Tuesday. A family has two children, and at least one is a boy born on a Tuesday. Show that the probability that both are boys is (13)/(27) . (List the 14 × 14 equally likely possibilities, or count cleverly.) Monty Hall. Verify the frac23 by listing outcomes. What if the host does not know where the car is, opens one of the other doors at random, and it happens to show a goat? Two aces. A bridge hand of 13 cards contains at least one ace. What is the probability that it contains at least two? Compare with the probability given that it contains the ace of spades. Further reading Jason Rosenhouse, The Monty Hall Problem (Oxford University Press). The puzzle, its history and its many variations. Geoffrey Grimmett & Dominic Welsh, Probability: An Introduction (Oxford University Press), the chapters on conditional probability. Joseph Blitzstein & Jessica Hwang, Introduction to Probability (CRC Press; free online). Excellent on conditioning, with many paradoxes.

title: The Largest of Many
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on The Gumbel distribution Extreme value theory The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2025, Question 11 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP III paper in OCR’s download of the 2025 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/750486-2025-past-papers.zip The hook How high will the highest flood of the next century be? How long will the longest-lived of a thousand light bulbs last? How fast will the fastest marathon runner in a field of n be? Questions about extremes , the largest or smallest of many random values, matter enormously in engineering, insurance and climate science, and they behave very differently from averages. This question finds the distribution of the largest of n exponential lifetimes. Its typical size grows like n , slowly but without limit. Its spread, however, does not grow at all: the maximum of a thousand lifetimes is just as predictable, give or take, as the maximum of ten. In the limit, the shape of its distribution is the Gumbel distribution , the extreme-value counterpart of the normal curve. Before you start The largest of X_1, ldots, X_n is at most y exactly when what happens? Y ≤ y exactly when every X_i ≤ y . Independence then turns this into a product. Working it through Stage 1 The distribution of the maximum Each X_i has F(y) = 1 - e^-λ y for y ≥ 0 , and by independence G(y) = P(X_1 ≤ y, ldots, X_n ≤ y) = bigl(1 - e^-λ ybigr)^n. qed Stage 2 The quantiles Solve G(L) = α for L . Then solve G(U) = 1 - α . bigl(1 - e^-λ Lbigr)^n = α gives e^-λ L = 1 - α^1/n , so L(α) = -frac1λbigl(1 - α^1/nbigr), qquad U(α) = -frac1λbigl(1 - (1 - α)^1/nbigr). qed Stage 3 Large n Write α^1/n = e^(α)/n . For large n the exponent is small. What is 1 - α^1/n approximately? α^1/n = e^(α)/n approx 1 + (α)/(n) , so 1 - α^1/n approx (-α)/(n) = ((1/α))/(n) . Hence λ L(α) approx -((1/α))/(n) = n - Bigl(frac1αBigr). qed Similarly, λ U(α) approx n - bigl((1)/(1 - α)bigr) . Stage 4 Growth and spread The median is L(frac12) , with λ L(frac12) approx n - 2 → ∞ . But λbigl(U(α) - L(α)bigr) approx Bigl(frac1αBigr) - Bigl((1)/(1 - α)Bigr), in which the n terms have cancelled: the width does not depend on n . ■ Stage 5 A 90\% interval Take α = 0.05 . What are frac1α = 20 and (1)/(0.95) , approximately? With α = 0.05 , 20 approx 3 , so frac1α approx 3 . And (1)/(0.95) = -(1 - 0.05) approx 0.05 = (1)/(20) , so (1)/(1 - α) approx (1)/(20) approx -3 . The width is therefore about frac1λ(3 + 3) approx (4.1)/(λ) , and Y lies in [L(0.05), U(0.05)] , an interval of width about 4λ^-1 , with probability 0.9 . ■ Looking back The maximum is at most y when all are. Independence made the distribution of the maximum a power. Quantiles by inversion. Solving G(y) = α gave exact formulas for the interval ends. Approximate, then compare. The approximations for L and U both contained n , which cancelled in the width. What’s really going on The Gumbel distribution Since P(λ Y - n ≤ x) = bigl(1 - frace^-xnbigr)^n → exp(-e^-x) , the shifted maximum λ Y - n has, in the limit, the Gumbel distribution with distribution function exp(-e^-x) . Its mean is Euler’s constant γ approx 0.577 . You met it already: the time to collect all n coupons ( Section 9.11 ) is the maximum of n (nearly independent) waiting times, which is why it is about n n + γ n , with Gumbel fluctuations of order n . Extreme value theory A remarkable theorem of Fisher, Tippett and Gnedenko (1928–1943) says that, suitably shifted and scaled, the maximum of many independent identically distributed variables can have only three possible limiting shapes: Gumbel (for light tails, like the exponential or normal), Fréchet (for heavy tails, like the Cauchy) and Weibull (for variables with a hard upper limit). It is the extreme-value analogue of the central limit theorem ( Section 12.24 ). Engineers use it to design flood defences and offshore platforms for the “hundred-year wave”, insurers to price catastrophe cover, and climate scientists to estimate how heatwaves are changing. Gumbel and the floods Emil Julius Gumbel, a German statistician and an outspoken opponent of the Nazis, who was forced out of his university post in 1932 and eventually fled to the United States, applied extreme value theory to the flooding of rivers in the 1930s and 1940s. His book Statistics of Extremes (1958) made the subject a practical tool. The Dutch Delta Works, built after the North Sea flood of 1953 to protect the Netherlands, were designed using extreme value statistics to withstand a storm surge expected about once in 10\,000 years. The thinking skill Distributions of maxima and minima For the maximum of independent variables, P(max ≤ y) = prodP(X_i ≤ y) ; for the minimum, P(min > y) = prodP(X_i > y) . This one idea handles the nearest supermarket ( Section 12.19 ), the first bus ( Section 12.18 ) and the longest-lived bulb. At university it is the starting point of order statistics and extreme value theory. Try this next The expected maximum. Show that E(Y) = frac1λbigl(1 + frac12 + cdots + frac1nbigr) . ( Hint: by memorylessness, after the first of the n lifetimes ends, the remaining n - 1 start afresh.) The minimum. Show that the smallest of X_1, ldots, X_n is exponential with parameter nλ . The median exactly. Find the exact median of Y and compare it with the approximation frac1λ( n - 2) for n = 10 . Uniform maxima. If X_1, ldots, X_n are uniform on [0, 1] , find the distribution of their maximum M , and show that n(1 - M) is approximately exponential for large n . Which of the three extreme-value shapes is this? Further reading Stuart Coles, An Introduction to Statistical Modeling of Extreme Values (Springer). The standard introduction, with real data on floods and sea levels. Emil Julius Gumbel, Statistics of Extremes (Dover). The classic. David Spiegelhalter, The Art of Uncertainty (Pelican), on rare events and how to think about them.

title: Probability
headings: Why probability matters What you will meet at university The questions that run through this chapter Ideas in this chapter How to read this chapter
text: Chapter 12 · Introduction Reasoning About Chance Probability theory is nothing but common sense reduced to calculation. — Pierre-Simon Laplace, Théorie analytique des probabilités (1812) Laplace’s famous remark is half true. Probability is common sense made precise; but, as this chapter shows again and again, common sense left to itself goes wrong. People think a positive test for a rare disease means you probably have it; that the second passenger to board a plane is as badly off as the last; that a sequence of coin tosses cannot beat another sequence of the same length; that the average of many measurements always settles down. All of these are false, and in each case a short calculation reveals the truth and, better still, the reason for it. Probability began in the seventeenth century with questions about gambling, in the letters between Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat. It became a branch of rigorous mathematics only in 1933, when Andrey Kolmogorov set out its axioms. In between, and since, it has grown into one of the most widely used parts of mathematics. Why probability matters Every field that deals with uncertainty uses probability: medicine (diagnostic tests and clinical trials), law (the weight of evidence), finance (risk and insurance), engineering (reliability and floods), computer science (randomised algorithms, cryptography, machine learning), physics (quantum mechanics and statistical mechanics) and biology (genetics and epidemics). Modern artificial intelligence is, in large part, applied probability: a language model predicts the probability of the next word. And the ability to reason correctly about risk, chance and evidence is one of the most valuable skills any educated person can have. What you will meet at university First-year probability covers the axioms, conditional probability and Bayes’ theorem, independence, discrete and continuous random variables, expectation and variance, generating functions, and the two great limit theorems: the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem. Later courses study random processes (Markov chains, Poisson processes, random walks, branching processes), measure-theoretic probability (which puts limits and continuous distributions on a firm footing) and martingales, and connect probability with statistics, analysis, combinatorics and physics. The questions that run through this chapter Three big questions What exactly is the question? What is the random experiment, what is being conditioned on, and what does “at random” mean? What is the clever way in? When can symmetry, indicators, conditioning or a well-chosen state replace a long calculation? What happens in the long run? How do random processes behave over time, and what do sums, averages and maxima of many random quantities look like? The chapter has five parts. Thinking clearly ( Section 12.1 to Section 12.4 ) deals with the traps: conditioning, base rates, the meaning of “random” and the meaning of independence. Symmetry and clever arguments ( Section 12.5 to Section 12.9 ) collects problems with beautiful short solutions. Expectation, games and stopping ( Section 12.10 to Section 12.14 ) turns to averages and decisions: when to stop, whom to shoot at, how to randomise. Random processes ( Section 12.15 to Section 12.19 ) follows randomness through time and space. And Limits and continuous probability ( Section 12.20 to Section 12.25 ) ends with geometric probability and the great limit theorems. Ideas in this chapter § Topic Idea 12.1 Conditioning “A specific one” versus “at least one” 12.2 Bayes’ theorem Base rates and natural frequencies 12.3 Bertrand’s paradox “Random” needs a definition 12.4 Independence Pairwise is not mutual 12.5 The airline seat Symmetry between two seats 12.6 One more coin Complementary symmetric events 12.7 Tournaments Counting matches and pairs 12.8 Penney’s game First-step analysis; non-transitivity 12.9 Fair coins Extracting fairness from bias 12.10 Random loops A memoryless sum of indicators 12.11 Cups and e Factorials and the exponential series 12.12 Optimal stopping The frac1e rule 12.13 The truel Strategic weakness 12.14 Game theory Randomised strategies; minimax 12.15 Branching processes Extinction as a fixed point 12.16 Markov chains Stationary distributions; reversal 12.17 Banach’s matchboxes The negative binomial 12.18 The exponential Memorylessness and independence 12.19 Spatial randomness Nearest neighbours; Rayleigh 12.20 Buffon’s needle Geometric probability and π 12.21 Random triangles Probability as area 12.22 The Cauchy distribution A distribution with no mean 12.23 Stirling’s formula Factorials from the normal curve 12.24 Central limit theorem Moment generating functions 12.25 Extreme values The Gumbel distribution One section, Section 12.24 , uses moment generating functions, which were removed from the STEP specification in 2019; it explains what it needs. How to read this chapter When a probability question seems confusing, write down the sample space for a small case and count. When an answer comes out suspiciously simple, look for the symmetry that explains it. And when your intuition and the calculation disagree, trust the calculation, then find out why your intuition was wrong: that is where the learning happens.

title: Who Meets Whom in a Knockout
meta: Chapter 12 · STEP II Specimen paper Question 16
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Expected counts Seeded tournaments The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II Specimen paper, Question 16 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/spec-s2-q16 The hook At Wimbledon, 128 players enter the draw. Pick two at random: what is the chance that they meet at some point? You might try to add up the probabilities of meeting in each round, each a product of chances of surviving and being drawn together. That works, but there is a much better way. Count the matches: every match is between a pair of players, and there are exactly 127 matches. By symmetry, every pair of players is equally likely to be any of them. So the chance is 127 divided by the number of pairs. This question is a perfect example of solving a probability problem by counting the right thing. The answer, frac12^n-1 , comes out in one line. Before you start How many matches are played in a knockout tournament with 2^n players? (Each match eliminates one player.) Each match eliminates exactly one player, and all but one player is eliminated, so there are 2^n - 1 matches. Working it through Stage 1 The first round Call the two chosen players X and Y . In the first round, X ’s opponent is equally likely to be any of the other 2^n - 1 players, so P(meet in round 1) = (1)/(2^n - 1). Stage 2 The key symmetry The draw in each round is random and every match is a fair coin toss. Does the process treat any pair of players differently from any other? No. Relabelling the players does not change any probability, since draws are random and every match is 50 – 50 . So any particular match (say, the final) is equally likely to be between any of the binom2^n2 pairs. Stage 3 The final The final is one specific match, so the probability that it is between X and Y is frac1binom2^n2 = (2)/(2^n(2^n - 1)). (Check: both must reach the final, which needs them in different halves and each to win n - 1 matches.) Stage 4 At any stage X and Y can meet at most once. How does that let you add probabilities over matches? Let I_m be 1 if match m is between X and Y . Each of the 2^n - 1 matches has P(I_m = 1) = binom2^n2^-1 , and the events are mutually exclusive (they cannot meet twice), so P(meet) = frac2^n - 1binom2^n2 = (2(2^n - 1))/(2^n(2^n - 1)) = frac12^n-1. qed For Wimbledon, with n = 7 , the probability that two given players meet is (1)/(64) . As a check, the first round contains 2^n-1 of the 2^n - 1 matches, giving frac2^n-1binom2^n2 = (1)/(2^n - 1) , agreeing with Stage 1. Looking back Count the matches. The number of matches, 2^n - 1 , was the key fact. Symmetry among pairs. Every pair of players is equally likely to contest any particular match. Linearity over matches. Since two players meet at most once, the probability of meeting is the expected number of meetings, a sum over matches. What’s really going on Expected counts The argument in Stage 4 is really an expectation calculation: the number of times X and Y meet is a sum of indicators, one per match, and its expectation (which equals the probability of meeting, since it is 0 or 1 ) is the sum of the indicators’ expectations. This is linearity of expectation, used in Section 9.11 and Section 12.4 . Its great advantage is that it ignores all the complicated dependence between the rounds. Seeded tournaments Real tournaments are seeded : the strongest players are placed so that they cannot meet until the late rounds. And real matches are not 50 – 50 . Both destroy the symmetry, and calculating the chance that two given players meet becomes a genuine computation. Statisticians who model sport use exactly such calculations, with each match’s probability estimated from players’ ratings, to forecast tournaments. The symmetric case is the baseline against which the real effects are measured. The thinking skill Count the right thing A probability can often be found as (number of favourable objects) div (number of equally likely objects), once the right objects are chosen. Here they were matches and pairs. Choosing what to count is the art of combinatorial probability. At university the same idea appears as double counting ( Section 7.9 ) and in the probabilistic method, where the expected number of some structure proves that it exists. Try this next Round by round. Show directly that the probability that X and Y meet in round k is frac2^n-kbinom2^n2 , and check that these add up to frac12^n-1 . A fixed bracket. If instead the bracket is fixed in advance (as in the figure) but all players are placed in it at random, does the answer change? A strong player. Suppose player X wins every match. What is now the probability that X meets Y ? A league. In a league of 2n teams where every pair meets once, how many matches are there? What is the analogous “probability of meeting”? Further reading Frederick Mosteller, Fifty Challenging Problems in Probability (Dover), which includes tournament problems. David Spiegelhalter, The Art of Statistics (Pelican), on modelling and forecasting. Joseph Blitzstein & Jessica Hwang, Introduction to Probability (CRC Press; free online), on indicators and symmetry.

title: Tying Loose Ends
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Logarithmic growth Cycles of random permutations The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2008, Question 13 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/08-s3-q13 The hook Put a hundred pieces of string in a bag, so that only their ends poke out. Pick two ends at random and tie them; repeat until no loose ends are left. You end up with a tangle of loops. How many? A hundred strings could in principle make a hundred little rings, or one enormous loop. Remarkably, the expected number is only about 3.3 ; with forty thousand strings, it is still only about 6 . The key observation makes the problem almost trivial: after each knot, the box simply contains one fewer piece of string, whatever happened. The process “forgets” its history, and the number of rings becomes a sum of independent coin tosses with changing probabilities. Before you start After tying two ends together, how many pieces of string are left (counting a ring as no longer a “piece”)? Does it depend on whether a ring was made? If the two ends belong to the same string, it becomes a ring and n - 1 pieces remain. If they belong to different strings, those two become one longer piece, and again n - 1 pieces remain. Either way, we are left with n - 1 pieces of string, each with two ends. Working it through Stage 1 The first knot There are 2n ends. Choose one; its partner is equally likely to be any of the other 2n - 1 ends, and exactly one of these belongs to the same string. So the first knot makes a ring with probability (1)/(2n - 1) , and the expected number of rings created at the first step is (1)/(2n - 1) . Stage 2 All the knots By the observation above, what is the situation before the second knot? The third? Let I_k indicate a ring at the knot made when k pieces remain. What are the E(I_k) ? Before each knot the box contains k pieces for k = n, n - 1, ldots, 1 , and the knot makes a ring with probability (1)/(2k - 1) . (The last knot, with one piece left, always makes a ring.) The total number of rings is R = I_n + I_n-1 + cdots + I_1 , so E(R) = sum_k=1^n(1)/(2k - 1) = 1 + frac13 + frac15 + cdots + (1)/(2n - 1). qed Stage 3 The variance Are the indicators I_k independent? (Does the probability of a ring at one step depend on what happened earlier?) At each step, the probability of a ring is (1)/(2k - 1) whatever happened before, because the configuration is always “ k pieces of string”. So the I_k are independent, and variances add: Var(R) = sum_k=1^n(1)/(2k - 1)Bigl(1 - (1)/(2k - 1)Bigr) = sum_k=1^n(2k - 2)/((2k - 1)^2). qed Stage 4 Forty thousand strings Write the sum of the reciprocals of the odd numbers up to 2n - 1 using harmonic numbers. The sum of reciprocals of all numbers up to 2n , minus those of the even numbers, is sum_k=1^n(1)/(2k - 1) = H_2n - tfrac12H_n approx (2n) - tfrac12 n = tfrac12(4n).
