For n = 40\,000 , 4n = 160\,000 = 20^4 , so E(R) approx frac12 · 420 approx 6 . ■ (The exact value is 6.28 ; the difference comes from Euler’s constant, as H_n approx n + 0.577 .) Looking back Find what the process forgets. After each knot the box was “ k pieces of string”, regardless of history. Indicators again. The number of rings was a sum of indicators, one per knot. Independence gives the variance. Because each step’s probability did not depend on the past, the indicators were independent. What’s really going on Logarithmic growth The expected number of rings grows like frac12 n , and the variance is close to the mean (both are sums of small probabilities). By the central limit theorem ( Section 12.24 ), the number of rings is approximately normal for large n , with mean and variance about frac12(4n) . With 40\,000 strings, you will usually get between 2 and 11 rings. Cycles of random permutations The same logarithm appears in the number of cycles of a random permutation of n objects: on average H_n approx n (the strings problem is a close relative, with frac12 n ). Random permutations have few cycles: one giant cycle usually contains most of the elements, and the fraction of elements in the largest cycle averages about 0.62 , the Golomb–Dickman constant. Tangling strings at random behaves the same way: most of the string ends up in one or two long loops. These facts are part of the study of random combinatorial structures , which has connections to number theory (the prime factors of a random integer behave like the cycles of a random permutation). Random knots and polymers The string-tying problem is a toy model for physical systems. Long polymer molecules in a solution join end to end to form rings and chains, and the statistics of loop formation follow similar rules. In knot theory, mathematicians ask the harder question of how likely a random closed loop is to be knotted; for long random loops, the answer tends to 1 , a result proved by De Witt Sumners and Stuart Whittington in 1988. The thinking skill Find the memoryless structure If, after each step, the system is in a state that depends only on the number of steps taken, then the steps behave independently, and expectations and variances simply add. This is the idea behind the coupon collector ( Section 9.11 ), where each stage is a fresh geometric wait, and it reappears in the theory of Markov chains, where only the current state matters. Try this next Small cases. For n = 2 , list the possibilities and check that the expected number of rings is frac43 . One big loop. Show that the probability that the process ends with a single loop containing all the strings is prod_k=2^nbigl(1 - (1)/(2k - 1)bigr) , and that this is approximately sqrt(π)/(4n) for large n . ( Hint: relate the product to binom2nn .) Cycles of permutations. Show that the expected number of cycles of a random permutation of n objects is H_n , by building the permutation one element at a time (the “Chinese restaurant” construction). The variance. Show that Var(R) = E(R) - sum_k=1^n(1)/((2k - 1)^2) , and that the subtracted sum tends to (π^2)/(8) . Further reading Peter Winkler, Mathematical Puzzles: A Connoisseur’s Collection (A K Peters), which includes the string-tying puzzle. Richard Arratia, Andrew Barbour & Simon Tavaré, Logarithmic Combinatorial Structures (European Mathematical Society). Cycles, primes and random structures, for later. Colin Adams, The Knot Book (American Mathematical Society). An introduction to knot theory, including random knots.

title: Markov Chains Forwards and Backwards
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Convergence to equilibrium Reversibility The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 1996, Question 12 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/96-s3-q12 The hook Professor Ecks’s theorems follow a pattern: what she proves next depends only on what she proved last. A process whose future depends on the present but not on the past is a Markov chain , and Markov chains are everywhere: in weather models, in the board game Snakes and Ladders, in models of DNA, in Google’s original PageRank algorithm, and in the methods statisticians use to simulate complicated probability distributions. This question finds the long-run mix of theorem types, the stationary distribution : in the long run, one in six of her theorems is new and correct, and half are false. Then it runs the chain backwards in time, and asks: given today’s theorem, what was yesterday’s? Before you start What does the condition “each row adds up to 1 ” mean? Do the columns add up to 1 ? Row i lists the probabilities of the next type, given that the current type is i ; one of the three must occur, so each row adds to 1 . The columns need not: the second column adds to exactly 1 , but the first adds to 0.6 and the third to 1.4 . Working it through Stage 1 One step By the law of total probability, conditioning on the type i of the current theorem, b_j = sum_iP(current i)\,P(next j mid current i) = a_1p_1j + a_2p_2j + a_3p_3j. qed In matrix terms, the row vector mathbf b = mathbf aP . Stage 2 The stationary distribution We want mathbf a = mathbf aP with a_1 + a_2 + a_3 = 1 . Write out the equations. Which are the simplest? The equations are beginaligned a_1 &= 0.3a_1 + 0.2a_2 + 0.1a_3, \\ a_2 &= 0.3a_1 + 0.4a_2 + 0.3a_3, \\ a_3 &= 0.4a_1 + 0.4a_2 + 0.6a_3. endaligned (They are not independent: adding them gives a_1 + a_2 + a_3 on both sides.) The second gives 0.6a_2 = 0.3(a_1 + a_3) = 0.3(1 - a_2) , so a_2 = frac13 . The first gives 7a_1 = 2a_2 + a_3 = frac23 + a_3 , and a_1 + a_3 = frac23 , so 8a_1 = frac43 , a_1 = frac16 , a_3 = frac12 : (a_1, a_2, a_3) = bigl(tfrac16, tfrac13, tfrac12bigr). qed Stage 3 Running the chain backwards q_ij = P(previous i mid current j) . Use Bayes’ theorem, with the stationary distribution for both the previous and the current theorem. By Bayes’ theorem, q_ij = (P(previous i)\,P(current j mid previous i))/(P(current j)) = fraca_ip_ija_j. For example q_11 = (frac16 × 0.3)/(frac16) = 0.3 and q_21 = (frac13 × 0.2)/(frac16) = 0.4 . Altogether (with i labelling rows and j columns): (q_ij) = beginpmatrix 0.3 & 0.15 & (2)/(15) \\ 0.4 & 0.4 & (4)/(15) \\ 0.3 & 0.45 & 0.6 endpmatrix. qed Each column now adds to 1 , since column j lists the possible types of the previous theorem. Looking back The law of total probability, as a matrix. One step of the chain is multiplication of a row vector by the matrix P . Stationarity is an eigenvector. mathbf a = mathbf aP says that mathbf a is a left eigenvector of P with eigenvalue 1 . Reverse with Bayes. The backwards probabilities are another stochastic matrix, built from the forwards one and the stationary distribution. What’s really going on Convergence to equilibrium Start Professor Ecks with any theorem; after n more, the distribution of the type is mathbf a_0P^n . For a chain like this one, in which every type can follow every other, P^n converges to a matrix with every row equal to the stationary distribution (frac16, frac13, frac12) , whatever the starting point. The speed of convergence is governed by the other eigenvalues of P (here 0.2 and 0.1 ), which shrink geometrically: after just a few theorems, her past is forgotten. This ergodic theorem for Markov chains is a central result of a second-year probability course, and it is what makes Markov chain Monte Carlo methods work: to sample from a complicated distribution, design a Markov chain with that stationary distribution, and run it for a long time. Reversibility The backwards chain (q_ij) is different from the forwards chain (p_ij) : you can tell the direction of time from a long record of her theorems. Chains whose backwards and forwards versions agree, a_ip_ij = a_jp_ji for all i , j , are called reversible ; they include random walks on networks and the models of physical systems in thermal equilibrium. Reversibility is a powerful property, because it makes the stationary distribution easy to find. Markov and Pushkin Andrey Markov introduced his chains in 1906, partly to show that the law of large numbers does not require independence, in a dispute with the mathematician Pavel Nekrasov, who had claimed it did. In 1913 Markov applied his idea to the first 20\,000 letters of Pushkin’s verse novel Eugene Onegin , classifying each as a vowel or consonant and showing that the type of each letter depends on the type of the previous one in a way well described by a two-state chain. It was the first statistical analysis of a text, and the ancestor of every predictive-text system. The thinking skill Probabilities as vectors, transitions as matrices When a system moves between states with fixed probabilities, write the distribution as a vector and the transitions as a matrix. Then long-run behaviour becomes a question about eigenvectors. At university, this brings the linear algebra of Chapter 7 into probability. The Perron–Frobenius theorem guarantees the stationary distribution, and the other eigenvalues measure how quickly it is reached. Try this next A rabbit warren. Try STEP III 2003, Question 13 : a random walk on the corners of a square with an exit at each corner, solved by first-step equations. Two steps. If Professor Ecks’s last theorem was new and correct, find the probabilities of the three types for the theorem after next. Eigenvalues. Show that the eigenvalues of P are 1 , 0.2 and 0.1 . Reversible? Check whether a_ip_ij = a_jp_ji for Professor Ecks’s chain. What does the answer tell you? Further reading James Norris, Markov Chains (Cambridge University Press). The standard undergraduate text. Olle Häggström, Finite Markov Chains and Algorithmic Applications (Cambridge University Press). Short, and good on Markov chain Monte Carlo. Brian Hayes, “ First links in the Markov chain ” , American Scientist 101 (2013). Markov’s Pushkin analysis, retold.

title: Banach's Matchboxes
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Banach’s matchboxes The negative binomial distribution The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 1992, Question 16 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/92-s2-q16 The hook The mathematician Stefan Banach, so the story goes, was a heavy smoker who kept a box of matches in each pocket. Each time he wanted a match he chose a pocket at random. One day he found a box empty. How many matches were left in the other box? This is Banach’s matchbox problem , devised by Hugo Steinhaus in Banach’s honour, and this question is the taxi driver’s version with sweets. The subtlety is in the word “discovers”. The driver does not notice that a packet is empty when she takes its last sweet, only when she next reaches for it. So the event is: she reaches for a toffee, and all n toffees have already gone. Counting the ways this can happen on the N th reach is a neat exercise in the binomial distribution, and the answer to Banach’s problem has a surprising feature: the most likely number of matches left in the other box is 0 (tied with 1 ). Before you start For the driver to discover on the N th reach that the toffees have run out, what must the N th reach be? What must the previous N - 1 reaches contain? The N th reach must be for a toffee, and the previous N - 1 reaches must have taken exactly n toffees (all of them) and N - 1 - n mints. Also, she must not have discovered the mints empty earlier. Working it through Stage 1 Discovering the toffees are gone In what order can the first N - 1 reaches occur? What condition on N - 1 - n ensures she never found the mint packet empty? The n toffee-reaches can be any n of the first N - 1 reaches. She never reached for a mint after the mints were gone provided she took at most m mints: N - 1 - n ≤ m . So, for n + 1 ≤ N ≤ n + m + 1 , P(T_N) = binomN - 1np^n+1q^N-1-n, where T_N is the event “on the N th reach she discovers the toffees are gone” (the factor p^n+1 includes the N th reach itself). Stage 2 Discovering the mints are gone By the same argument with the roles swapped, for m + 1 ≤ N ≤ n + m + 1 , P(M_N) = binomN - 1mq^m+1p^N-1-m. Stage 3 The conditional probability We are told that a discovery happens on the N th reach. What is the probability that it was a toffee? The events T_N and M_N are exclusive, so P(toffee mid discovery at N) = fracbinomN-1np^n+1q^N-1-nbinomN-1np^n+1q^N-1-n + binomN-1mq^m+1p^N-1-m, where a binomial coefficient is taken to be 0 outside the ranges above. (If N ≤ m , only the toffees can have run out, and the probability is 1 ; similarly it is 0 if N ≤ n but N > m .) ■ Check the formula when n = m and p = q = frac12 . By symmetry the answer should be frac12 for every possible N . Is it? Looking back Read the event precisely. “Discovers” meant reaching for an empty packet, not taking the last sweet. Fix the last step, count the rest. The N th reach was fixed; the first N - 1 could be in any order, giving a binomial coefficient. Check the boundaries. The constraints N - 1 - n ≤ m and N - 1 - m ≤ n excluded impossible histories. What’s really going on Banach’s matchboxes In Banach’s version, each box starts with n matches and each pocket is equally likely. When he first finds a box empty, let K be the number of matches in the other box. For K = k , he must have taken n from the empty box and n - k from the other, in any order, before reaching for the empty box once more; and either box could be the empty one: P(K = k) = 2binom2n - knBigl(frac12Bigr)^2n - k + 1 = binom2n - knBigl(frac12Bigr)^2n - k. These probabilities decrease with k , except that P(K = 0) = P(K = 1) (Figure 12.17.1). The expected number left is about 2sqrtn/π - 1 : with 50 matches in each box, about 7 . The sqrt n is the typical size of the imbalance between the two boxes after 2n random choices, the same square-root law as in the birthday problem ( Section 9.9 ) and the random walk. The negative binomial distribution The number of trials needed to obtain the r th success in independent trials, each succeeding with probability p , has the negative binomial distribution : P(N = k) = binomk - 1r - 1p^rq^k-r . The taxi driver’s problem is a race between two negative binomial processes (the toffees and the mints), each needing one more “success” than it has sweets. The negative binomial appears in insurance (numbers of claims), ecology (clustered counts of animals) and genetics, often as a more flexible alternative to the Poisson distribution. Banach and the Scottish Café Stefan Banach, one of the founders of functional analysis, did much of his mathematics in the Scottish Café in Lwów (now Lviv), where he and his colleagues wrote problems in a notebook kept by the waiter, the Scottish Book , with prizes ranging from a beer to a live goose. Hugo Steinhaus, Banach’s mentor, devised the matchbox problem for a speech honouring Banach’s smoking. The problem was first analysed in print by William Feller in his celebrated probability textbook of 1950. The thinking skill Fix the final event, count the paths to it To find the probability that a process ends in a particular way at a particular time, fix what happens at the last step and count the histories that lead there. At university this is the basis of the negative binomial distribution, of first-passage times for random walks, and of the reflection principle in Section 9.10 . Try this next Small case. With n = m = 1 and p = frac12 , list the possible sequences and find the distribution of N . Banach’s formula. Verify that sum_k=0^nbinom2n - kn2^-(2n-k) = 1 for n = 1 and n = 2 . Equal tops. Show that P(K = 0) = P(K = 1) for every n in Banach’s problem. Which runs out first? For the taxi driver, find the probability that the toffees are the first packet to be discovered empty (at any time), when n = m = 2 and p = frac23 . Further reading William Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications , Vol. 1 (Wiley), Chapter VI, which introduced Banach’s problem to the world. R. Daniel Mauldin (ed.), The Scottish Book (Birkhäuser). The problems from the Scottish Café, with commentary. Geoffrey Grimmett & Dominic Welsh, Probability: An Introduction (Oxford University Press), on the negative binomial distribution.

title: Memorylessness
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Why the exponential is special Minima and the waiting-time paradox The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2021, Question 11 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP III paper in OCR’s download of the 2021 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/696588-2021-past-papers.zip The hook A radioactive atom has been sitting in a laboratory for a million years without decaying. Is it “due” to decay soon? No: its chance of decaying in the next second is exactly the same as that of a freshly made atom. Radioactive atoms do not age. The waiting time until decay has the exponential distribution , and its defining property is that it has no memory. This question shows the memorylessness in a striking form. Split an exponential waiting time into its whole number of units and its fractional part. These two pieces turn out to be independent : knowing how many whole hours you waited tells you nothing about the minutes. The question also explains, in the exercises, why your wait for a bus can seem longer than the gap between buses. Before you start What is P(X > x) for x ≥ 0 ? What is P(X > s + t mid X > s) ? P(X > x) = int_x^∞λ e^-λ u\,du = e^-λ x . Then P(X > s + t mid X > s) = frace^-λ(s + t)e^-λ s = e^-λ t = P(X > t) : having already waited s , the remaining wait has the same distribution as a fresh one. This is the memoryless property . Working it through Stage 1 The whole part Y = n exactly when n ≤ X < n + 1 : P(Y = n) = e^-λ n - e^-λ(n + 1) = (1 - e^-λ)e^-nλ. qed So Y has a geometric distribution: each whole unit is “survived” with probability e^-λ . Stage 2 The fractional part Z < z means X lies in one of the intervals [n, n + z) . Add up their probabilities. P(Z < z) = sum_n ≥ 0bigl(e^-λ n - e^-λ(n + z)bigr) = (1 - e^-λ z)sum_n ≥ 0e^-λ n = frac1 - e^-λ z1 - e^-λ. qed Stage 3 The mean of Z For a random variable on [0, 1] , E(Z) = int_0^1P(Z > z)\,dz . Use it. With c = 1 - e^-λ , P(Z > z) = 1 - frac1 - e^-λ zc , so E(Z) = 1 - frac1cBigl(1 - frac1 - e^-λλBigr) = 1 - frac1c + frac1λ = frac1λ - frace^-λ1 - e^-λ = frac1λ - (1)/(e^λ - 1). qed (For small λ , long waits, this tends to frac12 : the fractional part is nearly uniform. For large λ it is close to frac1λ , because X is almost always less than 1 .) Stage 4 Independence P(Y = n, z_1 < Z < z_2) = P(n + z_1 < X < n + z_2) = e^-λ nbigl(e^-λ z_1 - e^-λ z_2bigr). Compare with P(Y = n)\,P(z_1 < Z < z_2) , using parts (i) and (ii). From (i) and (ii), P(Y = n)P(z_1 < Z < z_2) = (1 - e^-λ)e^-nλ·frace^-λ z_1 - e^-λ z_21 - e^-λ , which is the same. So Y and Z are independent. ■ Looking back Sum over pieces. Both the distribution of Z and the joint probabilities came from adding probabilities over the intervals [n, n + 1) . The tail formula. E(Z) = intP(Z > z)\,dz avoided finding the density. Factorisation means independence. The joint probability split into a function of n times a function of z_1 , z_2 . What’s really going on Why the exponential is special The independence of Y and Z comes straight from e^-λ(n + z) = e^-λ ne^-λ z , and that is the memoryless property in disguise. In fact the exponential is the only continuous distribution without memory: if P(X > s + t) = P(X > s)P(X > t) for all s, t ≥ 0 , then g(t) = lnP(X > t) satisfies g(s + t) = g(s) + g(t) , and (for a monotonic g ) this forces g(t) = -λ t . That is why the exponential models waiting times for events that happen “at random”, with no build-up: radioactive decays, the arrival of customers, the failure of electronic components that do not wear out. Minima and the waiting-time paradox If X_1 and X_2 are independent exponentials with rates λ_1 and λ_2 , then P(min > x) = e^-λ_1xe^-λ_2x , so the minimum is exponential with rate λ_1 + λ_2 . Waiting for the first of two independent random events is like waiting for one event at the combined rate (STEP III 2002 Q13, in the exercises). Memorylessness also explains the waiting-time paradox : if buses arrive at random with an average gap of 10 minutes, then a passenger arriving at a random time waits on average 10 minutes, not 5 , because the remaining wait is memoryless; and the gap they arrive in is on average 20 minutes long, since long gaps are more likely to be landed in. Rutherford and the Poisson process In 1910 Ernest Rutherford and Hans Geiger counted the alpha particles emitted by a radioactive source in intervals of 7.5 seconds, and found that the counts followed the Poisson distribution, as the mathematician Harry Bateman showed they should if the emissions occurred independently at a constant rate. The times between emissions are then exponential. The Poisson process , a stream of events with exponential gaps, is now the basic model of randomness in time, used for telephone calls, insurance claims and the firing of neurons; the next section, Section 12.19 , extends it to space. The thinking skill Test independence by factorising Two random variables are independent if their joint probabilities factorise into a function of one times a function of the other. At university, factorisation of a joint density is the standard test for independence, and it is how you will recognise independent components in multivariate problems, such as the radius and angle of a normally distributed point in Section 12.22 . Try this next Two bus routes. Try STEP III 2002, Question 13 . It uses the minimum of two exponential random variables to find the wait for the next bus. Memoryless discrete. Show that the geometric distribution is memoryless: P(Y ≥ m + n mid Y ≥ m) = P(Y ≥ n) . The waiting-time paradox. Buses arrive as a Poisson process with rate λ . Show that the gap containing a fixed time t (for large t ) has expected length frac2λ , twice the average gap. The density of Z . Find the probability density of Z , and sketch it for λ = 1 and λ = 5 . Further reading Geoffrey Grimmett & Dominic Welsh, Probability: An Introduction (Oxford University Press), on the exponential distribution and the Poisson process. Sheldon Ross, Introduction to Probability Models (Academic Press). Exponential distributions, Poisson processes and queues. David Spiegelhalter, The Art of Uncertainty (Pelican). Randomness and waiting in everyday life.

title: Mixed Strategies
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on The minimax theorem Why randomise? The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP I 1989, Question 16 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/89-s1-q16 The hook In rock–paper–scissors, any fixed choice can be exploited: play rock every time and your opponent will learn to play paper. The only safe strategy is to randomise. This question is a more intricate version, where the payoffs are unequal and the right randomisation is not obvious. It turns out that by guessing 1 , 2 , 3 with probabilities frac14 , frac12 , frac14 , a player can guarantee not to lose in the long run, whatever the opponent does. This is a first glimpse of John von Neumann’s minimax theorem of 1928, the founding result of game theory: in every two-player game where one player’s gain is the other’s loss, there is a randomised strategy for each player that guarantees the best possible result against an opponent who plays perfectly. Before you start Write down a table of B’s winnings for each pair of guesses (B’s guess down the side, A’s across the top). Working through the rules (for instance, if B says 1 and A says 3 , they differ by 2 and B, the smaller, pays £2): B backslash A 1 2 3 1 0 +1 -2 2 -1 0 +1 3 +2 -1 0 The table is antisymmetric (swapping the players changes the sign), so the game is fair in the sense that neither player has a built-in advantage. Working it through Stage 1 Against a fixed guess If A always says 1 , B should say 3 and win £2 every round. If A always says 2 , B says 1 and wins £1. If A always says 3 , B says 2 and wins £1. Any fixed guess can be exploited. Stage 2 Against random guessing If A guesses uniformly at random, what is B’s expected gain when B says j ? (Average along row j of the table.) The row averages are frac13(0 + 1 - 2) = -frac13 for j = 1 , 0 for j = 2 and frac13(2 - 1 + 0) = frac13 for j = 3 . So B’s expected winnings per round are -tfrac13b_1 + 0· b_2 + tfrac13b_3, which is maximised by b_3 = 1 : always say 3 , winning frac13 of a pound per round on average. Uniform randomisation does not protect A. Stage 3 The general case Now A plays j with probability a_j . Collect B’s expected winnings by A’s guess: what is the coefficient of a_1 (the average of column 1 with weights b_j )? Reading down the columns of the table, B's expected winnings = (-b_2 + 2b_3)a_1 + (b_1 - b_3)a_2 + (-2b_1 + b_2)a_3, so X = -b_2 + 2b_3 , Y = b_1 - b_3 and Z = -2b_1 + b_2 . Can you make all three zero? (Three equations, but they are not independent; why not?) They are not independent: X + 2Y + Z = 0 identically (check it). So Y = 0 , giving b_1 = b_3 , and X = 0 , giving b_2 = 2b_3 , force Z = 0 as well. With b_1 + b_2 + b_3 = 1 : b_1 = tfrac14, qquad b_2 = tfrac12, qquad b_3 = tfrac14, giving X = Y = Z = 0 . Then B’s expected winnings are 0 whatever the a_j , and B loses nothing in the long run. ■ Looking back Write the payoff table. All the reasoning was about rows and columns of a 3 × 3 matrix. Pure strategies are exploitable. Against any fixed guess, and even against uniform guessing, the opponent has a profitable reply. Equalise. The safe strategy makes the opponent indifferent: every one of A’s choices gives the same expected result. What’s really going on The minimax theorem In a two-player zero-sum game, given by a payoff matrix M , B choosing probabilities b and A choosing a , B’s expected winnings are b^mathsf TMa . Von Neumann’s minimax theorem says max_mathbf bmin_mathbf ab^mathsf TMa = min_mathbf amax_mathbf bb^mathsf TMa. In words: the amount B can guarantee by announcing a randomised strategy in advance equals the amount A can hold B to by announcing his. This common value is the value of the game. Here, by antisymmetry, the value is 0 , and the strategy (frac14, frac12, frac14) is optimal for both players. The theorem is proved using linear algebra and convexity (it is equivalent to the duality theorem of linear programming), and its generalisation to many players, the Nash equilibrium , won John Nash the Nobel Prize in economics. Why randomise? Randomness here is not about luck but about information. If B’s choice can be predicted, A can exploit it; by randomising with the right probabilities, B makes his choice unpredictable and ensures that no prediction would help. Real examples include penalty kicks in football, where studies of professional players have found kickers and goalkeepers randomising between left and right in proportions close to the game-theoretic optimum, and tennis serves. Von Neumann’s 1928 paper John von Neumann proved the minimax theorem in 1928, in a paper “On the theory of games of strategy”, motivated by poker, where bluffing is a form of randomisation. In 1944 he and the economist Oskar Morgenstern published Theory of Games and Economic Behavior , which founded game theory as a subject. Von Neumann later recalled that he had regarded the minimax theorem as the key result, without which there would be no theory of games worth publishing. The thinking skill Randomise to remove an opponent’s advantage When any fixed choice can be exploited, choose at random, with probabilities that make the opponent indifferent between their options. At university, game theory, linear programming and the theory of algorithms all use this idea. Randomised algorithms, for example, protect themselves against worst-case inputs by making random choices that no adversary can predict. Try this next A’s best reply. If B uses (frac14, frac12, frac14) , show that every strategy of A gives expected winnings 0 . If instead B uses (frac13, frac13, frac13) , find A’s best reply. Rock, paper, scissors. Write the payoff matrix for rock–paper–scissors and find the optimal strategy. Why is it uniform here but not in the question? Uniqueness. Show that (frac14, frac12, frac14) is the only strategy for B that guarantees not losing. ( Hint: it must make X , Y , Z all non-negative; use X + 2Y + Z = 0 .) A modified game. If the penalty for differing by 2 is £3 instead of £2, find the optimal strategy. Further reading Ken Binmore, Playing for Real (Oxford University Press). A thorough but friendly introduction to game theory. Avinash Dixit & Barry Nalebuff, The Art of Strategy (Norton). Game theory with examples from sport and business. William Poundstone, Prisoner’s Dilemma (Anchor). Von Neumann, game theory and the Cold War.

title: One More Coin
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Symmetry and complements How likely is a tie? The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP I 2016, Question 12 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/16-s1-q12 The hook Bob tosses one more coin than Alice. What is the probability that he gets more heads? He has an advantage, but heads are not guaranteed, and ties go against him. Work out the first two cases by brute force and the answer is frac12 both times. Is that a coincidence? It is not, and there is a proof that takes one sentence, once you notice that Bob must get either more heads than Alice or more tails, but not both. This question is a model of how a calculation can suggest a pattern, and how a clever symmetry can then explain it. Before you start Alice tosses twice: what is the distribution of her number of heads? And Bob, tossing three times? Alice gets 0, 1, 2 heads with probabilities frac14, frac24, frac14 ; Bob gets 0, 1, 2, 3 with probabilities frac18, frac38, frac38, frac18 . Working it through Stage 1 Brute force For part (i), add up over Alice’s number of heads: beginaligned P(B > A) &= tfrac14\,P(B ≥ 1) + tfrac24\,P(B ≥ 2) + tfrac14\,P(B = 3) \\ &= tfrac14·tfrac78 + tfrac12·tfrac48 + tfrac14·tfrac18 = (7 + 8 + 1)/(32) = frac12. endaligned Part (ii) is the same calculation with more terms; counting the 8 × 16 = 128 equally likely outcomes, 64 have Bob ahead (Figure 12.6.1), so again the answer is frac12 . Stage 2 Splitting Bob’s tosses Think of Bob’s n + 1 tosses as n tosses followed by one extra toss. After his first n tosses, he is ahead of Alice, level with her, or behind. What happens in each case? After n tosses each, Bob is ahead with probability p_2 , level with probability p_1 , and behind with probability p_2 (by symmetry between Alice and Bob). If he is ahead, he stays ahead. If he is level, his extra toss puts him ahead with probability frac12 . If he is behind, one extra head can at best draw level. So P(Bob more heads) = p_2 + tfrac12p_1. Since the three cases cover everything, 2p_2 + p_1 = 1 , and so p_2 + frac12p_1 = frac12 . With one extra coin, Bob gets more heads with probability exactly frac12 , for every n . ■ Here is the one-sentence proof. Bob has n + 1 tosses, so his heads and tails add to n + 1 , one more than Alice’s. Show that Bob has more heads than Alice if and only if he does not have more tails than Alice. Since heads and tails are symmetric, these two events have equal probability, so each is frac12 . Indeed, writing H_A + T_A = n and H_B + T_B = n + 1 : if H_B > H_A then H_B ≥ H_A + 1 , so T_B = n + 1 - H_B ≤ n - H_A = T_A ; and conversely if T_B ≤ T_A then H_B ≥ H_A + 1 . So “more heads” and “more tails” are complementary, and swapping heads and tails (which does not change the probabilities, as the coins are fair) swaps them. Looking back Compute small cases. Two calculations suggested the answer frac12 . Condition on a natural split. Separating Bob’s extra toss reduced the problem to an even contest plus one coin. Find the complementary pair. “More heads” and “more tails” are complements and are swapped by a symmetry. What’s really going on Symmetry and complements The slick proof combines two facts: two events that are swapped by a symmetry have equal probabilities, and two complementary events have probabilities adding to 1 . If both hold, each has probability frac12 . The same reasoning appears throughout probability. In the airline problem ( Section 12.5 ), S_1 and S_n were swapped by a symmetry and exactly one of them is left at the end. In a game of Hex, the board’s symmetry and the fact that exactly one player must win show that the first player has the advantage, though nobody knows a winning strategy on large boards. How likely is a tie? For equal numbers of tosses the tie probability p_1 matters. Alice and Bob tie when Alice’s heads equal Bob’s heads, which (replacing Bob’s heads by his tails, by symmetry) has the same probability as Alice’s heads plus Bob’s heads equalling n : a total of n heads in 2n tosses. So p_1 = binom2nn(1)/(4^n) approx frac1sqrtπ n, using Stirling’s approximation ( Section 12.23 ). Ties become rare, but slowly: with 100 tosses each, the chance of a tie is still about 5.6\% . The thinking skill Calculate, conjecture, then explain When a calculation gives a suspiciously simple answer, look for a reason. A simple answer usually has a simple explanation. At university this habit separates understanding from computation. The first proof here confirms the answer; the second explains it, and generalises immediately (try exercise 2). Try this next Two extra coins. If Bob tosses n + 2 coins and Alice n , prove P(Bob more heads) = frac12 + frac12P(H' = H_A) , where H' is the number of heads in Bob’s first n + 1 tosses. Biased coins. If both use a coin with probability p of heads, is the answer still frac12 with one extra toss? Which step of the slick proof fails? Ties. Show that p_1 = binom2nn/4^n by the trick in the text, and evaluate it for n = 1, 2, 3 . Dice. Alice rolls n dice and Bob rolls n + 1 . Is the probability that Bob gets more sixes equal to frac12 ? Further reading Peter Winkler, Mathematical Mind-Benders (A K Peters). Many probability puzzles with symmetric solutions. Gabor Székely, Paradoxes in Probability Theory and Mathematical Statistics (Reidel). Frederick Mosteller, Fifty Challenging Problems in Probability (Dover).

title: Independent in Pairs, Not All Together
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Independence of several events Uncorrelated is not independent The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2021, Question 12 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP III paper in OCR’s download of the 2021 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/696588-2021-past-papers.zip The hook Players 1 and 2 roll the same number. Does that tell you anything about whether players 2 and 3 roll the same number? Surprisingly, no: the events are independent. The same goes for players 1 and 3 . But if 1 matches 2 and 2 matches 3 , then certainly 1 matches 3 . Three events, each pair independent, but not independent all together. Pairwise independence is weaker than full independence, and the difference matters. For variances, pairwise independence is all you need, which this question exploits. For many other purposes it is not enough. Computer scientists use pairwise independent random numbers deliberately, because they are much cheaper to generate than fully independent ones and are good enough for many algorithms. Before you start What is P(X_12 = 1) ? What is P(X_12 = 1 and X_23 = 1) ? Whatever player 1 rolls, player 2 matches it with probability frac16 . Both X_12 = 1 and X_23 = 1 means all three roll the same number: probability (6)/(216) = (1)/(36) . Working it through Stage 1 Pairwise independence Since P(X_12 = 1, X_23 = 1) = (1)/(36) = frac16 · frac16 = P(X_12 = 1)P(X_23 = 1) , and each variable takes only two values, X_12 and X_23 are independent. (For two-valued variables, one cell of the joint table determines the rest; exercise 1 makes this precise.) Pairs with no player in common, such as X_12 and X_34 , are clearly independent. So all the X_ij are pairwise independent. Stage 2 Mean and variance of the score The score is S = sum_i<jX_ij , a sum of binom n2 variables, each with mean frac16 and variance frac16 · frac56 = (5)/(36) . Expectation always adds, so E(S) = frac16binom n2 . When does the variance of a sum equal the sum of the variances? The variance of a sum is the sum of the variances plus twice the sum of the covariances, and independent pairs have zero covariance. Pairwise independence is enough: E(S) = (n(n - 1))/(12), qquad Var(S) = (5)/(36)binom n2 = (5n(n - 1))/(72). Stage 3 The variance formula If the Y_i have mean zero, then Var(sum Y_i) = Ebigl((sum Y_i)^2bigr) , and expanding the square gives every Y_i^2 once and every product Y_iY_j (with i < j ) twice. Taking expectations gives the formula. ■ Stage 4 The odd-and-even game What is E(Z_12) ? What values can Z_12Z_23 take, and when is it non-zero? Z_12 = 1 with probability (3)/(36) = (1)/(12) (both roll 2 , both 4 or both 6 ), and -1 with probability (1)/(12) ; so E(Z_12) = 0 and E(Z_12^2) = frac16 . Z_12Z_23 ≠ 0 only when all three players roll the same number, and then Z_12 = Z_23 (both +1 or both -1 ), so the product is 1 . Hence E(Z_12Z_23) = (1)/(36) , which is not E(Z_12)E(Z_23) = 0 : they are not independent. ■ (Even more directly, P(Z_12 = 1, Z_23 = -1) = 0 , while each event alone has probability (1)/(12) .) Stage 5 The variance The total score T = sum Z_ij has mean 0 . By part (ii), Var(T) is binom n2 · frac16 plus twice the sum of E(Z_ijZ_kl) over pairs of pairs. Pairs of pairs with no common player contribute 0 (they are independent, each with mean zero). Pairs of pairs sharing exactly one player each contribute (1)/(36) , and there are nbinomn-12 of them (choose the shared player, then two others). So beginaligned Var(T) &= (n(n - 1))/(12) + 2 · (1)/(36) · (n(n - 1)(n - 2))/(2) \\ &= (n(n - 1))/(36)bigl(3 + (n - 2)bigr) = (n(n^2 - 1))/(36). qed endaligned Looking back Indicators. Writing the score as a sum of indicator variables reduced everything to pairs of players. Variance needs only pairs. The variance of a sum depends only on the pairwise covariances, so pairwise independence is enough to add variances. Check independence, do not assume it. Two games that look alike had different dependence structures. What’s really going on Independence of several events Events A_1, ldots, A_n are independent if, for every subcollection, the probability of the intersection is the product of the probabilities. For three events this means four conditions: three for the pairs, and P(A cap B cap C) = P(A)P(B)P(C) . Sergei Bernstein gave the example in Figure 12.4.1 in the 1920s to show that the pairwise conditions do not imply the triple one. (Conversely, the triple condition alone does not imply the pairwise ones either.) The matching events X_12 , X_23 , X_13 in the question are exactly like Bernstein’s coins. Uncorrelated is not independent Zero covariance, E(XY) = E(X)E(Y) , is weaker still than independence. STEP III 2000 Q14 (in the exercises) shows that for variables taking only two values the two notions coincide, but with three values they do not. A simple example: let X be uniform on \-1, 0, 1\ and Y = X^2 . Then E(XY) = E(X^3) = 0 = E(X)E(Y) , yet Y is completely determined by X . Covariance measures only linear association. Cheap randomness Random numbers are expensive for a computer to generate. In 1979 Larry Carter and Mark Wegman showed that for many algorithms, such as hashing , which stores data at pseudo-random locations, pairwise independent random choices are just as good as fully independent ones. Pairwise independent values can be generated very cheaply: for example, a + bk pmod p for k = 0, 1, ldots, p - 1 , with a and b random, gives p values any two of which are independent. The variance calculation of this question is why it works: Chebyshev’s inequality needs only variances, and variances need only pairs. The thinking skill Decompose into indicators To find the mean and variance of a count, write it as a sum of indicator variables, one for each thing that might be counted. The mean needs single indicators; the variance needs pairs. This is one of the most useful techniques in probability, and it appeared already in Section 9.8 . At university it powers the analysis of random graphs, of algorithms and of statistical tests. Try this next Two values. Try STEP III 2000, Question 14 . It shows that for random variables taking only two values each, E(XY) = E(X)E(Y) forces independence, and asks for a counterexample with three values. A bigger team. For n = 7 in part (i), find the mean and standard deviation of the score, and compare the example score 7 with them. Birthdays again. Use indicators to find the mean and variance of the number of pairs sharing a birthday among k people ( Section 9.9 ). Are the indicators pairwise independent? Pairwise but not triple. Find three events, each of probability frac12 , with P(A cap B cap C) = frac18 but which are not pairwise independent. Further reading Geoffrey Grimmett & David Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes (Oxford University Press), the opening chapters on independence. Michael Mitzenmacher & Eli Upfal, Probability and Computing (Cambridge University Press). Pairwise independence and its uses in algorithms. Joseph Blitzstein & Jessica Hwang, Introduction to Probability (CRC Press; free online), on indicators and covariance.

title: Penney's Game
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Why some sequences are better Conway’s formula The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2001, Question 13 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/01-s3-q13 The hook You and a friend each choose a sequence of three coin tosses, and a coin is tossed until one of the sequences appears. Every sequence of three tosses is equally likely to occur at any given moment, so surely every choice is equally good? Not at all. Whatever sequence your friend chooses, you can choose one that beats it, sometimes with odds of 7 to 1 . This is Penney’s game , invented by Walter Penney in 1969. The question shows that A beats B , B beats C , C beats D , and D beats A : a cycle, like rock–paper–scissors. “Beats” is not transitive. Whoever chooses second can always win in the long run. Before you start Suppose the tosses so far end in TT and nobody has won yet. Can THH ever appear before TTH? From TT, every further T keeps the last two tosses as TT, and the first H completes TTH. For THH to appear we would need a TH, which can only arise from a T followed by an H, and that H already completes TTH. So once TT has occurred, A wins. Working it through Stage 1 States Neither sequence can be completed in two tosses. After two tosses, what is the next toss’s effect from each state? Since the game depends only on the last two tosses, we can track the state (last two tosses): From TT: A wins (shown above), so p_TT = 1 . From HT: the next toss gives TH or TT, so p_HT = frac12p_TH + frac12p_TT . From TH: an H completes THH ( B wins); a T gives HT. So p_TH = frac12 · 0 + frac12p_HT . From HH: an H gives HH again; a T gives HT. So p_HH = frac12p_HH + frac12p_HT , giving p_HH = p_HT . Stage 2 Solving Substituting p_TH = frac12p_HT into the HT equation: p_HT = frac14p_HT + frac12 , so p_HT = frac23 , p_HH = frac23 and p_TH = frac13 . Each of the four starting states has probability frac14 , so P(A wins) = tfrac14bigl(tfrac23 + tfrac23 + tfrac13 + 1bigr) = tfrac23. qed Stage 3 B against C C wants HHT and B wants THH. When does C win? (Look at what must come just before the first HH.) If the first two tosses are HH, then the first T after that completes HHT, before THH can appear: C wins. Otherwise, there is a T somewhere before the first occurrence of HH, and so the first HH is immediately preceded by a T: THH appears at that moment, before HHT (which needs a T after HH). So C wins only if the game starts HH: P(B wins) = tfrac34. qed Stage 4 The cycle The same method (or the shortcut in the What’s Really Going On section) shows that C (HHT) beats D (HTT) with probability frac23 , and D (HTT) beats A (TTH) with probability frac34 ; the last is the mirror image of Stage 3 with heads and tails swapped. So A beats B, qquad B beats C, qquad C beats D, qquad D beats A. qed Looking back Choose the right state. Only the last two tosses mattered, so four states and four equations captured the whole game. First-step analysis. Each equation conditioned on the next toss: the probability from a state is the average over where the next toss leads. Look for a decisive event. In Stage 3, “the first HH is preceded by a T” settled the game without equations. What’s really going on Why some sequences are better All sequences of three tosses are equally likely at any given position, and the expected waiting time for each is easy to compute. But the waiting times differ: you wait on average 8 tosses for TTH but 14 for TTT, because a sequence that overlaps itself (like TTT, where a near miss TTH ruins two tosses of progress) is slow to appear. And in a race between two sequences, what matters is how each overlaps the other . THH beats HHT because every occurrence of HHT (except at the very start) is preceded by a T, which means THH has just occurred. The second player’s trick is always the same: take the first two symbols of your opponent’s sequence, and put in front of them the opposite of the opponent’s middle symbol. Conway’s formula John Conway found a remarkable formula for the odds. For two sequences X and Y of length n , define the correlation XY as a binary number with n digits: reading from the left, the i th digit is 1 if the part of X starting at its i th symbol equals the beginning of Y of the same length. Then the odds that Y appears before X are (XX - XY) : (YY - YX). For X = HHT and Y = THH: XX = 100_2 = 4 (only the whole of HHT matches itself); XY = 001_2 = 1 (only the final T of HHT matches the start of THH); YY = 100_2 = 4 ; and YX = 011_2 = 3 (both HH and H at the end of THH match the start of HHT). So the odds that THH comes first are (4 - 1) : (4 - 3) = 3 : 1 , the frac34 of Stage 3. Conway’s formula works for sequences of any length and any alphabet, and its proof uses the theory of martingales : imagine a casino in which gamblers bet on the sequence appearing, and use the fact that a fair game has zero expected profit. Penney and Gardner Walter Penney described the game in a short note in the Journal of Recreational Mathematics in 1969. Martin Gardner made it famous in his Scientific American column in 1974, including Conway’s formula, which Conway had found but not published. Non-transitive relations of this kind (Efron’s dice, where die A beats B , B beats C , C beats D and D beats A , are another example) are a recurring source of surprise, and they matter in voting theory, where majority preferences can form cycles: Condorcet’s paradox. The thinking skill First-step analysis To find a probability or expectation for a process that moves between states, condition on the first step. This gives one linear equation per state. This is the basic technique for Markov chains, which you will meet in Section 12.16 and throughout a university course in probability. The same method finds the probability of reaching one state before another, the expected time to absorption, and the probability of ruin in gambling problems. Try this next Four players together. Try STEP II 2015, Question 12 : Penney’s game with four players at once. Waiting times. Show that the expected number of tosses until HH first appears is 6 , and until HT is 4 . (Use first-step analysis.) The best reply. For each of the eight sequences of length three, find the sequence that beats it with the greatest probability. Which sequence is beaten most easily? Conway’s formula. Use Conway’s formula to check that HHT beats HTT with probability frac23 . Further reading Martin Gardner, Time Travel and Other Mathematical Bewilderments (W. H. Freeman). Includes Penney’s game and Conway’s formula. Ronald Graham, Donald Knuth & Oren Patashnik, Concrete Mathematics (Addison-Wesley), Section 8.4. Penney’s game with generating functions. David Williams, Probability with Martingales (Cambridge University Press). The martingale proof, for later.

title: When to Stop Looking
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Optimal stopping Variations The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP I 2001, Question 14 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/01-s1-q14 The hook You are interviewing candidates one at a time, and must decide on the spot: accept this one, and stop, or reject them for ever and see the next. You want the very best. If you accept too early you probably miss someone better; if you wait too long the best has probably gone. What should you do? The answer, one of the most celebrated results in probability, is: reject the first 37\% of candidates, then accept the first one who is better than all of those. This succeeds about 37\% of the time, and 37\% is frac1e . This question computes the basic probabilities, and its companion from STEP II 2006 (in the exercises) analyses the simplest version of the strategy, rejecting just the first candidate. Before you start In a random order, what is the probability that the overall best candidate is among the first n interviewed? The best candidate is equally likely to be in any of the N positions, so the probability is frac nN . Working it through Stage 1 The best of the first n is the best The best among the first n is the best overall exactly when the overall best is among the first n : probability frac nN . ■ Stage 2 Best or second best The best of the first n is the second best overall exactly when the second best is among the first n but the best is not. What is that probability? The second best is among the first n with probability frac nN ; given that, the best is in one of the other N - 1 positions, of which N - n are after the first n . So P(best or second best) = frac nN + frac nN·(N - n)/(N - 1). qed For N = 4 , n = 2 : frac12 + frac12·frac23 = frac56 . Listing the positions of the top two candidates among the four places (all 12 ordered placements equally likely), the best of the first two is one of the top two in all but the 2 placements where both top candidates come in positions 3 and 4 : (10)/(12) = frac56 . Stage 3 The optimal strategy Strategy: reject the first r candidates, then accept the first candidate better than all of them. If the best candidate is in position k > r , when does the strategy pick them? The strategy picks the best candidate, in position k , if and only if no candidate in positions r + 1, ldots, k - 1 beats all of the first r , that is, if the best of the first k - 1 candidates is among the first r . By Stage 1 (with N replaced by k - 1 ), this has probability (r)/(k - 1) . Each position k has probability frac1N , so P(success) = frac1Nsum_k=r+1^N(r)/(k - 1) = frac rNBigl(frac1r + (1)/(r + 1) + cdots + (1)/(N - 1)Bigr). For large N , write x = frac rN . The sum is approximately (N)/(r) . What value of x maximises xfrac1x ? The success probability is approximately xfrac1x . Differentiating, frac1x - 1 = 0 when x = frac1e , and the maximum value is frac1e approx 0.368 (Figure 12.12.1). Looking back Symmetry of positions. In a random order, each candidate is equally likely to be anywhere, which gave frac nN immediately. Condition on where the best is. The strategy’s success was computed by conditioning on the position of the best candidate. Sums become integrals. For large N the harmonic sum became a logarithm, and an optimisation gave frac1e . What’s really going on Optimal stopping The secretary problem is the founding example of optimal stopping : deciding when to take an action, based on information arriving over time, to maximise an expected reward. It can be proved that among all strategies (not just “reject r , then take the next best-so-far”), this kind of threshold rule is optimal, by an argument working backwards from the last candidate. The same mathematics governs when to sell a share, when to exercise a financial option, and how long to search for a parking space. A remarkable feature is that the answer does not depend on N in the limit: you succeed with probability frac1e whether there are a hundred candidates or a million. Variations If you are satisfied with either of the top two candidates, the best strategy succeeds about 57\% of the time. If you want to maximise the expected rank of the chosen candidate rather than the chance of the very best, the optimal strategy is more complicated, and the expected rank tends to about 3.87 (Chow, Moriguti, Robbins and Samuels, 1964). If you can recall rejected candidates with some probability, or if you know the distribution of candidates’ scores (the “full-information” problem), the answers change again. The ice-cream question in the exercises is the simplest case: reject just one, then take the next improvement. Who solved it? The problem circulated among mathematicians in the 1950s, and Martin Gardner popularised it in 1960 as the “game of googol” (write numbers on slips of paper; your opponent turns them over one at a time and must stop at the largest). Thomas Ferguson’s article “Who solved the secretary problem?” (1989) traces its tangled history; one tradition says that the astronomer Johannes Kepler, choosing a second wife in 1611, interviewed eleven candidates and ended up proposing to the fifth. The thinking skill Parametrise a strategy and optimise When the best strategy is unknown, consider a natural family of strategies with a parameter, compute the success probability as a function of it, and optimise. At university this approach is used in decision theory, game theory and statistics. Showing that the best strategy in the family is the best overall is a harder and more interesting step, often done by backward induction . Try this next Ice-creams. Try STEP II 2006, Question 13 : a small version of the secretary problem with a simple rule. Reject the first, then take the first that beats it. Small N . For N = 4 , find the best value of r and the probability of success. Check by listing. Best or second best. Using part (ii), argue that “the best of the first n is one of the top two” is much more likely than “the best of the first n is the best”. What does this suggest about strategies for getting one of the top two? An exact maximum. For N = 10 , check from the figure that r = 3 is optimal. For N = 100 , show that r = 37 is optimal (to four decimal places the success probabilities for r = 36 , 37 , 38 are 0.3710 , 0.3710 , 0.3708 ). Further reading Thomas Ferguson, “ Who solved the secretary problem? ” , Statistical Science 4 (1989). History and variations; free online. Brian Christian & Tom Griffiths, Algorithms to Live By (William Collins). Optimal stopping and other algorithms applied to everyday decisions. Martin Gardner, New Mathematical Diversions (Mathematical Association of America). The game of googol.

title: Random Points in the Plane
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on The Poisson process in the plane In three dimensions The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 2012, Question 13 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/12-s2-q13 The hook If supermarkets, trees, stars or mobile-phone masts are scattered “at random” across a region, how far do you have to go to the nearest one? The answer depends only on the density k (the average number per unit area), and it has a characteristic shape, the Rayleigh distribution . On average the nearest is at distance (1)/(2sqrt k) : with one supermarket per square kilometre, 500 metres. The model is the spatial Poisson process , the two-dimensional version of random arrivals in time ( Section 12.18 ). The calculation is short and pretty, but its real interest is as a benchmark: ecologists compare real nearest-neighbour distances with this formula to decide whether trees or nests are clustered, randomly scattered or deliberately spaced out. Before you start A Poisson random variable with mean μ takes the value 0 with what probability? P(0) = e^-μ . A circle of radius y has area π y^2 , so the number of supermarkets inside it has mean kπ y^2 . Working it through Stage 1 No supermarket nearby The probability of no supermarket within distance y is e^-π ky^2 . Stage 2 The distribution of the nearest distance Y ≥ y means there is no supermarket within distance y . So what is P(Y < y) ? P(Y < y) = 1 - e^-π ky^2 , and differentiating gives the density f(y) = 2π kye^-π ky^2, qquad y ≥ 0. qed Stage 3 The mean Either integrate y\,f(y) by parts, or use E(Y) = int_0^inftyP(Y > y)\,dy . Then substitute to use the given Gaussian integral. E(Y) = int_0^∞ e^-π ky^2\,dy. Substituting x = ysqrt2π k , so that π ky^2 = frac12x^2 , gives E(Y) = frac1sqrt2π ksqrtfracπ2 = (1)/(2sqrt k) . ■ Stage 4 The variance E(Y^2) = int_0^∞ y^2·2π kye^-π ky^2\,dy. Substituting u = π ky^2 (so du = 2π ky\,dy ), this is int_0^∞(u)/(π k)e^-u\,du = (1)/(π k) . Hence Var(Y) = (1)/(π k) - (1)/(4k) = (4 - π)/(4π k). qed Looking back Turn a distance question into a counting question. “The nearest is further than y ” is “there are none within y ”. Cumulative first, density second. P(Y < y) came directly; differentiating gave the density. Substitutions to known integrals. Each moment reduced to the Gaussian integral or the exponential integral. What’s really going on The Poisson process in the plane A spatial Poisson process with intensity k is a random scatter of points such that the numbers in disjoint regions are independent, and the number in a region of area A is Poisson with mean kA . It is what you get from dropping a huge number of points independently and uniformly over a huge area, with the right average density: the “law of rare events” that also explains derangements ( Section 9.8 ). It is the natural model of complete spatial randomness, and real patterns are judged against it. The Clark–Evans test , devised by two ecologists in 1954, compares the observed mean nearest-neighbour distance with (1)/(2sqrt k) : much smaller suggests clustering (seeds falling near their parent tree), much larger suggests regular spacing (territorial birds, or competition between plants for water). In three dimensions The same calculation in three dimensions gives P(Y > y) = e^-frac43π ky^3 for the distance to the nearest star, molecule or galaxy. Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar used it in 1943 to study the gravitational forces on a star from its random neighbours, and physicists use it for the mean free path of molecules in a gas. Rayleigh The density (y)/(σ^2)e^-y^2/(2σ^2) is named after Lord Rayleigh, who met it in 1880 in the theory of sound: it describes the amplitude of the sum of many waves with random phases. It also gives the distance from the origin of a point whose two coordinates are independent normal random variables, which is another way to see why it appears here (exercise 3). Today it models the fading of mobile-phone signals, which reach the receiver along many paths with random phases. The thinking skill Find the distribution function first For the distribution of a minimum, a maximum or a nearest distance, P(Y > y) is often easy to write down directly. Differentiate to get the density. This approach recurs in Section 12.25 , for the largest of many random lifetimes. At university it is the standard first step for any “order statistic”. Try this next The median. Find the median distance to the nearest supermarket, and compare it with the mean. The second nearest. Find the distribution of the distance to the second nearest supermarket. ( Hint: P(Y_2 > y) is the probability of at most one supermarket within y .) Normal coordinates. If U and V are independent N(0, σ^2) , show that sqrtU^2 + V^2 has density (r)/(σ^2)e^-r^2/(2σ^2) . Which value of σ gives the supermarket distribution? Clark–Evans. In a survey of a 1 km ^2 wood containing 400 trees, the mean distance from a tree to its nearest neighbour is 35 m. Is this consistent with complete spatial randomness, or does it suggest clustering or spacing? Further reading Peter Diggle, Statistical Analysis of Spatial Point Patterns (Arnold). The standard reference, with the Clark–Evans test and its successors. John Kingman, Poisson Processes (Oxford University Press). A beautiful short book on Poisson processes in any number of dimensions. Geoffrey Grimmett & David Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes (Oxford University Press), the chapter on the Poisson process.

title: Stamps, Cups and e
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on The same distribution, in disguise Why e keeps appearing The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP I 1996, Question 13 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/96-s1-q13 The hook A strange way to sell a stamp: the buyer keeps guessing which cup hides it, with one more cup each round, and pays one pound per cup on the table when he first guesses wrong. On average he pays pounds e , about pounds 2.72 . The number e appears in probability with uncanny frequency: the chance that nobody gets their own shirt ( Section 9.8 ), the secretary problem ( Section 12.12 ), the Poisson distribution. This question is perhaps the simplest of all its appearances, and it turns out to have exactly the same distribution as another famous puzzle: how many random numbers between 0 and 1 must you add before the total exceeds 1 ? On average, e . Before you start For N = 4 , what must happen? With what probability? Jim must guess correctly with 2 cups (probability frac12 ) and with 3 cups ( frac13 ), then fail with 4 cups ( frac34 ). So P(N = 4) = frac12·frac13·frac34 = (3)/(4!) = frac18 . Working it through Stage 1 The distribution For N = k (with k ≥ 2 ), Jim succeeds with 2, 3, ldots, k - 1 cups and fails with k : P(N = k) = frac12·frac13cdots(1)/(k - 1)·(k - 1)/(k) = (k - 1)/(k!). (Check: (1)/(2!) + (2)/(3!) + (3)/(4!) + cdots = sum_k ≥ 2bigl((1)/((k-1)!) - (1)/(k!)bigr) = 1 , a telescoping sum.) Stage 2 The expectation Simplify k·(k - 1)/(k!) . What series do you get? E(N) = sum_k ≥ 2(k(k - 1))/(k!) = sum_k ≥ 2(1)/((k - 2)!) = (1)/(0!) + (1)/(1!) + cdots = e. qed Stage 3 The variance Find E(N^2) by writing k^2 = k(k - 1) + k , or by simplifying (k^2(k-1))/(k!) directly. E(N^2) = sum_k ≥ 2(k^2(k - 1))/(k!) = sum_k ≥ 2(k)/((k - 2)!) = sum_j ≥ 0(j + 2)/(j!) = sum_j ≥ 1(1)/((j - 1)!) + 2sum_j ≥ 0(1)/(j!) = e + 2e = 3e. So Var(N) = 3e - e^2 = e(3 - e) approx 0.766 . ■ Looking back Products of probabilities. A sequence of independent successes followed by a failure gave a product that collapsed to (k-1)/(k!) . Cancel factorials. Multiplying by k or k^2 and cancelling turned the sums into the exponential series. E(N^2) via a shift. Re-indexing with j = k - 2 split the sum into two copies of e . What’s really going on The same distribution, in disguise Choose random numbers U_1, U_2, ldots uniformly from [0, 1] , and let M be the number needed for their sum to exceed 1 . The probability that the first k numbers add up to less than 1 is the volume of the region \u_1 + cdots + u_k < 1, u_i ≥ 0\ , which is (1)/(k!) (a triangle of area frac12 , a tetrahedron of volume frac16 , and so on). So P(M > k) = (1)/(k!), qquad P(M = k) = (1)/((k - 1)!) - (1)/(k!) = (k - 1)/(k!), exactly the distribution of N . In both problems P(N > k) = (1)/(k!) : for the cups, that is the probability of k - 1 correct guesses in a row. Using E(N) = sum_k ≥ 0P(N > k) (a formula from Section 9.9 ) gives E(N) = sum(1)/(k!) = e in one line. Why e keeps appearing Whenever a probability involves (1)/(k!) , whether from k objects in a particular order, k successive events with probabilities frac12, frac13, ldots , or the volume of a simplex, sums over k produce the exponential series. Derangements ( Section 9.8 ) gave sum((-1)^k)/(k!) = e^-1 ; here we have sum(1)/(k!) = e . And limits of the form bigl(1 - frac1nbigr)^n → e^-1 , which come from many independent unlikely events, explain e in the secretary problem and the Poisson distribution. Monte Carlo e The “sum exceeds 1 ” problem gives a way to estimate e by experiment: generate random numbers, count how many are needed to exceed 1 , repeat many times and average. It is a cousin of Buffon’s needle ( Section 12.20 ), which estimates π . Such Monte Carlo methods, named after the casino, use random sampling to estimate quantities that are hard to compute directly; they are now used throughout science, from particle physics to finance, mostly for integrals in many dimensions. The thinking skill Recognise a series When an expectation is a sum involving factorials, simplify the terms until a standard series (exponential, geometric, binomial) appears. At university, generating functions systematise this: the probability generating function E(t^N) packages the whole distribution, and its derivatives at t = 1 give the mean and variance. Try this next The generating function. Show that E(t^N) = 1 + (t - 1)e^t , and use it to find E(N) and E(N(N - 1)) . The tail formula. Prove that E(N) = sum_k ≥ 0P(N > k) for a random variable taking non-negative integer values, and use it to find E(N) in one line. Starting with one cup. If the game starts with one cup (which Jim cannot get wrong), how does the distribution change? What is the expected price? The simplex. Show that the volume of \u_1 + u_2 + u_3 < 1, u_i ≥ 0\ is frac16 , and use induction to show the k -dimensional version is (1)/(k!) . Further reading Eli Maor, e: The Story of a Number (Princeton University Press). The history of e , including its appearances in probability. Geoffrey Grimmett & Dominic Welsh, Probability: An Introduction (Oxford University Press), on generating functions. Paul Nahin, Digital Dice (Princeton University Press). Probability puzzles solved by Monte Carlo simulation.

title: Stirling from Probability
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on How good is the approximation? Why factorials and normals are linked The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 2016, Question 13 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/16-s2-q13 The hook How big is 100! ? Multiplying out takes a while: it has 158 digits. Stirling’s formula , n! approx sqrt2π n\,(n/e)^n , gives it to within 0.1\% in a single line. It is one of the most useful approximations in mathematics, used constantly in probability, statistical physics and the analysis of algorithms. There are many proofs, using integrals ( Section 4.4 ) or the Euler–Maclaurin formula. This question gives the most surprising one: a proof by probability. The Poisson distribution with mean n is approximately normal, and comparing the two at the peak forces the value of n! . The sqrt2π in Stirling’s formula is literally the sqrt2π in the normal density. Before you start If a discrete random variable X with mean μ and variance σ^2 is approximately normal, roughly what is P(X = μ) ? (Think of the probability of an interval of width 1 centred at μ .) P(X = μ) approx P(μ - frac12 < X < μ + frac12) for the normal approximation, which is about the width 1 times the density at the peak: frac1σsqrt2π . Working it through Stage 1 Sixteen coins X sim B(16, frac12) has mean 8 and variance 16 · frac12 · frac12 = 4 , so σ = 2 . By the normal approximation, P(X = 8) approx frac12sqrt2π approx 0.1995. The exact value is binom168/2^16 = (12870)/(65536) approx 0.1964 , within 2\% . Stage 2 The central binomial coefficient For B(2n, frac12) , what are the mean and standard deviation? Write P(X = n) exactly and approximately. The mean is n and the variance frac n2 , so σ = sqrtn/2 . Exactly, P(X = n) = binom2nnfrac12^2n ; approximately, frac1sqrtn/2sqrt2π = frac1sqrtπ n . Equating, frac(2n)!(n!)^2\,2^2n approx frac1sqrtπ n, qquad (2n)! approx frac2^2n(n!)^2sqrtnπ. qed Stage 3 Stirling’s formula A Poisson distribution with parameter n has mean and variance both equal to n . Write P(X = n) exactly and approximately. Exactly, P(X = n) = e^-n(n^n)/(n!) . For large n the Poisson distribution is approximately normal (it is the sum of n independent Poisson (1) variables), with σ = sqrt n , so P(X = n) approx frac1sqrt2π n . Equating, n! approx sqrt2π n\,e^-nn^n. qed Looking back Probability at a point approx density times width. For a lattice distribution, the normal density at a point approximates the probability of that point. An exact formula meets an approximation. The binomial and Poisson probabilities are exact; equating them to their normal approximations gave estimates for factorials. Choose the distribution to fit the formula. binom2nn suggested B(2n, frac12) ; (n^n)/(n!) suggested Poisson (n) . What’s really going on How good is the approximation? This argument is a heuristic: it uses the normal approximation at a single point , which the usual central limit theorem does not justify. A rigorous version, the local central limit theorem , does exactly that, and makes this a genuine proof. Stirling’s formula is in fact remarkably accurate: the ratio fracn!sqrt2π n(n/e)^n is about 1 + (1)/(12n) , so even for n = 1 it gives 0.92 instead of 1 , and for n = 10 it is 0.8\% too small. The full series, 1 + (1)/(12n) + (1)/(288n^2) - cdots , is an example of an asymptotic series : it gives better and better approximations for large n , but for fixed n it eventually diverges. Why factorials and normals are linked The sqrt2π in Stirling’s formula and in the normal density are the same constant, because int_-∞^∞ e^-x^2/2\,dx = sqrt2π . Abraham de Moivre found the normal approximation to the binomial in 1733 in exactly this way, needing an approximation to binomnk for large n ; he found the form n! approx Cn^n + 1/2e^-n but not the constant. James Stirling showed that C = sqrt2π . The normal distribution was born from the asymptotics of factorials. De Moivre and Stirling Abraham de Moivre, a French Protestant who fled to London and earned a living tutoring and advising gamblers, published The Doctrine of Chances in 1718 and found the normal approximation to the binomial in a pamphlet of 1733, the first appearance of the normal curve. James Stirling, a Scottish mathematician, published the value of the constant in his Methodus Differentialis (1730), and de Moivre generously credited him. The approximation of factorials is still an active subject: computing n! for huge n is needed in combinatorics and cryptography. The thinking skill Use probability to prove something that is not about probability An exact probability, compared with an approximation, can give information about the numbers in the formula. This “probabilistic method” runs both ways. Here probability gave an estimate for factorials; Erdős used it to prove the existence of graphs ( Section 9.2 ). At university you will see probability used to prove theorems in analysis, number theory and combinatorics. Try this next Check the formula. Use Stirling’s formula to estimate 10! and 20! , and compare with the true values 3\,628\,800 and 2\,432\,902\,008\,176\,640\,000 . From (iii) to (ii). Show that Stirling’s formula in part (iii) implies the approximation in part (ii). Digits of 100! . Use log_10n! approx nlog_10frac ne + frac12log_10(2π n) to show that 100! has 158 digits. A tie in coin tossing. Use part (ii) to show that the probability of exactly 500 heads in 1000 tosses of a fair coin is about 0.025 . Further reading William Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications , Vol. 1 (Wiley), Chapter II, which proves Stirling’s formula. Ronald Graham, Donald Knuth & Oren Patashnik, Concrete Mathematics (Addison-Wesley), Chapter 9, on asymptotics. Stephen Stigler, The History of Statistics (Harvard University Press), on de Moivre and the birth of the normal curve.

title: The Truel
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Strategy and game theory Strength as a weakness The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 1995, Question 12 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/95-s2-q12 The hook Three people fight a duel with bread rolls. Cuthbert never misses, Bertie hits three times in five, and Algernon, the worst shot, only two times in five. Algernon throws first. Whom should he aim at? The surprising answer: nobody. He should throw his roll deliberately wide. The reason is strategic. While all three are in the game, Bertie and Cuthbert, the two dangerous throwers, aim at each other. If Algernon removes one of them, the survivor turns on him. By missing, he lets them fight it out, and then gets the first throw against whoever survives. In fact, with the best plan the worst shot becomes the most likely to win. This “truel” is a favourite example in game theory of how weakness can be an advantage. Before you start In a two-person duel, Percy throws first. Either he hits at once, or both miss and the situation repeats exactly. Write an equation for Percy’s probability of winning. Let P be Percy’s probability of winning. He hits at once with probability p ; otherwise (probability 1 - p ) Rodney throws, and misses with probability 1 - r , returning to the start. So P = p + (1 - p)(1 - r)P . Working it through Stage 1 The duel Solving, Pbigl(1 - (1 - p)(1 - r)bigr) = p , and 1 - (1 - p)(1 - r) = p + r - pr , so P = (p)/(p + r - pr). qed For Algernon ( p = frac25 ) against Bertie ( r = frac35 ), with Algernon throwing first, this is (2/5)/(2/5 + 3/5 - 6/25) = (10)/(19) ; with Bertie throwing first, Algernon wins with probability bigl(1 - frac35bigr)·(10)/(19) = (4)/(19) . Stage 2 Algernon’s three options In each case, who is left, and who throws next? Algernon hits Cuthbert. Bertie throws next, at Algernon. Algernon wins the duel with Bertie throwing first: probability (4)/(19) . Algernon hits Bertie. Cuthbert throws next, at Algernon, and never misses. Algernon’s chance is 0 . Algernon misses. Bertie throws at Cuthbert. With probability frac35 he hits, leaving Algernon and Bertie with Algernon to throw: Algernon wins with probability (10)/(19) . With probability frac25 Bertie misses, Cuthbert hits Bertie, and Algernon faces Cuthbert with one throw: he wins only if he hits, probability frac25 . Altogether, tfrac35·tfrac1019 + tfrac25·tfrac25 = tfrac619 + tfrac425 = tfrac150 + 76475 = tfrac226475 approx 0.476. Stage 3 Advice If Algernon aims at Cuthbert, he might hit (probability frac25 ) or miss. What is his overall chance? Compare with deliberately missing. Aiming at Cuthbert gives frac25·(4)/(19) + frac35·(226)/(475) = (200 + 678)/(2375) = (878)/(2375) approx 0.370 . Aiming at Bertie is worse still. Deliberately missing gives (226)/(475) approx 0.476 , the best. So Algernon should throw wide, and then his probability of winning is (226)/(475) . ■ Looking back Repeated situations give equations. The duel “starts again” after two misses, giving a linear equation for the winning probability. Think about the opponents’ responses. Each of Algernon’s options changes what Bertie and Cuthbert do next. Compare all options, including doing nothing. The best move was the one that looked worst. What’s really going on Strategy and game theory The truel shows the central idea of game theory : the best action depends on how the other players will respond. Hitting Cuthbert, the most dangerous opponent, is the obvious move, but it changes the game in a way that hurts Algernon. In this question Bertie’s and Cuthbert’s strategies are fixed (they aim at each other); in a full game-theoretic analysis each player would choose their own strategy, knowing that the others are doing the same. Such analyses, starting with the work of John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern in 1944 and John Nash in 1950, now underpin economics, evolutionary biology and political science. Strength as a weakness Who wins the truel? With Algernon’s best plan, the probabilities are (226)/(475) for Algernon, (135)/(475) for Bertie and (114)/(475) for Cuthbert. The best shot is the least likely to survive, because everyone with a choice aims at him. The same pattern appears in elections with several candidates, in competition between firms, and in nature, where the strongest competitor can be the first target. Martin Shubik, who introduced truels into game theory in the 1950s, used them to ask whether the fittest necessarily survive. The thinking skill Think one move ahead Before choosing an action, work out how it changes the situation for everyone else, and what they will do in response. At university, this becomes backward induction in game theory: analyse the end of the game first, then work back to decide the best opening move. Try this next Bertie and Cuthbert. Verify that, with Algernon missing deliberately, Bertie wins with probability (135)/(475) and Cuthbert with (114)/(475) . A better shot. If Algernon hit with probability a instead of frac25 , for which values of a is deliberately missing still his best first move? Should Bertie aim at Cuthbert? Given that Algernon misses deliberately, is it in Bertie’s interest to aim at Cuthbert rather than at Algernon? (Assume Cuthbert’s behaviour is unchanged.) A duel with a fixed number of throws. In a duel where each player has only two throws, find Percy’s probability of winning, and compare with the unlimited duel. Further reading D. Marc Kilgour & Steven Brams, “ The truel ” , Mathematics Magazine 70 (1997). An accessible survey of three-way duels. Avinash Dixit & Barry Nalebuff, Thinking Strategically (Norton). Game theory for a general reader, including the truel. Ken Binmore, Game Theory: A Very Short Introduction (Oxford University Press).

title: A Fair Decision from a Biased Coin
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Von Neumann’s trick Extracting randomness The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP I 2019, Question 11 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP I paper in OCR’s download of the 2019 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/696590-2019-past-papers.zip The hook You need to make a fair decision, but the only coin available is bent, and you do not know how biased it is.
