Can you still make a fair choice? John von Neumann’s answer, from 1951: toss it twice. If it comes up HT, choose the hotel; if TH, the tea shop; if HH or TT, toss twice more. Since HT and TH both have probability pq , the decision is perfectly fair, whatever p is. The procedure in this question is the opposite: it decides on HH and TT, which is quick but unfair (hotel with probability (p^2)/(p^2 + q^2) ). The question shows that it never takes long, whatever the coin. Comparing the two procedures shows a basic trade-off in generating randomness: speed against fairness. Before you start In one round, what is the probability of a decision? Of no decision? What is the largest value 2pq can take? A decision is made if the coins agree, with probability p^2 + q^2 ; otherwise, with probability 2pq , they continue. Since pq = p(1 - p) ≤ frac14 (with equality at p = frac12 ), we have 2pq ≤ frac12 . Working it through Stage 1 Decision on the n th round Rounds are independent. A decision on the n th round needs n - 1 rounds of disagreement followed by agreement: P(decision on round n) = (2pq)^n-1(p^2 + q^2). qed Stage 2 Decision by round n What is the probability of no decision in the first n rounds? No decision in n rounds has probability (2pq)^n ≤ bigl(frac12bigr)^n , so a decision by round n has probability at least 1 - (1)/(2^n) , whatever p . ■ Stage 3 Three people After a first round with two heads and one tail, the third person turns the tail over to a head. What must happen in round two for a decision? And after two tails and one head? Round one decides with probability p^3 + q^3 . Otherwise two coins agree and one differs. If the majority showed heads (probability 3p^2q ), the odd coin is turned to heads, and the round-two decision needs the other two to toss heads: probability p^2 (all tails is now impossible). Similarly with a tails majority (probability 3pq^2 ), a decision needs two tails: q^2 . So P(decision by round 2) = p^3 + q^3 + 3p^2q· p^2 + 3pq^2· q^2. Write everything in terms of s = pq . (Use p + q = 1 .) We have p^3 + q^3 = (p + q)^3 - 3pq(p + q) = 1 - 3s , and 3p^4q + 3pq^4 = 3s(p^3 + q^3) = 3s(1 - 3s) . So P = 1 - 3s + 3s - 9s^2 = 1 - 9s^2 ≥ 1 - (9)/(16) = (7)/(16), since s ≤ frac14 . ■ Looking back Complements. “At least once by round n ” was easiest as 1 - (“never in n rounds”). Bound the worst case. The unknown p was handled by the inequality pq ≤ frac14 . Symmetric functions. Expressions symmetric in p and q simplify when written in terms of p + q = 1 and pq . What’s really going on Von Neumann’s trick The procedure in the question is quick but biased. Von Neumann’s procedure is fair: toss twice, decide on HT or TH, repeat on HH or TT. Each attempt succeeds with probability 2pq , so it takes on average (1)/(2pq) attempts, which is slow when the coin is very biased (Figure 12.9.1). The question’s procedure decides with probability p^2 + q^2 ≥ frac12 per round, but its answer favours the hotel when p > frac12 . Extracting randomness Von Neumann’s trick is the first randomness extractor : a procedure that turns imperfect randomness into perfect randomness. It wastes a lot (each pair of tosses yields at most one fair bit, and often none), and better methods recycle the discarded HH and TT pairs to extract almost all the randomness the coin contains, which is measured by its entropy -plog_2p - qlog_2q bits per toss. Extractors are used in computers’ hardware random number generators, which harvest unpredictable but biased physical noise and must turn it into unbiased bits for cryptography. Von Neumann and random numbers John von Neumann described the trick in a 1951 paper, “Various techniques used in connection with random digits”, written when he and his colleagues were running some of the first computer simulations (the “Monte Carlo method”) for the design of nuclear weapons. In the same paper he made a famous remark about generating random numbers by arithmetic: “Anyone who considers arithmetical methods of producing random digits is, of course, in a state of sin.” The thinking skill Use symmetry to cancel an unknown When a parameter is unknown, look for events whose probabilities are equal whatever its value, and base decisions on those. HT and TH have the same probability pq , so comparing them removes p altogether. At university, the same idea appears in statistics as pivotal quantities and in the design of experiments, where randomisation and symmetry cancel out unknown effects. Try this next Expected rounds. Find the expected number of rounds for the procedure in part (i), and for von Neumann’s procedure. For which p is von Neumann’s procedure slower? Fair three-way choice. Using a biased coin, devise a procedure that chooses one of three options, each with probability exactly frac13 . A biased die from a fair coin. Using a fair coin, devise a procedure that simulates a coin with probability of heads exactly frac13 . What is the expected number of tosses? Three people again. In part (ii), what is the probability that they go to the hotel, as a function of p ? Is the procedure fair when p = frac12 ? Further reading John von Neumann, “Various techniques used in connection with random digits” , National Bureau of Standards Applied Mathematics Series 12 (1951). Short and famous. Donald Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming , Vol. 2 (Addison-Wesley), Chapter 3, on random numbers. Michael Mitzenmacher & Eli Upfal, Probability and Computing (Cambridge University Press), on extracting randomness and entropy.

title: What We Have Learned
headings: 1. What exactly is the question? 2. What is the clever way in? 3. What happens in the long run? 4. A toolkit for probability Where next
text: We began by saying that uncertainty can be reasoned about exactly, but intuition cannot. We asked three questions: what exactly is the question, what is the clever way in, and what happens in the long run? Here is what the chapter’s twenty-five questions showed. 1. What exactly is the question? The first four sections were about getting the question right. “Given that a numbered disc is taken” and “given that the disc numbered 3 is taken” gave different answers ( Section 12.1 ). A 90\% accurate test for a rare disease left a positive patient only 9\% likely to be ill, because base rates matter ( Section 12.2 ). “A random chord” had no expected length until we said how it was chosen ( Section 12.3 ), and the broken stick ( Section 12.21 ) made the same point. And “independent” turned out to have several meanings: events can be independent in pairs but not all together ( Section 12.4 ), and uncorrelated variables need not be independent. In every case, the cure was to write down exactly which outcomes are possible and how they arise. 2. What is the clever way in? Many questions had a long calculation and a short insight. Symmetry. Two seats that the process cannot tell apart ( Section 12.5 ); “more heads” and “more tails” as complementary mirror images ( Section 12.6 ); every pair of players equally likely to contest any match ( Section 12.7 ); HT and TH equally likely for any coin ( Section 12.9 ); a radially symmetric point whose direction is uniform ( Section 12.22 ). Indicators and linearity. Counting pairs ( Section 12.4 ), knots ( Section 12.10 ) and matches ( Section 12.7 ) as sums of indicators gave means and variances without the full distribution. States and first-step analysis. Penney’s game ( Section 12.8 ), the rabbit warren and Professor Ecks ( Section 12.16 ), and the extinction of family names ( Section 12.15 ) were all solved by conditioning on the next step. Strategy. The worst shot in the truel should miss on purpose ( Section 12.13 ); a randomised strategy cannot be exploited ( Section 12.14 ); rejecting the first frac1e of the candidates is optimal ( Section 12.12 ). 3. What happens in the long run? The last parts of the chapter followed randomness over time and across many trials. A branching process either dies out or explodes, and even an exploding one can die by chance ( Section 12.15 ). A Markov chain settles into a stationary distribution and forgets its past ( Section 12.16 ). Exponential waiting times have no memory at all ( Section 12.18 ). Averages usually settle down, but not for the Cauchy distribution, which has no mean ( Section 12.22 ). Sums of many independent effects become normal, by the central limit theorem ( Section 12.24 ), and that normality hides Stirling’s formula for n! ( Section 12.23 ). Maxima behave differently again: they grow like n with a spread that does not grow at all ( Section 12.25 ). And the constants e , π and γ kept appearing, in cups and stamps, needles and loops. 4. A toolkit for probability Method Where you used it Write down the sample space Conditioning (12.1); Bertrand (12.3) Bayes’ theorem and odds Base rates (12.2); Markov reversal (12.16) Symmetry 12.5, 12.6, 12.7, 12.22 Indicators and linearity 12.4, 12.7, 12.10 First-step analysis Penney (12.8); warren (12.16); branching (12.15) Complement and bounds Fair decisions (12.9) Series for expectations Stamps and e (12.11) Parametrise and optimise Secretary (12.12) Game-theoretic reasoning Truel (12.13); mixed strategies (12.14) Counting paths to the end Matchboxes (12.17) Distribution function first 12.18, 12.19, 12.25 Probability as area or integral Buffon (12.20); broken stick (12.21) Normal approximation Stirling (12.23); CLT (12.24) Where next Chapter 13 turns from probability to statistics: estimating unknown quantities from data, starting with Section 13.1 . The counting problems of Section 9.8 , Section 9.9 and Section 9.11 are the combinatorial side of this chapter. Markov chains use the linear algebra of Chapter 7, and the fixed points of branching processes the dynamics of Section 8.7 . If you want to go further before university Joseph Blitzstein & Jessica Hwang, Introduction to Probability : a superb first course, free online, with video lectures. Geoffrey Grimmett & Dominic Welsh, Probability: An Introduction : concise and rigorous, at first-year level. Frederick Mosteller, Fifty Challenging Problems in Probability : classic puzzles with full solutions. David Spiegelhalter, The Art of Statistics and The Art of Uncertainty : probability and risk in the real world. Laplace called probability common sense reduced to calculation. This chapter has shown that the calculation is often needed precisely because common sense fails, and that the best calculations do more than produce numbers: they explain. A symmetry, an indicator, a well-chosen state or a limit theorem turns a puzzle into an insight, and those insights are what a university course in probability is built on.

title: Answers to Try This Next
headings: 13.1 Reading the Headlines 13.2 Counting Voles 13.3 The German Tank Problem 13.4 Mean or Median? 13.5 Asking Awkward Questions 13.6 Errors That Add Up 13.7 Manufacturing Correlation
text: These are brief answers and hints, not full solutions: they give the result and the key step, so that you can check your own work. Try each exercise properly before looking. 13.1 Reading the Headlines 1 - sum_k=0^6e^-2.96(2.96^k)/(k!) approx 0.0315 , so seven or more deaths happen on about 11 days a year. P(X ≥ 9) approx 0.0035 : about one day a year. Deaths are 150K with K Poisson with mean 1.2 : mean 180 , variance 150^2 × 1.2 = 27\,000 , standard deviation about 164 . A year with 125 deaths or fewer is a year with no crashes, which has probability e^-1.2 approx 0.30 : entirely ordinary. But exactly 125 deaths is impossible in this model, since deaths come only in multiples of 150 . The mean and standard deviation do not show this: clustering makes the distribution lumpy, with all its probability on 0 , 150 , 300 , and so on. z = (1349.5 - 1080)/(33) approx 8.2 : a probability of order 10^-16 . A steady rate cannot explain 1350 ; something really changed (or the way deaths were counted did). For example: (i) “Totals alone cannot say whether flying or walking is safer”; (ii) “Air deaths in 1990 within the normal range”; (iii) “Seven pedestrian deaths on Tuesday: a bad day, but one that happens about eleven times a year”; (iv) “Pedestrian deaths up sharply in 1990: cause must be investigated”. 13.2 Counting Voles fracp_Np_N-1 = ((N - M)(N - C))/(N(N - M - C + R)) , which is at least 1 exactly when NR ≤ MC . So p_N increases up to N = (MC)/(R) and then decreases, and the maximum is at its integer part. Count committees of c from a women and b men by the number j of women: binom ajbinombc - j for each j . (d)/(dp)bigl(h p + (n - h)(1 - p)bigr) = frac hp - (n - h)/(1 - p) = 0 gives p = frac hn . With R = 0 , p_N increases for ever, and the estimate is infinite. The method only works if the second sample contains enough marked animals; with few recaptures the estimate is very unstable. 13.3 The German Tank Problem With M the maximum, E(M) = (nN)/(n + 1) and Var(M) = (nN^2)/((n + 1)^2(n + 2)) , so E(M - N)^2 = (2N^2)/((n + 1)(n + 2)) . This is (2n)/(n + 1) times Var(Z_1) = (N^2)/(n(n + 2)) : worse. The best multiple is c = (NE(M))/(E(M^2)) = (n + 2)/(n + 1) , with mean squared error (N^2)/((n + 1)^2) , slightly better than Z_1 . E(min) = (N)/(n + 1) , and min has the same variance as M , so Varbigl((n + 1)minbigr) = (nN^2)/(n + 2) . This does not shrink as n grows: a poor estimator. The maximum is at most m exactly when all k numbers come from \1, ldots, m\ . For k = 1 the estimator is 2X - 1 , with mean 2 · (N + 1)/(2) - 1 = N . 98 + (98)/(5) - 1 = 116.6 : about 117 tanks. 13.4 Mean or Median? Choose which value is the median ( 2n + 1 ways) and which n of the rest are below it ( binom2nn ways). The probability is (2n + 1)binom2nny^n(1 - y)^n\,δ y = ((2n + 1)!)/((n!)^2)y^n(1 - y)^n\,δ y . Var(Y) = (1)/(4(2n + 3)) = (1)/(20) and Var(bar X) = (1)/(12(2n + 1)) = (1)/(36) . The mean is better. Var(max) = Var(min) = (m)/((m + 1)^2(m + 2)) and Cov(max, min) = (1)/((m + 1)^2(m + 2)) , giving (1)/(2(m + 1)(m + 2)) . This shrinks like (1)/(m^2) , much faster than the mean’s (1)/(12m) : for uniform data the extremes carry the information, as with the tanks. The mean is about 18.6 , wrecked by one typing error; the median is 10.1 , unaffected. 13.5 Asking Awkward Questions Let t = ap + bq , the probability of a true answer. “Yes” has probability frac12t + frac12(1 - t) = frac12 , so P(heads mid yes) = t , which is frac12 exactly when 2t = 1 . If the same twin answers twice, “yes” then “no” has probability pa(1 - a) + qb(1 - b) whether the coin showed heads or tails, so the posterior is frac12 . Two “yes” answers have probabilities pa^2 + qb^2 (heads) and p(1 - a)^2 + q(1 - b)^2 (tails), which are equal exactly when 2(ap + bq) = 1 . P(yes) = frac34π + frac14(1 - π) , so hatπ = (0.4 - 0.25)/(0.5) = 0.3 . The standard error is fracsqrt0.4 × 0.6/4000.5 approx 0.049 . E(Y^2) = sum_cP(C = c)bigl(Var(Y mid c) + E(Y mid c)^2bigr) ; subtracting E(Y)^2 = bigl(sum_cP(C = c)E(Y mid c)bigr)^2 gives E(Var(Y mid C)) + Var(E(Y mid C)) . Z_2 is close to frac n6 (heads) or (5n)/(6) (tails), each with probability frac12 . So P(Z_2 > frac n2) → frac12 , although Z_2 is almost never near frac n2 . 13.6 Errors That Add Up Each truncation error is uniform on (-1, 0] ; adding frac12 to each makes it uniform on (-frac12, frac12] , exactly like rounding. So the corrected VOZ is as good as LEP. Each error is uniform on (-0.05, 0.05) , with variance (0.1^2)/(12) , so the total has standard deviation sqrt10\,000 × 0.01/12 approx 2.9 . 3000 × 250 × 0.0005 = 375 points. For two errors, 1 - |x| on [-1, 1] . For three: frac34 - x^2 for |x| ≤ frac12 and frac12bigl(frac32 - |x|bigr)^2 for frac12 ≤ |x| ≤ frac32 , already close to a normal curve. 13.7 Manufacturing Correlation For standardised variables, Var(X_1 + X_2 + X_3) = 3 + 6rho ≥ 0 , so rho ≥ -frac12 . For n variables, n + n(n - 1)rho ≥ 0 gives rho ≥ -(1)/(n - 1) . With b = fracrho_23 - rho_12rho_13sqrt1 - rho_12^2 , (1 - rho_12^2)(1 - rho_13^2 - b^2) = 1 - rho_12^2 - rho_13^2 - rho_23^2 + 2rho_12rho_13rho_23 = det R . Since 1 - rho_12^2 > 0 , the two conditions are equivalent. Var = frac14(0.04 + 0.09 + 0.12rho) : standard deviations 0.05 , 0.18 and 0.25 for rho = -1 , 0 , 1 . Unless the shares are perfectly correlated, the mix is less risky than the average of the two risks ( 0.25 ). Z_2 = dfracY_2 - rho_12Y_1sqrt1 - rho_12^2 .

title: Asking Awkward Questions
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Randomised response Differential privacy The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 2023, Question 11 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP II paper in OCR’s download of the 2023 STEP papers (a zip file): www.ocr.org.uk/Images/707102-2023-past-papers.zip The hook How do you find out what fraction of students have cheated in an exam, or of employees have stolen from work? Ask them directly and many will lie. In 1965 the statistician Stanley Warner invented an ingenious solution, randomised response . Each person secretly tosses a coin or rolls a die, and the outcome decides whether they answer the sensitive question truthfully or answer its opposite. The interviewer never knows which, so no individual answer is incriminating; yet, because the randomisation probabilities are known, the overall proportion can still be estimated. This question explores the mathematics behind it. Randomising each person independently (part (ii)) gives a well-behaved total that pins down the proportion. Randomising everyone with a single coin toss (part (iii)) produces a total with the same mean but a completely different, two-humped distribution, which tells us almost nothing. Where you put the randomness matters. Before you start Y is X_1 with probability p and X_2 with probability q . What is E(Y) ? What is E(Y^2) ? Conditioning on which variable is chosen, E(Y) = pμ_1 + qμ_2 , and E(Y^2) = p\,E(X_1^2) + q\,E(X_2^2) = p(σ_1^2 + μ_1^2) + q(σ_2^2 + μ_2^2) . Working it through Stage 1 The variance of a mixture Var(Y) = p(σ_1^2 + μ_1^2) + q(σ_2^2 + μ_2^2) - (pμ_1 + qμ_2)^2. The μ terms are pμ_1^2 + qμ_2^2 - p^2μ_1^2 - 2pqμ_1μ_2 - q^2μ_2^2 = pqμ_1^2 + pqμ_2^2 - 2pqμ_1μ_2 , using p - p^2 = pq and q - q^2 = pq . So Var(Y) = pσ_1^2 + qσ_2^2 + pq(μ_1 - μ_2)^2. qed The variance of a mixture is the average variance within the components, plus the variance between their means. Stage 2 Independent randomisation What is P(B = 1) ? Are the n values of B independent? P(B = 1) = frac12·frac16 + frac12·frac56 = frac12 . The n values are independent, each with success probability frac12 , so Z_1 sim B(n, frac12) , with mean frac n2 and standard deviation (sqrt n)/(2) . Within 10\% of the mean means |Z_1 - frac n2| < (n)/(20) . In standard units, this is |Z| < (n/20)/(sqrt n/2) = (sqrt n)/(10) , which tends to infinity, so the probability tends to 1 . ■ Stage 3 One coin for everybody Now one coin toss decides for all n dice. Given heads, what is the distribution of Z_2 ? Given tails? Use part (i). Given heads, Z_2 sim B(n, frac16) : mean frac n6 , variance (5n)/(36) . Given tails, Z_2 sim B(n, frac56) : mean (5n)/(6) , variance (5n)/(36) . By part (i) with p = q = frac12 , E(Z_2) = frac n2, qquad Var(Z_2) = (5n)/(36) + frac14Bigl((4n)/(6)Bigr)^2 = (5n)/(36) + (n^2)/(9). Where is most of the probability? Is there much near the mean frac n2 ? Z_2 has two humps, near frac n6 and (5n)/(6) , each of width about sqrt n (Figure 13.5.1), and almost nothing in between. A normal distribution with the same mean and variance would be a single hump centred at frac n2 , exactly where Z_2 almost never is. For Z_2 to be within 10\% of frac n2 , a B(n, frac16) or B(n, frac56) variable must lie in [0.45n, 0.55n] . For B(n, frac16) that is at least 0.28n above its mean, which is about (0.28n)/(0.37sqrt n) approx 0.75sqrt n standard deviations, so the probability tends to 0 ; similarly for B(n, frac56) . ■ Looking back Condition on the hidden choice. The mixture’s mean and variance came from conditioning on which component was chosen. Variance within plus variance between. The extra term pq(μ_1 - μ_2)^2 measured the spread between the two components. Mean and variance are not the whole story. Z_2 had the same mean as Z_1 , but a completely different shape. What’s really going on Randomised response In Warner’s scheme, each respondent answers “Do you belong to group A ?” with probability p , and “Do you not belong to group A ?” with probability 1 - p , choosing privately. If a fraction π belong to A , the probability of a “yes” is λ = pπ + (1 - p)(1 - π), so from the observed fraction of yeses, hatλ , we can estimate hatπ = (hatλ - (1 - p))/(2p - 1) (provided p ≠ frac12 ). Part (ii) of the question is exactly this, with each person’s own die deciding. The price of privacy is precision: dividing by 2p - 1 inflates the variance, so a randomised survey needs more respondents than a direct one. But each person randomises independently, so the law of large numbers works. Part (iii) shows what goes wrong if the randomisation is shared: the uncertainty about the single coin never averages out. Differential privacy Randomised response is the ancestor of differential privacy , a mathematical definition of privacy introduced by Cynthia Dwork and colleagues in 2006: a procedure is private if adding or removing any one person’s data changes the probability of any output by at most a small factor. Technology companies use it to collect usage statistics, and the United States Census Bureau used it for the 2020 census, adding carefully calibrated random noise to published figures so that no individual’s answers could be reconstructed. The law of total variance The identity in part (i) is a special case of the law of total variance : Var(Y) = Ebigl(Var(Y mid C)bigr) + Varbigl(E(Y mid C)bigr) , where C is the hidden choice. It underlies the analysis of variance (ANOVA), introduced by Ronald Fisher in the 1920s for agricultural experiments at Rothamsted, which splits the variation in crop yields into the part explained by fertilisers or varieties and the part left unexplained. The thinking skill Look at the whole distribution, not just its summaries A mean and variance describe a single-humped distribution well, but can be badly misleading for a mixture. Ask where the probability actually lies. At university, mixture models are used to describe populations made of several groups, and the law of total variance is a standard tool in statistics, from survey design to hierarchical models. Try this next The twins. Try STEP II 2005, Question 12 . It is a randomised-response puzzle in disguise: when does an answer tell you nothing about the coin? Estimating π . In a Warner survey with p = frac34 , 400 people answer and 160 say yes. Estimate the proportion π in group A , and find the approximate standard error of your estimate. Total variance. Prove the law of total variance for a discrete hidden variable C with several values. Shared coins. In part (iii), what is the probability that Z_2 > frac n2 ? Explain why, for large n , it is close to frac12 even though Z_2 is almost never close to frac n2 . Further reading Stanley Warner, “ Randomized response: a survey technique for eliminating evasive answer bias ” , Journal of the American Statistical Association 60 (1965). Cynthia Dwork & Aaron Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy (free online). The modern theory; the first chapters are accessible. David Spiegelhalter, The Art of Statistics (Pelican), on surveys and their pitfalls.

title: Manufacturing Correlation
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on The Cholesky decomposition Which correlations are possible? The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 2010, Question 13 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/10-s3-q13 The hook A bank wants to know how likely it is to lose money on a portfolio of shares. Share prices move together: when one falls, others tend to fall too. To simulate thousands of possible futures, the bank must generate random numbers that are correlated in exactly the right way. How do you manufacture random variables with prescribed correlations, starting from independent ones? This question gives the recipe, step by step, for three variables. Each new variable is a combination of the previous independent ingredients, plus a fresh independent ingredient to make up the variance. The construction is a famous piece of linear algebra in disguise, the Cholesky decomposition , and it also reveals a hidden constraint: not every set of correlations is possible. A note on the syllabus Covariance and correlation were removed from the STEP specification in 2019. The covariance is Cov(U, V) = E(UV) - E(U)E(V) ; it is zero for independent variables, and it is linear in each argument: Cov(aU + bV, W) = a\,Cov(U, W) + b\,Cov(V, W) . Also Var(U) = Cov(U, U) . The correlation always lies between -1 and 1 . Before you start Z_1 and Z_2 are independent. What is their covariance, and so their correlation? Independent variables satisfy E(Z_1Z_2) = E(Z_1)\,E(Z_2) . So the covariance is 0 , and Corr(Z_1, Z_2) = 0 . Working it through Stage 1 Two variables E(Y_2) = 0 . Since Z_1 and Z_2 are independent with variance 1 , Var(Y_2) = rho_12^2 + (1 - rho_12^2) = 1, qquad Cov(Y_1, Y_2) = Covbigl(Z_1, rho_12Z_1 + sqrt1 - rho_12^2\,Z_2bigr) = rho_12. Both variances are 1 , so Corr(Y_1, Y_2) = rho_12 . ■ Think of Z_1 and Z_2 as perpendicular unit vectors. Where is Y_2 ? What is the cosine of the angle between Y_1 and Y_2 ? Y_2 = rho_12Z_1 + sqrt1 - rho_12^2\,Z_2 is a unit vector making angle θ with Z_1 = Y_1 , where cosθ = rho_12 . Correlation is the cosine of the angle between the variables, viewed as vectors (Figure 13.7.1). Stage 2 The third variable Write down the three conditions Var(Y_3) = 1 , Cov(Y_1, Y_3) = rho_13 , Cov(Y_2, Y_3) = rho_23 in terms of a , b , c . Using linearity and independence: a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 1, qquad a = rho_13, qquad rho_12a + sqrt1 - rho_12^2\,b = rho_23. So a = rho_13, qquad b = fracrho_23 - rho_12rho_13sqrt1 - rho_12^2, qquad c = sqrt1 - rho_13^2 - frac(rho_23 - rho_12rho_13)^21 - rho_12^2. qed (Taking the non-negative square root, as c ≥ 0 .) Stage 3 Any means and variances Scaling and shifting do not change correlations, so X_i = μ_i + σ_iY_i qquad (i = 1, 2, 3) have means μ_i , variances σ_i^2 and correlations rho_ij . ■ The formula for c needs the quantity under the square root to be non-negative. Try rho_12 = rho_13 = rho_23 = -0.6 . What goes wrong, and why does it make sense that three variables cannot all be strongly negatively correlated with each other? Looking back Build up one variable at a time. Each new variable copied the right amount of the previous ingredients and added a fresh, independent one. Covariance is linear. All the conditions became simple equations in the coefficients. Correlation is a cosine. Thinking of standardised variables as unit vectors makes correlations into angles. What’s really going on The Cholesky decomposition In matrix form, the construction says Y = LZ with a lower triangular matrix L = beginpmatrix 1 & 0 & 0 \\ rho_12 & sqrt1 - rho_12^2 & 0 \\ a & b & c endpmatrix, and the correlation matrix of Y is R = LL^mathsf T . Writing a symmetric matrix as LL^mathsf T is the Cholesky decomposition , found by the French military engineer André-Louis Cholesky around 1910 for solving the equations of geodetic surveys (published after his death in the First World War). It works whenever R is positive definite , and the computation is exactly what we did by hand: each row is solved in turn. It is the standard way to simulate correlated variables in finance, engineering and climate modelling. Which correlations are possible? The number under the square root for c must be non-negative. Multiplying out, the condition is 1 - rho_12^2 - rho_13^2 - rho_23^2 + 2rho_12rho_13rho_23 ≥ 0, which is the condition that the determinant of the correlation matrix is non-negative. Geometrically: three unit vectors with pairwise angles θ_ij (where cosθ_ij = rho_ij ) must actually fit together in space. If rho_12 = rho_13 = rho_23 = -0.6 , the angles are all about 127^circ , and three vectors at 127^circ to each other would need angles summing to more than 360^circ : impossible. In general a matrix can be a correlation matrix only if it is positive semi-definite, all its eigenvalues non-negative ( Section 7.2 ). When correlations are estimated separately from incomplete data, this can fail, and statisticians must find the nearest valid correlation matrix, a problem solved by Nicholas Higham in 2002. Galton, Pearson and correlation Francis Galton introduced correlation in 1888, while studying how the heights of parents and children are related, and Karl Pearson gave the product moment formula used in this question in 1896. Galton also noticed regression to the mean ( Section 13.1 ). Pearson founded the world’s first university statistics department, at University College London, in 1911. The warning that “correlation does not imply causation” is almost as old as correlation itself. The thinking skill Construct step by step, using fresh independent ingredients To build objects with prescribed relationships, add them one at a time, each a combination of what came before plus something new and independent. This is the Gram–Schmidt process of linear algebra, run in reverse, and the Cholesky decomposition. At university it appears in least squares, in the theory of multivariate normal distributions and in the simulation of random processes. Try this next Impossible correlations. Show that three random variables cannot all have pairwise correlation rho unless rho ≥ -frac12 . What is the corresponding statement for n variables? Check the determinant. Show that 1 - rho_13^2 - b^2 ≥ 0 is equivalent to det R ≥ 0 , where R is the 3 × 3 correlation matrix. Portfolio risk. Two shares have returns with standard deviations σ_1 = 0.2 and σ_2 = 0.3 and correlation rho . Find the standard deviation of a portfolio half in each, for rho = -1 , 0 and 1 . What does diversification achieve? Recover the ingredients. Given Y_1 , Y_2 as in the question, express Z_2 in terms of Y_1 and Y_2 . (This is the Gram–Schmidt step.) Further reading Gilbert Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra (Wellesley-Cambridge), on positive definite matrices and the Cholesky factorisation. Paul Glasserman, Monte Carlo Methods in Financial Engineering (Springer). Simulating correlated variables in practice; advanced but the early chapters are readable. Theodore Porter, Karl Pearson: The Scientific Life in a Statistical Age (Princeton University Press).

title: Errors That Add Up
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Bias and variance Floating point The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 1993, Question 15 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/93-s2-q15 The hook In 1982 the Vancouver Stock Exchange launched a new index, starting at 1000 . Every time a share price changed, the index was recalculated and truncated to three decimal places. Each truncation lost on average 0.0005 , which seems negligible. But there were about 3000 recalculations a day, and after twenty-two months the index stood at around 520 , even though the market had risen. When it was recomputed correctly, overnight it jumped to about 1100 . This question explains what happened. Truncation errors all point the same way, so they add up steadily, in proportion to the number of operations. Rounding errors point both ways and largely cancel: they grow only like the square root of the number of operations, the random-walk behaviour that the central limit theorem ( Section 12.24 ) predicts. Before you start If a number’s fractional part U is uniform on [0, 1) , what is the error when it is truncated? When it is rounded? What are the mean and variance of each? Truncation replaces a by lfloor arfloor , an error (true minus approximate) of U , uniform on [0, 1) : mean frac12 , variance (1)/(12) . Rounding gives an error uniform on (-frac12, frac12] : mean 0 , variance (1)/(12) . Working it through Stage 1 The total errors The total error after 1500 numbers is the sum of 1500 independent errors, approximately normal by the central limit theorem: LEP (rounding): mean 0 , variance (1500)/(12) = 125 , standard deviation sqrt125 approx 11.18 . VOZ (truncation): mean (1500)/(2) = 750 , the same standard deviation 11.18 . Stage 2 The probability of a large error For LEP, what is P(|E| > 15) with E sim N(0, 125) ? For VOZ, where is the error almost certainly? For LEP, (15)/(11.18) approx 1.342 , so P(|E| > 15) approx 2bigl(1 - Phi(1.342)bigr) approx 2 × 0.090 = 0.18. For VOZ, the error is about 750 11 ; the probability that it is less than 15 in magnitude is essentially zero, so P(|E| > 15) approx 1 . ■ Stage 3 How many additions? After n additions, LEP’s error has standard deviation sqrtn/12 . When is P(|E| < 10) ≥ 0.9 ? We need frac10sqrtn/12 ≥ 1.645 (since P(|Z| < 1.645) = 0.9 ), that is (n)/(12) ≤ bigl((10)/(1.645)bigr)^2 approx 36.95 , so n ≤ 443 . LEP can perform about 443 additions. ■ Looking back Model each error. Uniform fractional parts gave each error a simple distribution. Add means and variances. Means add (giving the bias frac n2 ) and, for independent errors, so do variances. Normal approximation. The central limit theorem turned a sum of 1500 uniform errors into a normal distribution. What’s really going on Bias and variance Truncation is biased : its errors have non-zero mean, and bias accumulates linearly. Rounding is unbiased , and its errors behave like a random walk, growing like sqrt n . After a million operations, the difference is between an error of order 500\,000 and one of order 300 . This is the same distinction as between a systematic error in an experiment (a miscalibrated instrument) and random measurement error: averaging many measurements reduces random error but does nothing to systematic error. Floating point Every computer stores real numbers to limited precision, and every arithmetic operation rounds its result. Modern computers follow the IEEE 754 standard, which rounds to the nearest representable number, with ties broken towards an even last digit precisely so that rounding is unbiased on average. Even so, careless summation of many numbers can lose accuracy; William Kahan’s compensated summation algorithm (1965) keeps track of the lost low-order digits and adds them back. In the Gulf War in 1991, a Patriot missile battery failed to intercept an incoming missile because its clock counted time in tenths of a second, a number that cannot be stored exactly in binary; after 100 hours of operation the truncation error had grown to about a third of a second, enough to misjudge the target’s position by over half a kilometre. The Vancouver index The Vancouver Stock Exchange index was created in January 1982 with a value of 1000.000 . By November 1983 it had fallen to about 524 , despite a generally rising market. Consultants found that the index was being recalculated thousands of times a day and truncated (not rounded) to three decimal places each time. Recomputed correctly over a weekend, the index reopened at about 1098 . The episode is a standard warning in courses on numerical computation. The thinking skill Separate systematic from random error Errors with a consistent sign accumulate linearly; independent errors with mean zero accumulate like a square root. Identify which kind you have. At university, numerical analysis studies how errors propagate through calculations, and statistics distinguishes bias from variance; the “bias–variance trade-off” is central to modern machine learning. Try this next VOZ corrected. If VOZ adds frac n2 to its answer at the end, what is the distribution of its error? Is it now as good as LEP? Rounding to one decimal place. If numbers are rounded to one decimal place, with uniformly distributed discarded digits, find the standard deviation of the total error in adding 10\,000 numbers. The Vancouver index. If the index was recalculated 3000 times a day and each truncation lost on average 0.0005 , how much would it lose in a year of 250 trading days? The exact distribution. For the sum of two rounding errors, find the exact density (a triangle). For three, sketch it. How quickly does it start to look normal? Further reading Nicholas Higham, Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms (SIAM). The authoritative book on rounding errors; the opening chapter is accessible. David Goldberg, “ What every computer scientist should know about floating-point arithmetic ” , ACM Computing Surveys 23 (1991). A classic, free online. Tim Harford, How to Make the World Add Up (Bridge Street), on systematic errors in data.

title: The German Tank Problem
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Sufficiency The discrete version The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP III 1998, Question 14 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/98-s3-q14 The hook During the Second World War, Allied intelligence wanted to know how many tanks Germany was producing. Spies’ reports suggested about 1400 a month. Statisticians took a different approach: captured tanks carried serial numbers on their gearboxes and other parts, and serial numbers are, in effect, a random sample from 1, 2, ldots, N . From the numbers alone, they estimated production at about 250 a month. In the figures usually quoted, German records examined after the war gave 245 . The statisticians had been far more accurate than the spies. This question compares two ways of estimating N from serial numbers. Both are right on average. But one uses the data much more efficiently than the other, and working out which leads to the central idea of estimation theory: among estimators that are correct on average, prefer the one that varies least. Before you start If M is the largest of n independent uniform values on [0, N] , what is P(M ≤ m) ? M ≤ m exactly when every X_i ≤ m , so P(M ≤ m) = bigl(frac mNbigr)^n for 0 ≤ m ≤ N (compare Section 12.25 ). Differentiating, M has density fracnm^n-1N^n . Working it through Stage 1 Both are unbiased For M : E(M) = int_0^N m·fracnm^n-1N^n\,dm = (n)/(n + 1)N, qquadsoqquad E(Z_1) = (n + 1)/(n)·(n)/(n + 1)N = N. For the mean: each X_i has mean frac N2 , so E(Z_2) = frac2n· n·frac N2 = N . ■ Both estimators are unbiased : on average, they give the right answer. The factor (n + 1)/(n) corrects for the fact that the largest serial number seen is always a little below N . Stage 2 Their variances Find E(M^2) and hence Var(M) . For Z_2 , what is the variance of a single uniform variable on [0, N] ? E(M^2) = int_0^N m^2·fracnm^n-1N^n\,dm = (n)/(n + 2)N^2 , so beginaligned Var(M) &= (n)/(n + 2)N^2 - (n^2)/((n + 1)^2)N^2 = (nN^2)/((n + 1)^2(n + 2)), \\ Var(Z_1) &= ((n + 1)^2)/(n^2)Var(M) = (N^2)/(n(n + 2)). endaligned A uniform variable on [0, N] has variance (N^2)/(12) , and the X_i are independent, so Var(Z_2) = (4)/(n^2)· n·(N^2)/(12) = (N^2)/(3n). qed Stage 3 Which is better? Compare (1)/(n(n + 2)) with (1)/(3n) . How do they behave as n grows? The ratio is (Var(Z_1))/(Var(Z_2)) = (3)/(n + 2) , which is less than 1 for n ≥ 2 (and equal for n = 1 , when the two estimators coincide). So Z_1 is better, and much better for large n : its standard deviation shrinks like frac1n , while that of Z_2 shrinks only like (1)/(sqrt n) (Figure 13.3.1). With n = 10 serial numbers, Z_1 has a standard deviation about 9\% of N , and Z_2 about 18\% . There is another reason to prefer Z_1 : Z_2 can be absurd. With the serial numbers 10 , 20 and 300 , Z_2 = frac23 · 330 = 220 , less than a serial number we have actually seen. Z_1 = frac43 · 300 = 400 can never be smaller than the largest observation. ■ Looking back Unbiasedness. Each estimator was scaled so that its expected value is exactly N . Compare variances. Among unbiased estimators, the one with smaller variance is more reliable. Use the most informative statistic. The maximum contains all the information about N that the sample holds; the mean wastes much of it. What’s really going on Sufficiency Why is the maximum so much better? Given the largest value M , the other values are just uniform on [0, M] , whatever N is: they carry no further information about N . The maximum is a sufficient statistic . A theorem of C. R. Rao and David Blackwell (1945–47) says that any unbiased estimator can be improved, or at least not made worse, by replacing it with its expected value given a sufficient statistic, and here that turns Z_2 into Z_1 . The Lehmann–Scheffé theorem then shows that Z_1 is the unbiased estimator with the smallest possible variance. Notice too that the variance of Z_1 falls like (1)/(n^2) , faster than the frac1n of most estimators: that happens because N is an endpoint of the distribution, and the data pile up against it. The discrete version Real serial numbers are whole numbers 1, 2, ldots, N , sampled without replacement. The best unbiased estimate is then hat N = m + frac mk - 1 , where m is the largest of k observed serial numbers: the maximum plus the average gap between observations. Using estimates of this kind, based mainly on the serial numbers of gearboxes and wheels, the Allied statisticians estimated German production at about 246 tanks a month, against the 245 later found in German records and the 1400 suggested by intelligence reports. Serial numbers in history The method has been used many times since, for example by analysts estimating how many units of a new consumer product had been made from the serial numbers of the first few sold. Manufacturers learned the lesson: many now encode serial numbers so that they cannot be read as a simple sequence. Richard Ruggles and Henry Brodie described the wartime work in the Journal of the American Statistical Association in 1947. The thinking skill Judge an estimator by its sampling distribution An estimator is a random variable. Ask whether it is right on average (bias) and how much it varies (variance), and prefer the one with smaller error. At university this leads to the theory of efficient estimation: the Cramér–Rao bound says how small the variance of an unbiased estimator can be, and sufficiency explains how to reach it. Try this next Mean squared error. The biased estimator M has E(M - N)^2 = Var(M) + bigl(E(M) - Nbigr)^2 . Compute it and compare with Var(Z_1) . Find the constant c that minimises E(cM - N)^2 . The minimum too. Show that (n + 1)min\X_i\ is also an unbiased estimator of N , and find its variance. Is it any good? The discrete formula. For serial numbers 1, ldots, N , sample k without replacement, with maximum m . Show that P(max ≤ m) = binom mkbig/binom Nk , and verify that m + frac mk - 1 is unbiased when k = 1 . Tanks. If 5 captured tanks have serial numbers 19 , 40 , 42 , 60 , 98 , estimate the number of tanks made. Further reading Richard Ruggles & Henry Brodie, “ An empirical approach to economic intelligence in World War II ” , Journal of the American Statistical Association 42 (1947). The original account. John Rice, Mathematical Statistics and Data Analysis (Duxbury), on bias, variance and sufficiency. David Spiegelhalter, The Art of Statistics (Pelican).

title: Reading the Headlines
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Signal and noise Regression to the mean The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP I 1992, Question 14 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/92-s1-q14 The hook Statistics is the science of learning from data, and its first lesson is that numbers do not speak for themselves. “Six times safer”, “alarming rise”, “carnage increasing”: every day, headlines turn numbers into claims, and the claims are often wrong, not because the numbers are false but because they are compared with the wrong thing, or because ordinary random variation is mistaken for a trend. This question has no formulas in it at all, which makes it unusual for STEP. It asks you to think like a statistician: what would we need to know to justify each headline, and how much variation should we expect by chance alone? The answers use the Poisson distribution ( Section 12.18 ), and the reasoning is the foundation of the rest of this chapter. Before you start If deaths occur independently and at random at a steady rate, how much should the yearly total vary? If the average is 1080 a year, what is a typical deviation from year to year? Counts of independent rare events are approximately Poisson, and a Poisson count with mean μ has variance μ and standard deviation sqrtμ . With μ = 1080 , the standard deviation is about 33 : yearly totals between about 1015 and 1145 would be unremarkable. Working it through Stage 1 “Six times safer to fly than to walk” 1080 pedestrian deaths and 180 air deaths per year. Six times what, exactly? The headline compares total deaths, but safety is about risk : deaths per unit of exposure. Almost everyone walks every day, while relatively few people fly, and then only occasionally. A fair comparison would use deaths per kilometre travelled, per hour of travel, or per journey, and these can give very different answers (air travel is extremely safe per kilometre, less impressively so per journey, since most air deaths happen at take-off and landing). The figures given cannot “prove” anything about relative safety. Also, “pedestrians killed in road accidents” is a narrow category; road deaths overall are much larger. Stage 2 “Our skies are safer: only 125 killed in 1990” Are air deaths like independent rare events? How variable would you expect the yearly total to be? Air deaths come in clusters: a single crash may kill hundreds of people. So the yearly total depends mainly on the number of crashes, which is small, and is extremely variable from year to year. One year with 125 deaths, against an average of 180 , is entirely consistent with no change at all: a single extra crash would have changed the figure completely. One year’s data cannot show a trend. Stage 3 “Road carnage increasing: 7 killed on Tuesday” On average, how many pedestrians are killed per day? If daily deaths are Poisson, how often would you see 7 or more in a day? The average is (1080)/(365) approx 2.96 pedestrian deaths per day. If daily counts are Poisson with this mean, P(≥ 7) approx 0.031 : about 11 days a year would have 7 or more pedestrian deaths purely by chance. (And “road carnage” presumably includes drivers and passengers too, making 7 road deaths in a day even less remarkable.) A single day says nothing about a trend. The headline picks an extreme value out of a highly variable series, a classic error. Stage 4 “Alarming rise: 1350 pedestrians killed in 1990” Compare 1350 with the Poisson standard deviation. Is this just chance? If not, what else could explain it, and does it justify “alarming rise”? This is the substantial part. Under a steady Poisson model, 1350 is 270 above the mean of 1080 , about 8 standard deviations: it is wildly unlikely to be chance. So something has probably changed. But the headline still overreaches, in several ways: A trend hidden by an average. The figure 1080 is an average over 16 years. If deaths rose steadily from about 900 in 1974 to about 1260 in 1989, the average would still be 1080 , and 1350 in 1990 would simply continue an existing trend, not a sudden “alarming” rise (Figure 13.1.1). We need the year-by-year figures. Exposure. Population growth, more walking, more traffic or an ageing population would all increase deaths without the roads becoming more dangerous per journey. A rate per head, or per kilometre walked, is the right measure. Definitions. A change in how deaths are recorded or classified (for example, how long after an accident a death is counted) can produce a jump. Over-dispersion. Real yearly counts vary more than the Poisson model suggests, because conditions (weather, economic activity) vary. The “ 8 standard deviations” should be treated with some caution. The rise is probably real, but whether it is alarming, and what causes it, needs more data. Looking back Compare like with like. Risks need a denominator: deaths per person, per kilometre or per journey. Know the natural variation. Poisson variability, and the much larger variability of clustered events, tell us when a change is noteworthy. An average hides a trend. A single summary number cannot describe how a quantity has changed over time. What’s really going on Signal and noise Every statistical question is, at bottom, a question of separating signal (a real effect or trend) from noise (random variation). The Poisson model gives a yardstick for the noise in counts of independent events: a standard deviation of sqrtμ . Rare events have large relative variation: a count of 9 varies by about 3 , a third of its size, while a count of 10\,000 varies by only about 1\% . That is why small numbers (deaths on one day, crashes in one year) are so often over-interpreted, and why cancer “clusters” in small towns usually turn out to be chance. Regression to the mean There is a further trap. Road-safety cameras are often installed at sites that have just had an unusually bad year. The following year, accidents fall, and the cameras get the credit. But an unusually bad year is likely to be followed by a more ordinary one anyway: this is regression to the mean , first described by Francis Galton in the 1880s. Separating the effect of a camera from regression to the mean requires comparison with similar sites that did not get cameras, the idea behind controlled experiments. Florence Nightingale’s statistics Florence Nightingale, famous as a nurse in the Crimean War, was also a pioneering statistician. Her “rose diagrams” of 1858 showed that far more soldiers were dying of preventable disease than of wounds, and persuaded the government to reform army sanitation. She insisted on rates (deaths per thousand soldiers per year) rather than raw totals, and on comparing like with like, the very points this question tests. She was the first woman elected a Fellow of the Royal Statistical Society. The thinking skill Ask “compared with what?” Before accepting a statistical claim, ask what the comparison is, what the denominator is, and how much variation would be expected by chance. At university, statistics courses turn these questions into precise methods: hypothesis tests ask whether an observation is consistent with chance; confidence intervals say how precisely a quantity has been measured; and the design of experiments ensures that comparisons are fair. Try this next Poisson tails. Check that P(X ≥ 7) approx 0.031 for X Poisson with mean 2.96 . How many days a year would you expect 9 or more pedestrian deaths? Clustered deaths. Suppose air crashes occur as a Poisson process at 1.2 per year, and each kills 150 people. Find the mean and standard deviation of yearly air deaths. Is a year with 125 deaths or fewer unusual? Could a year have exactly 125 deaths? A significant rise? If the 1974–1989 figures had been steady at 1080 33 , find (using a normal approximation) the probability of 1350 or more in a single year. Write a better headline. For each of the four headlines, write a headline that the data actually support. Further reading David Spiegelhalter, The Art of Statistics (Pelican). How to learn from data, with many examples from the news. Tim Harford, How to Make the World Add Up (Bridge Street). Ten rules for thinking about numbers in the media. Darrell Huff, How to Lie with Statistics (Penguin). A short classic from 1954, still relevant.

title: Statistics and Randomness in the World
headings: Why statistics matters What you will meet at university The questions that run through this chapter Ideas in this chapter How to read this chapter
text: Chapter 13 · Introduction Learning from Data All models are wrong, but some are useful. — George Box, statistician In probability, we know how the dice are loaded and ask what will happen. In statistics, we see what happened and ask how the dice must be loaded. Probability reasons from causes to effects; statistics reasons back from effects to causes. Every estimate of a population, every opinion poll, every clinical trial and every scientific measurement is a statistical inference: a conclusion about the world drawn from limited, noisy data. Statistics is a young subject compared with most of mathematics. Its modern form was created in the early twentieth century by Karl Pearson, Ronald Fisher, Jerzy Neyman and others, often driven by practical problems: brewing beer (the t -test was invented at the Guinness brewery), growing crops, testing medicines. Today, with the explosion of data, statistics and its close relative machine learning are among the most important applications of mathematics. Why statistics matters Decisions about medicines, public health, economic policy, climate and justice all rest on statistical evidence. Misreading it has real consequences: a patient frightened by a false positive ( Section 12.2 ), a policy based on a chance fluctuation ( Section 13.1 ), a computer system whose small errors pile up ( Section 13.6 ). Understanding what data can and cannot tell you, and how uncertain any conclusion is, is part of being an informed citizen, and a professional necessity for scientists, doctors, engineers and economists. What you will meet at university A first course in statistics covers estimation (finding good estimates of unknown quantities and saying how precise they are), hypothesis testing (deciding whether data are consistent with a hypothesis), confidence intervals, regression (relating one variable to others), and the design of experiments and surveys. The central ideas are sampling distributions (an estimate is a random variable), bias and variance , and likelihood . Later courses add Bayesian inference, multivariate analysis, time series and the methods of machine learning, which are statistics at enormous scale. The questions that run through this chapter Three big questions Is it real or is it noise? How much variation should we expect by chance, and when is a change worth taking seriously? How should we estimate? Given data, what is the best estimate of an unknown quantity, and how do we compare different methods? How does randomness enter the data? What do the ways data are collected, protected or processed do to our conclusions? The chapter starts with reading newspaper statistics critically ( Section 13.1 ), then turns to estimation: counting voles by capture–recapture, estimating a total from serial numbers, and comparing the mean with the median. It ends with three questions about how randomness enters data: randomised surveys that protect privacy, rounding errors that accumulate or cancel, and the construction of variables with prescribed correlations. Ideas in this chapter § Topic Idea 13.1 Reading statistics Rates, natural variation, trends 13.2 Capture–recapture Maximum likelihood 13.3 Serial numbers Bias, variance and sufficiency 13.4 Estimating a centre Efficiency and robustness 13.5 Randomised response Mixtures and total variance 13.6 Rounding errors Systematic versus random error 13.7 Correlation The Cholesky construction Section 13.7 uses covariance and correlation, which were removed from the STEP specification in 2019; it explains what it needs. How to read this chapter Remember that every estimate is a random variable: if the data had come out differently, so would the estimate. For each method in this chapter, ask what its distribution would be over many repetitions: is it right on average, and how much does it vary? That single question is the heart of statistical thinking.

title: Mean or Median?
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Efficiency Robust statistics The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 2000, Question 14 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/00-s2-q14 The hook To estimate the centre of a set of measurements, you could take the mean or the median. Which is better? The answer depends on the data. For measurements with occasional wild errors, the median is far more reliable: one absurd value can drag the mean anywhere, but barely moves the median. For well-behaved data, the mean usually wins. This question measures how much it wins by, for uniformly distributed data: the median’s variance is three times as large, so you would need three times as many observations to make the median as precise as the mean. The comparison introduces efficiency , one of the main ideas in choosing statistical methods, and the beta integral, which also appeared in Section 4.4 . Before you start Why is the density of the median proportional to y^n(1 - y)^n ? (For Y to be near y , how many of the 2n + 1 values must be below y , and how many above?) For the median to be at y , one value must be at y , n values below (each with probability y ) and n above (each with probability 1 - y ). That gives the factor y^n(1 - y)^n ; the constant counts the ways of choosing which values are which. Working it through Stage 1 The constant The density must integrate to 1 : kint_0^1y^n(1 - y)^n\,dy = k·(n!\,n!)/((2n + 1)!) = 1, qquad k = ((2n + 1)!)/((n!)^2). qed Stage 2 Mean and variance The density is symmetric about frac12 (replace y by 1 - y ), so E(Y) = frac12 . Compute E(Y^2) = kint_0^1y^n+2(1 - y)^n\,dy using the beta integral, and simplify the factorials. E(Y^2) = ((2n + 1)!)/((n!)^2)·((n + 2)!\,n!)/((2n + 3)!) = ((n + 2)(n + 1))/((2n + 3)(2n + 2)) = (n + 2)/(2(2n + 3)). So Var(Y) = (n + 2)/(2(2n + 3)) - frac14 = (2(n + 2) - (2n + 3))/(4(2n + 3)) = (1)/(4(2n + 3)). qed Stage 3 Comparing with the mean What are the mean and variance of bar X , the average of 2n + 1 independent uniform variables? Each X_i has mean frac12 and variance (1)/(12) , so E(bar X) = frac12 and Var(bar X) = (1)/(12(2n + 1)) . For large n , Var(Y) approx (1)/(8n), qquad Var(bar X) approx (1)/(24n). If Y and bar X are normal with mean frac12 and standard deviations σ_Y and σ_bar X , write both probabilities in terms of the standard normal distribution function Phi . Pbigl(|Y - frac12| < (d)/(sqrt n)bigr) = 2Phibigl((d)/(sqrt n\,σ_Y)bigr) - 1 , and sqrt n\,σ_Y → (1)/(sqrt8) ; similarly for bar X with sqrt n\,σ_bar X → frac1sqrt24 . So the probabilities tend to 2Phi(dsqrt8) - 1 and 2Phi(dsqrt24) - 1 . Since Phi is increasing and sqrt24 > sqrt8 , the second is larger, and so the inequality holds for all sufficiently large n . ■ The mean is more likely to be close to the true centre. Looking back The beta integral. int_0^1y^r(1 - y)^s\,dy gave the normalising constant and the moments in one formula. Symmetry gave the mean. No integration was needed for E(Y) . Compare spreads on the right scale. Multiplying standard deviations by sqrt n made the comparison independent of n . What’s really going on Efficiency The relative efficiency of two unbiased estimators is the ratio of their variances; it says how many times as many observations one needs to match the other. For uniform data the median has efficiency frac13 relative to the mean. For normal data it is frac2π approx 0.64 : the median needs about 57\% more observations. But for heavy-tailed data the tables turn. For the Cauchy distribution ( Section 12.22 ) the mean is useless, since the average of n observations is no better than one, while the median works well. For the Laplace distribution ( Section 12.24 ) the median is twice as efficient as the mean. Robust statistics The median is robust : you can change almost half the data to arbitrary values without moving it far. The mean has no such protection: one wrong value can spoil it. In the 1960s and 1970s John Tukey, Peter Huber and others developed robust statistics , estimators that are nearly as efficient as the mean for clean data but resistant to outliers, such as the trimmed mean (discard the largest and smallest 10\% and average the rest), which is used in judging sports like diving and gymnastics. Laplace and the median Laplace showed in 1774 that if errors follow the double exponential (Laplace) distribution, the best estimate of the true value is the median; Gauss showed in 1809 that if they follow the normal distribution, the best estimate is the mean, which led him to the method of least squares. Which is right depends on how errors behave, a question that statisticians still debate for each new kind of data. The thinking skill Compare methods by their variability Two methods may both be right on average; compare how much their answers vary, and how quickly that variation shrinks with more data. At university, asymptotic efficiency, the comparison of variances for large samples, is a standard tool for choosing between statistical methods, together with robustness for when the model might be wrong. Try this next The median’s density. Derive the density ((2n + 1)!)/((n!)^2)y^n(1 - y)^n by counting: one value in [y, y + δ y] , n below and n above. Three observations. For n = 1 (three uniform observations), find Var(Y) and Var(bar X) exactly. Which is smaller? The midrange. Another estimator of the centre is the midrange frac12(max + min) . Show that for uniform data its variance is (1)/(2(m + 1)(m + 2)) with m = 2n + 1 observations. How does it compare with the mean? (Compare Section 13.3 .) An outlier. Eleven measurements are 9.8 , 9.9 , 10.0 , 10.0 , 10.1 , 10.1 , 10.2 , 10.2 , 10.3 , 10.4 and 104 (a typing error). Compare the mean and median. Further reading John Rice, Mathematical Statistics and Data Analysis (Duxbury), on order statistics and efficiency. Rand Wilcox, Fundamentals of Modern Statistical Methods (Springer). Why robust methods matter, for non-specialists. Stephen Stigler, The Seven Pillars of Statistical Wisdom (Harvard University Press). Aggregation, the mean and the median, in historical perspective.

title: Counting Voles
headings: The hook Before you start Working it through Looking back What’s really going on Maximum likelihood How precise is the estimate? The thinking skill Try this next Further reading
text: The question STEP II 2000, Question 13 Read the question before you go on. It is in the STEP Support Programme’s question database: step.maths.org/questions/00-s2-q13 The hook How many voles live on an island? Counting them is impossible: they hide, they move, they look alike. But you can catch some, mark them, let them go, and catch some more. If 200 are marked and, in a second catch of 200 , 11 turn out to be marked, then roughly (11)/(200) of the population is marked, so the population is about 200 × (200)/(11) approx 3636 . This capture–recapture method is used to estimate populations of fish, birds and whales, and also of drug users, homeless people and casualties of war, any population that cannot be fully counted. The question puts the intuitive estimate on a firm footing using the principle of maximum likelihood , the most important idea in statistical estimation: choose the value of the unknown that makes the observed data most probable. Before you start The population has N voles, 200 of them marked. A random sample of 200 is taken. What is the probability that exactly 11 are marked? Choose 11 of the 200 marked voles and 189 of the N - 200 unmarked ones, out of binomN200 equally likely samples: p_N = fracbinom20011binomN - 200189binomN200. This is the hypergeometric distribution . Working it through Stage 1 The likelihood Writing out the binomial coefficients that involve N , binomN - 200189 = ((N - 200)!)/(189!\,(N - 389)!), qquad binomN200 = (N!)/(200!\,(N - 200)!), so p_N = binom20011(200!)/(189!)·(bigl((N - 200)!bigr)^2)/(N!\,(N - 389)!) = k(bigl((N - 200)!bigr)^2)/(N!\,(N - 389)!). qed Seen as a function of the unknown N , with the data fixed, p_N is called the likelihood . Stage 2 Maximising over a whole number N is a whole number, so calculus is awkward. Instead compare p_N+1 with p_N . When is their ratio bigger than 1 ? Most of the factorials cancel: fracp_N+1p_N = ((N - 199)^2)/((N + 1)(N - 388)). This exceeds 1 when (N - 199)^2 > (N + 1)(N - 388) , that is N^2 - 398N + 39601 > N^2 - 387N - 388 , or 11N < 39989 , N < 3635.4 . So p_N increases up to N = 3636 and decreases afterwards: the maximum likelihood estimate is hat N = 3636. qed This is the integer part of (200 × 200)/(11) = 3636.4 , the intuitive estimate. Stage 3 A third sample After the second sample, the 189 unmarked voles in it are marked too, so 389 voles are now marked. Taking N = 3636 , there are 3636 - 389 = 3247 unmarked. A third sample of 200 contains exactly j marked voles with probability fracbinom389jbinom3247200 - jbinom3636200. These probabilities, for j = 0, 1, ldots, 200 , must add up to 1 , which gives the identity. ■ Looking back Probability of the data, as a function of the unknown. The likelihood reverses the usual viewpoint: the data are fixed and the parameter varies. Ratios for discrete maximisation. Comparing consecutive terms located the maximum of a function of an integer. Probabilities add to 1 . Summing a distribution over all outcomes proved a combinatorial identity (Vandermonde’s identity). What’s really going on Maximum likelihood The principle of maximum likelihood , developed by Ronald Fisher in the 1910s and 1920s, says: estimate an unknown parameter by the value that makes the observed data most probable. It is by far the most widely used method of estimation, from fitting curves to data to training the neural networks of machine learning, whose “loss functions” are usually negative log-likelihoods. Fisher showed that, for large samples, maximum likelihood estimates are approximately normal and as precise as any reasonable estimator can be, provided the model is well behaved in ways that hold for most everyday models. There are important exceptions. In the next section ( Section 13.3 ) the unknown is the largest possible value, an endpoint of the distribution, and there the maximum likelihood estimate behaves quite differently: its error is not approximately normal, and it shrinks like frac1n rather than (1)/(sqrt n) . How precise is the estimate? Figure 13.2.1 shows that the likelihood is broad: 11 recaptures is not much information. A rough calculation: the number of marked voles in the second sample is approximately Poisson with mean (200 × 200)/(N) , so its standard deviation is about sqrt11 approx 3.3 , a relative error of about 30\% , which carries over to the estimate of N . To estimate N to within 10\% , the biologists would need about 100 recaptures. Statisticians also correct for the small bias of the simple estimate, using the Chapman estimator ((M + 1)(C + 1))/(R + 1) - 1 , where M and C are the sizes of the two catches and R the number recaptured. Laplace counts France Laplace used the same idea in 1802 to estimate the population of France without a census. He knew the number of births registered in the whole country in a year, and, for a sample of communes, both the population and the births. Assuming the ratio of population to births was the same everywhere, he estimated the population of France at about 28 million, and even gave a measure of the uncertainty. The method was rediscovered for animal populations by C. G. J. Petersen, who marked plaice in Danish fjords in the 1890s, and by Frederick Lincoln, who used bird rings in the 1930s; it is still often called the Lincoln–Petersen estimator. The thinking skill Choose the parameter that makes the data most likely To estimate an unknown, write the probability of what you observed as a function of the unknown, and maximise it. At university, maximum likelihood is the backbone of statistical inference, with a theory of how precise the estimates are (the Fisher information) and how to compare competing models (likelihood ratio tests). Try this next General formula. If M animals are marked and a second sample of C contains R marked, show that the maximum likelihood estimate of N is the integer part of (MC)/(R) . Vandermonde. Prove sum_jbinomajbinombc - j = binoma + bc by counting committees of c people chosen from a women and b men. Coin tosses. In n tosses of a coin with unknown probability p of heads, h heads are observed. Show that the maximum likelihood estimate of p is frac hn . No recaptures. What happens to the maximum likelihood estimate if the second sample contains no marked voles? What does that tell you about the method? Further reading David Spiegelhalter, The Art of Statistics (Pelican), on estimation and uncertainty. George Seber, The Estimation of Animal Abundance (Blackburn). The standard reference on capture–recapture. John Rice, Mathematical Statistics and Data Analysis (Duxbury). A first course in mathematical statistics, including maximum likelihood.

title: What We Have Learned
headings: 1. Is it real or is it noise? 2. How should we estimate? 3. How does randomness enter the data? 4. A toolkit for statistics Where next A last word
text: We began by saying that probability goes from a model to data, and statistics goes from data back to the world. We asked three questions: is it real or is it noise, how should we estimate, and how does randomness enter the data? Here is what the chapter’s seven questions showed. 1. Is it real or is it noise? In Section 13.1 , four headlines turned numbers into claims. Comparing totals without denominators, reading a trend into one year or one day, and hiding a trend inside an average were all errors, and the Poisson model gave a yardstick for the natural variation of counts. A rise of 8 standard deviations was almost certainly real; seven deaths on a Tuesday almost certainly was not. Regression to the mean and the need for fair comparisons completed the picture. 2. How should we estimate? Three questions developed the theory of estimation. Maximum likelihood ( Section 13.2 ): choose the value of the unknown that makes the observed data most probable. For capture–recapture it gave the natural estimate (200 × 200)/(11) approx 3636 , with a broad likelihood showing how uncertain it was. Bias and variance ( Section 13.3 ): two unbiased estimators of the number of submarines, one based on the maximum and one on the mean. The maximum, a sufficient statistic, was far more precise, with variance shrinking like (1)/(n^2) rather than frac1n . The same reasoning outwitted wartime intelligence about German tanks. Efficiency and robustness ( Section 13.4 ): for uniform data the mean is three times as efficient as the median, but for heavy-tailed data the median wins, and it is robust to wild errors. 3. How does randomness enter the data? Randomness can be added deliberately: randomised response ( Section 13.5 ) protects each respondent’s privacy while still estimating the population, provided each person randomises independently; a single shared coin would produce a two-humped mixture that tells us almost nothing. Randomness also enters through processing: rounding errors cancel and grow like sqrt n , while truncation errors accumulate linearly, as the Vancouver Stock Exchange discovered ( Section 13.6 ). And randomness can be engineered: independent ingredients, combined by the Cholesky construction, produce variables with any valid set of correlations ( Section 13.7 ), but not every set of correlations is valid. 4. A toolkit for statistics Method Where you used it Poisson variation Headlines (13.1) Likelihood and its maximum Voles (13.2) Unbiasedness and variance Serial numbers (13.3); median (13.4) Sufficient statistics Serial numbers (13.3) Normal approximation 13.4, 13.5, 13.6 Law of total variance Randomised response (13.5) Bias versus random error Rounding (13.6) Linearity of covariance Correlation (13.7) Where next Bayes’ theorem ( Section 12.2 ) is the basis of Bayesian statistics, the main alternative to the methods of this chapter. The central limit theorem ( Section 12.24 ) justifies the normal approximations used throughout; the Cauchy distribution ( Section 12.22 ) shows when they fail. Correlation matrices are positive semi-definite matrices, studied with the eigenvectors of Section 7.2 . If you want to go further before university David Spiegelhalter, The Art of Statistics : the best introduction to statistical thinking for a general reader. Tim Harford, How to Make the World Add Up : how to read numbers in the news. John Rice, Mathematical Statistics and Data Analysis : a first university course in mathematical statistics. Stephen Stigler, The Seven Pillars of Statistical Wisdom : the big ideas of statistics and where they came from. George Box said that all models are wrong, but some are useful. This chapter has tried to show how to make models useful: by knowing how much variation to expect, by judging methods by how they behave over many repetitions, and by thinking about how the data came to be. These are the habits that turn numbers into knowledge. A last word This is the end of the book. Over thirteen chapters, we have used STEP questions as doorways into the mathematics of a first university course: number theory and analysis, calculus and complex numbers, algebra and linear algebra, differential equations and dynamics, combinatorics, mechanics, probability and statistics. Each question was an invitation to ask what lies behind it, and almost every time the answer was a whole subject. If you have worked through even a few of these sections with a pencil in hand, asking the questions in the margins and trying the problems at the end, you have already begun to think like a mathematician. The rest of the journey is yours.

title: Glossary
headings: A B C D E F G H I L M N O P Q R S T U V W
text: University mathematics has its own vocabulary, and much of it will be new to you. This glossary collects the words in this book that you are unlikely to have met at school, with a short explanation of each and, where it helps, a pointer to the section where the idea is used or explained properly. The explanations are meant to get you started, not to be precise definitions; where a word has a careful definition, the section it points to gives it. A few words, such as set , function and proof , will be familiar, but are used at university with more care than at school, and they are included for that reason. Words in italics within an entry have entries of their own. A Adiabatic invariant A quantity that stays almost constant when a system is changed slowly. A molecule bouncing in a slowly compressed cylinder keeps its speed multiplied by the length of the cylinder nearly fixed ( Section 10.4 ). Algebraic number A number that is a root of a polynomial equation with integer coefficients (positive, negative or zero), not all zero. sqrt2 , i and frac12(1 + sqrt5) are algebraic; numbers that are not algebraic are transcendental ( Section 6.3 ). Analysis The branch of mathematics that puts calculus on a rigorous footing: limits, continuity, differentiation, integration and infinite series, all defined precisely and proved from first principles. Chapters 2 to 4 are an introduction to it. Angular momentum The rotational counterpart of momentum. For a body spinning about an axis it is the moment of inertia multiplied by the angular velocity, and it is conserved when there is no turning effect from outside ( Section 11.6 ). Arithmetic–geometric mean The common limit of two sequences formed by repeatedly replacing a pair of numbers by their arithmetic mean and their geometric mean. It converges extraordinarily fast ( Section 2.6 ). Associative An operation ast is associative if (a ast b) ast c = a ast (b ast c) for all a , b , c , so that brackets can be left out. Addition and multiplication of numbers are associative; subtraction is not. Asymptotic Two expressions are asymptotic, written f(n) sim g(n) , if their ratio tends to 1 as n → ∞ . Stirling’s formula says that n! sim sqrt2π n\,(n/e)^n , even though the difference between the two sides grows without limit ( Section 12.23 ). Axiom A statement taken as a starting point, without proof, from which everything else is deduced. Much of university algebra starts from a short list of axioms and asks what follows from them ( Section 7.3 , Section 6.5 ). B Base case The first step of a proof by induction : checking that the statement is true for the smallest value, usually n = 0 or n = 1 . The inductive step then shows that truth for one value implies truth for the next. Base-rate fallacy The mistake of judging the probability of something from the evidence alone while ignoring how common it was to begin with. If a disease is rare enough, even a positive result from an accurate test can be more likely to be a false alarm than not; whether it is depends on how rare the disease is and how accurate the test is ( Section 12.2 ). Basis A set of vectors such that every vector in the space can be written in exactly one way as a combination of them. In the plane, i and j form a basis; so does any pair of vectors that are not parallel. The number of vectors in a basis is the dimension of the space ( Section 6.3 ). Bayes’ theorem The rule for turning one conditional probability round: P(A mid B) = P(B mid A)\,P(A)/P(B) . It tells you how to update a belief in the light of evidence ( Section 12.2 ). Bias An estimator is biased if, on average over many samples, it comes out too high or too low; it is unbiased if its expectation is exactly the quantity it estimates ( Section 13.3 ). Bijection A one-to-one correspondence: a rule that pairs off every member of one set with exactly one member of another, with nothing left over on either side. Two finite sets have the same size exactly when there is a bijection between them, and this is how the size of an infinite set is defined ( Section 1.8 , Section 9.10 ). Binary operation A rule for combining two objects to give a third, such as addition of numbers, multiplication of matrices, or composition of functions. Bound An upper bound for a set or sequence of numbers is a number that none of them exceeds; a lower bound is one that none of them falls below. A sequence is bounded if it has both ( Section 2.2 ). Branching process A model of a population in which each individual independently has a random number of offspring. The central question is whether the family line dies out, and the answer comes from a probability generating function ( Section 12.15 ). C Calculus of variations The study of problems in which the unknown is a whole function or curve, chosen to make some quantity as small or as large as possible: the shortest path, the quickest slide, the curve enclosing the most area ( Section 4.7 ). Catenary The shape of a hanging chain, the graph of y = acosh(x/a) . It looks like a parabola but is not one ( Section 11.14 ). Cauchy distribution A continuous distribution, with a bell-shaped graph, whose tails are so heavy that it has no mean. The average of a sample from it is no more reliable than a single observation ( Section 12.22 ). Central limit theorem The theorem that the sum of a large number of independent random quantities with the same distribution and finite variance, suitably shifted and scaled, has approximately a normal distribution, whatever that common distribution is.
