Versions exist for quantities with different distributions, provided no few of them dominate the sum. It explains why the bell curve appears everywhere ( Section 12.24 ). Chaos Behaviour of a deterministic system that is so sensitive to its starting point that long-term prediction is impossible in practice: two starting points that are very close together lead to completely different futures ( Section 8.7 , Section 8.8 ). Closed A set is closed under an operation if combining two members of the set always gives another member. The even numbers are closed under addition; the odd numbers are not. Commutative An operation ast is commutative if a ast b = b ast a always. Multiplication of numbers is commutative; multiplication of matrices and of quaternions is not ( Section 7.1 , Section 6.7 ). Completeness The property of the real numbers that they have no gaps: every increasing sequence that is bounded above converges to a real number. The rational numbers lack it, since a sequence of fractions can close in on sqrt2 . Much of analysis rests on it ( Section 2.2 ). Congruence a equiv b pmod n , read “ a is congruent to b modulo n ”, means that a and b leave the same remainder on division by n ; equivalently, n divides a - b . Arithmetic with congruences is called modular arithmetic ( Section 1.5 ). Conjecture A statement that is believed to be true but has not been proved. Conservation law A statement that some quantity, such as energy, momentum or angular momentum, does not change as a system evolves. Conservation laws often let you solve a problem without following its details ( Section 10.1 ). Continuous A function is continuous if small changes in the input produce small changes in the output; informally, its graph can be drawn without lifting the pen. Precisely, f is continuous at a if f(x) → f(a) as x → a ( Section 3.1 , Section 8.8 ). Contradiction, proof by A proof that assumes the statement is false and deduces something impossible. The classic example is the proof that sqrt2 is irrational ( Section 1.3 ). Contrapositive The contrapositive of “if P then Q ” is “if not Q then not P ”. The two statements are logically equivalent, and proving the contrapositive is often easier. It is not the same as the converse , “if Q then P ”, which may well be false. Converge A sequence converges if its terms get, and stay, as close as you like to a fixed number, its limit . A series converges if its partial sums converge. A sequence or series that does not converge diverges ( Section 2.1 , Section 2.3 ). Convex A function is convex if the chord joining any two points on its graph lies on or above the graph, as for x^2 or e^x . Many inequalities, including AM–GM, are consequences of convexity ( Section 3.3 ). Corollary A result that follows quickly from a theorem just proved. Correlation A number between -1 and 1 measuring how close two random quantities are to having a straight-line relationship. It is the covariance scaled by the two standard deviations ( Section 13.7 ). Countable A set is countable if its members can be listed as a first, second, third, and so on, possibly for ever. The whole numbers and, surprisingly, the fractions are countable; the real numbers are not ( Section 1.8 ). Counterexample A single example showing that a general statement is false. One counterexample is enough to disprove a claim, however many examples support it. Covariance Cov(X, Y) = E(XY) - E(X)E(Y) , a measure of how two random quantities vary together. It is zero for independent quantities, though zero covariance does not imply independence ( Section 12.4 , Section 13.7 ). Cycle A set of points that a repeated function visits in turn: x_1 mapsto x_2 mapsto cdots mapsto x_n mapsto x_1 . The number n is its period , and the points are periodic points ( Section 8.8 ). Cycloid The curve traced by a point on the rim of a rolling wheel. Turned upside down, it is both the curve of quickest descent and the curve along which every slide takes the same time ( Section 11.4 ). Cyclotomic polynomial The polynomial Phi_n(x) whose roots are exactly the primitive n th roots of unity . It has integer coefficients and is irreducible , and x^n - 1 is the product of the Phi_d(x) for all divisors d of n : for example, x^4 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1)(x^2 + 1) ( Section 6.1 ). D Derangement A rearrangement of a list in which nothing stays in its original position ( Section 9.8 ). Derivation An operation D on functions (or on other objects) with D(f + g) = Df + Dg and the product rule D(fg) = f\,Dg + g\,Df . Differentiation is the standard example, and much of its behaviour follows from these two rules alone ( Section 6.5 ). Determinant A number calculated from a square matrix, which measures the factor by which the corresponding transformation scales areas or volumes. It is zero exactly when the matrix has no inverse ( Section 7.3 ). Differentiable A function is differentiable at a point if its graph has a well-defined tangent there, so that the limit defining the derivative exists. Every differentiable function is continuous , but not the other way round: |x| is continuous but not differentiable at 0 . Dimension The number of vectors in a basis : the number of independent directions in a vector space . Diverge See converge . Dynamical system A rule describing how the state of a system changes with time, either step by step (a sequence defined by x_n+1 = f(x_n) ) or continuously (a differential equation). Chapter 8 is about them. E Eigenvalue, eigenvector A non-zero vector v is an eigenvector of a matrix M if Mv = lambdav for some number λ , its eigenvalue: the transformation stretches v without turning it ( Section 7.2 ). Envelope A curve that touches every member of a family of curves. The envelope of all the trajectories of a ball thrown at a fixed speed is the safety parabola , the boundary of the region the ball can reach ( Section 11.9 ). Equilibrium A state of a system that does not change. It is stable if small disturbances stay small, and asymptotically stable if they also die away, as they do for a pendulum with friction; a frictionless pendulum hanging straight down is stable, but a small push makes it swing for ever. It is unstable if some small disturbances grow ( Section 8.3 , Section 11.8 ). Estimator A rule for calculating, from data, a guess at an unknown quantity, such as the size of a population or the mean of a distribution ( Section 13.3 ). Euler characteristic For a polyhedron with V vertices, E edges and F faces, the number V - E + F , which is always 2 for a polyhedron without holes ( Section 7.9 ). Existence proof A proof that something exists that does not necessarily say how to find it. The pigeonhole principle and the intermediate value theorem both give existence proofs. Expectation The mean value of a random quantity X , written E(X) : the long-run average of many independent repetitions. Expectation is additive, E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y) , whether or not X and Y are independent ( Section 9.11 ). Extremal principle The strategy of looking at the smallest, largest, first or last object of some kind, and showing that it has a property that leads either to the result or to a contradiction ( Section 1.3 ). F Field A number system in which you can add, subtract, multiply and divide (except by zero), with all the usual rules holding. The rational, real and complex numbers are fields; so are the integers modulo a prime. The integers are not, because you cannot always divide ( Section 6.3 ). Field extension A larger field containing a smaller one, such as the numbers a + bsqrt2 with a , b rational, which contain the rationals. Its degree is its dimension as a vector space over the smaller field ( Section 6.3 ). Fixed point A point x with f(x) = x , which the function leaves where it is. On a graph, fixed points are where y = f(x) meets y = x ( Section 2.2 , Section 8.8 ). Frame of reference A point of view from which positions and motions are measured. An inertial frame is one in which Newton’s first law holds; in an accelerating frame, such as a train speeding up, there appear to be extra forces ( Section 11.5 ). Function A rule that assigns to each member of one set, the domain , exactly one member of another set, the codomain . At university a function is not the same as a formula: many important functions have no formula, and some formulae do not define functions. Functional equation An equation whose unknown is a function, such as f(x + y) = f(x)f(y) ( Section 3.8 ). Fundamental theorem of algebra Every polynomial of degree at least 1 with complex coefficients has a complex root, and so factorises completely into linear factors over the complex numbers. G Gamma function A function Gamma that extends the factorial to non-integers: Gamma(n + 1) = n! for whole numbers n , and Gamma(frac12) = sqrtπ , which in a sense says that (-frac12)! = sqrtπ ( Section 4.4 ). Gaussian integer A complex number a + bi with a and b integers. They behave much like ordinary integers, with their own primes and unique factorisation ( Section 1.6 ). Generating function A power series a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2 + cdots whose coefficients are the terms of a sequence. Operations on the series, such as multiplication, correspond to useful operations on the sequence ( Section 9.4 ). A probability generating function does this for the probabilities of a random whole number ( Section 9.6 , Section 12.15 ); a moment generating function is a close relative ( Section 12.24 ). Group A set with a binary operation that is associative , has an identity element and gives every element an inverse . The symmetries of a shape form a group, as do the non-zero complex numbers under multiplication. Groups are the language of symmetry ( Section 6.6 , Section 6.7 ). H Hyperbolic geometry A geometry in which, through a point not on a given line, there are infinitely many lines that never meet it, and the angles of a triangle add up to less than π . A disc with a suitable way of measuring distance is a model of it ( Section 5.8 ). I Identity An identity element for an operation ast is an element e with e ast a = a ast e = a for every a : 0 for addition, 1 for multiplication, the identity matrix I for matrix multiplication. Separately, an identity is an equation that holds for every value of its variables, such as cos^2θ + sin^2θ equiv 1 . If and only if “ P if and only if Q ”, often written “ P iff Q ” or P iff Q , means that P and Q are either both true or both false. Proving it needs two arguments, one in each direction. Independent Two events are independent if knowing that one has happened does not change the probability of the other: P(A cap B) = P(A)P(B) . Three or more events can be independent in pairs without being independent all together ( Section 12.4 ). Induction A method of proving a statement for every whole number n : prove it for the first value (the base case ), then prove that whenever it is true for one value it is true for the next (the inductive step ). In strong induction , the inductive step may use the statement for all smaller values, not just the previous one ( Section 1.2 ). Infinite descent A form of proof by contradiction: show that any solution of a problem in whole numbers would lead to a smaller one, and so to an endless decreasing sequence of positive whole numbers, which is impossible ( Section 1.5 ). Intermediate value theorem If a continuous function takes the values a and b , it takes every value in between. So a continuous function that changes sign must have a root ( Section 8.8 ). Invariant A quantity that does not change while a process runs, or under some transformation. Finding an invariant is one of the most powerful ways to prove that something is impossible, or to solve a problem without following every step ( Section 7.7 , Section 10.4 ). Inverse An inverse of an element a , for an operation with identity e , is an element b with a ast b = b ast a = e . An inverse function undoes a function: f^-1(f(x)) = x . Irrational A real number that cannot be written as a fraction frac pq with p and q integers ( q ≠ 0 ), such as sqrt2 , π or e ( Section 1.4 ). Irreducible A polynomial is irreducible if it cannot be written as the product of two polynomials of lower degree with coefficients of the same kind. x^2 - 2 is irreducible over the rationals, but factorises as (x - sqrt2)(x + sqrt2) over the reals ( Section 6.1 ). Isomorphic Two structures, such as two groups , are isomorphic if there is a bijection between them that matches their operations exactly: they are the same structure with different labels ( Section 6.7 , Section 6.8 ). Iteration Applying the same function again and again, so that x_1 = f(x_0) , x_2 = f(x_1) , and so on. The sequence x_0 , x_1 , x_2 , … is the orbit of x_0 ( Section 8.7 ). L Law of large numbers The theorem that the average of many independent repetitions of a random quantity tends to its expectation , provided the expectation exists ( Section 12.22 ). Lemma A result proved mainly as a step towards a larger theorem . Limit The value that a sequence or function gets, and stays, arbitrarily close to. Making this idea precise was one of the great achievements of nineteenth-century mathematics, and it is the starting point of analysis ( Section 2.1 ). Limit cycle A closed loop in the motion of a system that nearby motions spiral towards (or away from), such as the steady rhythm of a heartbeat or a clock ( Section 8.4 ). Linear map A function T between vector spaces with T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) and T(lambdau) = λ T(u) . Every linear map can be represented by a matrix, and linear algebra is the study of them ( Section 7.2 ). Logistic map The rule u_n+1 = ru_n(1 - u_n) , a simple model of a population limited by its food supply, and the standard example of chaos ( Section 8.7 ). M Markov chain A random process that moves between states in steps, in which the probability of the next step depends only on the present state, not on how the process got there ( Section 12.16 ). Maximum likelihood A way of estimating an unknown quantity: choose the value that makes the observed data most probable ( Section 13.2 ). Memoryless A random waiting time is memoryless if, however long you have already waited, the remaining wait has the same distribution as it did at the start. The exponential distribution is the only continuous memoryless distribution ( Section 12.18 ). Minimal polynomial The polynomial of lowest degree, with rational coefficients and leading coefficient 1 , that has a given algebraic number as a root. The minimal polynomial of sqrt2 is x^2 - 2 ( Section 6.3 ). Modular arithmetic See congruence . Moment of inertia The rotational counterpart of mass: a measure of how hard it is to change a body’s rate of rotation about an axis. It depends on how far the mass is from the axis, not just on how much mass there is ( Section 11.7 ). Monotonic A sequence or function is monotonic if it never goes down (increasing) or never goes up (decreasing). A monotonic sequence that is bounded must converge ( Section 2.2 , Section 11.10 ). N Necessary and sufficient P is a necessary condition for Q if Q cannot happen without P ( Q Rightarrow P ); it is sufficient if P guarantees Q ( P Rightarrow Q ). A condition that is both is equivalent to Q . Normal modes The special patterns of vibration of a system in which every part moves in step at the same frequency. Any vibration of the system is a combination of its normal modes ( Section 11.2 ). O Order The order of an element g of a group is the smallest positive whole number n for which g^n is the identity : the number of times you must apply it to get back to the start ( Section 7.4 ). If there is no such n , as for the number 1 in the integers under addition, g has infinite order . The order of a finite group is the number of elements it has. Orthogonal Perpendicular. At university the word is extended beyond vectors: two functions f and g can be called orthogonal if int f(x)g(x)\,dx = 0 over a suitable range ( Section 8.6 ). P Parameter A quantity that is fixed within a particular problem but can vary from one problem to another, such as r in the logistic map . Many STEP questions ask how the answer depends on a parameter. Partial sum The sum a_1 + a_2 + cdots + a_n of the first n terms of a series. The series converges if its partial sums do ( Section 2.3 ). Pigeonhole principle If more than n objects are put into n boxes, some box contains at least two of them. Simple as it is, it proves some remarkable existence results ( Section 9.2 ). Poisson process A model of events that occur at random, independently, at a constant average rate, in time or in space: radioactive decays, phone calls, stars in the sky ( Section 12.19 , Section 12.18 ). Primitive root of unity An n th root of unity whose powers give all n of the n th roots of unity; equivalently, one that is not an m th root of unity for any smaller m ( Section 6.1 ). Probability density function For a continuous random quantity, the function f whose integral over an interval gives the probability of landing in that interval. Proof A complete logical argument that a statement is true, starting from definitions, axioms and results already proved. At university, a calculation that gives the right answer is not a proof unless each step is justified. Q Quaternions A number system discovered by William Rowan Hamilton in 1843, extending the complex numbers with three square roots of -1 , written i , j , k , which satisfy i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = ijk = -1 . Their multiplication is not commutative . They are used to describe rotations in three dimensions ( Section 6.7 , Section 7.5 ). R Random variable A quantity whose value is determined by the outcome of a random experiment, such as the number of heads in ten tosses of a coin. Random walk A path made of successive random steps, such as a counter that moves one place left or right on the toss of a coin ( Section 9.10 , Section 12.17 ). Rapidity A measure of speed in special relativity that, unlike velocity, simply adds when one motion is combined with another in the same direction. If c is the speed of light, velocity v has rapidity artanh(v/c) ( Section 7.6 ). Recurrence relation An equation giving each term of a sequence in terms of earlier ones, such as F_n+1 = F_n + F_n-1 for the Fibonacci numbers. Resonance The large response of a system that is pushed periodically at, or near, its own natural frequency, as when a child on a swing is pushed in time with the swing ( Section 11.1 ). Riemann integral The precise definition of the integral as the limit of sums of areas of thin rectangles, when that limit exists ( Section 4.1 ). Rigour The standard of argument in which every step is justified and nothing is taken for granted because it looks obvious or is true in the examples you have tried (Chapter 3). Root of unity A complex number z with z^n = 1 for some positive whole number n . The n th roots of unity are e^2piik/n for k = 0 , 1 , …, n - 1 , which form a regular n -gon on the unit circle ( Section 5.2 ). S Sample space The set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment. Events are subsets of it ( Section 12.1 ). Set A collection of objects, its elements , considered as a single thing. The order of the elements does not matter, and nor does repetition: \1, 2, 3\ and \3, 1, 2, 2\ are the same set. Simple harmonic motion Motion in which the acceleration is proportional to the displacement from a fixed point and directed towards it, ddot x = -ω^2x . The solution is x = Acos(ω t + ε) , and the period, 2π/ω , does not depend on the size of the swing ( Section 11.4 ). Stable, unstable See equilibrium . Stirling’s formula The approximation n! approx sqrt2π n\,(n/e)^n , whose percentage error tends to zero as n grows ( Section 12.23 ). Subgroup A subset of a group that is itself a group under the same operation ( Section 6.6 ). Symmetry argument An argument that two quantities must be equal because nothing in the problem distinguishes between them. A good symmetry argument can replace pages of calculation ( Section 12.5 ). T Theorem An important statement that has been proved. Lesser results are often called propositions , those proved on the way to a theorem lemmas , and quick consequences corollaries . Trace The sum of the entries on the leading diagonal of a square matrix. Like the determinant , it does not change when the matrix is written in a different basis , and it equals the sum of the eigenvalues ( Section 7.4 , Section 7.7 ). Transcendental A number that is not algebraic : it is not the root of any polynomial equation with integer coefficients, not all zero. e and π are transcendental, though proving it is hard ( Section 1.4 ). Triangle inequality |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b| , for real numbers, complex numbers or vectors: one side of a triangle is never longer than the other two together. U Unique factorisation The property that every whole number greater than 1 can be written as a product of primes in only one way, apart from the order of the factors. It is not as obvious as it looks: there are number systems in which it fails ( Section 1.7 ). Uniqueness theorem A theorem saying that a problem has only one solution. For differential equations, uniqueness can fail when the equation is not well behaved, so that a single starting point leads to several different futures ( Section 8.1 ). V Vector space A collection of objects, called vectors, that can be added together and multiplied by numbers, following the familiar rules for arrows in the plane. Polynomials, functions and solutions of many differential equations all form vector spaces, so the methods of linear algebra apply to them ( Section 6.3 ). W Well-defined An object or rule is well-defined if its definition really does specify a single unambiguous thing: if it does not depend, for example, on an arbitrary choice made along the way. Well-ordering principle Every non-empty set of positive whole numbers has a smallest member. It is equivalent to the principle of induction , and it lies behind every argument that begins “take the smallest counterexample” ( Section 1.3 ). Without loss of generality A phrase, often shortened to WLOG, meaning that the argument considers only one case because the other cases are the same apart from relabelling. “Without loss of generality, a ≤ b ” means that if a > b you can swap their names.

title: Introduction
headings: What STEP is, and why it exists Stephen Siklos How I met STEP Some gems What this book is for How the book is organised How to use this book as a student How to use this book as a teacher Copyright and corrections A last word before you start
text: I can’t teach you mathematics with this book, but I believe that much hard work on your part, chipping away at the problems, will eventually reveal the mathematician that is within you. — Stephen Siklos, Advanced Problems in Mathematics This is a book of hard problems, and of what lies behind them. Every one of its 136 sections starts with a question from a past STEP paper. But the question is only the way in. Behind almost every good STEP question is a piece of mathematics that you will meet properly at university, and the aim of this book is to take you through the door and show you what is on the other side. What STEP is, and why it exists STEP, the Sixth Term Examination Paper, is a set of mathematics examinations taken in the summer of the final year of school. It was introduced by the University of Cambridge in 1987, and its job is to help decide who should study mathematics there: almost all Cambridge offers for Mathematics are conditional on STEP grades, and over the years other universities, notably Warwick, have used it too. At the start there were STEP papers in many subjects, but by 2001 only mathematics remained. For most of its history there were three papers, I, II and III; Paper I was last set in 2019, and today candidates take Papers II and III. The examination was run for many years by Cambridge Assessment, and since 2024 it has been administered by OCR. A STEP paper looks nothing like a school examination. Instead of ten short, compulsory questions, there are a dozen or so long ones, of which candidates attempt six, and a strong candidate who makes real progress on four will do very well. The questions do not tell you how many marks each part is worth, and they rarely ask you to do something you have practised. They ask you to take the mathematics you already know and use it somewhere new. Stephen Siklos, who knew STEP better than anyone, described its purpose like this. It is a hurdle: success in STEP turns out to predict success in a university mathematics degree remarkably well (he reported a correlation of 0.63 between STEP rank and first-year Cambridge examination rank, very high by the standards of such things). It is a preparation: the style of thinking that STEP rewards is the style of undergraduate mathematics. And it is a test of motivation: preparing for STEP takes real effort, and a student who is not willing to make that effort is unlikely to enjoy a demanding mathematics degree. Stephen Siklos It is impossible to write about STEP without writing about Stephen Siklos. He was a Cambridge mathematician, a former research student of Stephen Hawking who worked on the mathematics of the early universe and of gravitational waves, a lecturer in the Department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics, and later Senior Tutor and then President of Jesus College. He became the Senior Examiner for STEP Mathematics when it began in 1987, and held the post for thirty-two years, until his death in August 2019. In that time he drafted questions, “knocked other people’s questions into shape” (his own phrase, for something he said had long been a source of interest and entertainment), scrutinised every paper and oversaw the marking. He was also the driving force behind the STEP Easter School and the STEP Support Programme , which give free help to students whose schools cannot. One obituary said that he did more than anyone to make the Cambridge entrance examination in mathematics accessible to students whatever their school background. His book Advanced Problems in Mathematics: Preparing for University , published free online by Open Book Publishers, is still the best introduction to STEP, and I strongly recommend it. Two things he wrote in it have shaped this book. The first is his view of what a good STEP question is: one in which the first part shows you an unfamiliar idea, and the later parts ask you to show that you have understood it by using it again in a harder setting; or one whose answer depends on a parameter that you have to discover for yourself; or one that starts with special cases and ends with a general result. Those are exactly the questions that lead somewhere, and most of the questions in this book are of those kinds. The second is his insistence that solutions should be “springboards rather than feather beds”. You learn nothing by reading a solution you have not first fought with yourself. How I met STEP I first came across STEP in the early 1990s, when my mathematics teacher gave me some of the papers as an extra challenge. I worked through them for the fun of it rather than for an offer, and never sat the real examination, but I remember those papers as being extraordinarily hard: questions that seemed to have nothing to do with anything I had learned, that went on for a page, and that I could start but rarely finish. I also remember the feeling, on the occasions when something finally worked, that I had seen something that school mathematics had not shown me. Many years later I came back to STEP from the other side, helping students to prepare for it. Working through hundreds of questions with them, I came to see the papers differently. Not every question is a gem. Some are, frankly, long tests of stamina: a page of careful algebra, a demanding but routine calculation, with not much insight or pleasure at the end. Stamina matters, and university mathematics needs it, but those questions are not what make STEP special. What makes it special is that, scattered across the more than 1,500 questions set since 1987, there are hundreds of genuinely beautiful ones. The best way to explain what I mean is to show you some. Some gems Here are seven of the questions you will meet later in the book, chosen to span its range: two from combinatorics, two from dynamical systems, two from mechanics and one from probability. Each starts with something you can picture, ends with something you might not have believed, and opens onto a piece of mathematics that is studied seriously at university. Order hiding in chaos. Draw six dots on a page and join every pair with a line, fifteen lines in all, colouring each line gold or silver however you like. Now try to avoid creating a triangle whose three sides are all the same colour. You will fail, every time. With five dots it can be done (colour the sides of a pentagon gold and the five diagonals silver), but with six it is impossible, however cunning your colouring. A 1989 STEP I question asks you to prove this, with a single hint: look at the five lines that leave one dot. Three of them must share a colour, and from there the proof takes a few lines. There are 2^15 = 32\,768 ways to colour the lines, and the argument deals with all of them at once, without checking a single case. The result is the smallest case of Ramsey’s theorem, proved by Frank Ramsey in 1928, which says that complete disorder is impossible: any large enough structure, however haphazardly it is put together, contains a pocket of perfect order. How large is “large enough”? To guarantee four dots joined entirely in one colour you need 18 dots, a fact proved in 1955. For five dots, nobody knows: the answer lies somewhere between 43 and 46 , and the upper bound was proved only in 2024. Paul Erdős joked that if aliens threatened to destroy the Earth unless we told them this number, we should set every computer and mathematician to work on it; but if they asked for the answer for six, we should try to destroy the aliens. You will meet Ramsey theory in a university combinatorics or graph theory course, and the pigeonhole principle that powers the STEP proof in almost every course you take ( Section 9.2 ). Strange dice. With two ordinary dice, a total of 7 is the most likely and totals of 2 and 12 the least, in the familiar pattern of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 ways. Is there any other way to number a pair of dice with positive whole numbers that gives exactly the same chances for every total? It seems unlikely, but there is exactly one: 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4 on one die and 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 on the other. These are Sicherman dice , named after George Sicherman, who found them, and made famous by Martin Gardner in 1978. In any game that depends only on the total thrown, you could swap them for ordinary dice and nobody would ever know. A 1993 question approaches the idea from the other end. It gives you a table showing how many ways each total can be thrown with two oddly numbered dice, and asks you to work out the numbering, like a detective reconstructing a crime from its traces. The section then shows the idea that makes the whole subject simple: turn each die into a polynomial, with a term x^k for each face showing k . Throwing two dice corresponds to multiplying their polynomials, because x^i × x^j = x^i+j adds the numbers on the faces. Finding new dice with the same totals becomes a matter of factorising a polynomial in a different way, rather as 36 can be split as 4 × 9 instead of 6 × 6 . And because polynomials, like whole numbers, factorise in only one way into pieces that cannot be broken down further, the factorisation also proves that Sicherman’s dice are the only alternative. This trick of encoding a counting problem in a polynomial, a generating function , is one of the most powerful tools in combinatorics, and the unique factorisation behind it is a central theme of a first university course in algebra ( Section 9.6 ). Chaos with a formula. Start with a number between 0 and 1 , multiply it by 4 and by one minus itself, and repeat: u_n+1 = 4u_n(1 - u_n) . This is the logistic map , a crude model of a population that grows but is limited by its food supply. The rule could hardly be simpler, yet the numbers it produces jump around with no visible pattern, and two starting values that agree to ten decimal places typically give completely different sequences within a few dozen steps. The biologist Robert May drew attention to it in 1976, in a famous paper with the title “Simple mathematical models with very complicated dynamics”, and it became the standard example of chaos, usually explored by computer. A 2014 question reveals something unexpected: the sequence has an exact formula. If the starting value is sin^2θ , then u_n = sin^2(2^nθ) , which you can prove with nothing more than the double angle formulae and induction. (The formula was known to Stanisław Ulam and John von Neumann in the 1940s.) You might expect an exact formula to tame the chaos. Instead it explains it completely. Each step doubles the angle, so any tiny uncertainty in the angle doubles at every step, and errors in the starting value grow just as fast on average: after fifty steps an error has grown about a million billion times. Writing the angle, as a fraction of π , in binary makes this vivid: each step of the map shifts the binary digits one place to the left and throws away the first, so the sequence reads off the digits of the starting value one by one, and to predict a hundred steps ahead you need to know the starting value to a hundred binary places. The same formula also finds every cycle of the map, and shows that there are cycles of every length, packed densely into [0, 1] , every one of them unstable. This is the subject of dynamical systems, which you will meet in university courses on differential equations and, later, in courses on chaos itself ( Section 8.7 ). Period three implies chaos. Take the function f(x) = 7 - 2|x| , start with a number, and keep feeding the answer back in. Starting at 1 gives 1, 5, -3, 1, 5, -3, ldots : a cycle of length three. A 2025 question asks you to hunt for cycles like this one, by sketching the graphs of f , f(f(x)) and f(f(f(x))) and finding where they cross the line y = x . Each extra application of f doubles the number of zigzags in the graph, and the section turns that observation into a proof that this function has cycles of every length: two, three, four, a hundred, a million. That is not a special feature of this function. In 1975 Tien-Yien Li and James Yorke proved that any continuous function with a cycle of length three must have cycles of every other length, in a paper with the irresistible title “Period three implies chaos”. The proof needs nothing more than the intermediate value theorem, which you already use whenever you argue that a continuous function that changes sign must cross zero, together with a clever diagram showing which intervals the function stretches over which. It later turned out that a Ukrainian mathematician, Oleksandr Sharkovsky, had proved a stronger result in 1964: he found a strange ordering of the whole numbers, beginning 3, 5, 7, 9, ldots , such that a cycle of any length forces cycles of every length that comes after it. The intermediate value theorem is one of the first results proved carefully in a university analysis course; this question shows how much it can do ( Section 8.8 ). Why a bicycle pump gets warm. Pump up a bicycle tyre and then feel the pump: it is warm. Squeezing a gas heats it, which is how a diesel engine ignites its fuel without a spark. But why? A 2002 question answers this by following a single air molecule as it bounces back and forth between the end of the pump and the piston being pushed in. Each time the molecule bounces off the advancing piston, it picks up a little speed, like a tennis ball hit by a moving racket. The question asks you to describe one bounce exactly, turn that into a recurrence for the length of the cylinder at each collision, and then solve the recurrence. The solution reveals a hidden law: the molecule’s speed multiplied by the length of the cylinder hardly changes. Halve the length and you double the speed, and since temperature measures the energy of the molecules, the gas heats up. Quantities like this, which stay almost constant when a system is changed slowly, are called adiabatic invariants , and with a little more work the same argument leads to the law of adiabatic compression of a gas that you will meet in university thermodynamics. The idea reaches a long way. Enrico Fermi suggested in 1949 that cosmic rays reach their enormous energies in exactly this way, by bouncing repeatedly between moving magnetic fields in space; and Paul Ehrenfest argued in 1916 that adiabatic invariants are the quantities that quantum mechanics must quantise. A question about a bicycle pump turns out to touch statistical physics, astrophysics and the beginnings of quantum theory ( Section 10.4 ). A ball that comes back. Throw a ball gently forwards and it moves steadily away from you until it lands. Common sense says this is always so: the ball is always moving forwards, so how could it get closer? But throw it steeply enough, at more than about 70.5^circ to the horizontal, and something odd happens. For part of its flight, as it comes down, the ball gets closer to you, even though it is still moving away horizontally. Its height is falling faster than its horizontal distance is growing. A 2019 question asks you to prove this and to find the critical angle exactly. The method is one you will use again and again: instead of the distance itself, differentiate its square, which avoids square roots; the derivative turns out to be a quadratic in time, and the question of whether the distance ever decreases becomes the question of whether that quadratic has real roots. Its discriminant gives the answer, and the critical angle turns out to be the angle whose sine is exactly (2sqrt2)/(3) . The lesson goes well beyond projectiles. Many quantities that “obviously” increase do not, and at university, showing that something is monotonic, by finding the sign of a derivative, is a key step in proving inequalities, in proving that sequences converge, and in showing that the solutions of a differential equation settle down ( Section 11.10 ). The last passenger. A train is fully booked. The first passenger to board ignores their ticket and sits in a seat chosen at random. Everyone after that sits in their own seat if it is free, and in a randomly chosen free seat if it is not. What is the chance that the last passenger to board finds their own seat free? With a hundred seats the possibilities branch bewilderingly: one displaced passenger can displace another, who displaces another, in a chain of any length. A direct calculation looks hopeless. Yet the answer is exactly frac12 , whatever the number of seats. A 2021 question reaches this answer step by step: it asks you to find the answer for two and three seats, to set up a recurrence by conditioning on where the first passenger sits, and then to prove by induction that the answer is always frac12 . That is a perfectly good proof, but it leaves you wondering why the answer is so simple, and the section then gives a one-line argument that explains it. Whenever a passenger has to choose at random, the first passenger’s seat and the last passenger’s seat are treated in exactly the same way; the process cannot tell them apart until one of them is taken. So the last free seat is equally likely to be either, and it must be one of them, because every other seat is taken by its owner, or by someone displaced, before the last passenger boards. Arguments from symmetry like this, which replace pages of calculation with a single observation, run all through university probability ( Section 12.5 ). Taken together, questions like these touch every one of the main areas of a first-year mathematics degree: number theory, analysis, calculus, complex numbers, algebra, linear algebra, differential equations, combinatorics, mechanics, probability and statistics. What this book is for That observation is the reason for this book. Most STEP preparation, quite reasonably, aims at passing the examination: learn the techniques, practise the papers, build up speed and stamina. This book aims at that too, and working through it will make you better at STEP. But its real purpose is different. It is to help you prepare for STEP with university mathematics in mind : to see each question not as an obstacle to be cleared but as an invitation, and to follow the invitation as far as it goes. The students who do best at STEP, and who flourish at university afterwards, are almost always the ones who love mathematics for its own sake. They enjoy the moment when a hard problem gives way. They want to know why a trick works, not just that it does. When an answer comes out to be suspiciously simple, like frac12 or frac1e or π^2/6 , they suspect that something deeper is going on, and they go looking for it. Those are the habits this book tries to encourage. Each question is chosen because it leads to a discovery: an idea, a theorem, a way of thinking, that is bigger than the question itself. The ways of thinking matter as much as the theorems. University mathematics asks you to think in ways that school mathematics rarely does: to prove things rather than calculate them, to argue by contradiction or by infinite descent, to count the same thing in two ways, to find a quantity that never changes, to construct a counterexample, to show that something exists without finding it. STEP questions train exactly these habits, often without saying so. In this book every section names the thinking skill at its heart, so that you can recognise it when you meet it again. How the book is organised The book has thirteen chapters, organised by the area of university mathematics that the questions lead to, rather than by the STEP paper they came from. Pure mathematics (Chapters 1 to 9): number theory and proof; sequences, series and convergence; functions, inequalities and rigour; calculus done properly; complex numbers; algebra and structure; linear algebra and geometry; differential equations and dynamical systems; and counting and chance, which also draws on the combinatorial questions from the probability papers. Mechanics (Chapters 10 and 11): conservation laws, collisions and gravity; and oscillations, rotation and moving frames, ending with a set of surprising trajectories. Probability and statistics (Chapters 12 and 13): probability, from clear thinking about conditioning to the central limit theorem; and statistics and randomness in the world. Each chapter opens with an essay: why the area matters, what you will meet in it at university, and three big questions that run through the chapter. Each closes with a wrap-up that returns to those questions, a toolkit of the methods used, pointers to other chapters, and suggestions for reading before university. At the end of each chapter are brief answers to the exercises. Before Chapter 1 there is a glossary of the terms in the book that are unlikely to be familiar from school, and a table of the mathematical symbols it uses; if a word or a symbol stops you, look it up there. Every section follows the same pattern. It begins with the question : a link to the STEP question, exactly as it was set, at its official source. The hook explains why the question is more interesting than it looks. Before you start gives you a first foothold. Working it through is a guided solution in stages, interrupted by boxes headed Ask yourself and Pause and try , which are the questions a good teacher would ask you at that point; they are there to be answered, not skipped. Looking back picks out the key moves. What’s really going on is the heart of the section: the university mathematics behind the question, its history and its surprises. The thinking skill names the habit of mind the question exercises. Try this next gives follow-up problems, often including related STEP questions, and Further reading suggests books and articles at a level a strong school student or first-year undergraduate can manage. The book treats 136 questions in full, but STEP has set more than 1,500. The website has a worked solution to every one of them, from the specimen papers to 2025. They are written in the same spirit as the book but are much shorter. Each gives the key idea that unlocks the question, a complete solution part by part, a few checks you can make on the answers, the slips that are easy to make, and a pointer to the university mathematics that the question touches. Where a question has a full treatment in this book, its solution says so and links to it. A few sections use topics that are not on the current STEP specification, such as groups, moments of inertia and moment generating functions. They are included because the questions are too good to leave out, and each gives the facts it needs. How to use this book as a student Do the question first. Open it from the link at the start of the section and keep it beside you as you read, since the solutions refer to its parts and wording throughout. Give each question at least half an hour of honest effort before you read further. Being stuck is not a sign of failure; it is where the learning happens. If you are completely stuck, read Before you start , then try again. Answer the boxes. When the text asks you a question, stop and answer it, on paper. The guided solutions are written to be read with a pencil in your hand. Do not skip the “What’s really going on” sections. They are not examinable, but they are the reason the book exists, and they are what you will remember. Read the sections in any order. Each section stands on its own, and cross-references point you to related ideas elsewhere. Follow your curiosity. Try the exercises, then check the answers. The answers at the end of each chapter are brief: they give the result and the key step, not a full write-up. Use the worked solutions as springboards. When you practise on past papers, try each question properly before you open its solution on the website, and then read only as far as you need to get moving again. If the key idea is enough, close the solution and finish the question yourself. Use the worksheets. The website has a printable worksheet for every section, with a link to the question, the hints in order, the What’s really going on part and the exercises, for working away from a screen. Read beyond the book. Siklos’s book, the STEP Support Programme and the past papers themselves are all freely available. The further reading in each section is chosen to be accessible before university. How to use this book as a teacher As a source of extension work. Each section is a self-contained session: the question, a guided path through it, and somewhere interesting to go afterwards. The thinking skills make good themes for a sequence of sessions. As a discussion guide. The Ask yourself and Pause and try boxes are natural prompts for a class or small group. Pose them before revealing the next stage. With the worksheets. Each worksheet gives a link to the question, the hints in order, the What’s really going on part and the follow-up exercises; students can choose how many hints to take. For STEP preparation. Questions from all three papers, from the specimen papers to 2025, are included, many with related questions in the exercises. The chapter wrap-ups and toolkits help students to see connections across topics. For students without STEP support. The book is written so that a determined student can work through it alone. If your school does not offer STEP preparation, it can do much of that job. Copyright and corrections Everything in this book that is my own work, including the text, the guided solutions, the figures, the exercises and the answers, is dedicated to the public domain under the Creative Commons CC0 1.0 Universal licence: you may copy, adapt and share it for any purpose, without asking permission. The STEP questions themselves are the copyright of Cambridge University Press & Assessment, and are not covered by that licence. For that reason they are not reproduced in this book. Instead, each section links to its question at an official source: the STEP Support Programme’s question database for the specimen papers and the papers from 1987 to 2018, and OCR’s downloads of each year’s papers from 2019 onwards. Exercises that use further STEP questions link to them in the same way. I have tried hard to make the mathematics correct, but a book of this size will certainly contain errors. If you find one, however small, please report it as an issue on the book’s GitHub repository, github.com/keithmcnulty/step_book_mcnulty . Corrections will be made on the book’s website as they come in. A last word before you start Siklos ended the introduction to his book with the story of Michelangelo’s David , carved from a block of marble that had lain untouched for decades, and said that he could not teach you mathematics, but that hard work chipping away at problems would reveal the mathematician within you. I cannot improve on that. This book offers you the marble, and some tools, and a few pictures of what other people have found inside. The chipping is up to you. I hope you enjoy it as much as I have enjoyed putting the book together. Keith McNulty November 2026

title: Worked Solutions
text: Have a proper go at a question before you open its solution: STEP rewards the struggle, and a solution read too early teaches much less than one read after an hour of trying. Each solution starts with the key idea , so you can read just that and go back to the question. The questions themselves are not reproduced here. Each Question link goes to the official source: the STEP Support Programme’s question database for papers up to 2018, and OCR’s downloads (zip files of the year’s papers) from 2019. Where a question has a full guided treatment in the book, the § link takes you to that section, with hints, a worksheet and the university mathematics behind it. Each year’s solutions also come as a single book, with a cover, a contents page and every solution for that year’s papers: use the link under the year’s heading. Every answer has been checked numerically, but with this many solutions some slips are inevitable: if something looks wrong, trust your own working and check it carefully. Corrections are very welcome as GitHub issues . title: Mathematical Symbols
headings: Logic and proof Sets and number systems Numbers, divisibility and approximation Functions Sums, limits and calculus Complex numbers Vectors and matrices Probability and statistics The Greek alphabet Mechanics
text: Mathematical writing packs a lot of meaning into a few marks, and university lecturers use many symbols that school textbooks rarely do. The tables below list the symbols used in this book, grouped by topic, with what each one means and how it is read aloud. Most of them will become second nature within a few weeks of starting a degree; until then, this is somewhere to look them up. Two conventions are worth knowing from the start. First, this book follows STEP in printing some letters upright rather than in italics when they have a fixed meaning: e for the base of natural logarithms, i for sqrt-1 , d in dy/dx , and the names of functions, as in f(x) and P(A) . Italic letters are variables. Secondly, the same symbol sometimes means different things in different contexts; equiv and sim are the main culprits, and the tables point out where. Logic and proof Symbol Meaning Example or reading P Rightarrow Q P implies Q : if P is true, so is Q x = 2 Rightarrow x^2 = 4 ; “ P implies Q ” P Leftarrow Q P is implied by Q “ P if Q ” P iff Q P if and only if Q : each implies the other x^2 = 4 iff x = 2 ; also written “iff” forall for all, for every forall x mathbbR,\ x^2 ≥ 0 exists there exists exists\, n mathbbZ with n^2 = 9 neg P not P , the negation of P the negation of “ forall x,\ P(x) ” is “ exists\, x with neg P(x) ” := is defined to equal f(x) := x^2 + 1 blacksquare end of proof; also written QED from the Latin quod erat demonstrandum , “which was to be shown” Sets and number systems Symbol Meaning Example or reading \\,ldots\ the set whose elements are listed \1, 2, 3\ \x : ldots\ the set of all x such that …; also written \x mid ldots\ \x : x^2 < 2\ ; “the set of x such that x^2 < 2 ” x A x is an element of A sqrt2 mathbbR ; “ sqrt2 is in mathbbR ” x notin A x is not an element of A sqrt2 notin mathbbQ A subseteq B A is a subset of B : every element of A is in B mathbbZ subseteq mathbbQ A cup B union: elements in A or B (or both) \1, 2\ cup \2, 3\ = \1, 2, 3\ A cap B intersection: elements in both A and B \1, 2\ cap \2, 3\ = \2\ A setminus B elements of A that are not in B \1, 2, 3\ setminus \2\ = \1, 3\ A' complement: everything not in A also written A^c or bar A varnothing the empty set, with no elements \x mathbbR : x^2 < 0\ = varnothing |A| the number of elements of a finite set A |\a, b, c\| = 3 A × B the set of all pairs (a, b) with a A , b B mathbbR × mathbbR is the plane, also written mathbbR^2 mathbbN the natural numbers 1, 2, 3, ldots some authors include 0 mathbbZ the integers ldots, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ldots from the German Zahlen , “numbers” mathbbQ the rational numbers (fractions) from quotient mathbbR the real numbers mathbbC the complex numbers mathbbH the quaternions after Hamilton ( Section 6.7 ) mathbbZ[i] numbers a + bi with a, b mathbbZ the Gaussian integers ( Section 1.6 ) [a, b] closed interval: a ≤ x ≤ b includes its endpoints (a, b) open interval: a < x < b excludes its endpoints; also a pair or a point Numbers, divisibility and approximation Symbol Meaning Example or reading a mid b a divides b : b is an integer multiple of a 3 mid 12 ; “ 3 divides 12 ” a nmid b a does not divide b 5 nmid 12 a equiv b pmod n a and b leave the same remainder on division by n 17 equiv 2 pmod 5 ; “ 17 is congruent to 2 modulo 5 ” equiv (without a modulus) is identically equal to: true for all values (x + 1)^2 equiv x^2 + 2x + 1 lfloor x rfloor floor: the greatest integer ≤ x lfloor 3.7 rfloor = 3 , lfloor -3.7 rfloor = -4 lceil x rceil ceiling: the least integer ≥ x lceil 3.2 rceil = 4 n! n factorial, 1 × 2 × cdots × n 0! = 1 by convention binomnr the binomial coefficient (n!)/(r!\,(n - r)!) “ n choose r ”; also written ^nC_r approx is approximately equal to π approx 3.1416 sim is asymptotic to: the ratio tends to 1 n! sim sqrt2π n\,(n/e)^n (but see also Probability) propto is proportional to v propto 1/d , plus or minus; minus or plus cos(A B) = cos Acos B sin Asin B 0.overline01 recurring digits 0.overline01 = 0.010101ldots Functions Symbol Meaning Example or reading f : A → B f is a function from the set A to the set B f : mathbbR → mathbbR x mapsto ldots x is sent to … x mapsto x^2 - 2 ; “ x maps to x^2 - 2 ” f circ g composition: do g , then f (f circ g)(x) = f(g(x)) f^-1 the inverse function of f not 1/f f^n in this book, usually f applied n times f^3(x) = f(f(f(x))) ; but sin^2 x means (sin x)^2 |x| modulus, or absolute value |-3| = 3 exp x the exponential function e^x x natural logarithm, to base e at university often written log x sec , cosec , cot 1/cos , 1/sin , 1/tan arcsin , arccos , arctan inverse trigonometric functions also written sin^-1 , etc. sinh , cosh , tanh hyperbolic functions: sinh x = frac12(e^x - e^-x) , cosh x = frac12(e^x + e^-x) , tanh = sinh/cosh read “shine” (or “sinch”), “cosh” and “than” (or “tanch”) artanh inverse of tanh artanh x = frac12(1 + x)/(1 - x) max , min the largest, smallest of max(3, 7) = 7 Gamma(x) the gamma function Gamma(n + 1) = n! ( Section 4.4 ) Sums, limits and calculus Symbol Meaning Example or reading sum sum sum_k=1^n k = frac12n(n + 1) prod product prod_k=1^n k = n! ∞ infinity: not a number, but shorthand for “without limit” sum_k=1^∞ frac1k^2 = (π^2)/(6) x → a x tends to a frac1n → 0 as n → ∞ lim limit lim_x→0(sin x)/(x) = 1 f'(x) , f''(x) first and second derivatives “f dash”, or “f prime” dot x , ddot x derivatives with respect to time dot x = (dx)/(dt) ; “ x dot”, “ x double dot” (partial f)/(partial x) partial derivative: differentiate with respect to x , holding other variables fixed “partial f by partial x ” int_a^b definite integral from a to b oint integral round a closed loop oint p\,dq ( Section 10.4 ) δ x , Delta x a small change in x ; a change in x ε , δ conventional names for small positive numbers in analysis “for every ε > 0 there is a δ > 0 such that …” Complex numbers Symbol Meaning Example or reading i a square root of -1 engineers write j Re z , Im z real and imaginary parts if z = 3 + 4i , Re z = 3 , Im z = 4 z^* , bar z complex conjugate (3 + 4i)^* = 3 - 4i ; both notations are used |z| modulus: distance from 0 |3 + 4i| = 5 arg z argument: angle from the positive real axis arg i = fracπ2 e^iθ cosθ + isinθ e^iπ = -1 ω conventionally, a complex cube root of unity ω = e^2pii/3 , 1 + ω + ω^2 = 0 Vectors and matrices Symbol Meaning Example or reading a , overrightarrowAB a vector; the vector from A to B handwritten as underlinea hatn a unit vector, of length 1 “ n hat” |a| the length (magnitude) of a a · b scalar (dot) product a · b = |a||b|cosθ a × b vector (cross) product perpendicular to a and b M a matrix I the identity matrix Iv = v for every v M^-1 the inverse matrix MM^-1 = I det M the determinant of M detbeginpmatrix a & b \\ c & dendpmatrix = ad - bc tr M the trace: sum of the diagonal entries trbeginpmatrix a & b \\ c & dendpmatrix = a + d λ conventionally, an eigenvalue Mv = lambdav Probability and statistics Symbol Meaning Example or reading P(A) the probability of the event A P(A mid B) the probability of A given B P(A mid B) = P(A cap B)/P(B) ; “ A given B ” E(X) the expectation (mean) of X also written μ Var(X) the variance of X E(X^2) - E(X)^2 ; also written σ^2 Cov(X, Y) covariance E(XY) - E(X)E(Y) Corr(X, Y) correlation Cov(X, Y)/sqrtVar(X)Var(Y) ; also written rho X sim ldots X has the distribution … X sim B(16, frac12) ; “ X is distributed as …” B(n, p) binomial distribution number of successes in n trials N(μ, σ^2) normal distribution, mean μ , variance σ^2 f(x) , F(x) probability density function;
